Papillon; or any Six, Five, Four, Three, Two, or One of them; my Deputies, and Deputy, in my Place and Stead, to tender and administer the Oaths mentioned in the Statute, made in the First Year of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, intituled, An Act for removing and preventing all Questions and Disputes concerning the Assembling and Sitting of this present Parliament; according to the Direction of the Statute, of the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty. Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the Security of her Majesty’s Person and Government, and of the Succession to the Crown of Great Britain in the Protestant Line, and of all and every other Statute and Statutes, directing the Taking of the said Oaths before me; to all and every Person and Persons, which is, are, or shall be, electea or appointed a Knight, Citizen, Burgess, Baron of any of the Five Ports, or Commissioners of Shires or Burghs, for the present Parliament; and to take and receive the Oaths of all and every the said Person and Persons, which is, are, or shall be elected or appointed a Knight, Citizen, Burgess, Baron of any of the Five Ports, or Commissioners for Shires or Burghs aforesaid, for the said Parliament; giving them, Six, Five, Four, Three, Two, or One of them, full Power and Authority to execute and perform the fame; ratifying and confirming all and whatsoever my laid Deputies, or Deputy, any Six, Five, Four, Three, Two, or One of them, shall do and perform in this Behalf, in as ample, perfect, and full Manner, as if I myself had personally been present, and done the fame. In Testimony whereof I have hereunto set my Hand and Seal. Given this First Day of August, in the First Year of the Reign of our Sovereign Lord George, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, King, Defender of the Faith, 8$c. IT having pleased Almighty God to call to his Mercy our late most gracious Sovereign Lady Queen of blessed Memory, this Morning between Seven and Eight of the Clock, at her Palace at and her late Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council having met at the Palace of St. James's, and having directed, That his illustrious Highness the Elector of wick-Lunenburg should be proclaimed King; and the Privy-Council, with the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Sheriffs, of the City of London, having, between the Hours of Two and Four of the Clock, in the usual Manner, published and proclaimed his laid Highness King, by the Name of George, King of Great Britain, , and

Ireland (the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain, Lord President of the Council, Lord Steward of the Houshold, and others, Lords and Commons, going in the Procession); about Six of the Clock in the same Afternoon, the Parliament met at Westminster, pursuant to the Statute, made in the Sixth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for the Security of her Majesty’s Person and Government, and of the Succession to the Crown of Great Britain in the Protestant Line: And the Right honourable John Earl Poulett, Lord High Steward of his Majesty's Houshold, came into the Room, belonging to the Clerk of the House of Commons, called the Inner Court of Wards, the usual Place of administering the Oaths appointed to be taken by the Members returned to serve in Parliament, before they go into the House of Commons; and, Paul Jodrell Esquire, Clerk of the House of Commons, and Mr. Stables, Clerk-Assistant, and other Clerks attending according to their Duty, the Lord High Steward did himself, in Person, administer the said Oaths appointed to all such Members as then appeared; and afterwards made a Commission, or Deputation, under his Hand and Seal, hereunto annexed, impowering the Members lb sworn to administer tire Oaths to those Members as are, or should be, returned: Which being done, the Members repaired to their Seats in the House of Commons; where, being seated, they were acquainted, That Sir Thomas Hanmer Baronet, their Speaker, had been gone into the Country some Time; but that a flying Packet was gone to him; and it was hoped he would be in Town speedily: And therefore it was moved, That the House would adjourn till Tomorrow, T welve of the Clock.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended at the House of Lords: Where the Lord Chancellor, being One of the Lords Justices of Great Britain appointed and impowered by Act of Parliament to administer the Government till his Majesty shall arrive, did, in the Name of the said Ix>rds Justices, make a Speech to both Houses of Parliament; of which, for preventing Mistakes, he had obtained a Copy.

Mr. Speaker read the Speech to the House; which is as follows; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

' It having pleased Almighty God to take to himself our late most gracious Queen, of blessed Memory, we hope, that nothing has been omitted, which might contribute to the Safety of these Realms, and the Preservation of our Religion, Laws, and Liberties, in this great Conjuncture: As these invaluable Blefiings have been secured to us by those Acts of Parliament which have settled the Succession to these Kingdoms in the most Illulirious House of Hanover, we have regulated our Proceedings by those Rules which are therein prescribed.

The Privy Council, soon after the demise of the late Queen, Afleinbled at St.James's; where according to the said Acts of Parliament, the three Instruments were produced and opened, which had been deposited in the Hands of the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord Chancellor, and the Resident of Brunj: Those who, either by their Offices, or by virtue of these Instruments, had the Honour of being appointed Lords Justices, did, in conjunction with the Council, immediately proceed to the Proclaiming of our lawful and rightful Sovereign, King George; taking, at the same time, the necessary Care to maintain the Publick Peace.

In pursuance of the Acts before-mentioned, this Parliament is now assembled; and we are persuaded, you all bring with you so hearty a Disposition for his Majesty’s Service, and the Publick Good, that we cannot doubt of your Assistance in every thing which may promote, those great Ends.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

We find it necessary to put you inAnind, That several Branches of the Publick Revenue are expired, by the Demise of her late Majesty; and to recommend to you the making such Provisions in that Respect, as may be requisite to support the Honour and Dignity of the Crown: And we allure ourselves, you will not be wanting in any thing that may conduce to the establishing and advancing of the Publick Credit.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

We jbrbear laying beibre you any thing that does not require your immediate Consideration; not having received his Majesty’s Piealure: We shall only exhort you,

' worth, Mr Sheppard:And they are to meet upon Mon-

day Sevennight at Five a Clock in the Afternoon, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and to fit every Wednesllay, Friday, and Monday, in the Afternoon: And all that come are to have Voices: And they are to take into Consideration all such Matters as shall or may come in Question touching Returns, Elections, and Privileges; and to proceed upon Double Returns in the first Place; and to report their Proceedings, with their Opinion therein, to the House, from time to time: And all Persons that will question any new Returns, are to do it in Fourteen Days next after such Return shall be brought in: And the Committee are to have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records, for their Information: And all Members who are returned for Two or more Places, are to make their Elections, within Fourteen Days next, for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place: And if any thing shall cotne in Question touching the Return, Election, or Matter of Privilege, of any Member, he is to withdraw during the time the Matter is in Debate: And that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

UfvudOrdfre. Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear any Person hath Voi. 18.

procured himself to be elected, or returned as a Member of this House, or endeavoured lb to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practice, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or directly, or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of, to be in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers* into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables and other Officers of MiddlesexwaA Westminster do take care, That, from Nine

of the Clock in the Morning to Three in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets, between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall, be kept free and open; and that no ObstruCfcion be made by Cars,

Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care, there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in -

hall, or Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High-Bailiff of Westminster: And that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Mr Secretary Bromley reported from the Committee Addrefo to appointed Yesterday to draw up an humble Address, to tho Kin*, be presented to his Majesty, That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where it was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, having a just Sense of the great Lois the Nation has sustainea by the Death of our late Sovereign Lady

Queen Anne, of blessed Memory, humbly crave Leave to condole with your Majesty on this lad Occasion.

It would but aggravate our Sorrow, particularly to enumerate the Virtues of that pious and most excellent Princess; The Duty we owe to your Majesty, and to our Country, oblige us to moderate our Grief, and heartily to congratulate Your Majesty’s Accession to the Throne; whole Princely Virtues give us a certain Prospect of future Happiness, in the Security of our Religion, Laws and Liberties; and engage us to assure Your Majesty, That we will, to our utmost, support Your undoubted Right to the Imperial Crown of this Realm, against the Pretender, and all other Persons whatsoever.

Your faithful Commons cannot but express their impatient Desire for Your Majesty’s safe Arrival and Prelence in Great Britain.

In the mean time, we humbly lay before Your Majesty the unanimous Resolution of this House, to maintain the publick C redit of the Nation; and effectually to make good all Funds which have been granted by Parliament, for the Security of any Money which has been, or shall be, advanced for the publick Service; and to endeavour, by every thing in our Power, to make Your Majesty’s Reign happy and glorious.

The said Address being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House doth

agree with the Committee in the said Address.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most Honourable Privy-Council, do present the said Address to the Lords Justice$, with the Desire of this House, That they do transmit the same to his Majesty with all convenient Speed.

Message to attend Lords Justices.

A Message from the Lords Justices, by Sir William Oldes, Gentleman-Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords Justices command the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And, being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended in the House of Peers: Where the Lord Chancellor did, in the name of the Lords Justices of Great Britain, deliver a Speech to both Houses of Parliament; of which, for preventing Mistakes, be had obtained a Copy.

Mr. Speaker read the Speech to the House: Which is as follows; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Lord Chan- It is with great Satisfaction we can now tell you. That cellor’s we have, this Morning, received a Letter from the King;

Speech. wherein his Majesty is graciously pleased to acquaint us.

That his Majesty is battening hither to employ his utmost Care for putting these Kingdoms into a happy and flourishing Condition.

He has commanded us, in the mean time, to continue our Care of every thing that may conduce to the Peace and Safety of his Dominions: And we are assured, that, if this had required his more immediate Presence, he would, without the least Delay, have repaired hither, for the Support of so dutiful and faithful Subjects; for his Majesty does very particularly express his great Satisfaction in the Loyalty and Affection which his People have universally shewn upon his Majesty’s Accession to the Crown.

At the opening this Session, we did not mention to you the Apprehensions we then had, from the Smallnefe of the Sum at that time advanced, that the Lottery would not be full; being desirous, in the first Place, to try to make it effectual in the manner the Parliament had established it: But we are obliged now to acquaint you, That all our endeavours have failed of the desired Succels, though 23

the Contributions have been thereby considerably increased.

We must therefore earnestly recommend to you, Gentlemen of the House of Commons, to take this into your Consideration; and to give such further Encouragement as you shall think proper, for raising the whole Sum which was intended, and is absolutely necessary, for carrying on the Service of the Year.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That an humble Ad- Address to drels be presented to his Majesty, to return the humble tte Kin&-Thanks of this House for the Satisfaction his Majesty has been pleased to express in the Loyalty and Affection which his Subjects have universally shewn upon his Majesty’s Accession to the Throne; and for his gracious Intentions of making his People speedily happy with his Royal Presence; and also to assure his Majesty of the Continuance of the same Zeal and Affection to his Majesty, upon all Occasions; and that this House will contribute their utmost Endeavours for preserving the publick Peace, until his Majesty shall arrive.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to the Lords Justices, with the Delire of this House, That they will transmit the same to his Majesty with all convenient Speed.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to the Lords Justices by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy-Council.

and to be transmitted to the King

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, Lords Justict resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to Speech to b consider of that Part of the Speech of the Lords Justices, coa^dered‘ which relates to the Lottery.

Ordered, That the Lords Justices Speech be referred to the said Committee.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Conyers, according to Order, repotted, froitt the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of that Part of the Speech of the Lords Jufe tices to both Houses, which relates to the Lottery, the Resolutions of the said Committee; which they had di-rested him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and areas follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That for railing so much as is wanting to complete the full Sum of One Million Four hundred thousand Pounds, which was intended to be raised for the publick Service, by way of a Lottery, by virtue of the late Act of Parliament in that behalf, the Time for receiving the Contributions on that Act be prolonged.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of One hundred Five thousand Pounds a Year, by that Act granted, be increased, and made up, to be a yearly Fund of One hundred Sixteen thousand Five hundred Seventy-three Pounds Twelve Shillings, during the Term of Thirty-two Years therein mentioned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the publick Monies which shall, from time to time, come into the Receipt of the Exchequer, not appropriated to any particular Use or Uses by any Act or Acts of Parliament made before the Act for the said Lottery, be made an additional Security (over and above the Revenues and Branches settled by the said Act) for making good the said Fund of One hundred Sixteen Thousand Five hundred Seventy-three Pounds Twelve Shillings per Annum; and that the same unappropriated publick Monies, or lo much thereof as shall, from time to time, be necessary for completing and making up the said increased Fund, be, from time to time, applied thereunto.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Interest, after the Rate of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, for the Blank Tickets in the said Lottery, be increased by an Addition after the Rate of One Pound per Cent, per Annum; and allowed as well in respect of the Contributions which have been made, as those which shall hereafter be made, in the said Lottery, out of the said increased yearly Fund.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for rectifying Mistakes 'in the Commissioners Names for putting in Execution the Act, passed the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for granting an Aid to her Majesty, to be raised by a Land Tax in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen, is committed. That they have Power to receive a Clause, or Clauses, pursuant to the said Resolutions.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they Have Power to receive a Clause, or Clauses, for confining the Number of Managers for putting in Execution the Powers and Trusts in them re-posed by the Lottery-Act to One-and-twenty; and for providing, That their Allowance shall not exceed One hundred Pounds each.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable Persons now residing in Great Britain to take the Oaths, and do all other Acts, in Great Britain, requisite to qualify themselves to continue their respective Places, Offices and Employments, in Ireland: And that Mr. Annefey, Mr. Lowndes, and Mr. Ward, do prepare, and bring so, the lame.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nbe of the Clock.

By the KING.

A PR OCLAMATION

For Calling a new Parliament

GEORGE R.

IT having pleased Almighty GOD, by most remarkable Steps of his Providence, to bring Us in Safety to the Crown of this Kingdom, notwithstanding the Deligns of evil Men, who shewed themselves disaffected to Our Succession, and who have since, with the utmost Degree of Malice, misrepresented Our firm Resolution, and uniform Endeavours, to preserve and defend Our most excellent Constitution both in Church and State; and attempted, by many false Suggestions, to render Us suspected to Our People; We cannot omit, on this Occasion, of First summoning Our Parliament of Gre Britain (in Justiceto Ourselves, and that the Miscarriages of others may not be imputed to Us, at a Time when false Impressions may do the greatest and irrecoverable Hurt before they can be cleared up), to signify to Our whole Kingdom, That We were very much concerned, on Our Accession to the jublick Affairs of Our Kingdoms

Crown, to find f under the greatest Trader and the Interj great Debts of the observe. 'had bee lion of the last War:

iculties, agXpell in respect of Our Iption of Q^r'Navigation, as of the prtion, which'"We were surprized. to much4ftereased since the Conclu-We do not, therefore, doubt, that if the ensuing Elections shall be made by Our loving Subjects with that Safety and Freedom which, by Law, they are intitled to, and We are firmly resolved to maintain to them, they will fend up to Parliament the fittest Persons to redress the present Disorders, and to provide for the Peace and Happinets of Our Kingdoms, and the Ease of Our People for the future; and therein will have a particular Regard to such as shewed a Firmnels to the Protestant Succession when it was most in Danger: We have, therefore, found it necessary, as well for the Causes aforesaid, as for other weighty Considerations concerning Us and Our Kingdoms, to call a new Parliament; and We do accordingly declare, That, with the Advice of Our Privy Council, We have this Day given Order to Our Chancellor of Great Britain, to issue out Writs, in due Form, for the Calling a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Tefie on Monday the Seventeenth Day of this instant January, and to be returnable on the

Seventeenth Day of March next following.

Given at Our Court at St. James's, the Fifteenth Day of January 1714, in the First Year of Our Reign.

GOD save the King.

Lord Chancellor’s Speech.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I am commanded by his Majesty to acquaint you, That his Majesty does not intend to declare the Causes of calling this Parliament, till there be a Speaker of the House of Commons:

And therefore, you, the Gentlemen of the House of Commons, are to repair to the Place where the Commons usually fit, and there proceed to the Election of a fit Person to be your Speaker, whom you are to present to his Majesty here, for his Royal Approbation, on Monday next, at Twelve of the Clock.

And the House being returned;

Mr. Compton The Right honourable Algernoon Earl of Hartford,

chosen Son and Heir apparent to the most Noble Charles

Speaker. Duke of Somerset, Knight of the Shire for the County of

Northumberland, laid;

That the House having received his Majesty’s Commands to return, and immediately choose a Speaker; although he was himself very unfit to recommend any Per-ibn; yet he should take upon him to name one, of whole Abilities and Virtues, he thought, no one need be better convinced, though it very ill became him to recommend: And thereupon the honourable Spencer Compton Esquire, who had already made known his Experience in the House, and given lo many Occafioas of knowing his Abilities in every thing of that Kind; and as he had already, with the

freateft Honour, filled the Chair of the Committee of 'rivileges and Elections, which next to that of the Speak-' era, is the highest we have'; there was no occasion to say

more of him; and therefore moved, That Spencer Compton Esquire might take the Chair of the House.

Then the Lord Finch, Son and Heir apparent to the Right honourable Daniel Earl of Nottingham, Knight of the Shire for the County of Rutland, said;

That, after the honourable Mention, which the Noble Member had been pleased to make of Mr. Compton, whole Abilities were lo well known to every Gentleman in the House, his Addition would be a Mif-spending of Time; But, however, on this Occasion, he could not but take notice of him, as be was a Person defeended of a very noble and honourable Family, in all Times famous for their steady Adherence to the Constitution in Church and State; for their inviolable Loyalty to a deserving Master, though an unfortunate Prince; that he had eminently distinguished himself in the true Interest of his Country, by his firmly adhering to, and supporting with Resolution, those Measures, that were necessary to maintain the Protestant Succession, when in the utmost Danger; upon which alone the -Security of the Church of Englanthe Protestant Religion

abroad, and the Liberties of his Country, could depend; without which, they might not have had an Opportunity this Day to choose a Speaker: That, by these Virtues, and his great Abilities in Parliamentary Affairs, he had so well deserved of his Country, as to merit all Marks of Esteem that they could shew him: That he had already discharged the Duty of the Second Chair, when intruded with the Rights and Liberties of the Commons, with such Temper, Candour, and Impartiality, as must satisfy every Gentleman in the House, that he will support the Dignity of the Chair, and shew himself entirely equal to the Trust they should repole in him. Unless such Merit fills the Chair, in vain would it be for a Speaker, at the Bar of another House, to insist upon the Rights and Privileges of Parliaments, Freedom of Speech, and Liberty of Debating; for it would ever be in the Bread of a Speaker to obstruct that Freedom of Speech, which the Crown has not a Right to deny: Since, therefore, to complete his Character, he has already distinguished himself by these Virtues, so necessary to every one who is to preside in a free Assembly, he begged Leave to second the Motion, That Spencer Compton Esquire, do take the Chair.

Then Mr. Compton stood up in his Place; and laid;

That Excuses upon these Occasions were generally lo much suspected, that, notwithstanding the just Sense ha had of his own Inabilities, he should have chose to have iat silent, and submitted himself to the Pleifure of the House, had nothing but his own Reputation, however dear that was to him, been concerned in the Decision of this Question: But when he considered, that the future Prosperity and Tranquillity of this Kingdom would entirely depend on many difficult and important Points, which must necessarily come under the Consideration of this Parliament, he must own he trembled, left the just Expectation the Nation had of Relief, of Security, and of future Happiness, from the Deliberations of this House of Commons, should be any ways obstructed, if not dil-appointed, by his Want of Capacity; and that he should therefore think himself inexculable, did he not lay before Gentlemen how unequal he found himself to so great a Weight: And since there were so many Gentlemen in this House (he might venture to lay there never were more iq any House of Commons), whole Experience, added to their Abilities, did fitly qualify them' to promote those

That they may have Privilege from Arrests, and Disturbance, for their Persons, Estates, and Servants; Liberty of Speech, for the better Management of their Debates; and free Access to Your Majesty’s Royal Person, as Occasion shall require.

Mr. Speaker reported, That, on Monday last, when the House attended his Majesty in the House of Peers, his Majesty was graciously pleased to declare, from the Throne, That he had ordered the Lord Chancellor to declare the Caules of calling this Parliament, in his Majesty’s Name

-2 30 Martii. A. 1714.

and Words: And that, accordingly, the Lord Chancellor did declare the Causes of calling this Parliament, as they are mentioned in a Speech delivered into his Hands by his Majesty from the Throne: Which Speech he read to both Houses: and of which, to prevent Mistakes, Mr. Speaker said he had obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as follow’s;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

This being the first Opportunity that I have had of meeting my People in Parliament, since it pleased Almighty God, of his good Providence, to call me to the Throne of my Ancestors, I most gladly make use of it, to thank my faithful and loving Subjects for that Zeal and Firmnels that hath been shewn in Defence of the Protestant Succession, against all the open and secret Practices that have been used to defeat it: And I shall never forget the Obligations I have to those who have distinguished themselves upon this Occasion.

It w’ere to be wished, that the unparalleled Successes of a War, which was so wifely and cheerfully flip ported by this Nation, in order to procure a good Peace, had been attended with a suitable Conclusion: But it is with Concern I must tell you, that feme Conditions even of this Peace, essential to the Security and Trade of Great tain, are not yet duly executed; and the Performance of the Whole may be looked upon as precarious, until we shall have formed defensive Alliances, to guaranty the present Treaties.

The Pretender, who still resides in Lorrain, threatens to disturb us; and boasts of the Assistance which he still expeXs here, to repair his former Dilappointments.

A great Part of our Trade is rendered impracticable: This, if not retrieved, muftdestroy our Manufactures, and ruin our Navigation.

The Publick Debts are very great; and surprisiugly in-created, even since the fatal Cessation of Arms: My first Care was, to prevent a farther Increase of these Debts, by paying off forthwith a great Number of Ships, which had been kept in Pay, when there was no Occasion for continuing such an Expence.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I rely upon you for such Supplies as the present Cir-> cuinstances of our Affairs require for this Year’s Service, and for the Support of the Publick Faith: The Estimates shall be laid before you, that you may consider of them; and what you shall judge necessary for your Safety, I shall think sufficient for mine.

I doubt not but you will concur with me in Opinion, That nothing can contribute more to the Support of the Credit of the Nation, than a ftriX Observance of all Parliamentary Engagements.

The Branches of the Revenue formerly granted for the Support of the Civil Government, are 1b far encumbered and alienated, that the Produce of the Funds which remain, and have been granted to me, will fall much lliort of what w’as at first: designed, for maintaining the Honour and Dignity of the Crown: And since it is my Hap-pinefe, as I am confident you think it yours, to fee a Prince of Wales who may in due time succeed me on the Throne; and to fee him blessed with many Children, the heft and most valuable Pledges of our Care and Concern for your Prosperity; this must occasion an Expence to which the Nation has not of many Years been accustomed; but such as, surely, no Man will grudge: And, therefore, I do not doubt, but you will think of it with that Affection which I have Reason to hope for from you.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Eyes of all Europe are upon you, waiting the Issue of this First Session: Let no unhappy Divisions of Parties here at home divert you from pursuing the common Interest of your Country; let no wicked Insinuations dif-quiet the Minds of my Subjects: The established Constitution in Church and State shall be the Rule of my Government; the Happiness, Ease, and Prosperity, of my People shall be the chief Care of my Life: Those who assist me in carrying on these Measures. I shall always

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to express our just Sense of the Divine Providence in placing his Majesty on the Throne of his Ancestors: To return his Majesty the Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; for his Assurances, that the established Constitution in Church and State shall be the Rule of his Government; and for his Goodness expressed to-those who distinguished themselves by their Zeal and Firmness for the Protestant Succession: To express our Concern, that any Conditions of the late Peace, essential to the Security and Trade of Great Britain, are not yet duly executed; that such Alliances have not been formed, as are necessary to render the Peace durable; that our Manufactures and Navigation are in such Hazard, by the Difficulties brought upon our Commerce; and that the Publick Debts are greatly increased, even since the Cessation of Arms: To declare our highest Resentinent against the presumptuous Declaration of the Pretender, and the Encouragement he boasts to have received from hence: And to allure his Majesty, ITiat we will demonstrate our just Sense of the great Blessings derived to these Nations in the Person of the Prince of , and his Issue, by enabling his Majesty to support the Dignity of the Crown, and to make an honourable Provision for the Royal Family; and that we will likewise grant such Supplies as shall be requisite for the Service of the Year, and for maintaining Parliamentary Credit; and will support his Majesty in such Alliances as* he shall judge necessary to make, for preserving the Peace of Europe.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned as a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practice, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter, or hinder, any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemea-nor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed, with the utmost Severity, against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of, to be in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee t>f the whole House, is fitting.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker's Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked Up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the Hoi^e, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of

Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Nine

of the Clock in the Morning to Three in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets, between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall, be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in hall, or Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherw ife, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster:And that he do fee the same put

in execution.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Resolved, That, notwithstanding the Oath taken by any Candidate at, or after, any Election, his Qualification may be afterwards examined into.

Resolved, That the Person whose Qua;ification is expressly objected to, in any Petition relating to his Election, shall, within Fifteen Days after the Petition read, give to the Clerk of the House of Commons a Paper, signed by himself, containing a Rental, or Particular, of the Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, whereby he makes out his Qualification; of which any Person concerned may have a Copy.

Resolved, That, of such Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, whereof the Party hath not been in Possession for Three Years before the Election, he shall also insert in the same Paper, from what Person, and by what Conveyance, or Act, in Law, he claims and derives the fame; and also the Consideration, if any paid; and the Names, and Places of Abode, of the Witnesses to such Conveyance and Payment.

Resolved, That if a Sitting-Member shall think fit to question the Qualification of a Petitioner, he shall, within Fifteen Days after the Petition read, leave Notice thereof in Writing, with the Clerk of the House of Commons; and the Petitioner shall, in such Case, within Fifteen Days after such Notice, leave, with the said Clerk of the House, the like Account, in Writing, of his Qualification, as is required from a Sitting Member.

A Petition of George Ashby Esquire, and Thomas Byrd Esquire, was read; letting forth. That the Petitioners, with Sir Geofrey Palmer, and Sir Thomas Cave, stood Candidates for the County of Leicester, on Tuesday the First of February last: And that, on the said Day, and on Wednesday the Second Day, the Freeholders, who offered to poll for the Petitioners, were insulted by several Persons unknown; and feme, upon their Refusal to vote for the said Sir Geofrey Palmer and Sir Thomas Cave, for which they were offered considerable Stuns of Money, were grievously wounded and ill-treated; and, oh Wednesday Night, the Under-Sheriff was insulted by the Friends of Sir Geofrey Palmer and Sir Thomas Cave, and threatened with Death by several Persons to him unknown, unless he would appoint a Deputy to carry on the Poll in his Absence, whom they should nominate; and, for fear of his Life, he was compelled to swear one Mr. Busby, Brother-in-Law to Sir George Beaumont, a Member of the House, as Deputy; and the Poll was carried on accordingly, in the Under-Sheriff's Absence j but none were admitted to poll on the Petitioners Side: That the Petitioners had several Hundreds of Freeholders in Town, who came to vote for them; and a great many more came on Thursday the Third of February, intending to do the fame; and several more upoa the Road, for that Purpose; so that the Petitioners doubt not, but if the Freeholders who would have voted for them had been suffered to give their Votes, the Petitioners would have been duly elefiled Knights for the said County: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Preuiifes.

Mr. Walpole reported from the Committee appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address, to be presented to his Majesty, That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House: and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

YOUR Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return Your Majesty their unfeigned Thanks, for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

’Tis with inexpressible Joy that we approach Your Majesty, peaceably leated upon the Throne of Your Royal Ancestors; and, being thoroughly sensible of the many open and secret Practices that have, of late Years, been uled to defeat the Protestant Succession, we cannot sufficiently adore the Divine Providence, that so interposed, and saved this Nation, by Your happy Accession to the Crown.

Your faithful Commons receive, with the highest Gratitude, Your most gracious Assurances, that the established Confutation in Church and State shall be the Rule of Your Government; and the Safety, Ease, and Prosperity, of Your People, the chief Care of Your Lite: We are sensible of Your Goodness, expressed to those w ho have distinguished themselves by their Zeal and Firm-ness for the Protestant Succession: And as we doubt not, but the Wisdom and Steadinels of Your Government w ill unite the Hearts of all Your faithful Subjects in Duty and Affcction to Your sacred Person, lb we most humbly beg Leave to allure Your Majesty, That we not only highly resent the wicked Insinuations uled to disquiet the Minds of Your Subjects; but are resolved, to the utmost of our Power, to suppress and exlinguish that evil Disposition that is still at work to deprive Your Majesty of the Affections of Your People.

We are sensibly touched, not only with the Disappointment, but with the Reproach, brought upon the Nation, by the unfuitabl? Conclusion of a War which was carried on at lb vast an Expense, and was attended with such unparalleled Successes: But, as that Diffionour cannot, in Justice, he imputed to the whole Nation, so we firmly hope and believe, that, through Your Majesty’s great Wisdom, and the faithful Endeavours of Your Commons, the Reputation of theft; Your Kingdoms will, in due time, be vindicated and restored.

We are under Astonishment to find, that any Conditions of the late Peace, cfiential to the Security and Trade 14

seasonably

Majesty’s

of Great Britain, should not yet be duly executed; and that Care w as not taken to form such Alliances, as might have rendered that Peace not precarious: And as no Care shall be wanting in Your loyal Commons to inquire into these fatal M ifearriages, so we entirely rely on Your Majesty’s Wisdom to enter into such Alliances as You shall judge necessary to preserve the Peace of Europe: and we faithfully promise to enable Your Majesty to make good all l’uch Engagements.

It is with just Rclentment we observe, that the Pretender still relides in Lorrain; and that he has the Pre-fumption, by Declarations from thence, to ltir up Your Majesty’s Subjects to Rebellion: But that which railes the utmost Indignation of Your Commons, is, that it appears therein, that his Hopes were built upon the Measures that bad been taken for feme timepaftin Great Britain: It shall be our Business to trace out those Measures whereon he placed his Hopes, and to bring the Authors of them to condign Punishment.

Your Commons are under the deepest Concern, that a great Part of our Trade is rendered impracticable, which, if not retrieved, must destroy our Manufactures, and ruin our Navigation: But, though we are too lbnlible of those fatal Consequences, we are not yet without Hopes, that Your Majesty’s great Wisdom, by the Abidance of Your Commons, may find Means to extricate Your People from their present Difficulties.

The Blessings derived to these Nations from Your Majesty’s auspicious Reign are not confined to the present Times: We have a Prospect of future and lasting Happiness entailed upon Your People, by a long Succession of Your Royal Progeny: And as this is a Blessing which these Kingdoms have a long time wanted, lb they could never hope to have seen - it so well supplied, as in the Person of his Royal Iiighness the Prince of and his Issue: Your faithful Commons shall therefore think it their Duty to enable your Majesty to support the Dignity of the Crown, and to make an honourable Provision for the Royal Family.

The surpriling Increase of the Publick Debts, even since all Thoughts of carrying on -the War were laid aside, shall not dil’courage us from granting fuel) Supplies as shall be necessary for the Service of this Year, and for the Support of Publick Faith: And we do entirely concur with Your Majesty in Opinion, That nothing can contribute more towards preserving the Credit of the Nation, than a strict Observance of all Parliamentary Engagements; which we are firmly resolved, upon all Occasions, inviolably to maintain.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Address be re-committed;

The House divided.

Waller Bacon Esquire, being chosen a Citizen to serve St. Germans in this present Parliament for the City and County of the Writ. City of Norwich; and also a Burgess for the Borough of St. Germans, in the County of Cornwall; made his Election to serve fur the City of Nprwick.

All the Silver above-mentioned was extracted out of English Lead; and all the Gold came to the Mint in the Form of Bars, or Ingots, the several Denominations and Species of which are not entered in our Books; but, by the Shape and Allay of the Bars, we conceive great part thereof to have been imported from Portugal, in the Form of Bars; and the rest to have been melted into Bars by the Goldsmiths in London. from various Sorts of foreign Gold, and chiefly from the Monies of France and Portugal, before it came to the Mint

Return to his Under-Sheriff in London; giving the Petitioner a Letter to him, or his Deputy, with Directions, to receive the Return and Precept, and annex the same to his General Return for the County: Which Letter, with the Return so affixed, the Petitioner delivered, according to the Sheriff’s Direction, here in Town: And that Person was desired to annex the same accordingly; who acquainted the Petitioner, that the General Return was not then come to Town: Upon which the Petitioner left the Letter and Return with the Person: But the Petitioner finds, that the General Return for the County is delivered to the Clerk of the Crown, without the Petitioner’s Return on the Precept, and with an Indenture signed by the Mayor of Newport, and others, to whom the Precept was not directed, of JVm. MR. Secretary Stanhope reported to the House, That Answer to their several Addresses of the Thirty-first of Addresses. March, and of Yesterday, had been presented to his Majesty, That his Majesty would be graciously pleased to direct the several Accounts and Matters therein mentioned to be laid before this House; and that his Majesty had been graciously pleased to give Directions for the laying the same before this House accordingly.

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Ten thousand Men be allowed for the Sea-Service for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fifteen, beginning from the First Day of January One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Ten thousand Men for Thirteen Months; including the Ordnance for Sea-Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Five hundred thirty-eight thousand Six hundred Seventy-eight Pounds One Shilling, be granted to his Majesty, to make good, for the Services of the Navy, the like Sum which, in the Year commencing from Chmtmas 1714, is to be paid by the Treasurer of the Navy, by quarterly Payments, to the South-Sea Company, pursuant to the Act of Parliament in that behalf.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That this House, will, upon Monday Mom- \Vay» ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole and Means. House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty/

Proclamation A Motion being made, That the House will appoint for calling a Day to take , into Consideration his Majesty’s Royal meat!Parlia* Proclamation, of the Fifteenth of January last, for the Calling of a new Parliament;

Resolved, That the said Proclamation be read.

And the same was accordingly read; and is as followed!; viz.

G. R.

IT having pleased Almighty God, by most remarkable Steps of his Providence, to bring us in Safety to the Crown of this Kingdom, notwithstanding the Designs of evil Men, who shewed themselves disaffcCted to our Succession, and who have since, with the utmost Degree of Malice, misrepresented our firm Resolution, and uniform Endeavours, to'preserv and defend our most excellent Constitution both in Church and State; and attempted, by many false Suggestions, to render us suspected to our People; we cannot omit, on this Occasion of first fumtnoning our Parliament of Great Britain (in Justice to ourselves, and that the Miscarriages of others may not be imputed to us, at a time when false Impressions may do the greatest and irrecoverable Hurt before they can be cleared up) to signify to our whole Kingdom, That we were very much concerned, on our Accession to the Crown, to find the publick Affairs of our Kingdoms under the greatest Difficulties, as well in respect of our Trade, and the Interruption of our Navigation, as of the great Debts of the Nation, which, we were surprised to observe, had been very much increased since the Conclusion of the last War. We ' Vot. 18.

do not, therefore, doubt, that if the ensuing Elections shall be made by our loving Subjects with that Safety and Freedom which, by Law, they are intitled to, and we are firmly resolved to maintain to them, they will fend up to Parliament the fittest Persons to redfefo the present Dif-orders, and to provide for the Peace and Happiness of our Kingdoms, and the Ease of our People, for the future; and therein will have a particular Regard to such as (hewed’ a Firmnels to the Protestant Succession, when it was most in Danger: We have, therefore, found it necessary, as well for the Causes aforesaid, as for other weighty Con. siderations concerning us, and our Kingdoms, to call a new Parliament; and we do accordingly declare, That, with the Advice of our Privy Council, we have this Day given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain, to iflu<3 out Writs, in due Form, for the calling a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Tefe on Monday the Seventeenth Day of this instant January, and to be returnable on Monday the Seventeenth Day of March next following. Given at our Court at St. James's, the Fifteenth Day of January One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen, in the First Year our Reign.

GOD fove the King.

Sir William Wyndhamattending in his Place, according to Order;

Mr. Speaker called upon him by his Name (Mr. Speaker litting in the Chair covered); and Sir William Wyndham standing up in his place uncovered, Mr. Speaker lpoke to him to the Effect following;

Sir William Wyndham,

I am to acquaint you, That Yesterday, after you were withdrawn, the House came to this Resolution;

" That Sir William Wyndham, having reflected upon his Majesty’s Proclamation, of the Fifteenth of January " last, for calling a new Parliament; and having refused to justify his Charge, although often called upon so to " do; is guilty of a great Indignity to his Majesty, and " of a Breach of the Privilege of this House."

Sir, The arraigning a Proclamation, issued by his Majesty, for calling this present Parliament; and refilling to assign any Caule, why such Proclamation is blameable; the House thought an Indignity to his Majesty, and so unwarrantable an Use of that Freedom of Speech, which is the undoubted Privilege of Parliament, that the House thought they could not let it^iafs without Animadversion: But, being willing their Moderation should appear, notwithstanding their Lenity has been too much despised and contemned, they have inflicted the mildelt Censure your Offence was capable of; and have commanded me to reprimand you in your Place; and, in Obedience to their Command, I do reprimand you accordingly.

Whereupon Sir William Wyndham said,

Mr. Speaker,

I very truly return my Thanks to you for performing that Duty which is incumbent upon you, from your Office, in so candid and gentleman-like a Manner.

As I am a Member, I know I mult acquiesce in the Determination of the House; but, as I am not confeious to myself of having offered any Indignity to his Majesty, or of having been guilty of any Breach of the Privilege of this House, I have no Thanks to return to those Gentlemen, who, under a Pretence of Lenity, have brought me under this Censure.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock,

Ross, Thomas Craig, Ballizes there; John Gordon, Trea-fnrer; James Anderson, James Lines, John Duff, Janies Duncan, James Warden, Michael Black, Convenees; and James Bannerman, Deacon; all Councilors; being Ten in Number, the Council confuting of Seventeen, whereof Sixteen being present, which is in the Terms of their Commission: The said Robert Dunbar craved, under Form of Instrument, that he might be received as Commissioner for the Town of Elgin to choose a Member for the ensuing Parliament, with the other Towns, by virtue of the above Commission, and the Plurality therein mentioned; and Protests against the Town Clerk of in case

he shall make any Return which is not founded upon this Commission: and the said Archibald Dunbar pro-telts, That his Commission should be received, and he be allowed to vote by virtue thereof, it being the only legal Commission; the other having been procured by Practices forbidden by Law; as to which, and the Objections made against these Practices, and the Commission procured by them, he refers to the Minutes of the Town Council of Elgin, and he protests against the Clerk, That he make no Return founded upon the other Commission, illegal as aforesaid, in regard also that it was objected, that the said Robert Dunbar should not be chosen Delegate, in regard he threatened several of the Members of the Council of that Town, as is more fully contained in the Minutes of the said Meeting, to which he refers: To which it is answered by Robert Dunbar, of Grangehill, That he never was guilty of any undue Practices in procuring the Delegacy of the Town of Elgin; nor that he ever threatened any Members of the Council of Elgin , but that he undertakes to prove, that there was undue Practices used upon the other Side; and that there was Threatenings against several of the Council; and granting, that either Whole or Part of these Objections were true, as they are all false, the Delegate from the other Towns, nor the Returning Clerk, are not the proper Judges; but that his Commission should be received, being signed by the Majority, as above, and the Return made according: In Answer to which, Archibald Dunbar, of Thunderton, repeated his Protestation: James Murray Esquire protested, That no Commission in favour of Robert Dunbar, of Grangehill, could be received as by Authority, the above-mentioned William John Gordon, James Anderson, James Inncs, John Duff, Michael Black, James Bannerman, James Warden, unless it is in order to vote for the said James Murray, becaul'e they were under Obligation so to do, signed under their Hands, at the Twenty-fifth Day of September; which I desire to be read, and answered, as the Ground of my said Protestation: — Our Provost, Dunkcnlie, did, some time ago, signify to several of us his Inclinations of your succeeding him as Provost of that Burgh; and the Proposal was so relishing and well-pleasing, that nothing but insupportable Difficulties could have interrupted our asking the Favour of such a worthy and honourable Countryman to have Vol. 18.

done us the Honour to have accepted of the Trouble of El that Office; but we are so hemmed in by a Set, and such ® Eyes of our common Enemies upon us, as that we would utterly risk a total Depravation of our Council, in case we give them Opportunity, or the least Foundation of a Process, at this Juncture; and we hope this Matter, and the quiet Settlement of this Burgh, is what you will think concerns yourself; and you would not be pleased, that we should give any Occasion or Opportunity to a certain Set of People to reign over us; and therefore it is expected you will weigh our Interest in the same Balance with your own, and not in the leait have any Thought of us, as that we will not, in any thing lies in our Power, contribute for your Interest, especially as to your continuing to your being Member of Parliament for this District of Boroughs; and, in as far as concerns us, we hope, ye will not neglect your own Friends; but will accept an unanimous Vow for you to represent this District in the ensuing Parliament; and you may be allured, and by these we do, as one Man, certify and declare to you, that no Delegate shall go froui this Borough, but such as shall be allured by your own; for we have such fixed Resolutions as to this Matter, which so nearly concerns us and the Nation, that nothing shall (hake us from the same: We wish you good Succels in your good and virtuous Inclination; and we give you hearty Thanks for the Trouble and Pains you were at to l'erve some of our Friends, and we are much honoured: Your most humble Servants, the Provost, Ballizes, and Council, of Elgin; Sicfubferibitur; George Lines, Kenneth MKenize, William Ross, John Gordon, Alexander

Rejoined, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be allowed Nine thousand Nine hundred Fifty-six Men, Commission and Non-commission Officers included, for Guards and Garrisons in Great Britain, Jersey, and Guernsey, and for his Majesty’s Plantations in America, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fifteen, over and above the Twelve Companies of Invalids, and Three Independent Companies in North Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four hundred twenty-five thousand Nine hundred Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining Guards and Garrisons in Great Britain, Jersey, and Guernsey, and his Forces in America, and the Twelve Companies of'Invalids, and Three Independent Compa- nies in North Britain, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fifteen.

A Petition of Wm.Paterson Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That by the Fifteenth Article of the Treaty of Union it is agreed, That, next after the necessary Allowance for any Losses which private Persons may sustain by reducing the Coin of Scotland to the Standard and Value of the Coin of England, the capital Stock, or Fund of the African and Indian Company of Scotland, advanced, together with the Interest for the said capital Stock, after the Rate of £!] per Cent, per Annum, from the respective Times of the Payment thereof, shall be paid; upon Payment of which capital Stock and Interest, it is agreed the said Company be dissolved, and cease: That, loon after passing the Treaty of Union by the Parliaments of both Kingdoms, the Parliament of Scotland, by an Act, intituled, Act concerning the Payment of the Sums out of the Equivalent to the African Company, did limit and restrict the Payment of such Interest at £.5 per Cent, per Annum to the ift Day of May 1707 then next following; and the whole Sums of Principal and Interest to be paid to the Creditors and Proprietors of the Joint-Stock of the said Company, to the gross Sum of £. 232,884. 5 s.o-^d. only; appointing the Directors of the said Company, or any Five of them, with their Secretary, to state the Account of such Debts and Stock advanced; but so as, in the Whole, not to exceed the said grols Sum of £.232,884. 5s. o \d.on or before the said First Day of May, on Pain of Letters of Horning; in which Proceedings, the Petitioner’s Claim and Demand upon the said Company was omitted; That, by an Act of the First Parliament of Great Britain, intituled, An Act for the further directing the Payment of the Equivalent-Money, it is particularly declared and enacted, That no Omission or Neglect of the Directors of the said Company, or of others concerned in Hating, adjusting, or certifying, the Claims or Demands upon the Equivalent, shall prejudice the Right, Interest, Claim, or Demand, of the Petitioner in and upon the said Company; but that the several Sums due to him by the said Company shall be certified, and thereupon fully satisfied and paid, in the Terms of the Treaty of Union, as the same shall be proved before the Judges of die Court of Exchequer in Scotland: That, by the Proofs since made before the said Judges, pursuant to the above-recited special Direction (a Certificate whereof is hereunto annexed) it appears, that the Petitioner hath not received the Considerations stipulated in and by his First Contrafts and Agreements with the said Company, nor had Satisfaction for his further and other Services, Expences, and Losses, for and on their Account: And praying such Relief as in your great Wisdom shall seem meet.

Exchequer-Chamber, Edinburgh, 171-f.

And whereas it appears, That the Accounts of the Stock advanced, and Debts due, by the African and Indian Company of Scotland, have been made up without Re-

Strd i to the Claim of Wm. Paterson Esquire, for his xpences, Pains, and Losses, on Account, and at the Instance, of the said Company; Be it Enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That no Omission or Neglect of the Directors of the said Company, or of others concerned in stating, adjusting, or certifying, the Claims or Demands upon the Equivalent, shall prejudice the Right, Interest, Claim, or Demand, of the said in and upon

the said Company; but that the several Sums due to him by the said Company shall be certified, and thereupon fully satisfied and paid, in the Terms of the Treaty of Union, as the same shall be proved before the aforesaid Judges of the Court of Exchequer in Scotland. And in regard that, since the making of the first Contrafts and Vo 1. 18.

Agreements, the said Wm. Paterson hath been at further Expences, and sustained olher Losses and Damages, for and on account of the said Company; Be it therefore further Enacted, That the said Judges of the Court of Exchequer in Scotland shall and are hereby required to take an Account of those his Expences and Losses, and likewise of his good Services and publick Cares, and make a full and fair Representation thereof to her Majesty: And, to the end the more full and free Inquiries may be made, and Information had of the Premises, the said Judges of the Court of Exchequer in Scotland shall and may, from time to time, direct their Commission, or Commissions, to any Commissioner or Commissioners within this Kingdom of Great Britain, or Dominions or Territories thereunto belonging, for taking the requisite Examinations, or Informations, to the Purposes aforesaid; and for reporting the same to the said Judges of the Court of Exchequer in Scotland: That, after passing the said Act of Parliament, viz. in the Months of June and July 1708, the Petitioner made his humble Application to this Court; upon which Application, the Court was pleased to give Orders and Directions: That, upon such Order, James Dunlop and John Symmer, Accountants to the said Company, did, on the 2d Day of July 1708, lay before this Court a State of the Petitioner’s Accounts of Debt and Credit; which was by the said James Dunlop and John Symmer sworn unto, before Mr. Baron Maitland, upon the 5th Day of August then next following: That Mr. Roderick Mackenzie, late Secretary to the said Company, did, by like Order, on the 83d Day of the same Month of July, lay before this Court a Report, with Extracts out of the Re-: gifter-Books of the said Company, relating to the Petitioner’s Claim; which was sworn unto by the said Mr. Mackenzie, before Mr. Baron Scrope, on the 29th Day of the said Month of July; the Originals of which Reports, and Extracts out of the Register-Books and Books of Accounts of the said Company, are now in the Hands of Paul Jo dr ell Esquire, Clerk of the House of Commons; to which honourable House the Petitioner hath since been obliged to apply for Relief: That, towards being still the better enabled to examine Witnesses, and bring his Proofs together, the Petitioner did, in Michaelmas .....1710, exhibit a Bill in this Court against the Commissioners of the Equivalent, her then Majesty’s Lord Advocate, and Lord Clerk Register: That, upon Interrogatories in relation to the Matter of the said Bill, the Depositions of Mr. Roderick Mackenzie were taken on or about the 30th Day of December following, together with the like Extracts directly from the said Company’s original Register-Books: That it appears from the before-mentioned Proofs, that the Petitioner hath been at great Expence and Pains, and sustained very considerable Losses, in the Service of the late African and Indian Company of Scotland; and that it doth not appear, that he hath received the Two per Cent. Premium stipulated in the Preamble or Conditions of Subscriptions, marked N° 1. in the above-mentioned Extracts out of the Register-Books of the said Company, or had other Satisfaction for his said Expences, Pains, and Losses, only that the Sum of £.435. 155. i-j-d. with the Interest thereon from the 7th of November 1701, remains in his Hands: That die many Obstructions, and long-continued Hardships, that the Petitioner hath hitherto laboured under in the Matter of obtaining his Right upon the said Company, do now indispensably oblige him again to make his humble Application to this Court: The Petitioner humbly prays their Lordships to make such Report, or Representation of the said Proofs, as they, in their Wisdom and Justice, shall judge proper for his Relief.

Upon Consideration whereof, and of the Proofs made in this Court upon the Matters therein let forth, since, both at the time when the Company, in the said Petition mentioned, was beginning to be formed, and after it w’as carried into a Settlement, it was intended by those interested therein, that the Petitioner should have aconliderable Recompence for his extraordinary Services, in projecting the said Company, and carrying on the Interests thereof; as, by the particular Proposals made for that Purpose,

R fully

TCennet

Navigation.

Privilege.

6l 140 Aprilis. 1715.

fully appears, though they were never perfected, or carried into an Execution; we are of Opinion, That the Petitioner had a just Right to have had the said intended Recompence made good to him out of the Equivalent-money appointed to make good the Losses of the Persons concerned in the said Company: And, since he hath been, excluded from any Share thereof, and also in regard that he hath been very instrumerital in carrying on other Matters of a publick Nature, which seem to us to have been very much for his Country’s Service, we think it just and reasonable, that some Way should be found out to give him that Recompence for his said Services, which he appears to have merited, and of which he hath hitherto been disappointed of.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Mr. Hampden accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which Report he j;ead in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: And the Re-]3ort and Resolution are as followeth; viz.

Upon the Complaint, That Robert Parker and others bad entered upon the Pofiession of Richard Clowder, Tenant to Hugh Cholmly Esquire, a Member of this House:

That the Committee have examined the Matter of the said Complaint; and heard Counsel for and against the Persons complained of

Richard Clowder said, That he holds from Mr. Cholmly a Wood at Sydenham, in Kent, for which he has paid his Rent to Mr. Cholmly, and hisTrufiees, Sixteen Years; and that, upon the Twenty-fifth Day of March last, the said Robert Parker came, with John Kither, a Sheriff’s Bailiff, and turned him out of Pofiession.

John Kither said, That Mr. Parker employed him to take the Pofiession; which he did by virtue of a Warrant f rom the Sheriff of Kent, brought to him by Mr. Parker, who went with him to take the Pofiession;

18

That the Warrant is dated the Twenty-fourth Day of March last; and is in Execution of a Judgment in Ejectment, obtained by Default upon the Demise of the said Robert Parker.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee cams to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Robert Parker, having, upon the Twenty-fifth Day of March last, entered upon, and taken Possession of, a Wood at Sydenham, in the County of Kent, then in Possession of Richard Clowder, Tenant to Hugh Cholmly Esquire, a Member of this House, is guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the said Robert Parker be, for the said. Breach of Privilege, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, and other the chief Inhabitants, of the Borough of Whitchurch, in the County of Southampton, was presented to the Iioule, and read; setting forth, That the making the River Kemiet navigable from Reading to Newbury, in the County of Berks, will emphatically answer those great Ends, and . highly advantageous to the Publick; and tend very much to the Preservation of the Highways, and Improvement of Trade; and be serviceable to this and the neighbouring Countries, and to this Borough, and Parts adjacent: And praying, That the Bill, now depending, for making the said River navigable, may pass into a Law.

A Petition of Thomas Crosby, Under-Sheriff of the County of Cumberland, in Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for neglecting to return the Writ for electing the Members of the said County by the Seventeenth Day of March last, being the Day appointed for the Return thereof, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner is deeply sensible of his Fault; and extremely lorry that he has so justly incurred the Censure of this House; but, as he professes to have had no evil Intention in the Delay of this Return, humbly hopes you will {hew a ifterciful Disposition towards him: lie heartily asks Pardon for his Fault; and begs, in regard the Duty of his Office, and his own pressing Affairs, require his Presence in the Country: And praying, That-he may be released, from his Confinement.

Ordered, That the said Thomas Crosby be brought to the Bar of this House on Friday Morning next, in order to his being discharged out of Custody.

Woollen Ma- A Petition of the Buyers and Dealers in mixed or nufacture. medley Broad Cloths; complaining of many Abuses and Frauds put upon them by the Makers and Manufacturers of the fame, to the great Disresputation of the Woollen ' Trade, and the manifest Injury of the Petitioners; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That an Act passed in the Tenth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, for regulating, improving, and encouraging, the Woollen Manufacture of mixed or medley Broad-Cloths; and for the better Payment of the Poor employed therein; it is enacted, That all mixed or medley Broad-Cloths, to be made after the Twenty-fourth Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and twelve, shall be measured at the Fulling-Mill by the Master, &;c. upon Oath; who is also to rivet a Seal of Lead on every such Cloth; and to seal and stamp in Figures, the Length and Breadth of the fame, to be and remain the Rule of Payment for the Buyer to accept the said Cloths; under a Penalty of1Twenty Shillings for every Refusal: And that through the Un-ilfulness of feme Owners of the said Fulling-Mills, or through the Covetoulness in the Clothier who employs them, that frequently these mixed or medley Cloths is short in Measure of what is fixed on the Seals of the said Owners of the Mills; and that the Clothiers lie under the Penalty of Twenty Shillings only, if any mixed or medley Broad-Cloth is fully wet, lealed, and stamped, and the said Clothiers shall stretch any such Broad-Cloth above One Yard in Twenty Yards Length, and One Nail of a Yard in Breadth: That the said Penalty is . of sufficient Weight to enforce the Observation of the said Law; besides, that the Manner of Recovering thereof renders the Law ineffectual in this Point j for that no Forfeiture is to be paid, unless the Offender. convicted before such mixed or medley Broad-Cloths is exposed to Sale: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to amend or repeal Part of the said Law; and to prevent the Abuses done under Colour, and by Pretext of the said Law; and for the Preservation of the Woollen Trade; and for the equal Benefit and Relief of the Buyers and Dealers therein.

And several Clauses in the said Act were read.

A Petition of the High-Sheriff, Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen of the Grand Jury, and other Gentlemen, of the County of Wilts, assembled at the Quarter-Sessions held at the Devizes, in the said County, the Twenty -sixth Day of April, Anno Domini One thousand Seven hundred and Fifteen, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That whereas it appeareth unto the Petitioners, that there is a Bill nowr depending before this House, for making the River Kennet navigable from Reading to Newbury, in the County of Berks; which, we humbly suggest, will be of great Advantage to all the Inhabitants of this County, if it passes into a Law, not only for the Benefit of Trade in general, but by easing us of the great Rates we pay for the Carriage of bulky Goods from the City of London to all Parts hereabouts; as also by preventing the great Damage continually done to our Highways, so very much impaired by the heavy Loads carried in Waggons from the City of London to the City of Bristol: And praying, That the said Bill may pass, in order to pass into a Law; which will be of great Advantage to the Petitioners, and highly tend to the Advancement of Trade in this Part of the Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to w hom the Bill to make the River Kennet navigable from Reading to Newbury, in the County of Berks, is committed.

That it appeared to the Committee, That by an Act passed in the Tenth Year of her late Majesty s Reign,

That all mixed or medley Broad-Cloth, to be made after the Twenty-fourth Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Twelve, shall be measured at the Fulling-Mill by the Matter, Owner, or other Occupier thereof, upon Oath; who is also to rivet a Seal of Lead on every such Cloth, and to seal and stamp in Figures the Length and Breadth of the fame; which is to be and remain the only Rule and Payment for all and every Buyer or Buyers whatsoever, to accept the said Cloths; subject to a Penalty for every Refusal:

That it also appeared to the Committee, That these mixed or medley Cloths frequently come into the Petitioners Hands short m Measure, both in Length and Breadth of what is fixed and stamped on the Seal of the said Owners or Occupiers of the Mills: Several of the said Clothe being produced before the Committee; the false Measurment whereof was attefied by various Witnesses who had measured the same:

And that, upon Consideration of the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of the said Petition.

The House divided.

The Yeas go forth.
