A Paper Ihevting how the Civil List Branches have been abridged, altered, taken away, or incumbered, by any Act

or Acts of Parliament, since the granting thereof.

9* W. Cap. 23.,) By an Act of Parliament, intituled,

Sec. 13. jAn Act for granting to his Majesty a further Subsidy of Tonage and Poundage, towards railing the yearly Sum of 700,000l. for the Service of his Majesty’s Houshold, and other Uses therein mentioned, during his Majesty’s Life, it is recited, That it was intended the yearly Sum of 700,000l. should be supplied to his said late Majesty King William, for the Service of his Houshold and Family, and for other his necessary Expences and Occasions, out of the Hereditary and Temporary Excise, after all the Tallies charged upon the weekly Sum of 6,000 /. bluing out of the said Branches of Excise, by an Act made in the 7th Year of his Majesty’s Reign, with the Interest thereof, should be fully paid off and cleared; and out of the Revenue of the Poll Office, after all the Tallies charged upon the weekly Sum of 600l. then issuing out of that Revenue, and all the Interest thereof, should be fully paid and discharged; and out of the small Branches of his Majesty’s Revenues after-mentioned; that is to say; First fruits and Tenths of the Clergy, the Fines payable in the Alienation Office, the Poll Fines, the Revenue of Wine Licences, the Money arising by Sheriffs Proffers, Compositions in the Exchequer, Seizures of uncustomed and prohibited Goods, the Duchy of Cornwall, and other Land Revenue in England or Wales, and the Duty of and f per Cent, in Barbadoes and the Leeward J/lands;and out of the further Subsidy of Tonage and Poundage granted by that Act: And it was thereby Enacted, That, if the said Revenues should produce in clear Money more than the yearly Sum of 700,000l. from the 25th Day of December 1699, the Overplus should not be dispoied without Authority of Parliament, and the Grants thereof should be void.

12* W. Cap. 12.] By this Act of Parliament, 3,700l. weekly out of the said Branches of Excise is appropriated for publick Uses: And it was thereby Enacted, That all the Residue of the said particular Branches of Excise, which should remain after the said weekly Payments made out of the fame; and the said Revenue of the Poll Office, and the several small Branches before expressed; and the said further Subsidy of Tonage and Poundage; should, during his Majesty’s Life, be for the Service of his Hous-hold and Family, and other his necessary Expences and Occasions; any Clause in the said former Act to the contrary notwithstanding: And that all the Clauses contained in the said former Act, for, touching, or concerning, the said Overplus, over and above the said yearly Sum of 700,000l. were and should be repealed and void.

i# Anna, Cap. 7.] By an Act, intituled, An Act for the better Support of her Majesty’s Houshold, and of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown, it is Enacted, That the Hereditary Duties of Excise, and the Duties of Excise thereby granted to her Majesty for her Life, subject nevertheless to the Payment of 3,700l. a Week for publick Uses; and the said Revenue of the Post Office, and the several small Branches before enumerated; and the said further Subsidy of Tonage and Poundage; and all other Duties which were chargeable with the said yearly Sum of 700,000l. the said Duty of and $ per Cent. excepted; should be. for the Support of her Majesty’s Houshold, and of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown.

3* Anna.’] The Queen, by Letters Patents dated the 3d Day of November, 3® Anna, pursuant to an Act 2® Anna, Cap. 11. created the Corporation for the Augmentation of the Maintenance of the poor Cleray; and thereby granted to the same the Revenue of First fruits and Tenths, and the Arrears thereof, subject to the Pensions before that time charged thereupon.

9® Anna.] By this Act of Parliament, the Rates of Postage of Letters, Pacquets, and Advices, were increased; and, out of the Revenues so increased, a weekly Sum of 700l. was appropriated for 32 Years, from Michaelmas 1711, for publick Uses; which weekly Sum of 700l. amounting to 36,400l. per Annum, jiyas supposed, would have been the Increase, by the additional Duties granted by that Act; but,.by the Accounts transmitted from the Post Office, it appears, that the grols Produce of the said Revenues have not been increased, by the additional Duties, more than 8,000 /. per Annum, or thereabouts.

12® Anna.] By an Act for raising 500,000l. by way of a Lottery, for Payment of Arrears due to her Majesty’s Servants, Tradesmen, and others; and by Letters Patents, thereupon grounded, bearing Date the 13th Day of

October, 12° Anna; the yearly Sum of 35,000l. out of all the Civil List Branches, was appropriated for 32 Years, from Michaelmas 1713, to pay the principal Sum of 633,000l. and Interest, at 4/. per Cent, to the Adventurers in the said Lottery, or their Assigns.

Major-General Gust. Hamilton — at 182/. 10$. per Annum-, by her Majesty’s Letter, dated the 8th of July 1706; in consideration of his storming the Town of Athlone, at the head of the Grenadiers 5 and thereby obtained from his late Royal Majesty King William the Third the government thereof, with a salary of Fourteen Shillings a Day: This Pension to continue during her Majesty’s pleasure.

Lord Slane — at 500l. per Annum; by her Majesty’s Letter, bearing date the 7th of 1707: This

Pension to continue during her Majesty’s pleasure.

Colonel Wm. Cullyford — at 250/. per Annum; by her Majesty’s letter, bearing date the 3d of August 1706; upon consideration that he served the Crown very well for many Years; and being infirm: This Pension to continue during her Majesty’s Pleasure.

Major Edmund Power — at 73/. per Annum;. by her Majesty’s Letter, bearing date the 8th at July 1706; in regard to his services: This Pension to continue during her Majesty’s pleasure.

Captain Adam Blair — at 100l. per Annum; in consideration of the loss of his right leg, two wounds in his left thigh, and a wound in his face; all received at the siege of Alicant.

Captain John Claverie — at 45/. 1 is. 6d. per Annum; by her Majesty’s Letter, bearing date the 13th March 1709; upon consideration that he is a French Protestant, and quitted the French King’s service: This Pension to continue during her Majesty’s pleasure.

Lieutenant-Colonel Hugh Owen — at 91/. 5s. per Annum; by her Majesty’s Letter, bearing date the 3d of July 1711; upon consideration of the wounds he received in Spain, at the battle of Stephens: This Pension to continue during her Majesty’s pleasure.

Captain Robert Phillips — at 50/.; by her Majesty’s Letter, bearing date the 3fl of July 1711; upon consideration of having served long with honour and fidelity, till disabled by his wounds; and that he is now very old, and in extreme want: This Pension to continue during her Majesty's pleasure.

Colonel Wm. Coward — at 182/. 10 per Annum; by her Majesty’s Letter, bearing date the 29th of September 1709; in consideration of his past services, and the hardships he hath laboured under: This Pe'nsion to continue during her Majesty’s Pleasure, or until such time as her Majesty shall otherwise provide for him.

Letter, bearing date the 12th of November 1707, at the request of the House of Commons of Ireland: This Pension to continue during her Majesty’s pleasure.

Captain George Lyndon — at 54/. 15 per Annum: by her Majesty’s Letters, bearing date the 13th of March 1709; in consideration of his not being able to attend the service; that he is a gentleman of a very good family, and of a very fair character; and having a wife and five children to maintain: This Pension to be paid during her Majesty’s pleasure.

ANNE R.

WHEREAS, in or about the Month of November 1711, we did, by Commission under our Seal appointed to be kept in place of our Great Seal of nomi-

nate and constitute our Right Trusty and Well-beloved John Lord Balmerino, and several others therein named, during our Pleasure only, to be Commissioners for executing die Office of High Chamberlain of Scotland, with such Powers and Authorities, and in such Manner, as by the said Commission, Relation being the reunto had, may appear: And whereas we are graciously pleased to allow unto the said Lord Balmerino, in Confederation thereof, a Sum of 1,000l.: Our Will and Pleasure now is, and we do hereby direct, authorize, and command, That, out of the Sum of 5,040/. lately paid to your Hands by die Representatives of Sir George Hume, and others, for the Causes mentioned in our Letters of Privy Seal in that behalf, you forthwith pay over to the said John Lord Bat-merino, or his Assigns, the said Sum of 1,000l. without any Account, Imprest, or other Charge, to be set upon him in our Exchequer, for the fame: And this shall be, as well to you for Payment, as to the Auditors, and all others concerned, for Allowing thereof, upon your Account, a sufficient Warrant. Given at our Court at St. James's, the 14th Day of May 1714, in the Thirteenth Year of our Reign.

By her Majesty's Command,

To our Trusty and Well-beloved

Archibald Douglas, of Cavers,

Esquire, Receiver General of our Land Rents, and Casualties in Scotland.

Alexander Earl of Eglington, David Earl of Wm. Lord Haddo, the like Warrants, mutatis mutandis.

27th July 1714. Andrew Cockburn, Merchant, a like Warrant for 1,000l.: mentioned to be in Satisfaction of Money expended by him for her late Majesty’s Service.

24th July 1714. A Warrant signed by her late Majesty, directed to Mr. Nicholas, for paying 1,000l. to David Earl of Northesk, as of her Majesty’s Bounty.

etith July 1714. A like Warrant, directed to Mr. Nicholas, for paying to Thomas Paterson j,oooo/. as of like Bounty.

ANNER.

WHEREAS we directed you, our High Treasurer, to signify our Commands to the Commissioners for managing our Revenues of Excise in Scotland to advance and pay to our Trusty and Well-beloved Henry Maule Esquire, a Sum of 4,000l. out of that Part of our Revenue of Excise applicable to the Ufesof our Civil Government: And whereas you our said High Treasurer have laid before us the annexed Acquittance of the said Henry Maule, given to our said Commissioners, acknowledging the Receipt of the said Sum; and we being fully satisfied, not only that the said Sum hath been paid to the said Henry Maule, but also with the Expenditure thereof by him for such our Service, as we had directed: Our Will and Pleasure therefore is, and we do hereby direct, authorize, and command, That, in pursuance of our Letters of Privy Seal in this behalf, you, and every of you, and all others herein concerned, do make and give full and plenary Allowance and Discharge to the said Commissioners of Excise, in their Accounts of that Part of the Excise which is applicable to the Uses of the Civil Government, of the said Sum of 4,000l. paid to the said Henry Maule, without setting him the said Maule insuper for the fame, or any Part thereof: And for so doing, this shall be your Warrant Given at our Court at Kensington, the 27th July 1714, in the 13th Year of our Reign.

By her Majesty’s Command,

To our Right Trusty and Right Well- OXFORD. beloved Cousin and Counsellor Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer, our High Treasurer now being, and to our High Treasurer, or Commissioners of the Treasury for the time being; and to the Barons of our Court of Exchequer in Scotland, now, and for the time being.

The Receipt.

I do hereby acknowlege to have received, of the Commissioners of Excise in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, the Sum of 4,000l. being Money arising out of such Part of the Revenue of Excise, under their Management, as is applicable to the Uses of her Majesty’s Civil Government, pursuant to her Majesty’s Pleasure, and the Commands of the Right honourable the Lord High Treasurer, signified by Lowndes, Esquire,

in his Letter dated the 19th of September last. Witness my Hand, the 4th Day of November 1713.

(Signed)

Witness ColinAlifon,

Louis Groeme. Lorcndes.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Thirty-five thousand Five hundred Seventy-four Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for Half Pay to the Sea Officers for the Year 1715.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Ninety-seven thousand Eight hundred Ninety-six Pounds Seventy Shillings and Five Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy, for the Year 1715.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred Thirty-seven thousand Two hundred Seventy-seven Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, for the extraordinary Repairs of the Navy, Rebuilding of Ships, and other extraordinary Works; as also completing the Furniture and Stores of the Ships in Repair, and to be repaired; in the Year 1715.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ninety thousand Seven hundred Ninety-seven Pounds Eleven Shillings and Three Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance for Land Service, for the Year .1715.

A Petition of the People called Quakers, in behalf of Quaker many of their Friends in South Britain, and of their Affirm*Uon' Friends in general in North Britain, who conscientiously scruple the taking the present Affirmation, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in the Year 1696, King William, and the then Parliament, were pleased to grant us a solemn Affirmation, instead of an Oath; whereby many of us have been delivered and defended from Imprisonments, vexatious Suits, Lois of Goods and Estates, as well as enabled to serve our Country, and piomote the Trade and Wealth of it; though many of our Friends, ferupling to attest the sacred Name of God, and all other his divine Attributes, hive, by means thereof, been deprived of its intended Benefit; and have been, and still are, if not relieved, liable tq great Sufferings and Discouragements in their lawful Callings, and Manufactures of this Kingdom: And praying to make such an Alteration in the present Bill before the House, that our Affirmation may be in these Words; " I do fin-

" cerely declare and aftirm which, on Inquiry, we find will be generally easy to our Friends; and which, we humbly conceive, will very well answer the Intent of the Law, and Justice, since the Penalties in case of Falshood carry the same legal Security as in Perjury.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put,

That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed;

It passed in the Negative.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Army Debts. A Petition of Francis Beaumont, Undertaker for Forage, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner entered into a Contraft with his Grace the Duke of Marlborough, and afterwards with Lieutenant General Cadogan, for delivering Forage to the Troops in the Pay of her late Majesty serving in Flanders, in their Winter Quarters l yfi, and the Spring following, upon express Condition, That he iliould forthwith receive the Advance-money, and his intire Payment in a Month after the Delivery of the Forage; and, upon the repeated Assurances of a punctual Payment, he furnished the Forage cheaper than any former Contractors had done, or even than the States General allowed their Undertaker for the same time: The Petitioner, having performed his Part of the Contraft to the intire Satisfaction of all the General Officers of the Army, had Reason to hope for a punctual Payment, the Parliament having provided, in the Sessions 17if, for the greatest part of this Service; but that Money, as the Petitioner has -been informed, being applied to other Uses, he is lb far from receiving the Satisfaction he expected, that, after Three Years continual Solicitation, he has not yet received the Advance-money: The Petitioner’s Account has passed several Examinations, and has always been reported in his Favour: It was first referred to Mr. Watkins in Flanders; then to the Comptrollers of the Accounts of the Army; afterwards to Mr. Bridges, now Earl of Caernarvon; then to Mr. Watkins again, who had a particular Commission from her late Majesty for that Purpose; whole Report, being laid before the select Committee of the House of Commons in the lall Parliament, was there approved of, and reported

to the House as a Debt amounting to 54,750/. 2 8

Sterling: The said Parliament having granted 300,000l.

Sterling upon Account of the Debts of the Army, the Petitioner had Reason to hope, that he should have been speedily paid; but, instead thereof, his Account was ordered to be re-examined by the Right honourable Mr.

Walpole, Mr. Pulteney, and the Comptrollers of the Accounts of the Army j who do not only report, That the said Debt appears to be justly due; but, also, that it defences to be paid preferably to others; and do therefore propose, that it shall be paid out of the Remainder of the said 300,000l.: The Petitioner humbly hopes, that this honourable House will consider the irreparable Damages he has suffered by this long delay; the Interest and Charges of what is so justly due to him having more than funk the Profit he proposed to make by the said Undertaking, having been obliged to fell the greatest Part of his Effects to support his Credit; and, by his long Attendance at London to solicit this Business, has loft the belt Employment he had at Maestricht, and is in Danger of being

thrown into a Gaol for the Debts he has contracted for the Service of the Crown of England: And praying. That this honourable House will be pleased to give Leave to insert a Clause in such Bill as they shall think proper, that he may be paid out of the Remainder of the said 300,000l. granted by Parliament upon Account of the Debts of the Army; without which, the Petitioner is in Danger of being still postponed from time to time, to the intire Ruin of himself, and numerous Family, as well as many more in Holland, Flanders, and Brabant, who are engaged with him in this great Undertaking.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report of the Referrees concerning the Debts of the Army, be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Frederick Tilney Esquire, be at liberty Whitdmrtk to withdraw his Petition, complaining of an undue Elec- Ele&o*. tion and Return for the Borough of Whitchurch, in the County of Southampton.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee of Privileges and Elections, That they be discharged from proceeding upon the said Petition.

[Debtors Petitions.]

A PETITION of many poor Prisoners in the King's Bench Prison, in behalf of themselves and several Thousands, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have been great Traders both by Sea and Land, and paid great Customs and Taxes; meeting with Misfortunes by Trading in so long and tedious War, are become insolvent; not capable of making Satisfaction to their Creditors, are willing to surrender their All, for the Relief of their Bodies: And praying, That this honourable House will give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in for the Relief of the Petitioners.

A Petition of the poor Prisoners for Debt in his Majesty's Prison in the County of Leicester, on Behalf of themselves, and many Thousands poor distressed Debtors, in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners did most humbly represent their sad deplorable Conditions and long Confinements, in Gaol, the last Parliament, with such good Effect, that the then honourable House ordered a Bill to be brought in, and passed it, for the Relief of the Petitioners; which was sent up to the House of Peers, read there a First time, and ordered a Second Reading; but, by the sudden and unexpected Prorogation of that Parliament, the Bill was dropped, and lost; to the great Disappointment and Mortification of all the Petitioners: That the Petitioners, with Hearts filled with Gratitude, and a true Sense of the charitable and good Intentions of this honourable House, the last Sessions of her late Majesty’s Reign, are thereby encouraged to present themselves again to this honourable House; most humbly imploring your Honours Aid and Assistance for; what is most desired and dear to all the World, their Liberty, upon the same just and equitable Considerations as the former Bill; they being willing and ready to make the utmost Satisfaction they are capable of at present, by surrendering up their All to their Creditors, and upon the feverell Penalties: And praying, that your Honours win be pleased to take the distressed and deplorable Condition of so many Thousand poor Prisoners into your Honours Considerations; To the End that a Bill may be ordered to be brought into this House, for their Relief.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petitions: And that Mr. Bracebridge and Sir Thomas Cave do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of George Blagrave Esquire, Owner of Two several Mills, called St.Giles and Minster Mills, both within the Borough of Reading, in the County of Berks, Handing upon the River Kennet, and also One other Mill, called Calcat Mill, in the Parish of Tilehurst, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner's aforesaid Mills are ancient Corn-Mills, and were lately new-built, which cost at least 3,000l.; and are now let at 300 annum’, and grind at least ninety Load of Wheat per Week for London Market, more than what is ground for the Neighbourhood; and in case the said River should be made navigable, the Water will be so much diverted, that the Petitioner's said Mills will not have Water enough to grind for the Families of the Inhabitants of the said Borough; to the great Damage of the Petitioner: And praying to take such effectual Care, that the Petitioner may, in case such Bill shall pass, have a Clause inserted in the said Bill, That all Damages which shall at any time or times hereafter happen, as aforesaid, shall be made good to the Petitioner, in such Manner as to your Honours, in your great Wifi-dom, shall seem meet: And that the Petitioner may be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, before the same shall pass.

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Freemen not receiving Alms.

The Question was, touching the Qualifications of the Freemen:

It was agreed, That Persons are intitled to Freedom, by Birth after their Father’s Freedom; or by Marriage with the Daughter of a FreemanTo born; or by Seven Years Servitude as Apprentices to Freemen; and the Difference was, Whether Freemen by Redemption have a Right-to vote?

That the Petitioners Counsel alleged, This is a Borough by Prescription; and that Freemen by Redemption had no Right.

That the Sitting Members Counsel alleged, This is a Borough, and a Corporation, by Prescription; and that all Freemen had a Right to vote.

That, to prove this to be a Borough by Prescription, the Petitioners Counsel produced the following Returns to Parliament;

That, to prove the ancient Usage of admitting honorary Freemen, the Town-Books were produced, and 75 Instances were read of Admissions to Freedom for Fines, or gratis, in the several Reigns of R. 2. H. 4, 5, and 6. Ed. 4. H. 7. Ph. and M. Eliz. and J. 1.: And the Petitioners Counsel admitted there were Inffances of the same Nature in all subsequent Reigns.

From whence the Sitting Members Counsel inferred this to be a Corporation by Prescription; or that, at lealt, they had, Time out of Mind, admitted honorary Freemen, which was what they contended for.

And, to prove farther, that such Freemen had always voted in Elections, they called,

Mr. Richard Freeman, the Town-Clerk; who laid. That honorary Freemen had voted in all Elections for Ten Years past; and produced the Polls taken in 93, and 95, and another without Date, when several honorary Freemen voted.

And that the Committee came to the following Resolution;

That Mr. Mayfant, another Voter, seconded him in this' Demand; and while they were talking, the Bailiff went on with the Poll:

Being cross-examined, he owned, That Serjeant Comyns gave him a Particular of his Qualification in the Time of the Poll; which being Five hundred Pounds, he said. That he thought liirely the Serjeant was qualified; but that, the others insisting on his Qualification, and again demanding the Oath, the Serjeant replied. An Oath was a weighty Thing; and that he would not take- a false Oath for all the World, much less for that Election:

Mr. Coe said farther. That he staid till the Poll was over; and then they again demanded the Qualification; and that Sir William Jollyjfe demanded the same thing: That he did not remember the Serjeant named any Time to take the Oath, but he refused to take it then:

Mr. Coe being farther examined, owned, That, when he first received the Particular from Serjeant Comyns, he promised to deliver it back again; but carried it away with him; and that night, after the Court was adjoumea, he returned the Particular to the Bailiff, at whole House the Serjeant was to lie.

Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Malden, in the County of wilfully refused to take the Oath of Qualification, as is directed by an Act of Parliament, of the 9th Year of the late Queen, intituled, An Act for securing the Freedom of Parliaments, by the farther qualifying the Members to fit in the House of - Commons, though duly required so to do; and not having at any time before the Meeting of this Parliament taken the said Oath; his Election is thereby void.

A Petition of the Sea-Chaplains, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of their Brethren unprovided for in time of Peace, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in the 12th Year of her late Majesty, intituled, An Act for laying additional Duties on Soap, 8$c. for raising the Sum of 1,400,000l. by way of Lottery, there is a Clause inserted in these Words, Page 322.; " And any further Sum, not exceeding 3,000l. to be equally distributed among the " Chaplains that served in the Fleet during the late War, and are not otherwise provided for That the Petitioners, pursuant to the Advertisements of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, did lay in their several Claims; and were in Hopes to have had a Distribution of the said Sum at the time fixed, by their last Advertiso-ment, for receiving any further Claims; but, after several Applications to their Lordships, they were at length pleased to declare themselves unable to determine the Import of the general Terms in which the said Act, with regard to the Petitioners, is conceived; and therefore are resolved to make no Distribution of the said Sum among the aforesaid Chaplains, without a more full Explication of the Words of the said Act, from "this honourable House: And praying to take into Consideration the hard Circumstances of the Petitioners; and, by giving a more full Explanation of the Import of the said Act, to enable their Lordships to make a speedy Distribution of the above-mentioned Sum among such Chaplains as are unprovided for.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table*

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the poor distressed Prisoners for Debt in the Sheriff's Ward, or Prison, at the Parish of St.Thomas the Apofile, in and for the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the said poor distressed Prisoners, being about 107 in Number, being in a very dismal and despicable Estate and Condition by Imprisonment, occasioned chiefly through the malicious Prosecutions of our Creditors; for some of us have been, in some measure, able to satisfy our Creditors, and have offered so to do; which they would not accept of/in such reasonable manner as we were able to do; and others of us, who would have satisfied our Creditors, if we might have had reasonable Time from them so to do; and others of us, who, through Losses, and Impoverishments by long absconding for Debts (who, in that time of such Abfeonding, we endeavoured with the utmost Diligence to reconcile ourselves to our Creditors), long Voj.. 18.

Imprisonment, and rigorous Prosecutions, our Estates are either wasted, wholly gone, ourselves almost starved, and our Families in a perishing Condition; and all of us utterly disabled to make Satisfaction of our Debts: And praying your Honours to consider our miserable Condition, and to give us your Assistance in procuring an Act of Parliament for our Relief, and Freedom from Imprisonment, as to your Honours shall think meet and convenient

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the poor distressed Prisoners for Debt in the Castle of Lincoln was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by great Losses and Disappointments in Trade, and otherwise, are become incapable of paying their respective Creditors full Debts; but the Petitioners are ready and willing to make them the utmost satisfaCHon they are capable of, by delivering up unto each respective Creditor, or to their Use, upon Oath, all the Petitioners Substance or EffeCls, without Fraud or Concealment, under the severest Penalties that can be inflicted upon them, so as they may be discharged of their Imprisonments: And praying your Honours will not stop your Ears at the Cry of the Poor, but, as it is in your Powers, will undo the heavy Burden many of us having so long groaned under.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of above Four hundred insolvent Debtors in the Alarshalfea, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners Insolvency is chiefly by Badness of Trade, occasioned by a long, though neceifery War: That the Petitioners, to obtain their Liberty, are willing to give their respective Creditors the utmost Satisfaction they are able, by delivering up their All, on the strictest Oaths and Obligations; which Terms are humbly conceived to be agreeable to Religion, Reason, and Humanity: That a great Number of miserable Debtors have been starved to Death in the said Prison; on which account poor Insolvents have reason to envy the Condition of Felons, and other Criminals, who are either punished, or discharged, soon after their Commitment and, in the mean time, supported with Bread; which your unhappy Petitioners want: And praying, That a new Bill may be brought in for their Relief this happy Juncture, now the Crown is demised on a Prince endued with so much Justice, Mercy, and Clemency, whom God grant long to reign.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table*

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in the Sheriflf1 Ward, and County-Prison, in , in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That your poor Petitioners, or most of us; have been several Years in Prison, occasioned by many Loffe$ and Disappointments; and, by reason of the Largenefil of our Debts, could not take the Benefit of the late Act of Parliament, made in the Tenth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, which was restrained to the Sum of Fifty Pounds; whereby Two-thirds of us were incapable of being dise charged; ourselves and Families are likely to starve, and suffer inevitable Ruin, unless timely relieved: Some of us have served in the late War several Years, and most of us largely contributed towards the carrying on of the fame, which was so very expensive, long, and tedious: And praying your Honours to take our miserable Condition into your most serious Consideration; and bQ pleased to grant us such an Act for our Relealemen^ as in your great WiiUom shall think meet; we being ready to deliver up to our Creditors all that we have in the World, that we may be freed from the heavy Misery of Imprisonment.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Upon the Petition of William Paterson Esquire;

The Committee having taken into Consideration the Matters of the said Petition, it appeared;

That, by the Fifteenth Article of the Treaty of Union, it is agreed, That, in the First place, out of the aforesaid Sum, what Consideration shall be found necessary to be had for any Losses which private Persons may sustain by reducing the Coin of Scotland to the Standard and Value of the Coin of England, may be made good: In the next place, That the capital Stock, or Fund, of th and

Indian Company of Scotland, advanced, together with the Interest for the said capital Stock, after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, from the respective Times of the Payment thereof shall be paid; upon Payment of which capital Stock and Interest, it is agreed the said Company be dissolved, and cease: And also, That, from the time of passing the said Act of Parliament in England, for raising the said Sum of 398,085/. 10s. the said Company shall neither trade, nor grant Licence to trade; providing, That if the said Stock and Interest shall not be paid in Twelve months after the Commencement of the Union, that then the said Company may from thenceforward trade, or give Licence to trade, until the said whole capital Stock, and Interest, shall be pud.

That, soon after passing the Treaty of Union by the Parliaments of both Kingdoms, the Parliament of Scotland, by an Act, intituled. Act concerning the Payment of the Sums out of the Equivalent to the African Company, did, among other Things, limit and restrict the Payment of such Interest of 51, per Centum per Annum to the 1 ft Day of May 1707 then next following; and the whole Sums of Principal and Interest to be paid to the Creditors and Proprietors of the Joint-Stock of the said Company, to the gross Sum of 232,884 /. 5 s. o^d. only; appointing the Directors of the said Company, or any Five of them, with their Secretary, to; stato the Account of such Debts and Stock advanced of the said Company j butfo as, in the Whole, not to exceed the said grofe Sum of 232,884/. 5 s. 0\d. on or before the said First Day of May, on Pain of Letters of Homing; in which Proceedings, the Petitioner’s Claim and Demand upon the said Company was omitted.

That by the before-mentioned Report, and Extracts out of the Register-Books of the said Company, and Depositions of Mr. Roderick Mackenzie, their late Secretary, it particularly appears;

That in regard the Petitioner, and others concerned with him, had been at great Pains and Expence in making several considerable Discoveries of Trade, and Improvements in and to both Indies-, and like wife, in procuring ‘ needful Powers and Privileges for a Company of Commerce from several sovereign Princes and States; and for which, he and they had contrived, suited, and designed, the said Company; in Consideration whereof, by the Preamble, or Conditions of Subscriptions, bearing Date at London, the 6th Day of November 1695, it was agreed That the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, or Assigns, should, out of the First Payment, have and receive Two per Cent, of the Money to be subscribed to the capital Stock of the said Company; which was to con-lift of 600,000l. Sterling; as also 3 per Cent, of the Issues, Profits, and Product, of the said Fund, for the Space of Twenty-one Years; which was to be redeemable for 2 per Cent, more of the said capital Fund any time in Five Years:

That, afterwards, it was principally by the Petitioner’s Interest that the Sum of 300,000l. was first, in the said Month of November 169.5, subscribed to the capital Stock of the said Company at London; and that One Fourth-part thereof was at the Time of Subscription paid, either in Money, Bank-Notes, or Notes payable on Demand to the Company’s Order and Use:

That, after the Proceedings in Parliament against the Subscriptions taken at London, the Petitioner was prevailed upon to leave his Effects and Business in London, then very considerable, and to goto Scotland; where, by his Countenance and Influence, the Subscriptions to the feud capital Stock of 600,000/ was completed on or before the First Day of August 1696:

That, the Sums subscribed in London, and those in Scotland, were always understood and reputed to be Parts of the same Joint-Stock, and subjefit to the same Rules and Conditions:

That, after the Subscriptions in Scotland were completed, the Petitioner did not only continue very much to support and promote the Company’s Affairs at home; hut was further prevailed upon to go to Holland and Hamburgh, to negotiate the Transferring of such Subscriptions, as, by reason of the before mentioned Opposition, were relinquished:

That the Petitioner was still further prevailed upon to embark in the said Company’s Expedition to Darien; where, by his Condufit and Credit, he contributed much to the Support of that Colony whilst it subsisted:

That at his Return, he gave aparticular Journal, or Report, of his Negotiations and Traniafilions there: That the Petitioner hath often expressed his Concern for foe Lolfes and Misfortunes of foe said Company, and was very instrumental in having them made good out of the Equivalent-money, as stipulated in the 15th Article of foe Treaty of Union.

That he, foe said Mackenzie, had Occasion to be lo thoroughly versed in all the Transafctions relating to that Company, as having been foie Secretary thereto, both in England and Scotland, from the Time of its Institution, in the Year 1695, to its Dissolution, by the Union, in the Year 1707; that he dares confidently aver, it will always be found, upon the ftriQeft Examination that can be made, that, as the Petitioner had no Equivalent, or valuable Consideration, given him before, or at the Time of making such Release; so it was originally, according to his Apprehension, and the best Information he ever had, only a Contrivance towards defeating foe said invidious Calumny, as aforesaid.

A PETITION of the poor insolvent Debtors confined in the Prison at Anger, in the County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That whereas the Number of poor insolvent Debtors daily increasing, even to a prodigious Number, some of which is of long Standing, and in a very perishing and miserable Condition, in the said Prison: And whereas the Misfortunes of those who are not Traders, and others who owe but small Sums, are greater than those of large Extent, inasmuch as the Act concerning Bankrupts do, at once, on surrendering what they have, or are possessed of, free them from Confinement; but, on the other hand, those to whom the said Act do not extend itself, and others who owe smaller Sums, are wholly left to perish in Confinement: And praying your Honours to grant us Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the poor distressed Prisoners for Debt in the Prison of Gloucester, for the County of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the poor Petitioners, by reason of great Losses and Misfortunes in Trading, and by Fire, Lois of Cattle, bad Debts, and by Water, are become uncapable of paying their respective Creditors their full Demauds... the one Moiety thereof; by reason our Creditors have run us up to such a great and large Expence of Law-Proceedings; but the Petitioners, under their deplorable Condition, are ready and willing to make our Creditors our utmost Satisfaction, by delivering up our Substance and Effects, without Fraud or Concealment, so as we may be discharged of our Imprisonment, and to be at Liberty to exercise our respective Trades, for the Maintenance of ourselves, Wives, and Families: And praying your Honours will be pleased to take into your tender Considerations our submissive Suit and Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

By the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain and Ireland, 8cc.

THG Honourable House of Commons having, on /he 2lit of this Month, upon a Petition of the Sea-Chaplains, praying an Explanation of the Clause, granted the last Sessions of Parliament, for appropriating 3,000l. for their better Support, voted an humble Address to his Majesty, That he would be pleased to give Directions to us, to lay before them an Account how the said 3,000l. hath been distributed; We do, in Obedience to his Majesty’s Commands, hereby humbly represent, That, upon the directing the said Sum, we caused a List of the Names of all the Sea-Chaplains to be prepared, in order to the coming to as clear a Light as ’twas possible, which of them out of Employment had a Right to partake of the aforesaid 3,000l.; Which Lifts we having taken into our Consideration, and several Particulars occurring to us, upon debating this Matter, which we judged necessary to be explained by the House of Commons, before we gave any final Directions for the Distribution of the said Sum of Money among the Chaplains; we do humbly lay the following Queries before the House: And pray, That we may receive their Pleasure thereupon; viz.

ift. Whether, by these Words, " equally divided," in the Vote of the House, it is meant, That such Chaplains, who have served but a very little while, should have equal L Shares with those who have been many Years in the Service

2d. Whether all the Chaplains who shall appear to have a Right to Part of the aforesaid 3,000l. and have served in small or great Ships, shall be upon the same Foot ? Or whether they shall have a Proportion according to the Rates of the Ships wherein they have served

3d. Whether Curacies or Lectureships, from which they are liable to be removed* shall be deemed a Provision for any of them

4th. Whether the being unprovided for, when the House of Commons were pleased to vote the 3,000l. for their Support, or at any determined Day, shall entitle them to a Share of the said Money

5th. What Proof shall be required of the Value of their Livings? Or whnt Value of such Livings shall qualify or difoualify them, as to a share of the aforesaid 3,000l.?

6th. Whether the Widows of such deceased Chaplains who were entitled to part of the said Sum, when voted by the House, shall have the same Share thereof as their Husbands would have had if they were living

Admiralty-Office, Orford. Byng.

34th May 1715. Geo. Dodington. J. Jennings.

Ordered, That the said Estimate and Report do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

A Petition of the President, Treasurer, and Governors, Blackwell-of Christ’s Hospital, London, for and on behalf of the hall Woolla poor Children harboured in the said Hospital, was pre- Market* fented to the House, and read; letting forth, That Black-well-hall in London, is the Place that, for very many Years, hath been uied for a Common publick Market for Sale of English Cloth, brought to London for Sale; and has been set apart for this purpose; and, before the Fire of London, was very commodious for it; and since then,

the same has, at great Charge, been rebuilt, and new Ad-dititions made, to render it still more convenient for these Purposes; which it accordingly is: That, by Act of Parliament, in the 39th of Queen Elizabeth, Northern Cloths of all Kinds, brought to London for Sale, are to be brought to the said Market in Blackwell-hall; and, upon Application by the Clothiers of divers other Counties, an Act was obtained, in the 9th Year of his late Majesty,

King William, intituled, An Act to reliore the Market of Blackwell-hall to the Clothiers; and for regulating the Factors there; whereby it is enacted, That the Petitioners, Governors of the said Hall, and their Deputies,

shall set forth and appoint to the Clothiers of all Counties, that shall bring up Cloths to fell at the said publick Market, the most convenient Room in the said Hall, for the Sale of their Cloth; and likewise Warehouse-Room for the lodging and safe-keeping any Cloth of the said Clothiers, unfold; the Clothiers, or their Servants, paying unto the Hall-keepers the ancient Duties of the said Hall, and no more; and the Hall-keepers, Clerks, and Master-Porters, of the said Hall, are to keep their Books, and Weekly Register, of all the Cloths bought and sold in the said Market; in which they shall truly enter the Names, and Places of Habitation, of the Owner, Buyer, and Seller, of the said Cloths, together with the Time of the Sale thereof; and likewise of the FaCkor, or any other Person other than the Owner, buying or selling the fame; to the end Clothiers, and others, may be satisfied how their Cloths are fold and disposed of; without Fee or Reward:

And they are subjected to a Penalty of 101 for every Offence against the said Act; And that no Factor, or Person or Persons whatsoever, other than the Owner of the Cloth,

shall fell, cause to be sold, or expose to Sale, out of the said Market, any Cloth consigned, or directed, by the Owner thereof, to be brought to the said Market, or to any Factor there, to be sold, under the Penalty of 5/. for every Cloth so fold: That the keeping up the said Market for the Purposes aforesaid, tends greatly to the Encouragement of the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom; and is for the Benefit and Advantage of the Clothiers;

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, fend other Inhabitants, of the Borough and Parish of Barnstaple, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners labour under great Difficulties, by reason of the vast Quantities of Wool and Yarn being continually carried to France, and other foreign Parts, from this Kingdom, and more especially ' from Ireland; where several Ships of Wool, bound to

France, have of late been seized; and where the clandestine Runner saves the Duty, which is at least Twenty per Cent. which the fair Exporter for is obliged

to pay; by means whereof, the Woollen Manufacture of this Nation in general, and of this Town, and Country adjoining, in a more particular Manner, suffer under the greatest Hardships, and is in Danger of being loft; the many Thousands of poor Families, who were subsisted by their Labour in that Manufacture alone, must fall a grievous Charge to the Parishes where they dwell; and we; to our Grief, must lee the Subjects of the French King growing rich by our Ruin; and foreign Markets, formerly supplied from England with our Manufactures, are now supplied from France: And praying this honourable House, That such speedy and effectual Mefefures may be taken for our Relief

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are to consider the Laws in being for preventing the Exporting of Wodl from Great Britain and Ireland; and how the same may be made more effectual.

A Petition of the Mai tilers within the Borough of,

in the County of Derby, and Places adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That within the said Borough, and Places adjacent, there anciently hath been, and now is, a very great Trade of Malting; and that the Barley, with which the Maltsters theer are supplied to make Malt of, is very bold and good; and the Petitioners, and their Predecessors, have conilantly used to deep their Barley in the Ciftem much longer time than the Maltsters in other Places usually do; by reason whereof, and of the Goodnels of the Barley, it swells as much, or more, in the Cistern, as in most other Places it doth in the Couch: That, by reason the King's Officers may take as many Gauges as they please, the Petitioners are forced to let it lie, in a regular Form, in the Couch, 30 Hours; which is not only, in itself, very prejudicial to the Malt, but-also the Officers, in taking their Couch-Gauges, cannot avoid treading upon Part of it; which, being bruised, corrupts the red that it is mixed with, and proves prejudicial to the Petitioners: And praying your Honours to consider their Cafe, and give Leave, That a Clause may be added to the Bill, now before you, for continuing the Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, for the Service of the Year 1715, That the Gauge of the Petitioners Malt may be confined to the Gauge of the Cidem only.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the Petitioners Counsel objected to 61 of the Sitting Members Voters; viz.36 as disqualified Freemen;

That, on the Head of disqualified Freemen, the Petitioners Counsel alleged, There are Two Courts held in this Town; One called the General Common Day, the other the Private, or Summoned, Common Day:

That the General Common Day is held Five times a Year, on particular Days appointed by the Charter, when the Corporation auemble without Summons; and the Private, or Summoned, Common Day, is held as often as the Mayor thinks fit; of which, they infilled, there ought to be a reasonable Summons, by One Day’s Notice at the least; and that no Freemen could be admitted but at one of these General, or Summoned, Common Days, when a Majority of the Aldermen, being Six at lealt, must be present:

7* Jan. 1633. A Summoned Common Day, when a Freeman was admitted; and the Recorder, and Nine Aldermen, are mentioned to be present:

That, between the Years 1633 and 1653,-the Petitioners Counsel produced Nine Instances; viz. Four of Admissions of Freemen at Summoned Common Days; and Five other Instances of Business done on the like Days, when Six, or a greater Number of Aldermen are mentioned to be present:

That the Stile of these several Courts is, a Summoned Common Day; without mentioning before whom held:

In 1653, the Stile of the Summoned Common Days is altered; they are then mentioned to be held before the Mayor and Bailiffs:

And between the Years 1653 and 1660, the Petitioners Counsel produced 13 Instances; viz. Five of Admissions of Freemen at Summoned Common Days so held; and Eight Instances of Business done on the like Days, when Six, or a greater Number of Aldermen are mentioned to be present.

That in 1660, the Stile of these Courts is again altered; in that Year, they are mentioned to be held before the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses: Afterwards, that Stile is altered; and the nfual Stile is, a Summoned Common Day Court, such a one Mayor:

In the Years 1660, 1661* and 1662, the Petitioners Counsel produced 14 Instances; viz. Six Summoned Common Days, Two General Common Days, when Freemen were admitted; and Six other summoned Common Days, when Business was done; and another Summoned Common Day in 1713, when a Freeman was admitted: At-all which Days, Six* or a greater Number of-Aldermen are mentioned to be present That the Petitioners Counsel offered to produce many other Instances since the Year 1662, of Admissions of Freemen, when a Majority of Aldermen appeared to be present.

That the Sitting Members Counsel admitted. That, foom the Year 1662, whenever the Aldermen present are named, they are generally Six, or more, in Number.

' That the Petitioners Counsel produced an instance, 14 April \ 653, of a Summoned Common Day, when the Entry is thus; " Nothing done at the said Day, by Defest of a competent Number of Aldermen, most of " them being out of Town."

That the Sitting Members Counsel infilled, That the 36 Freemen admitted 14th of and 1 Qth November

last, when only Five Aldermen were present, with the Mayor, were regularly admitted: That the Common Day Courts are held before the Mayor and Bailiffs, and lb foiled; and that the Aldermen are no essential Part of those Courts: That the most ancient Entries do not shew any Number of Aldermen present; nor does it appear tohat Number they had, till their Charter in 1632 appointed 12 Aldermen: That the Admission of Freemen is an Act of the Common-Council: That here is a Mayor, Four Bailiffs, and 24 of the Common-Council; and that the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses assembled, can admit Freemen, without Six Aldermen present.

They produced the following Instances in the Town-Books; viz.

In Ed. VI. Three Common Days when Freemen were

admitted; and no mention made of any Aldermen being present.

The Stile of those Courts is thus; " A Common Day " held."

id and ad Ph. and Mary,a Common Day held, when a Freeman was admitted: And,

2d and 3d Ph.and Mary, a Summoned Common Day, when Members of Parliament were chose; and Notice is not taken of any Aldermen being present:

l° Eliz. a Summoned Common Day, when Freemen

were admitted, and other Business done, prafentibus tot a communitate.

Nineteen other Instances; viz. Seven tempore Eliz. and Eleven between the Years 1636 and 1649, Summoned Common Days, when Freemen were admitted, and Leases for 2t Years, or greater Terms, granted; a general Common Day held in 1683, when a Freeman was admitted: In all which Instances, no Notice is taken whether any Aldermen were present.

In the Stile of these Courts, the Mayor is but twice named; the rest are foiled Summoned Common Days, without mentioning either Mayor, or Bailiffs.

Two-and-twenty other Summoned Common Days held; viz.

Seventeen between the said Years. 1636 and 1649; at Three of which Days Freemen were admitted, and Leases for 21 Years granted, wh'eft ohly Five Aldermen are named to be present:

At Four other of the said Days Officers were elected, and other Business done, when the like Number of Five Aldermen are named to be present:

At Five other of the said Days, Freemen were admitted, and Leases for 21 Years granted, when only Four Aldermen are named to be present:

At another of the said Days a Mayor and Aldermen were defied; and, at another, a Treasurer defied; and the like Number of Four Aldermen named to be present:

At Three other of the said Days Freemen were admitted, when only Two Persons are named to be present

5 Mar. 1640, a Summoned Common Day, when Members of Parliament were chose, the greatest Part of the Burgesses of the Town being present; and no Notice is taken, whether any Aldermen w ere then present, or not

4 September 1643, Present, Mayor, Recorder, and Five Aldermen; and the Entry is, That nothing was done this Day for want of a Bailiff, One Bailiff only being present; upon which, the Day was adjourned.

1 & September 1678, a Summoned Common Day bfeld,

when a Freeman was sworn, and only Five Aldermen named to be present.

28 July 1691, a Summoned Common Day, in Mr.

Extent, Mayoralty, wheh Three Freemen were admitted, and other Business done, and only Five Aldermen named to be present: This is the Court where the Petitioners Counsel taken Notice of a Rasure among the Aldermens Names.

10 December 1695, a Summoned Common Day, w hen

a Freeman was admitted, and but Five Aldermen named to be present.

The Stile of these last mentioned 22 Common Days, heldfmce 1636, are thus; viz.

Five are foiled; Summoned Common Days, held coram majore et balivis; the rest, Summoned Common Days, such a one Mayor.

That the Sitting Members Counsel produced the old Book of Orders, established 16 March 1626; One of which is, that no Mayor shall, at any time hereafter, propound any thing to the House, unless he do first acquaint the Aldermen then present with his Purpose; and that the most Part of the Aldermen present do give theit Assent to the same:

This, they said; was the First time any Aldermen became necessary; but the Number is not named.

And they produced the new Book of Orders and Constitutions, established 20th April 1686; by which all Or*? ders contained in the former Book of Orders are made void, and new Orders established: One of which new Orders is, That the Mayor shall not propound any thing at a private Common Day, unless Five Aldermen be there then present, and all consenting: And

Another, That, from thenceforth, no Lease should be granted for longer than 21 Years, without the Consent of Six Aldermen, present at One of the General Common Days; under a Penalty upon the Mayor.

That the Sitting Members Counsel inferred from these Constitutions in 1686, That no certain Number of Aldermen were necessary before that time.

As to Notice of the Two Courts held in October and November last; they called,

Richard Excin, John JVish, and William Gunbay, Serjeants at Mace: Who said, They furamoned the Common Days of 14th October and 10th November last by Order of the Mayor: That the same Notice was given 01 those Courts as had been of all Courts in their Time; which was about Seven Years; and that they never knew Notice given but on the same Day the Courts w ere held; or any Court objected to for want of a legal Summons.

John Wardall said, He had been of the Common-

Council 27 Years, of the Corporation 40 Years, and had known the Town 79 Years: That, in all his time, the Common Days were summoned on the same Day they were held; he never knew any other Summons; or ever heard any body object to a Court so summoned for want of due Notice: And said. He did not know he had in his Life miffed uptimes attending the Courts.

Mr. Hampden, according to Order, reported, from the Westbory Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it Election. appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Westbury, in the County of Wilts, and the Refolt^ions

of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the Report, and Refelutions, were read; and arc as foHow-, viz.

Upon the Petition of George Evans, now Lord Carbery of the Kingdom of Ireland, and Charles Allanfon Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of the honourable Willoughby Bertie and Francis Annesley, Esquires, for the Borough of West bury, in the County of Wilts:

That it was agreed, That Westbu is a Borough by Prescription; and that only Burgage-Tenants have a Right to vote.

That the Petitioners Counsel infilled, They must be such Tenants only as hold in Fee for Life, or 99 Years determinable on Lives, or by Copy of Court-Roll, and pay an annual Rent of Four Pence, or Two Pence, to the Ix>rd; from which Rent they are called whole or half Burgages.

The Sitting Members Counsel infilled, That Tenants for Terms ablblnte, and Quarter-Burgages; viz. such a? pay a Peny Rent to the Lord; have also a Right to vote.

That the Petitioners Counsel called,

Zach. Bayly: Who said, He had known the Town 16 Years: Thatthofe who have an Estate of Inheritance, or for One, Two, or Three Lives, or 99 Years, determinable on Lives, or such a long Term as ordinarily extends to a Man’s Life, and who pay a whole or half Burgage-Rent, have a Right to vote: That he had known Two controverted Elections, when the Quarter-Burgages were refilled: That they were always refilled in his time: and he had heard, They were always refused before; but he could not say, whether the Quarter-Burgages had a Right, or not:

That the Leases for Terms were always for 99 Years determinable on Lives; and that he never heard of any Lease in the Borough for 99 Years absolute, or for any absolute Term, till, of late, the Leases have been short-ened, to make Votes.

Thomas Hayward said, He had known the Borough 25 Years, and had been at Five or Six Elections within these Ten Years; that the Quarter-Burgages were then allowed to vote, if they pleased Mr. Gibbs, and not else; but it was always looked upon, that they had no Right; and that only whole and half Burgages had a Right of Voting.

That the Petitioners Counsel produced the Town Book, wherein there is a Declaration entered, under the Hands and Seals of the Mayor and Burgesses, assembled at a General Council, held the 5th of January 1685,

That, by a Custom there, Time out of mind, the Right of Voting for this Borough is in Persons having, in any Messuage, or Messuages, within the Borough, out of which a yearly Rent of One, Two, or Four, Pence, or more, called Burgage-money, is issuing, any Estate in Fee, Fee-Tail, or for One, Two, or more Lives, or for any Number of Years determinable on One, Two, or more, Lives, or for any long Term of Years; and in no others.

Westbory It appears by the Book, That, in that Part of this De-Ele&iou. deration, which specifies the Rent, the Words " One, " To, or," are wrote upon a Rasure; and the Spelling differs from the rest of the Entry.

Mr. James Edgill said, That he was Steward of the Borough w'hen this Declaration was made: That it is all his Hand-writing, except the Alteration where the Rasure is; which is done since the making the Declaration;

That they keep the Books of Entries of the Burgage-Tenures; and that he has searched those Books down from the Time of Philip and and finds no mention of any Quarter-Burgage till the Year 1671:

That the Right of voting is in such as have a Freehold, or an Estate for Life, or a Term of 99 Years, or ,80 Years, or such a Term as ordinarily extends to a Man’s Life, determinable on Life, or Lives, out of which a Burgage Rent issues of Four Pence, or Two Pence, yearly:

That the Peny-Burgages have been objected to; but he never knew them rejected in his time; which is from 1684; nor did he know of any Leaies for Years absolute in the Borough:

Being cross-examined, he owned, That he polled the Peny-Burgages when he was Mayor; but first allied them, Who they would be for; and said, He did not remember, that he gave any Evidence for Terms of Years absolute, when he was a Witness in the controverted Election in 1702.

That, to prove that Quarter-Burgages, and Lease-holders for Years absolute, have a Right to vote, the Sitting-Members Counsel called,

Samuel Gibbs: Who said, He had known the Borough Sixty-four Years: That he was taken into Custody for refusing the Quarter-Burgages in his Mayoralty, about 37 or 38 Years ago; and ever since that time those Burgages have voted: That Tenants for Years also voted in that Election; but he could not say what Terms they held under.

Bayamin Bourn said, He has lived at Westbury Sixty Years; and that all Persons living within the Borough, whether Whole, Half, or Quarter, Burgages, or Tenants for Years, or Copyholders for Life, had voted in all his time; and that, 30 Years ago, William who was

reported to have only a Lease for 21 Years absolute, w as allowed to vote in a controverted Election.

That the Sitting-Members Counsel produced the Journals of the House of Commons, in the following controverted Elections; viz*

lft December 1702. When the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Owners of Burgage Houses; no Dif-tin&ion was then taken of Quarter-Burgages: The Objection was only to Leaseholders for Years absolute: And James Edgill and others gave Evidence, That Tenants for Years absolute were always reputed to have a Right; and gave an Instance of one Browne voting under aLeafo for 99 Years absolute: And the House then adjudged, That Leaseholders for Years absolute had a Right to vote.

26* November 1680. Samuel Gibbs, the Mayor, was sent for in Custody of the Serjeant at Arms, to answer, at the Bar of the House, for great Misdemeanors by him committed in that Election and Return.

William Cockle and Benjamin Bourne were called: And confronting each other, touching Cockle's voting;

Thomas Hodges and Thomas Potter said, That the House Richard Wheeler lives in is Two distinct Tenements, held by Two Tenants at different Rents, under Leases from different Lords: It was formerly Two Tenements, and both Tenants voted, till it was laid into an Inn, and held by one Tenant for some time; after which, it was, Twelve Years ago, divided again into Two Tenements, as it had been before; and both Tenants have since voted, and both have a Right to vote;

Thomas Waller,.on the other Side, said. He has lived

A Petition of the Clothiers of Bradford, in the County of Wilts, on the behalf of themselves, and several Thousands of People employed by them in the Woollen Manufacture, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That whereas an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for regulating improving, and encouraging, the Woollen Manufacture of mixed or medley Broad Cloth; and for the better Payment of the Poor employed therein; hath been complained of by the Dealers and Buyers of mixed or medley Broad-Cloth; and there being a Bill now depending in this honourable House, for making the said Act more effectual, for the Benefit of Trade in general: And praying. That the Measure of mixed or medley Broad-Cloth may be duly adjusted at Blackwell-hall, by the Keeper thereof, or by some other indifferent Person, that have no Dependence on the Buyers; or otherwise, as to your Honours Wisdom shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to make the Act, of the Tenth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for Regulating, Improving, and Encouraging, of the Woollen Manufacture of mixed or medley Broad-Cloth; and for the better Payment of the Poor employed therein; more effectual, for the Benefit of Trade in general j is committed.

Resolved, That the Bill do pals: And that the Title be, An Act for charging and continuing the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fifteen; and for making forth Duplicates of Exchequer- Bills, and Lottery-Tickets, loft, burnt, or destroyed; and for enlarging the Time for adjusting Claims in several Lotteries; and for making forth new Orders, in lieu of certain Lottery-Orders obliterated or defective; and for continuing certain Duties on Hops until the First Day of August One thousand Seven hundred and Fifteen.

An ingrossed Bill for making perpetual the Act, of the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of King William the Third, intituled, An Act, That the solemn Affirmation and Declaration of the People called Quakers shall be accepted, instead of an Oath in the usual Form, was read the Third time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for making perpetual the Act, of the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act, That the solemn Affirmation and Declaration of the People called Quakers shall be accepted, instead of an Oath in the usual Form; and for explaining and enforcing the said Act, in relation to the Payment of Tythes, and Church-Rates; and for appointing the Form of an . Affirmation to be taken by the said People called Quakers, instead of the Oath of Abjuration.

Ordered, That Mr. Hampden do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

and other foreign Parts, from this Kingdom, and Ireland, where several Vessels laden with Wool, bound to France, have of late been seized; and the clandestine Runner laves the Duty, which is at Jeaft Twenty per Cent.; which ,the fair Exporter for Rngfand is obliged to pay; so that the Woollen Manufacture of this Nation, in general, suffers under great Hardships, and is in Danger of being loft: And praying. That speedy and effectual Measures may be taken for our Relief.

A Petition of several Merchants, Importers of Tobacco and Wine, in behalf of themselves, and several others concerned in Bonds given for Part of the Duties on the fame, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That, the Importation of Commodities, Part of the Duties are generally bonded; the Goods are exported; and the Importers arc thereby intitled to the Customs, to be repaid them by Debenture, in order to discharge the Bonds; but they are from Four Months to Six Months before the Debentures pass the proper Offices; and the Crown allows no Interest for the fame; and the Bonds Handing out againfr the Petitioners, where the greatest Part of the Principal is discharged, are against Peiibns which have been Security for others, that, by Mis for-. tunes, are become dead, or insolvent: And the Wine-Merchants are the chief Exporters of Corn, for which they are intitled to a Bounty by Debenture; many of their Bonds w’ere paid by Certificates and Debentures, on which the Crown allowed no Interest, though they were as long due as the Bonds they discharged; and the Petitioners applied to Parliament, for the Discharge of those Bonds, in 1703; and a Bill passed the House of Commons for the fame; but was rejected by the Lords: And praying, That a Bill may be brought in to relieve them in the Premises.

Mr. Hampden, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Elections for the Borough of Horsham, in the County of Suffer, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report, and Resolutions, were read; and are as follow: viz.

Upon the Petition of the honourable Arthur Ingram and Arthur Ingram, Esquires, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir Harry Goring Barouet, and Charles Eversfeild Esquire, for the Borough of Horsham, in the County of Suffer:

That it was agreed, That Horsham is a Borough by Prescription; and that only Burgage-Tenants in Fee, or for Life, have a Right of voting:

But the Sitting Members Counsel insisted, It was e'flen-tially necessary they should be presented by the Homage-Jury: Which was denied by the Petitioners Counsel.

Jo. Wicker senior, Esquire, said, He was Bailiff 35 Years ago: That all Burgage-Tenants had a Right to be of the Homage; and none were ever refused till within these Six or Seven Years, during which time, one of the Sitting Members, has been Foreman of the Jury (who present), and the other has been Steward of the Borough (who admits), the Burgage-Tenants; and they have altered the ancient Usage of presenting and admitting all Burgage-Tenants, and taken such as would be for them, though they had no Right, and refused others who were against them, though they had a Right:

Being croft-examined, he said, That, at all Elections, the Voters were called over by the Burgage-Roll, and none others were, or could be, polled; because, till of late Years, none who had a Right were ever refused to be presented by the Homage:

Horsham

Election.

But he conceived all BurgagC-Tenants in Fee, or far Life, had a Right of voting, whether admitted by the Steward, or not; and gave an instance of a Pferlbn allowed to vote in the last Election but one, who had been refused by the Homage: And said, The Two Bailiffs of the Borough are appointed by the Steward, out of Four Persons nominated by the Homage.

That the Sitting Members Counsel called,

Mr. Thomas ryke, Mr. Nat. Sturt, Thomas White Esquire, Nat. Tredcroft Efauire, and Mr. John Warden-: Who spoke for 25 and 30 Years, and upwards; and said. That only Burgage-Tenants in Fee, or for life, had a Right to vote; and that it had always been usual, just before Elections, to summon all Burgage-Tenant6 to a Court-Baron, where the Homage present all new Titles; and they never knew any refused to be of the Homage who had a Right, except in some few Instances of late, when a great Number have appeared: That, at all Elections, the Voters were called over by the Burgage-Roll; and none others ever voted, or pretended to vote, except m a tingle instance or Two, to the contrary;

They thought a Presentment by the Homage was necessary, and, without it, a Person had no Right to vote; ‘ but they never knew this point contested: They-gave Instances of Candidates at several Elections, who were of this Opinion; and that this was the Opinion alto of a former Steward, who was an ancient Man.

That the Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election of Members to servein Parliament for the Borough of Horsham in the County of Suffer, is in all such Persons as have an Estate of Inheritance, or for Life, in Burgago-Houses, or Burgage-Lands, lying within the said Borough:

The Hoafe being moved, That the Account of what Proposals have been made, in relation to the Coinage of Farthings and Halfpence, which was ordered to lie upon the Table, might be read:

It was read accordingly; and is as follows;

An Account of what Propofols have been made, in relation to the Coinage of Farthings and Halfpence, and what has been done thereupon, from the Beginning of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Ann, to the Date hereof; that is to say,

Anno 1703, Abel Slaney, Citizen and Woollen-draper, of London, as principal Undertaker for the coining Halfpence and Farthings in the Reign, of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary; alleging, That he was a v.er^ great Sufferer in the Changing of Tin Halfpence and Farthings for Copper, by Tale; proposed to coin 700 Tons of Copper Halfpence and Farthings in Seven Years, of equal Value, Weight, and Fineness, of the last Halfpence and Farthings, to be melted, rolled, cut, and stamped, at her late Majesty’s Mint in the Tower, subject to a Comptroller to be appointed by her laid late Majesty, and at the Undertaker’s Expence:

In Consideration of such Grant, the said Slaney, for himself and Partners, proposed to give her late Majesty a Fine of 5,000l. and a Rent of 1,000l. per Annum, by Half-yearly Payments; and to be under such Restrictions and Regulations as her laid late Majesty should think reasonable:

Thomas Renda Esquire, E and Daniel

Barton, who were before Partners with the said Slaney in coining the former Halfpence and Farthings, understanding that the said Slaney designed to intitle a new Set of Partners to the Merit of another’s Patent, upon the Terms by him proppied* did petition, That, if her Majesty thought fit to grant a new Patent for making Copper Halfpence and Farthings, Strangers might not reap the Benefit of the Expences they had been at in performing the former Patent, which, they pretended, was done to their Lois; but that they might have some new Patent, paying for the same what was proposed by others.

Anno 1704, William Shepard, Shepard, and George

Freeman, did, in March 1704, petition to have a Patent to impower them to coin Forty or Fifty Tons every Year, for Eight or Ten Years; obliging themselves to make them of English Copper, of equal Weight and Fineness with those then current.

The Fellow-moneyers being poor and needy, and having no Work in the Mint, did, about the same time, petition to the same Effect, That out of the Profits of such Coinage, they might sustain themselves until the Mint was set to Work about Gold and Silver Monies.

Soon after the Union, Sir Talbot Clerke and Partners did represent, That having, in the Year 1686, obtained Letters-Patents for 14 Years, to put in Practice a new Invention of Furnaces for melting and refining Metals out of Ores j and that, by their Care and Expence, great Advantage had accrued to the Nation; hut that, by reason of great Difficulties they met wkb in the Management, and the Time being expired, they had not made the hoped Advantage; they, therefore, did petition, That, in lbrae Recompence for their Charges and Expences, they might fend in Two Tons of Copper Blanks per Week into the Mint, until they had-disposed of 700 Tons.

Mr. Chambers, hearing of this Propofol of Sir Talbot Clerke, represented, That he, and divers other Persons, had purchased, at a very dear Rate, of the said Sir Talbot Clerke, and others concerned with him, their Interest in

the said Patent; and were afterwards incorporated by their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, under the Name of the Governors and Company of Copper-Mines in England; and that, having very much improved the Copper-works, and, at the Charge of above 20,000l. having obtained the knowledge of making Copper fine; and having greater Stock in his Hands than could be disposed of; did propose to fend 100 Tons of Copper into the Mint* at the Rate of Twelve Pence per Pound, to be there coined into Halfpence and Farthings, at such Value as should be directed; so that the Charges of coining the lame, and other Incidents, might be borne out of the Surplus; and that he.might have Twelve Pence per Pound, to be paid him as salt, as the Copper-money should be disposed of

Anno 1708, William Morgan Gentleman, and others, did petition for a Grant for the coining 1,000 Tons of English Copper; one Half into Halfpence, and the other Half into Farthings and Halffarthings; within the Term of Seven Years, to be of Weight and Finenels according to a Standard to be agreed to; which Standard was to be at least 20/. per Cent, finer and better Copper than the 700 Tons formerly coined; and was to be melted, assayad, rolled, and cut and stamped, at the Mint in the Tou er; subject to a Comptroller to be appointed by her late Majesty, and at the Expence of the Undertaker:

By this Proposal, all the Copper Halfpence and Far* things formerly coined were to be taken and exchanged by the Proposer, in Tale, for those of the new Stamp, and so melted down.

1710, Mr. William Palmes did petition, That, towards a Recompence for the Losses he had sustained, he might have a Patent for the Coining of 700 Tons of Copper in 14 Years; subjefit to such Agreement, Limitations, and Covenants, as were made in the Patent granted for tho coining the former 700 Tons.

The several Reports, which were made by the Officers of the Mint, upon the aforegoing Petitions and Proposals, were to the Effect following; viz.

That, since the Year 1672, in the Reign of King the Second, and in the Beginning of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, all the Coinage of Farthings and Halfpence before the last Con-tra6l, were performed by Commissioners, who had Money imprested from the Exchequer to buy Copper and Tin; and coined the fame, at most, into Pound Weight

avoirdupois, the Copper being Swedish; and accounted, upon Oath, to the Government for the Charges and Produce thereof by Tale:

That, upon Complaints made against the Tin Halfpence and Farthings, Sir Joseph Hern, and others, contracted to change the fame; and, to enable them to bear that Charge, were allowed, by Patent, to coin 700 Tons of English Copper into Halfpence and Farthings at 21 per Pound Weight; with a Remedy of an Halfpeny, without being accountable to the Government for the Tale; which English Copper was cheaper than the Swedish: And, the Reason of this Allowance being ceasedK the said Patent ought not to be drawn into Precedent for coining the Money so much lighter than the intrinsick Value, and without Account; especially since the Money coined thereby were lighter, and of worse Copper, than by Agreement, and badly coined:

That it was belt to coin the Copper-money as near as could be to the intrinsick Value, including the Charges of Coinage, set Allowances, and Incidents, and reckoning the Copper at what it would fell for, if the new Money should be melted down again; for which Reason, it ought to be free from such Mixtures as would diminish -the Market-price; and that, whatever Profit should arise by the Coinage, the Crown might have it in its Power to gratify whom it please therewith; and therefore the for* mer Method, by Commissioners, and upon Account,' seemed the more lafe, commendable, and advantageous to the Government; especially if the Method used in th£ Coinage of Gold and Silver be observed, as nearly as con* ve nently can be, in the Coinage of Copper; for thaj
