A Petition of the Merchants of Whitehaven, trading in Tobacco, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That several of the Duties arising by the Importation. of Tobacco were, till of late, payable- at Three Months, Nine Months, and Eighteen Months, and secured by several Bonds; and the Payment of Interest upon those bonded Duties, accruing before the Expiration of the Eighteen Months, was a great Hardship upon the Merchant; and, by an Act of the Twelfth of her late Majesty, for encouraging the Tobacco-Trade, the Payment of the said several Duties is prejudicial to Trade, and a Lois to the Revenue, and are therefore all reduced to One Payment at the End of Eighteen Months; and consequently all Demands of Interest, before the End of Eighteen Months, are now cut off, after the Commencement, and during the Continuance, of that Act; and there is no Provision made in the said Act for discharging the Interest, before the said Eighteen Months, arising upon the Bonds made before the Act: and several of those Bonds being lately put in Suit against the Petitioners, notwithstanding the y have duly paid off all the Principal Money due thereon, upon the Expiration of the said Eighteen Months: And praying to be relieved in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Merchants, Importers of Tobacco and Wine, - in behalf of themselves, and several others concerned in Bonds given for Payment of the Duties on the fame, is referred.

Weobly The House proceeded, according to Order, to bear the Ekdion. Merits of the Election for the Borough of Weobly, in the County of Hertford:

And the Counsel on both Sides were called in:

And the Petition of Mr. Serjeant and also the

Petition of Simon Gough and John Moor, on behalf of themselves, and others the Electors, Burgesses of the said Borough of Weobly, complaining of the said Election and Return, were read:

And the Counsel for the Petitioner, Mr. Serjeant Birch, examined several Witnesses to disqualify several of the Voters for the Sitting Member, Mr. Foley, on account of Bribery; and femmed up their Evidence.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Member, Mr. Foley, proceeded, and called Mr. to give Evidence

touching what one William had confessed of Money offered him to vote for the Petitioner Mr. Serjeant Birch:

And the Petitioners Counsel objecting against the said Mr. Cooke's being examined touching the fame; for that he, the said William Bayly, was, by the said Petitioner’s Evidence, charged with having received Five Guineas to vote for the Sitting Member:

Touching which Matters, the Counsel on both Sides were heard.

And then they withdrew.

And the Question being put, That the Sitting Member’s Counsel be admitted to examine Mr. George Cooke as to any Discourse he had with William Bayly, in relation to Money offered to the said Bayly by the Petitioner;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Counsel were called in again; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them therewith.

Upon which, the Sitting Member’s Counsel acquainted the House, That they had other Witnesses, but that they w ere in the same Circumstances; and therefore they would not trouble the House therewith: But made their Observations upon the Petitioner’s Evidence.

And then the Counsel for Mr. Serjeant Birch and Mr. Foley withdrew.

After which, the Counsel for the Petitioners, Simon Gough and John Moor, opened the Nature of the Evidence they intended to give to the House.

Touching which Matter, the Counsel on both Sides were heard.

And then they withdrew.

A PETITION of the Woolcombers, Framework-knitters, and others, concerned in the Manufacture of Hole in and near the Borough of in the County of Leicester, in behalf of themselves and many others concerned in the said Manufacture, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the said Manufacture of Kofe hath, for many Years, been carried on by Persons inhabiting in and near the Borough of to the great Advantage of this Kingdom in general; there having been more than 20,00 worth of Wool yearly combed within and near the said Borough; which, when manufactured, and made into Hose, hath been worth 100,000 I.; whereby the poor of the said Borough, and Counties adjacent, hath been employed; but the said Trade is now greatly decayed, and die Hose, when lent abroad, cannot be sold at near the Prices they have been formerly; whereby the Price of Wool, and the Work-manship thereof have been much lowered; to the great Damage of the Petitioners, Landholders, and Poor, o the County and Borough: One cause of which Decay o Trade, ana lowering the Prices of the said Manufacture the Petitioners conceive to be, the great Quantities of Wool and Yam, which are feut out of this Kingdom, and Ireland, into France, and other foreign Parts; whereby die People of those Parts are unable to carry on the said Trade; to the great Damage of the Petitioners, and this Kingdom in general: And praying, That such other Laws may be made for the more effectual preventing the Exportation of Wool, and Woollen Yarn, from this Kingdom and Ireland.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Con-> deration of the Committee, who are to consider the Iaws being for preventing the Exporting of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland; and how far the same may be made more effectual: And that Mr. Carter be added to

Sir John Ward reported from the Committee, to whom Tobacco,

the Petition of several Merchants Importers of Tobacco Ac. bonded and Wine, concerned in Bonds given for Part of the Du- I,ut, es‘ tics on the fame, the Matter, as it appeared to them upon the said Petition; and also, upon the Petition of the Merchants of Whitehaven, trading in Tobacco; and also, upon

the Petitions of Thomas Haniond, Merchant, and Dean Cock, Merchant (the Consideration of which Petitions was referred to the said Committee ;) which lie read in his Place: and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the Reports upon the several Petitions of the Merchants Importers of Tobacco and Wine, and also of the Merchants of Whitehaven, were read; and are as' follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of several Merchants Importers of Tobacco and Wine, concerned in Bonds given for.

Part of the Duties on the same:

That, the Committee having taken into Consideration the several Matters contained in the said Petition; and examined die several Merchants, and Officers of the Custom-house, in order to prove the Allegations of the said Petition;

It appeared to the Committee, That, by a Clause in an Act, of the Fourth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Arm, for continuing an additional Subsidy of Tonage and Poundage, 8$c. the Lord Treasurer, or C’ommissioners of the Treasury, upon any Representation of the Commissioners of the Customs, if they judged it reasonable, might remit the Interest due upon Bonds given for Customs upon Goods and Merchandizes imported, or to be imported, upon Payment of the principal Money for which such Bonds were given.

It appeared to the Committee, That, on the Importation of these Commodities, Part of the said Duties are generally bonded; the Goods are exported; and the Importers are thereby intitled to the Customs, to be paid them by Debenture, in order to discharge the Bonds which -they entered into for the said Duties; but they are from Four Months to Six Months, before the Debentures pals the proper Offices; and the Crown allows no Interest for the fame:

That the Bonds standing out against the Petitioners, where the greatest Part of the Principal is discharged, are, many of them against Persons which have been Security for others, that, by Misfortunes, are become dead, or insolvent:

That the Wine Merchants are the chief Exporters’of Corn; for which they are intitled to a Bounty by Debenture: Many of their Bonds were paid by Certificates and Debentures, on which the Crown allowed no Interest, though they were as long due as the Bonds they dip-charged:

That the Crown never pays any Interest for Money ’ which lietfi in their Hands j nor the Law imposeth none

Upon the Merchant, but what ariseth upon the Penalty of the Bond; which never was demanded of them till of late.

It appeared to the Committee, That the Petitioners have laboured under many Difficulties and Hardships, which they have sustained, during the late War, by the great Duties and Impositions which have been laid upon them; and, by the Misfortunes of Persons failing, the Petitioners have not only lost their Goods, but great Duties they have paid the Crown for the lame.

That the Committee then proceeded to examine several of the Merchants, to prove the great Hardships and Difficulties they labour under, by reason of these Bonds; viz.

Mr. Richard Perry said, That, in the Year 1706, his Father Micajah Perry became bound, as a collateral Se-

Mr. Richard Lind fey said, That he had paid for Customs on Wines, at the Port of London, and Out-Ports, from the Beginning of the War to the Month of June 1715, as appears by his Books, the Sum of 118,400l.:

That he has sustained great Ix>ffes, during the War, as appeared by his Account delivered in to the Committee, amounting to the Sum of 14,795 /.:

That he has discharged Part of his Bonds, by Certificates for damaged Wines, and Debentures for Corn, $c. exported, to the Value of f6,.5oo /. which were due to him from the Crown, from Six to Eight Months, and some lourteen Months, when paid in to the Receiver-General of the Customs; and if the Interest of the said Certificates and Debentures had been computed, as well as that on his Bonds, there would remain but a very finall Sum for Interest due to the Crown.

Mr. Manly produced a Copy of the Report from the Commissioners of the Customs to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, dated the 31st of May last, upon the Petition of the Merchants concerned in Tobacco and Wine Bonds, about the Interest due on them; together with an Account of the Simple Interest due on all such Bonds, of which the Principal is paid j and of such only, where neither Principal nor Securities are become insolvent: By which account it appears, that there is due, for Simple Interest on the said Bonds, 4,412/. 18#. — id.

Mr. Fern said, That if the Merchants had had Interest allowed them on their Debentures and Certificates, it would have amounted to a much greater Sum than is now demanded on their Bonds:

And also said, That the augmenting the Time for Payment of the Principal due upon Bonds, and entirely

Remitting the Interest, was the Occasion, as he conceives, of bringing in, some time since, several Sums of Money,'

Which otherwise, in all Probability, would never have been paid: And that it was his Opinion, it would be a great Encouragement to Trade, and an Advantage to the Revenue, to remit the Interest:

That Mr. Fern likewise declared, That the Merchants were often kept out of their Money for their Debentures, after they had passed through the proper Offices, for want of Money upon the proper Branches for which the Debentures belonged, and no Consideration allowed the Merchants for the lame.

Mr. Metcalf said, That, upon Orders being formerly made at the Treasury, to remit the Interest, if the Principal was paid at the time mentioned in the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury's Warrant, great Sums of Money had been brought in, as well from the Port as the Out-Ports.

It appeared to the Committee, That the Petitioners did, in the Year 1713, apply to the Parliament for the Discharge of those Bonds; and the House thought their same so just and reasonable, that a Clause in the Tobacco- Bill palfed the House for their Relief; but, the same being clogged with so many Clauses of different Natures, the said Hill was laid afide by the Lords.

Upon the Petition of the Merchants of Whitehaven trading in Tobacco:

That the Committee, having considered of the Allegations of the said Petition, do find. That several of the Duties arising by the Importation on Tobacco were, till of late, payable at Three Months, Nine Months, and Eighteen Months; and secured by several Bonds:

That the Payment of Interest upon those bonded Duties, accruing before the Expiration of the Eighteen Months, have always been attended with great Hardships upon the Merchants:

That, by the Act, made it* the 12th Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, for encouraging the Tobacco-Trade, the Payment of the said several Duties at the different Times aforesaid, is declared to be prejudicial and burthensome to Trade, and a Loss to the Revenue; and are therefore all reduced to One Payment at the End of Eighteen Months:

But there being no Provision made, in the said Act, for discharging the Interest, before the said Eighteen Months arising upon the Bonds made before that Act, several of those Bonds are now lately put in Suit agair.ft the Petitioners, notwithstanding the y have duly paid off all the Principal Money due thereon, upon the Expiration of the Eighteen Months.

Mr. Metcalf, Solicitor of the Custams, attended the Committee, and delivered an Account of what Interest is demanded from the Tobacco-Merchants of Whitehaven upon Bonds and Notes in Process. where the Principal is paid, or discharged; which amounts to the Sum of 348/. 14 s-fid.

Mr. Drew reported from the Committee, who were to consider of the Laws for preventing the Exporting of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland; and how the same may be made more effectual; and to consider of proper Methods for the Encouragement of the Woollen M^nufafiture; That they had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were once read; and are as follows; viz.

iff. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee^ That the Act of Parliament, made in the Ninth and Tenth of his late Majesty King William, intituled, An Act for the Explanation, and belter Execution, of former Afits made against Transportation of Wool, Fullers-earth, and Scouring-clay, be made to extend to the Kingdom of Ireland.

ad. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Wool, Woollen Yarn, or Worsted, in Ireland, be, at any time, carried or conveyed within Miles of the Sea, unless direfilly to such Ports which are free for the exporting the same to England, under a Penalty; unless by special Licence or Permit first had from a proper Officer for carrying any Quantity of Wool to such Places where Wool is manufafitured; and which Place or Places shall be particularly mentioned in such Permits; and, in such Case, sufficient Security shall be first given in treble the Value of the Goods so licensed, that the whole Quantity shall be manufafitured in those Places; and the Proof of the Manufafituring thereof shall lie on the Persons who give such Security.

3d. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Licences, or Permits, for the removing Wool, Woollen Yarn, or Worsted, in Ireland, be made returnable to the proper Officer, within Days; and that all Persons shall return such Licences or Permits within such lime, under a Penalty; and the same Method to be observed in Great Britain; and, to prevent Collusion between the Officer and Grower, or First Owner, of such Wool, that the Officer, who gitrnts the same, shall transmit a Copy thereof to the next Collector of Excise or Customs, within Days

thereafter.

4th. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Person may seize any Wool, Woollen Yam, or Worsted, carried, lodged, removed, whether shipped . any-where in Ii'eland, contrary to any the Direfilions of the said Afit, of the Ninth and Tenth of his late Majesty King William, lb to be extended as aforesaid.

5th. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, of all Seizures and Forfeitures in Ireland, Three-fourths shall be to the Person or Persons who shall seize the same, to be intitled thereto, upon Convifition of the Party; and the other Fourth shall be to the King, for the Use and Encouragement of the Linen Manufofiture in Ireland; and that, of all Seizures and Forfeitures in Britain, the Seizer shall be likewise intitled to Three-fourths, and the other Fourth to the King; and the Crown to be at the Expence of Prosecutions in both Kingdoms.

6th. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Wool, Woollen Yarn, or Worsted, be, at any time, carried or conveyed any-where in Ireland, within Miles of the Sea, in any other Package than common Linen Packs or Bags; and that no lese Quantity be contained in each than Weight, under a

Penalty; except that a Grower give full SatisfofiVion to the Officer, that he had not lb much grown; and then the Quantity to be specified in his Permit.

7th. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That, instead of the great Ships and Sloops employed in England and Ireland against the Owlers, by virtue of the Tenth and Eleventh of his late Majesty King William, a greater Number of smaller Vessels be employed in Britain and Ireland for that Purpose; which may be a more effectual Method for preventing the exporting Wool to France, and may considerably lefl'en the yearly Charge of the Publick.

8th. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the same Duty now paid by the Exporter of Wool in Ireland, be paid by the Grow er, or First Owner, of such Wool, when fold, or within Months alter Sale.

9th. Resolved\That it k the Opinion of this Committee, That whosoever shall discover any Person or Persons, who shall export any Wool, Woollen Yarn, or Worsted, to the Value of from Great Britain or Ireland, contrary to Law, so as such Person or Persons be convifited, shall have and re1* ceive, over and above all Rewards given by any Law, the further Reward of Forty Pounds, to be paid oitt of the Treasuries of Great Britain and Ireland, rc-ijiefitively.

1 oth. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Comhiittee, That, for the better Encouragement of the Woollen Manufacture, the Port of Exeter be made a free Port for the Receiving of Wool from Ireland; and to continue so in the Time of Peace only.

1 ith. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the better Encouragement of the Linen Manir-fafiture in Ireland, which may tend to the Discouragement of exporting Wool from thence to France, lo much of the Afit, of the Third and Fourth of her late Majesty Queen Anne, relating to the Exportation of Irish Linen Cloth for the Plantations, be made perpetual; and that the Irish Linen Cloth, imported into Great Britain, may be re-exported Duty-free.

12th. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That no Licence-money may be taken hereafter for exporting Wool from Ireland to England, but the common Fee to the Secretary; and that his Majesty will be pleased to order an Equivalent for the same lo the Lord Lieutenant, or the Chief Governor for the Time being, in such manner as his Majesty shall think fit.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned until fVedncfday Morning next.

And the Sitting Member’s Counsel produced a Paper, as the Rate for the Land Tax in the Year 1714, for the Parish of Potton, to prove that One of the Sitting

Member’s Voters had been rated thereto for the said Year:

The Petitioner’s Counsel objected against the same; it not being signed by the Assessors, or Commissioners, but only by the Collectors, of the Land Tax:

And the Sitting Member’s Counsel insisting on its being read;

They were heard thereupon.

And then the Counsel on both Sides withdrew.

And the Question being put, That a Paper, intituled, " Potton Land Tax of Two Shillings in the Pound,

" for 1714," although not signed by the Assessors, or Commissioners, for the Land Tax, be read as Evidence;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the Counsel were called in again; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the said Resolution.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member proceeded in their Evidence, in order to add Two Persons to the Sitting Member’s Poll; and then examined several Witnesses, in order to disqualify several of the Petitioner’s Voters; one, as having polled twice; others, as having no Estates in the Places where they mentioned their Freeholds to lie; and others, as not paying to publick Taxes, or Rates.

After which the Counsel were directed to withdraw.

A Petition of James Campbell, of London, Merchant* Agent for tl*e publick Creditors of Scotland, in the Name and Behalf of them, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by the Fifteenth Article Vol. 18.

A Petition of the Commissioners of Equivalent was pre- pui,i;ck fented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Debts of said Commissioners, lately appointed by his Majesty, find Scotland^ such real Difficulties in the Execution of the Trust committed to them, as they, wdth all Submission, think can only be removed by Parliament; and therefore they humbly presume to lay before the honourable House of Commons a short View of the Agreements in the Treaty of Union, which relate to the Subject matter of their Commission; of the Manner in which it was intended, as they humbly apprehend, that these Agreements should have been brought to Execution; and of what has actually happened: That, by the Treaty and Articles of Union, it is agreed. That, towards preserving an Equality of Trade, the United Kingdom shall be subject to the same Customs, on Export and Import, upon exciseable Liquors: That neither Kingdom was to be subject to the Debts of the other, due and contracted before the Union; and several Branches of the Revenue of England were appropriated for Payment of their own Debts, some for ever, some for Eighty or Ninety Years yet to run; and other Branches of their Revenue were imposed, and to continue till June,

August, and September, One thousand Seven hundred and Ten; because it was computed, that the Debts for which they were imposed might then be paid off; whereby Scotland would become liable to several Customs and Excises

that.....payable in England, which would be applicable

towards Payment of the Debts of England contracted before the Union: Therefore, by the Fifteenth Article of Union, it was agreed, That Scotland should have an Equivalent for what the Subjects thereof should be so charged, towards Payment of the Debts of England, in all Particulars whatsoever; viz. Three hundred ninety-eight thousand Eighty-five Pounds and Ten Shillings, for such Parts of the Customs and Excise with which that Kingdom was

to be charged upon the Union, as would be applicable to the Payment of the said Debts of England, according to the Proportions which the then present Customs in land, being Thirty thousand Pounds per ,did bear

to the Cuuoms in England, computed at One Million Three hundred forty-one thousand Five hundred Fifty-nine Pounds per Annum; and the then present Excises in Scotlandbting Thirty-three thousand Five hundred Pounds per Annum, did bear to the Excises \c\England, computed at Nine hundred forty-seven thousand Six hundred and Two Pounds per Annum: 2°, It was agreed. That, from and after the Union, the whole Increase of the Revenues of Customs and Excise, over and above the annual Produce of the said respective Duties, as above-stated, should go, and be applied, for the Term of Seven Years, to the Uses mentioned in the said Fifteenth Article; and that, upon the said Account, there should be answered to Scotland annually, from the End of Seven Years after the Union, an Equivalent, in proportion to such Parts of the said Increase as should be applicable to the Debts of;

and generally, That an Equivalent should be answered to Scotland for such Parts of the Debts as Scotland

might thereafter become liable to pay by reason of the Union, other than such Debts in respeCfc whereof Equivalents are therein before provided: That it might be the better understood by what Rule the Equivalents above-mentioned were Hated, and to facilitate the subsequent Accounts to be made up, pursuant to the Agreements aforesaid, at the time of the Treaty, an Account was made out, of the Revenues of taken from a Me-

dium of Three Years; an Account of the Debts of England then provided for, with an Account of the Equivalents founded upon the Proportion between the Revenues of the respective Kingdoms; all which Accounts were, by Order of the Lords Commissioners of both Kingdoms, anuexed to the Minutes of their Proceedings, and signed by their respective Secretaries: That, towards executing these Agreements, it is, by the Fifteenth Article, further agreed, That her Majesty be im powered to appoint Commissioners, who shall be accountable to the Parliament of Great Britain for disposing of the said Sum of Three hundred ninety-eight thousand Eighty five Pounds and Ten Shillings, and all other Monies which should arise to Scotland upon the Agreements aforesaid, to the Purposes mentioned in that Article; which Commissioners are impowered to inspect the Books of the several Collectors of the said Revenues of Customs and Excise, and of all other Duties from whence an Equivalent might arise to Scotland; and that the Collectors and Managers of the said Revenues and Duties be obliged to give to the said Commissioners subscribed authentick Abbreviates of the Produce of the Revenues and Duties arising in their respective Districts; that the said Commissioners shall have their Office within the Limits of and, in such

Office, keep Books, containing Accounts of the Amounts of the Equivalents, and how the same shall be disposed of from time to time; which may be inspected by any of the Subjects who desire the fame: That, by an Act, of the 6th Year of her late Majesty Queen Ann, intituled, Act for further directing the Payment of the Equivalent-money, it is Enacted, That the Commissioners, Managers, Collectors, and other proper Officers, of the Customs and Excise, and of all other Duties and Revenues from whence an Equivalent may arise to Scotland, according to the Agreements contained in the aforesaid Treaty of Union, shall make and subscribe Two authentick Abbreviates of the Produce of such Revenues, with the Amount of the several Sums which shall be due, by way of Equivalent, according to the aforesaid Agreements, from the Commencement of the Union to the Twenty-fifth March One thousand Seven hundred and Eight, for the First time, and so from thenceforward half-yearly; and shall transmit one of the said Abbreviates to the Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain, or the Commissioners of the Treasury, for the Time being; and the other to the Commissioners of Equivalent in Scotland, for the Time being: It is further Enacted, That the Lord High Trea-

A. 1715.

surer, or Commissioners of the Treasury aforesaid, upon Receipt of such Abbreviates, shall and may grant his or their Warrants or Orders, for the Payment of such Sums as shall be so found due to the Commissioners of Equivalent, for the Time being, or to such Persons as they shall appoint to receive the same: That, by the same ACT of the 6th of the Queen, Provision was appointed for the Commissioners of Equivalent, out of the growing Equivalent, which was by that Act to have been paid half-yearly; but, no Payment having hitherto been made, thele Commissioners have not as yet got Payment of their Salaries; neitheris there any Fund for supporting the Charges of the present Commission: That the Commissioners of Equivalent, appointed by her said late Majesty, and velted with the aforesaid Powers, did begin the Distribution of the Money which they had received; and, tow ards being enabled to execute the other Part of their Trust, they demanded such Abbreviates and Accounts from the Treasury, and from the Managers and Officers of the Revenue, as the Article of the Union, and the afore-mentioned Act, directed; but never could obtain any other than half-yearly Abbreviates of the gross and net Produce of the Customs and Excise in Scotland; nor do these, as the Commissioners humbly think, come up to the Intention of the Article and Act aforesaid: That, since the Union, there is a very considerable Alteration in the State of the publick Revenues, and publick Debts; several Branches, which, at the time of the Treaty, were unappropriated for Debts, all the Branches which were temporary, and to have continued only till June, August, and 1710, have been, by several Acts since, further continued, and at length made perpetual; besides many Duties imposed since the Treaty, which are to continue for a long Term of Years; and the Monies arising from the said Appropriations, from the Continuance of the old, and Imposition of the new Duties aforesaid, have been applied promiscuously; that is, for paying and satisfying old Debts, and making Provision for the several Years since the Union, as appears by the several Acts of Parliament continuing, imposing, and appropriating, these Duties: And though, by comparing the Agreements in the Treaty of Union with the Acts of Parliament made since, it appears plain enough, that there is an Equivalent due, and growing due, to Scotland; yet the Commissioners of Equivalent, by not getting the half-yearly Abbreviates, appointed to be given them, have never been able to make up such Accounts of the Equivalents, as the Subjects of Scotland had Reason, from the 15th Article of Union, to expect; and, by this Delay, the Difficulty of making up such an Account will always growr greater: That, by an Act of the last Parliament of Queen Anne, the Commissioners of Equivalent were acquitted and discharged of the Sums by them duly issued; and, by the same Act, the publick Debts of Scotland, which were adjusted and certified, pursuant to the Direction of the several Acts therein recited, did amount, on the 24th June 1714, to 230,308/. 9*. 10 $d.to bear Interest thereafter at Five Pounds per Centum per Annum; for which no Provision is made, notwithstanding the above Claim; and that it is believed, there is scarce any Debt due before the Union but is provided for, except this; neither has any Care hitherto been taken of the Manufactures and Fifiling of Scotland, as was intended by the Treaty, and expected by the Subjects of Scotland That by the Agreements, and Manner of Execution of them above-expressed, it appears plainly, that the Subjects of Scotland believed themselves very secure in the publick Faith, for the Performance of all these Agreements and Conditions: And the Commissioners of Equivalent being accountable to the Parliament of Britain, and by no means able to obviate the Difficulties above-mentioned: And praying to make such further Provision for the dating the Accounts of the Equivalent for these Seven Years past, as may effectually answer that End; Mr. Hampden, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elefitions, the Matter touching the Election for the Town of Haverford West, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place: and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of John Barlow Efijuife, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir George Barlow Baronet, for the Town of Haverford West:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Freeholders, Burgesses, and Inhabitants, paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving Alms.

That the Poll was;

For the Sitting Member - - 222:

For the Petitioner - - 181:

That the Petitioner’s Counsel objected to 79 of the Sitting-Member’s Voters; v34 as illegal Burgesses; 20 receiving Alms; 15 Inhabitants not paying Scotland Lot; Eight neither Freeholders, Burgesses, or Inhabitants; and Two under Age.

On the Head of illegal Burgesses, the Petitioner’s Counsel produced,

Hat. 16 October 1629. A Collection of Orders agreed upon by the Mayor, Common Council, and other the Inhabitants; and confirmed and allowed by the King’s Justices of Assize;

By which no Person is to be admitted and Sworii Burgess (Apprentices and Freemens Sons only excepted), unlefe he be thereunto thought meet, first by the most Voice of the Common-Council of the Town, and afterwards by the Content, and most Voice of the Burgesses and Commons of the Town, under a Penalty of 10/. upon the Mayor; and further, that none shall be admitted or sworn Burgess at any Day or Time, laving the Days of Nomination and Election of the Mayor yearly, and at the Two Sheriffs Turns; and at no other time in the Year.

Against the 34 Burgesses objected to as illegal, the following Evidence was produced;

Hat. 11® Mar. 1714. An Order in the Town-Book for the Mayor’s swearing Eleven of them Burgesses when he thinks fit; viz.Thomas Gentleman, Simon Higda, Morgan Folland, John Hill, John junior,

George Hellier, and John Parrot, claiming Freedom as Burgesses Sons; Tho. Howell, claiming as Apprentice; and Mr. Lewis Powell, Mr. Lort, and the Reverend Mr. George Phillips, whole Titles are not mentioned:

Hat. 190 Afar. 1714. Another Order of the Mayor’s swearing Eleven others; viz.Thomas Bateman, George Jenkins, Henry Bowen Clerk, and David Lewis, being Freemens Sons; James Wilkin junior, having married a Freeman’s Daughter; Richard Llewellin, as Apprentice; Mark Roach Squire, Richard Esquire, John Stephens Gentleman, John Powell Gentleman, and Wm. Davids, whole Titles are not mentioned.

Hat. 20 Mar. 1714. Another Order for admitting and swearing 12 others; and the Order fays. They were then sworn accordingly; viz. Mr* Arnold,

Thomas Rees Taylor, Geo. Jones Glover, John Barnsly Butcher, Rowland Harries, and Thoihas Havies, Gen-

tlemen, (being Freemens Sons;) John Thomas, Thomas Knowles Esquire, Geo. Bowen Esquire, Thomas Edwards Gentleman, Joj'eph Allen Gentleman, and Richard Foley, whose Titles are not mentioned.

Vol. 18.

That the Petitioner’s Counsel objected against the Legality of these Admissions, as being clandestine and upon neither of the Three Days allowed by the Constitution: And against the Truth of these Entries they observed, That the 20th of March was upon a Sunday, when no Court w'as held; and called,

John Bateman and Richard Smith: Who spoke for 20 and 40 Years j and said, The Practice has always been to admit and swear Burgesses only upon the Three Constitution-Days; viz. the Election of the Mayor, and the Sheriffs Turns; and never at any other time, except sometimes in the same of Gentlemen of Quality, or the Mayor’s own Freeman:

That Burgesses cannot be admitted but by Conseqt of the Majority of the Common-Council; and also by Consent of the Majority of the Burgesses in the Common Hall: That all Members of the Common Council ought to be summoned to every Court; but only select Persons were summoned to the Courts in March last: Neither of them, though both of the Common Council, were then summoned: They never knew Burgesses admitted in any such manner before:.

And Smith laid, The Mayor declared. He would make as many new Burgesses as would serve his Turn.

Rowland Harries, who is entered in the Town-Book as admitted and sworn upon the 20th of March, laid, He was sworn upon the Day before the Election, being the Second of May last, at a Publick House, by the Mayor; and One of the Aldermen.

Mr. Hugh Fowler said, That Arnold Bowen, another of those mentioned to be admitted and sworn the 20th of March, polled as a Burgess; and hath, since the Election, contested, He never was sworn a Burgess.

Wm. Holloway named Twenty of the Sitting-Members Voters; and said, They received Alms, or publick Charity.

That the Petitioner’s Counsel proceeded to give Evidence of Partiality, and arbitrary Proceedings, of the Mayor and Sheriff; in favour of the Sitting-Member:

But the Sitting-Member’s Counsel alleged, They were surprised: And, having no Witnesses in Town to justify the Election, they withdrew.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committees came to these Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir George Barlow Baronet, is not duly elected a Bureefs to serve in this present Parliament for the Town of Haverford West.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Barlow, of Laxvrenny, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Jown of Haverford West.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the Proceedings of the Mayor and; Common Council of the Town of Haverford, West, in making Burgesses, without the Consent of the Commonalty, was illegal, and contrary to the Rights of the said Town: And that the Burgesses, so pretended to be made, have not thereby acquired any Right of Voting in any future Elections.

Mr. Dare’s Letter, dated from Calais, October 2 2d, 1708, directed to Mr. John James David and Company, in London-, purporting his hard Fortune of being taken by a French Privateer, under the Convoy of the Dover and Sunderland, and in Sight of them; and that, upon the First Appearance of the Privateer’s giving Chace to him, he fired a Gun, pursuant to his Sailing Orders received from the Dover: Which Orders were likewise produced; signed, Tho. Articles of Impeachment of High Treason, and other High Crimes and Misdemeanors, against Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer.

WHEREAS many Iblemn Treaties and Alliances have been formerly entered into, between the Crown of England and other Princes and Potentates of for

their mutual Safety, and from the Considerations of the common Danger which threatened all Christendom from the immoderate Growth of the Power of France:

And whereas the preventing the Monarchy of Spain from coming into the Hands of the House of Bourbon, has, for many Years, been a fundamental Principle and Maxim of Union among the Allies, in order to preserve a jult Balance of Power in Europe: And to that end, as the Designs of France on the Monarchy of Spain have, from time to time, appeared, new Treaties, and express Stipulations, have been entered into amongst the Allies, to strengthen themselves against that approaching Danger; and, oh this Foundation, a Treaty for an intended Partition, whereby a small Part only of the Dominions of the Crown of Spain was allotted to the House of Bourbon, was condemned by the Wisdom of Parliament, as being highly prejudicial, and fatal, in its Consequences, to England, and the Peace of Europe:

And whereas the Duke of Anjou, Grandson to the King of France, on the Demise of Charles the Second, King of Spain, took Possession of the entire Monarchy of Spain; whereby the Balance of Power, the Protestant Religion, and the Liberty of Europe, were threatened with immediate Danger:

Whereupon Leopold, then Emperor of Germany, his. late Majesty King William the Third, of ever-glorious Memory, and the states General of the United Provinces, finding, at that most critical Juncture, that a strict Conjunction and Alliance between themselves w’as become necessary for repelling the Greatness of the common Danger from so great an Accession of Power to the then common Enemy, did, in the Year of our Lord 1701, make, form, and conclude, a new Treaty and Alliance; whereby it was agreed,

That there shall be, and continue, between the said Confederates, his Sacred Imperial Majesty, his Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain, and the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, a constant, perpetual, and inviolable Friendftiip and Correspondence; and that each Party shall be obliged to promote the Advantages of the other, and prevent all Inconveniences and Dangers that might happen to them, as far as lies in their Power: That the said Allies, deliring nothing more earnestly than the Peace, and general Quiet, of all Europe, have adjudged, that nothing can be more effectual for the Estabishment thereof, than the procuring an equitable and reasonable Satisfaction to his Imperial Majesty, for his Pretension to the Spanish Succession; and that the King of Great Britain, and the States General, may obtain a particular and sufficient Security for their Kingdoms, Provinces, and Dominions, and for the Navigation and Commerce of their Subjects:

That the said Confederates therefore shall, in the First place, endeavour, by amicable means, to obtain the said Satisfaction; but if, contrary to their Expectation and Wifbes, the same is not had, the said Confederates do engage and promise to one another, That they will assist each other with all their Forces, according to a Specification to be agreed upon in a peculiar Convention for that Purpose:

That the Confederates, in order to the procuring the Satisfaction and Security aforesaid, shall, amongst other things, use their utmost Endeavours to recover the Provinces of the Spanish Low Countries, that they may be a Fence aid Rampart, commonly called a Barrier, separating and dividing France from the United Provinces, for the Security of the States General, as they have l'erved in all Tidies, till of late that the Most Christian King has seized theln by his Forces; as likewise the Duchy of Milan, with its Dependences, as a Fief of the Empire; and contributing to the Security of his Imperial Majesty’s hereditary Dominions; besides the Kingdoms of Naples and Sicily, and the Lands and islands upon the Coast of Tuf-cany, in the Mediterranean, that belonged to the Spanish Dominions; and may serve to the same Purpose; and will be also of Advantage to the Navigation and Commerce of the Subjects of the King of Great Britain, and of the United Provinces:

That, in case the Confederates shall be forced to enter into a War, for obtaining the Satisfaction aforesaid for his Imperial Majesty, and the Security of his Majesty of Great Britain, and the States General, they shall faithfully communicate their Designs to one another, as well in relation to the Actions of the War, as all other things wherein the common Cause is concerned:

That it shall not be permitted to eklrer Party, when! the War is once begun, to treat of Peace with the Enemy, unless jointly', and by a Communication of Councils; and no Peace shall be made, unless an equitable and reasonable Satisfaction for his Imperial Majesty, and the particular Security of the Kingdoms, Provinces, Dominions, Navigations, and Commerce, for his Majesty of Great Britain, and the States General, be first obtained; and unless Care be taken, by fitting Security, that the Kingdoms of France and Spain shall never come, and be united, under the same Government; nor that one and the same Person shall be King of both Kingdoms; and particularly, that the French shall never get into the Possession of the Spanish Indies; neither shall they be permitted to fail thither on the Account of Traffic k, directly or indirectly, on any Pretence whatl'oever; and lastly, unless full Liberty be granted unto the Subjects of the King of Great Britain, and the States General, to exercise and enjoy all the said Privileges, Rights, Immunities, and Franchises, of Commerce by Sea and Land, in Spain, the Mediterranean, and all Lands and Places which the King of Spain, last deceased, did possess at the time of his Death, as welt in Europe as elsewhere, which they used and enjoyed, or which the Subjects of both or either of them, by any Right, acquired by Treaties, Agreements, Customs, or any other Way whatsoever, might have used and enjoyed, before the Death of the late King of Spain:

That, at the same time that the said Agreement, or Peace, shall be made, the Confederates shall agree amongst themselves about all the things that they shall think ne-celfary for maintaining the Navigation and Commerce of the Subjects of his Majesty of and the

States General, in the Lands and Dominions they may acquire, and that were possessed by the late deceased King of Spain; and also in what manner the States General may be secured by the aforesaid Fence, or Barrier:

And whereas his said late Majesty King William, and the States General, seriously considering, that France was then become so formidable, from the Accession of Spain to the Duke of Anjou, that, in the Opinion of all the World, Europe was in Danger of losing her Liberty, and undergoing the heavy Yoke of universal Monarchy; and that the forest Means of effecting that Design were, to divide the King of Great Britain from the States General; for which Purpose, all imaginable Efforts would be made; they therefore thought it necessary to unite in the strictest Manner that was possible; and, to that End, a defensive Treaty and Alliance was concluded, and entered into, between them, in or about the Month of November, 1701; wherein it was, among other things, agreed,

And her Majesty having frequently declared from the Throne, That her Resolutions in entering into the said Negotiations were, to obtain a general, good, and lasting Peace; and the Plenipotentiaries at Utrecht being instructed to treat with France conformably to that End; he the said Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer, in order to remove the just Suspicions which had been conceived of his private and separate Negotiations with France, did advile her Majesty to make this further Declaration, in her laid Message, of the 17th of January,

" That the World will now fee how groundless those Reports are, which have been spread abroad by Men of " evil Intentions, to serve the worst Designs, as if a separate Peace had been treated; for which there has not been the least Colour given

Whereas a private and separate Negotiation had been carried on, for Five Months together, between England and France', and, during that time, private Propositions had been sent from England, and a private Treaty with a Minister of France signed, even by her Majesty’s Privity, exclusive of all the Allies, before the said Declaration made by her Majesty; and private and separate Measures were thenceforth carried on by the said Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer, and his Accomplices, on behalf of her Majesty, with the Ministers of France, evert to the Conclusion of the Peace.

Her Majesty was further prevailed on, by the wicked Advice of him the said Robei't Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer, in her Speech, of June the 6th, 1712, to declare, " That, to prevent the Union of the Two Crowns,

" foe would not be content with what was speculative;

" but infilled on something solidAnd, in the same Speech, to the Effect following; viz. " The Nature of " the Proposal for a Renunciation is such, that it executes " itself; and France and Spain are thereby more cftcctually divided than ever :"

Whereas the Ministers of France had, before that time, assured the Ministers of her Majesty, That, to accept of ,the Expedient proposed on her Majesty’s behalf, would be to build on a sandy Foundation; and that the Renunciation would be null and void by the fundamental Laws of France; and that they would deceive themselves, who

accepted it as an Expedient to prevent the Union of the Two Crowns:

And not only in the Particulars before-mentioned, but in many others contained in the said several Speeches and Messages, made, and sent to her Parliament, even while the said Negotiations of Peace with France were depending, the most essential Points relating to Peace and Commerce, and which concerned the Interest as well of the Allies as of Great Britain, were grossly mifirepresented:

By all which wicked, treacherous, and unexampled evil Counfete, he the said Robert Earl of and Earl

Mortimer, did most basely, ungratefully, and scandalously abuse the Favour of his Royal Mistress { and, by means of her Authority, did mislead her Parliament into ground-lese and fatal Resolutions; and thereby not only prevented the just Advice of die Parliament to her Majesty on that critical Juncture, but obtained the Approbation of Parliament to his mysterious and dangerous Practices; and did not only deprive her Majesty of the Confidence and Afieftion of her Allies, but exposed her Majesty, and her People, to the Contempt of the common Enemy.

Article 16.

That whereas the said Robert Earl of and Earl

Mortimer having, on all Occasions, used his utmost Endeavours to subvert the ancient established Constitution of Parliaments, the great and only Security of the Prerogatives of the Crown, and of the Rights, Liberties, and Properties, of the People; and being most wickedly determined, at one fatal Blow, as far as in him lay, to destroy the Freedom and Independency of the House of Lords, the great Ornament, and nearest Support, of the Imperial Crown of these Realms; and falfiy intending to disguise his mischievous Purposes, under a pretended Zeal for the Prerogative of the Crown; he the said Robert Earl of Oxfordand Earl , on or

about the Months of December or January 1711, whilst the House of Lords were under an Adjournment, and had Realbn to expefit, that, on their next Meeting, Matters of the highest Importance would be communicated to them from the Throne; they having, feme few Days before, given their humble Opinion and Advice to her Ma-jofty, That no Peace could be sese or honourable to Great Jiritain, or Europe, if Spain, and the West Indies, were to be allotted to auy Branch of the House of Bourbon; being then Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain, and One of her Majesty’s Privy Council, and aiTuming to himself an arbitrary Direction and Controul in her Majesty’s Councils, contrary to his Duty and his Oath, and in Violation of the great Trust reposed iu him, and with an immediate Purpose to render ineffectual the many earned Representations of her Majesty’s Allies against the said Negotiations of Peace, as well as to prevent the good Effects of the said Advice of the House of Lords, and in order to obtain such future Resolutions of that House of Parliament, on the important Subject of the Negotiations of Peace, as might flielter and promote his secret and unwarrantable Proceedings, together with other false and evil Counsellors, did advise her Majesty to make and create Twelve Peers of this Realm, and Lords of Parliament; and, pursuanl to his destructive Counsels, Letter Patents did forthwith pass, whereby Twelve Peers were made and created; and did likewise advise her Majesty immediately to call and summon them to Parliament; which being done accordingly, they took their Seats in the House of Lords on or about the Second Day of January 1711 $ to which Day the House then stood adjourned: Whereby the said Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer did most highly abuse the Influence he then had with her Majesty; and prevailed on her to exercise, in the most unprecedented and dangerous Manner, that valuable and undoubted Prerogative, which the Wisdom of the Laws, and Constitution of the Kingdom, hath intruded with the Crown, for the rewarding signal Virtue, % and distinguished Merit; by which desperate Advice he did not only, as far as in him lay, deprive her Majesty of the Continuance of those seasonable and wholsome Counsels in that critical Juncture, but wickedly perverted the true and only End of that great and useful Prerogative,

to the Dishonour of the Crown, and the irreparable Mif-chief to the Constitution of Parliaments.

All which Crimes and Misdemeanors were committed and done by him the said Earl, against our late Sovereign Lady the Queen, her Crown and Dignity, the Peace and Interest of this Kingdom, and in Breach of the several Trusts reposed in him the said Earl:

And he the said Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer was Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain, and One of her Majesty’s Privy Council during the time that all and every the Crimes before set forth were done and committed.

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, having, with the utmost Satisfaction, received your Majesty's gracious Message, recommending to us the providing a Maintenance for the Ministers, who are to attend the Service of the fifty new Churches intended to , be erected in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs thereof, beg Leave to allure your Majesty, That we will, with all Chearfolneis, set about the making such a Provision, as shall fully answer your Majesty’s pious Intentions, and the Wants of so many of the Inhabitants of your Two great and populous Cities It is very grateful to your obedient Commons, to be employed in a Work that is so much for the Honour of the Vox.. 18.

A PETITION of the Gentlemen, Clothiers, Wool-combers, Weavers, Fullers, and other the Inhabitants, of the Borough of Cullum, in Devon, was pre-

fented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the making Exeter a free Port for bringing in of Wool from Ireland, will be of no Advantage to that Town, or to the Petitioners; and the whole Business in the Manufactures depends on the Encouragement the Town of Tiverton finds from foreign Markets: And praying, That the Port of Exeter may not be opened for bringing in of Wool from Ireland.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, tiU the Report from the Committee appointed to consider the Laws in being for preventing the Exporting of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland; and how the same may be made more effectual; shall be taken into further Consideration.

A Petition of the Portreeve, Gentlemen, Clothiers, and other the Inhabitants, of the Borough of Honiton, in Devon, was prefen ted to the House, and read; setting forth, That the putting a Stop to the Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland to France, will be of very great Advantage to this Town, and the Parts adjacent; and the opening me Port of Exeter, for bringing in of Wool from Ireland, will obstruct the good Design of any Law against the Exporting of Wool for France; and the Woollen

Manufhfture of this Town depends chiefly on that of Tiverton, which can have no Advantage by opening the Port of Exeter: And praying, That the said Port of Exeter may full remain lhut up, with respect to the Fish-Trade.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, till the Report from the Committee, appointed to consider the Laws in being for preventing the Exporting of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland; and how the same may be made more effectual; shall be taken into further Consideration.

The House proceeded, according to Order, in the fur- Bedford ther Hearing the Merits of the Election for the County of Bedford:

And the Counsel on both Sides were called in:

And the Sitting Members Counsel proceeded, and examined Witnesses, in order to disqualify other of the Petitioner’s Voters, in regard they had no Freehold in the Places they voted for; or that they were not taxed or rated for their Freehold; or that their Freeholds were not lett for Forty Shillings a Year Rent; or that they were Purchasers within a Year before the Election; or that they were Copyholders: And also gave feme Evidence relating to Bribery.

And a Witness being called, to prove that one William Reynold voted contrary to what appears by the Sheriff’s Poll;

Which being objected to by the Petitioner’s Counsel:

And the Counsel on both Sides being heard;

They were directed to withdraw.

And the Question being put, That the Counsel for the Sitting Member be admitted to examine Edward Kemp, to prove That William Reynold voted otherwise than he is set down upon the Sheriff’s Poll;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Counsel were called in again; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the Resolution of the House.

Then the Sitting Member’s Counsel proceeded, and went through their Evidence, as to the Disqualifications of the Petitioner’s Voters.

And the Sitting Member’s Counsel summed up their Evidence touching the same.

After which, the Sitting Member’s Counsel proceeded to give Evidence, That the Petitioner was not qualified to be elected, according to the Act, of the Ninth Year of the late Queen, intituled, An Act for securing the Freedom of Parliaments, by the further qualifying the Members to fit in the House of Commons;

But a Witness, who had been summoned, not attending;

The Counsel were directed to withdraw.

Ordered, That the further Hearing the Merits of the Election for the County of Bedford be adjourned till Saturday Morning next

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Attorney General, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for preventing Tumults, and riotuous Afl’emblies; and for the more speedy and effefihaal punishing the Rioters; was committed; the Amendments they had made to the Bill; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were once read throughout: And the First Amendment was read a Second time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Amendments *be adjourned.

The House being informed of great Dilbrders in the County of Stafford by several evil-disposed Persons going from Place to Place, in a tumultuous and riotous manner; and that they had assaulted and wounded ibveral of his Majesty’s good Subjects, without any Provocation; and that one Mr. Bayly was able to give the House an Account thereof; and that he was at the Door;

He was ordered to be called in:

And he was called in accordingly; and, at the Bar (the Mace lying on the Table), gave the House an Account of what had happened in that Country.

And then he withdrew.

And Mr: Bracebridge,a Member of the House, acquainting them of a Letter wrote from that Country, relating to those Disturbances; which he read in his Place;

Ordered, That the said Letter be brought up to the Table.

And it was brought up accordingly; and read; and is as followeth;

Honoured Sir,

I Hope this will find you, and your good Lady, SO. in good Heath, as your Children here are, God be thanked.

Undoubtedly you have heard of several Passages, that followed upon -the Performance of the Mob; as, namely, the Demotifiiing of the Presbyterian Meeting Houses at Stafford and and ('tis laid) at

Stone and Langdon: Yesterday a Parcel of the

hampton Folks set forth in order to attack Bromwich Meeting-house: These People took Boston, and Wednesbury, in the Way; lo that they were a great

Number: But the Difienters, having Notice of what was intended, came together in great Numbers, Horse and Foot, furnished with Guns, Swords, &;c. and attackt the Rioters, and drove ’urn off; several of whom they have wounded: And the Mob has a Report among ’urn this Day, that one of their Fraternity is killed; and they seem resolved (as Fame goes) to venture another Pu(h for it. The Truth of it is, there is no such thing as appealing ’urn with good Words; and, I think, to cure it by Force will be but an uncomfortable Matter. As far as I can learn, these poor Fellows have got a Notion, that the Ministry and Difienters have ruined Trade, on Purpose to make the Nation out of Love with the late Peace, and Peace-makers; and, because the Ministry, and secret Committee, and their Friends, will not let the Country have Peace and Trade, they resolve (if they can hinder it) the Difienters shall not have a quiet Toleration. Hanger, and want of Sleep, perhaps, may tame ’um in a little while; but, if Things don’t mend in a little time, the Parishes may be burthened with their Families.

They will not be persuaded, that there is any Argument against Experience; and they say, that One Year’s Peace was better to them, and the Kingdom, than all the glorious Campaigns the D----- of M----- has ever made in

all his Life; that those were the belt Friends of the Government that made Peace; gnd that their Impeachers ought much rather to be impeached than the lait Alini-ftry; so that, in short, they look upon these Impeachments as nothing else but a Piece of Spight and Revenge in this military Ministry, because the Ratifications of Peace took feme Bread off their Treuchers: And they reason, that ’tis the itrangelt tiling in the World, that the Afitions and N egotiations of those worthy Patriots that made Peace,

should be called High Treason, High Crimes and Miftle-meanours, which have been approved by her Majesty’s subsequent Ratifications; for which her Majesty received the Thauks and Congratulations of the honourable House of Commons, and, indeed, of aluioft the w hole Nation. ’Tis impossible to recount their odd Speculations that they run into upon these Occasions; however, I was w illing you should not be wholly a Stranger to these Passages. I hope your Goodness will pardou the Interruption of thfe tedious Letter. 1 am, with due Commendations,

Honoured Sir,

Bilston, Your most obedient and

A Motion being made, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to give Directions to the several Magistrates throughout the Kingdom, That the Laws be put in a speedy and the most vigorous Execution against all such Persons, who shall be found any way concerned in the late rebellious and tumultuous Riots and Dilbrders committed, and now carrying on, in several Parts of this Kingdom, by Persons disaffefited to his Majesty, and his Government; and that a ftri6t Inquiry be made who are the Promoters and Authors of the said Tumults and Riots; and that an Account may be taken of such Justices of the Peace as have failed in die Discharge of their Duty on these Occasions; and that such Justices, who shall appear to his Majesty to have neglected their Duty, be forthwith put out of the Corn-millions of the Peace; and that such other Magistrates, as shall appear likewiseto have neglected their Duty therein, may be proceeded against with the utmost Rigour of the Law; and that his Majesty will likewise be pleased to di-refit, That an exafit Account may be taken of the Losses and Damages, which his Majesty’s Subjefitshave sustained by reasons of these tumultuous and rebellious Proceedings; and that the Sufferers may have full Compensation made them for their Damages; and to allure his Majesty, That all such Expences as his Majesty shall be at on that account, shall be made good to his Majesty out of the next Aids that shall be afterwards granted by Parliament; and also, that the Laws against Papists and Nonjurors may be effefitually put in Execution;

And the Question being put, That these Words be added to toe Question j . The House divided.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Merchants, and Clandefli* others, of the Borough of Barnstaple, trading in Wool, and Woollen Manufactures, was pretented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Committee, who are to prepare a Bill for the preventing the Exportation of Wool, have agreed to a Clause to be inserted, for making the Port of Exeter an open Port for the Importation of Wool from Ireland; and whether the said Clause will not be greatly prejudicial to the Design of such an Act, by giving Occasion to the Irish Owlers, and other ill-deligning Men, under pretence of carrying Wool to Exeter, to land it in France; and, by Bribes, and other ill Practices, get up their Bonds given in Ireland: And all the othejr Weltem Ports may well desire the same Liberty: which has formerly been the Occasion of exporting great Quantities of Wool to foreign Parts; the Distance from Ireland to Topfam being twice as far as from these Ports, the Hazard of the Seas consequently must be greater than this Side the Lands End; and, by the exactelt Computation the Petitioners can make,’ Wool may be rendered to fer by Way of this Port, Bideford, Mine head, as cheap as if carried by Ship directly to Topfam, without the Odds of the Hazard of the Seas, and Length of Time; the Freight, with Commission, and all Charges, from Ireland to Exeter, by the Way of these Ports, not exceeding Eight Pence Halfpeny a Stone; whereas the bare Freight to Exeter formerly was Eight Pence a Stone, betides other Charges, not to be esteemed less than a Peny or Two Pence a Stone; to that the carrying Wool about Land to Exeter will be a real Detriment to this, and the middle Part of the Country, without any Advantage to the Exeter Traders: And praying, That the same may be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, who were to con-lider the Laws in being for preventing the Exporting of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland; and how the same may be made more effectual; shall be taken into further Consideration.

elsewhere, ever since the Second Year of the Reign of King Edward the Sixth; and they are informed, that (bme Persons have petitioned to repeal and amend the said Act of Parliament, in order to remove the said Sessions to some other Place, as may be most conducive to the Ease and Safety of the said County in general; upon which it was ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for continuing several Laws therein is committed, That they have Power to receive a Clause to repeal and amend the said Act, made in the Second Year of the Reign of King Edward the Sixth, intituled, An Act for keeping the Great Sessions, and County-Courts, at the Town of Beaumorris, in the County of Anglesea: And the said Great Sessions, and County Courts, cannot be kept, to the Ease and Safety of the said County in general, as the Place where the same is now kept:

And praying to be heard, by Counsel, before the said Act of Parliament be repealed or amended.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill for continuing several Laws therein mentioned, is committed, shall be made.

Gentlemen,

I Thank you heartily for your Address, and the many Marks of Zeal and Affection which you express for my Honour and Safety, and the Security of the Kingdom.

I will give immediate Directions for putting in Execution the several Matters which you so justly recommend to me: And as I am resolved, on all Occasions, to follow the Advice of my Parliament; lb I have no doubt, but that, by the Blessing of Almighty God, and your fealbn-able and vigorous Assistance, I shall foort be enabled effectually to suppress that Spirit of Rebellion, which is so industriously fomented among us, and to establish the Peace and Prolperity of my People.

Words: And that die Lord Chancellor did accordingly read a Speech, delivered into his Hands by his Majesty from the Throne; and of which, to prevent Mistakfcs,

Mr. Speaker said, he had obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as follows;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

THE Zeal you have shewn for preserving the Peace ' of my Kingdoms, and your Wifdotn in providing so good a Law to prevent all riotous and tumultuous Proceedings, give me great Satisfaction; but I am sorry to find, that such a Spirit of Rebellion has discovered iliel^ as leaves no room to doubt but these Disorders are fft on foot, and encouraged, by Persons dif&ffected to my Government, in Expectation of being supported from abroad.

The Preservation of our excellent Constitution, and the Security of our holy Religion, has been, and always shall be, my chief Care; and I cannot question, but your Concern for these invaluable Blessings is so great, as not to let them be exposed to such Attempts as 1 have certain Advices are preparing by the Petender from abroad, and carrying on at home by a restless Party, in his Favour.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

In these Circumstances, I think it proper to alk your Assistance; and make no doubt but you will so far consult your own Security, as not to leave the Nation, under a Rebellion actually begun at home, arid threatened with an Invasion from abroad, in a defenceless Condition: And I shall look upon the Provision you shall make for the Safety of my People, as the bell Mark of your Affection to me.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Proposition presented by the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, and referred by the House to this Committee, for supplying, out of such a Fund as is therein mentioned, the additional yearly Sum of ne hundred Twenty thousand Pounds, during his Majesty’s Life (which God long preserve), for the Service of his Houshold and Family, and other his necessary Expences and Occasions; and a further yearly Sum of Fifty-four thousand Six hundred Pounds, to be a Fund or Security for raising a Sum, not exceeding Nine hundred Ten thousand Pounds, as Part of the Supply granted for publick Services, upon such Terms and Conditions, and in such Manner, as in the said Proposition are expressed; be accepted.

Resolved, Thai it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for answering the Sum of Twenty-eight thousand Pounds per Annum, or thereabouts, mentioned in the said Proposition, the Duties on Hops, which have Continuance until the First Day of August 1715, be further continued, and made payable to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors: subject nevertheless to Redemption by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such of the Duties and Revenues for raising the general Fund to be established, pursuant to the said Proposition, as are now temporary, be made perpetual; subject also to Redemption by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That if the Revenues settled by the Act of the First Year of his Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for the better Support of his Majesty’s Houshold, and of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown of Great Britain, together with the said additional Revenue of One hundred Twenty thousand Pounds per Annum, shall produce more, in clear Money, than the yearly Sum of Seven hundred thousand Pounds, to be reckoned from Michaelmas 1715, then the Overplus of such Produce to be made part of the general Fund to be established, as aforesaid; and be appropriated, issued, and applied, accordingly, until all the Exchequer Pills shall be paid off, or the said general Fund shall be redeemed by Parliament; and that afterwards such Overplus, exceeding Seven hundred thousand Pounds An. fium, be not issued, granted, disposed, or applied to any

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Sum of N ine hundred Ten thousand Pounds, for publick Uses, be raised by settling a perpetual Annuity) after the Rate of Six per Centum per Annum, to be redeemable by Parliament.

The said circular Letters are as follow;

From the House of Commons.

Sir,

THE House of Commons having taken Notice of the Absence of several of their Members, I am commanded to acquaint you with it, that you may give immediate Summons to the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs in the fame, That they do attend their Service in Parliament on Thursday the Eighth Day of August next,

notwithstanding any Order for Leave to be absent; the House of Commons intending to proceed with all Severity against all such of their Members as shall then neglect their Attendance, and whose Excuses shall not be allowed; And you are to give an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereupon, to,

Sir,

Your humble Servant.

From die House of Commons.

Gentlemen,

THE House of Commons having taken Notice of the Absence of several of their Members, I am commanded to give immediate Summons to all that are absent. That they do attend their Service in Parliament on the Day of next: You are there-

fore desired forthwith to fend the inclosed Letters, as they are directed; And you are to give an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereupon, to

Your humble Servant.

To Sir James Stuart, junior, and Thomas Ketinedy Esquire, or either of them, his Majesty’s Solicitors at Edinburgh.

in the Year 1711, he did enter 326,319 lb. of Virginia Tobacco at the Custom-house, London, and paid and secured the full Customs for the same; the greatest Part of which he afterwards exported; but the Remainder was unfortunately destroyed by a Hidden and dreadful Fire, 1712; fb could not have any Benefit by Sale, or Drawbacks upon Exportatiorf: And he, and his Sureties, being liable to the Customs of the said Tobacco, he did represent his same to the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury; which their Lordships did refer to the Commissioners of the Customs, who have certified the same to be as above set forth; but their Lordships, as the Law now Hands, could not give him any Relief therein; and the granting Debentures for the Tobacco so burnt is no more Detriment to his Majesty’s Customs, than if they had been thipped off to foreign Markets, by which he would have been intitled to Debentures for such Allowance as the Law directs; but, by this Calamity, lie is totally deprived of that Benefit: And praying to be relieved therein.

A Petition of the Trustees for settling the poor Palatines in Ireland was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they were constituted Trustees for settling several Families of poor Palatines in Ireland; and there are settled Two hundred and Thirteen Families, who m-dustriously follow their several Occupations, especially in propagating Hemp; and arc well settled on several Gentlemens Estates; and have Freeholds; but, being Strangers, they were ignorant of their being obliged to take the Oaths prescribed by the Act for Naturalization; and, the Act being repealed before they could be settled on their Freeholds, they are not capable of enjoying the m; but have since taken the Oaths, though the Time prescribed by the Act was elapsed: And praying, That a Time may be allowed them to take the Oaths.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the Petition: And that the Lord Coningsby, Mr. Molefaorth, and Mr. Strickland, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

- Sir James Bateman, Sub-Governor of the South Sea Company, presented to the House a Proposel from the General Court of the South Sea Company for raising the Sutn of Eight hundred Twenty-two thousand. Thirty-two Pounds Four Shillings Eight Pence, for the Service Of the Publick: And the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

Julii 1715.

1. THAT the said Company do consent, that their Stock be enlarged to Ten Millions, byadding 822,032/. 4s. 8 to the present Stock, by an Act, of this Session; for which an Annuity, after the Rate of Six per Cent, be allowed from 24 June 1715, over and above the present 8,0001, per Annum, for Management.

2. That this additional Stock be vested in feme Persons for the Purposes hereafter mentioned; and be written in the Book of the said Company accordingly,

3. That 558,678/. is. 4dbeing the Year’s Interest

for 9,177,967/. 15 r. 4</. the Company’s present Slock, from Christmas 1714 to Christmas 1715; and 24,660/,

1 gs.4 d.the Interest of the 822,032/. 4-s. 8 new Stock, from Midjiimmer last to Christmas next; making together 583,339/. os. 8 d.; be, upon passing the said Act, immediately assigned, by the Persons in whom it shall be vested, to the Cashier of the Company, or whom the Court of Directors may appoint to accept the fame, that due Discharge may be given for it.

4. That 238,693/. 4#. in Stock, the Remainder of the said 822,032/. 4 s.8 d. additional Stock, be for the Publick Service, as shall be directed.

5. That, from and after 25 December 1715, there be as is now provided, till 2 5 Decembe 1716, annually within Twenty Days after the 25 December an Estimate made of what the Funds, applicable to pay the Company their Annuity, will amount to, by a Medium of the 'three preceding Years; and what, the same shall fall short of 608,600l. shall be provided for by Parliament; and the Deficiency, at the End of every Quarter of each succeeding Year, shall be paid by the Treasurer of the Navy, out of the Money then in, or first coming to, his Hands.

6. That, after 25 December 1716, what the Funds shall produce short of the said 608,000l. in each Year, ending the 25 December, which, the Company are appre-hensive, will be considerable, shall be provided for by Parliament; and made good by the Treasurer of the Navy, out of the Money then in, or first coming to, his Hands,

7. That the Clauses for making good the said Deficiencies by the Treasurer of the Navy beeffectual, to the Satisfaction of the Company; and that thereby the Treasurer of the Navy be obliged to pay every Deficiency, as the same shall happen, whether the same be provided for by Parliament, or not; and that, in Default of Money in his Hands, he be authorized and obliged to dispolc of lo much of any Parliamentary Securities, which shall be> in, or first come to, his Hands, os will be sufficient to enable him to discharge the Deficiency due to the Company, and pay them the same in Money, without any Deduction from the Company.

8. That as for such Money as has been, or, on or before the 25 December 1715, shall be, paid into the Exchequer out of the Duties on Salt, above what may be sufficient to pay the Interest of unsubscribed Tallies 1710, and also out of the Duties on Candles, 8$c. Apprentices, which are at present applicable to the Payment of the Company’s Annuity, the ferae to be received by the Company weekly, out of the Exchequer; and be deducted out of the Quarter’s Annuity, which shall be due to the Company from the 25 December 1715 to the 25 March 1716.

By Order of the General Court,

39 July 1715. Ja. Bateman, Sub. Governor.

FURTHER Articles of Impeachment of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer.

Article I.

That whereas, in or about the Month of in the

Year 171 a dangerous and destructive Expedition hard been set on foot, and projected, under the Pretence of making a Conquest on the Possessions of the French King in North America; but with a real Design to promote his Interests, by weakening the Confederate Army in Flanders, and dissipating the Naval Force of this Kingdom; as well as for the fake of the private Interests, and corrupt Gain, of the Promoters of the said Expedition; he the said Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mor, being then One of her late Majesty’s Privy Council, and One of the Commissioners of her Majesty’s Treasury, was not only wanting in his Duty to her late Majesty, by wilfully and industriously absenting from the Meetings of other Persons then in high Trust under her Majesty, wherein the said Expedition was concerned; and by not advising her Ma-16

He the said Robert\Lsx\ of Oxford and Earl Mortimer, not regarding his Oath, or his high Trust, or the Laws of the Kingdom, did, most corruptly and scandalously combine with the said Matthew Prior for the defrauding her Majesty of very great Sums, under the Colour of his feid Employments in France; and, to that end, the said Earl did contrive, that the said Prior should be sent into France with the Character aforesaid, but without any settled Appointments or Allowances; but, in the stead and lieu thereof, he the said Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer did give the said Matthew Prior an unlimited Credit; and did promise to answer and pay such Bills as the said Prior should draw on him during his Residence in France.

Articles of Impeachment of High Treason, and other High Crimes and Misdemeanors, against Henry Viscount Bolingbrvke.

WHEREAS a Treaty of Alliance was made and concluded, on or about the Seventh Day of September One thousand Seven hundred and One, between Leopold then Emperor of Germany, his late Majesty King William the Third, of ever-glorious Memory, and their High Mighti-tiueffes the States General of the United Provinces, for repelling the Greatness of the common Danger, which threatened all Europe, from the Duke of Anjou's having taken Possession of the Monarchy of Spain; wherein it was, among other things, agreed, That, in case the said Confederates shall be forced to enter into a War, they
