Lord Boling- shall communicate their Designs to one another, as well in relation to the Actions of the War, as all other things 60 wherein the common Cause is concerned; and that it shall not be permitted to either Party, when the War is once begun, to treat of Peace with the Enemy, unlefe jointly, ana by a Communication of Councils: And in and by a defensive Treaty and Alliance, made and concluded in or dbout the Month of November One thousand Seven hundred and One, between his said late Majesty King William the Third and the States General, it was, among other things, expressly agreed, That, when the War is begun, the said Confederates shall act in Concert, according to the Seventh and Eighth Articles of the Treaty, of the Third of March 167^-, between England and;

and that no Peace, nor Truce or Suspension of Arms, shall be negotiated or made, but according to the Ninth and Tenth Articles of that Treaty; by which it was agreed, That when the Allies came once to open War, it shall be lawful for neither of them afterwards to come to any Cessation of Arms with him who shall be declared and proclaimed an Enemy, without it be done conjointly and with common Consent; and that no Negotiation of Peace shall be set on foot by one of the Allies, without the Concurrence of the other; and that each Ally shall continually, and from time to time, impart to the other every thing that passes in the said Negotiation: And in and by a Treaty, entered into and concluded on or about the Month of June 1703, between her late Majesty Queen Anne, of ever-blessed Memory, and the States General, it was, among other things, agreed, That all Treaties and Alliances, then subsisting between them, should be Renewed and confirmed: And whereas a long, bloody, and expensive, War had been carried on by her late Majesty, in ConjunQion with her said Allies, and other confederate Princes, against France and Spain, as well inRefentment of the Indignity offered to these Kingdoms, by their having acknowledged the Pretender King of these Realms, as for obtaining a just Satisfaction to his Imperial Majesty, and for the Preservation of the Protestant Religion, and the Balance and Liberties of Europe; and, from the great Sue-cedes with which it had pleased Almighty God to bless the Confederate Arms, they had just Reason to hope for an honourable, good, safe, and lasting Peace; and although the French King was encouraged, in or about the Month of April 1711, to make Proportions of Peace to her late Majesty, signed by Monsieur de , his Secretary of State; which her said Majesty having pleased to communicate to the Ministers of the States General, she did, however, graciously, declare, by Henry Viscount Bolingbroke, then Henry St. John Esquire, and One of her principal Secretaries of State, her Sentiments to them, That the said Propositions were too general; and, at the same time, the said Viscount did, in her Majesty’s Name, and by her special Command, give them her utmost and most solemn Assurances, That, m making Peace, as in making War, (he would act in perfect Concert with them; in which Sentiments the States concurring with her Majesty, reciprocal Assurances of mutual Confidence, lb necessary to prevent the Designs of the Enemy, were returned by them to her Majesty: notwithstanding which.

Article ill.

He the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke, then being One of her Majesty’s principal Secretaries of State, ana of her most honourable Privy Council; but, having entered into a most treacherous Confederacy with the Ministers and Emissaries of France, to frustrate the just Hopes and Expectations of her Majesty and her People, by dif-uniting the Confederacy at the most critical Juncture,-when they were ready to reap the Fruits of so many Triumphs over the common Enemy ? and most wickedly intending, as far as in him lay, to enable the French King, (o exhausted and vanquished as he had been on all Occasions, to carry his Designs, by a Peace glorious to him, and to the Ruin of the victorious Allies, and the Destruction of the Liberties of all Europe 1 and, having no Regard to the solemn Treaties her Majesty then flood engaged in, aor to the Honour or Safety of these Kingdoms, did, in 10

or about the Months of July or August in the Year of our Lord 1711, maliciously and wickedly from a most treacherous and pernicious Contrivance and Confederacy, with other evil-disposed Persons, then also of her Majesty’s Privy Council, to set on foot a private, separate, distio-nourable, and destructive, Negotiation of Peace between Great Britain and France, without any Communication thereof to her Majesty’s Allies, according to their said fe-verai Treaties; and was not only wanting in his Duty and Trust to her Majesty, by not opposing, and as far as was in his Power, by not advising her Majesty against going into any private, separate. Negotiation with Francebut, in Execution of his Purposes aforesaid, he the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke did advise her late Majesty to fend Mathew Prior Esquire directly to the Court of to make Propositions of Peace, without communicating the same to her Majesty’s Allies; and, accordingly, the said Mathew Prior, by the Advice and with the Privity of him the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke, and other false and evil Counsellors, in or about the Months of July or August in the Year of our Lord 1711, was sent, in a clandestine manner, from England to France, and did communicate the said Propositions of Peace to the Ministers of France', in which the particular Interests of Great,

as well as the common Interests of Europe, were fhume-fully betrayed; and, in Manifestation of his Design to exclude her Majesty’s Allies from their just Share in the said Negotiation, an express Article was inserted in the said Propositions, by the Privity and Advice of him the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke, That the Secret should be inviolably kept, till allowed to be divulged by the mutual Consent of both Parties; although the French King had, in the Propositions signed by Monsieur de , and transmitted in the Month of April preceding, offered to treat with the Plenipotentiaries of England and Holland alone,' or jointly with those of the Allies, at the Choice of England; By which treacherous and dangerous Advice, he the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke did not only contrive and set on foot a Negotiation of Peace, more advantageous to France than ever France itself had aiked; but thereby did put it into the Power of the common Enemy to create incurable Jealousies and Discords between her Majesty and her faithful Allies, and to destroy that Confidence which had so long, and so fuccelsfully, been cultivated between them, and which was so necessary for their common Safety.

Article 2d.

That the French King having, in or about the Months of August or September 1711, with the Privity and by the Contrivance of the said Viscount Bolingbroke, and others, lent over Monsieur Mefnager into England, to carry on a separate and clandestine Negotiation of Peace, he the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke did afterwards, in the said Month of September 1711, or thereabouts, secretly and unlawfully, and without any Colour of Authority, meet, confer, and treat, with the said Sieur Mefnager, on the Negotiations of Peace between Great Britain and;

and therein did advise and promote the making a private and separate Treaty, or Convention, on the said Subject of Peace between the said Crowns, without any Communication thereof to her Majesty’s Allies: And the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke did afterwards, in Violation of his Oath, and high Trust, falsly and treacherously advise her late Majesty to sign Powers to several Persons for concluding, on her behalfj a pernicious and destructive Treaty, or Convention, on the said Subject of Peace, with France; and, on or about the said 27th of September 1711, a dif-honourable, destructive, and fatal, Treaty, or Convention, was concluded and signed by the said Sieur Mefnager, on the Part of France, and by the Earl of Dartmouth and the said Viscount, being then Two of her Majesty’s principal Secretaries of State, and of her Privy Council, on the Part of her Majesty, by virtue only of a Warrant under her Majesty’s Sign Manual, under the Signet, directed to themselveSj but not countersigned, and without the lead Knowlege or Participation of the Allies; in which Treaty, the immediate Interests of Great Britain are given up

Article 6th.

That whereas her late Majesty Queen Anne, not only in pursuance of the Treaties ihe stood engaged in to her good Allies, and, in particular, to his Imperial Majesty, for the Recovery of the Monarchy of Spain to the House of Austria, thereby to preserve a due Balance of Power in Europe', but also, from her just Resentment against the Duke of Anjou, w ho then stiled himself King of Spain, and who, in Defiance of her Majesty’s Title to the Crown, had acknowledged the Pretender as King of/rratf;

and, on these just Foundations, her Majesty had, in Vindication of the Honour of the Crown, and in Justice to her People, at avail Expence of Blood and Treasure, and on the earned: and repeated Advices of her Parliament, prosecuted a vigorous War against the said Duke of Anjou; and whereas, in the Years of our Lord 1710, 1711, and 1712, the said open, bloody, and expensive War was carried on between her said late Majesty Queen Anne and the said Duke of Anjou, and during all the time aforesaid, the said War did continue, and for all that time, the said Duke of Anjou, and the Subjects of Spain adhere-ing to him, were Enemies of her late Majesty; he the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke, then being One of her Majesty’s principal Secretaries of State, and of her Privy Council, and a Subject of her said Majesty, not considering the Duty of his Allegiance, but hav ing withdrawn his true Obedience from her said late Majesty, did, at several times, in the said Years of our Lord 1710, 1711, and 171*, falsly, maliciously, wickedly, and traiterously, aid, help, assist, and adhere to, the said Duke of Anjou, then an Enemy to her said late Majesty, against her said Majesty; and, in Execution and Performance of his said Aiding, Helping, and Assisting, and Adhering, and in Confederacy and Combination with the then Enemies of her late Majesty, and with divers other wicked and evil-disposed Persons, did, at several times, in the Years aforesaid, advise and counsel the Enemies of her late Majesty, against her said Majesty; and, in such Counselling and Advising, did concert with them, and did promote, the yielding, and giving up Spain, and the West Indies, or some Part thereof, to the said Duke of Anjou, then in Enmity with her Majesty, against the Duty of his Allegiance, and the Law's and Statutes of this Realm.

All which Crimes and Misdemeanors were committed and done by him the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke, against our late Sovereign Lady the Queen, her Crown and Dignity, the Peace and Interest of this Kingdom, and in Breach of the several Trusts reposed in him the said Viscount: And he the said Henry Viscount Bolingbroke was One of her Majesty’s principal Secretaries of State, and One of her Privy Council, during the time that all and every the Crimes before let forth were done and committed.

Mr. Walpole, from the Committee of Secrecy, acquainting the House, That the Committee had, in Obedience to the Commands of the House, prepared Articles of Impeachment of High Treason, and other High Crimes and Misdemeanors, against James Duke of Ormond; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were once read throughout; and are as follows; viz.

Articles of Impeachment of High Treason, and other High Crimes and Misdemeanors, against James Duke of Ormonde.

Article 1.

THAT whereas James Duke of Ormonde, in or about the Month of April 1712, being appointed General of the Forces in the Netherlands of her late Majesty Queen Anne, with Orders to prosecute the War against France with all possible Vigour, in conjunction with her said Majesty’s Allies; and having, by her said Majesty’s Directions, and in her Name, given her said Allies the most lblemn Assurances to that Purpose; was thereupon admitted into the Counsels, and made privy to the most secret Designs, of the Generals of the Confederate Army against the common Enemy, and of the Measures they thought the most proper to carry on the War with Succels: And whereas, in the said Year 1712, the said War was carried on between her laid late Majesty Queen Anne and the said French King; and, during all the said Year, the War did continue, and, for all that time, the said French King, and his Subjects, were Enemies of her late Majesty; he the said James Duke of Ormonde, then General of her Majesty’s Army, and a Subject of her Majesty, not considering the Duty of his Allegiance, but having withdrawn his true and due Obedience from her said late Majesty, and Affection from his Country, did, during the said War, fallly, maliciously, wickedly, and traiteroully, aid, help, assist, and adhere to, the said French King, against her said late Majesty; and in Execution of his laid aiding, helping, assisting, and adhering, maliciously, fallly, and traiteroully, contrary to the Daty of his Allegiance, and the Laws and Statutes of this Realm, did, on or about the 26th Day of May 1712, fend private Intelligence and Information to Marechal Vtllars, then an Enemy to her said late Majesty, and General of the French King’s Army against her Majesty and her Allies, of a March the Army of her said Majesty, and of her Allies, was then going to make, and of the Design of the said Army in making that March.

Article the Second.

That whereas, in or about the Month of May 1712, a Vo j» 18.

traiterous Design was carried on between Henry John Esquire, then One of her said late Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, and other evil-disposed Persons, and the Ministers of France, to defeat the just Expectations of >the great Advantages over the common Enemy her Majesty and the Nation had then Reason to hope for from the great Superiority of the Confederate Forces in the Netherlands; to obtain which, very large Sums of Money had been chearfully contributed by Parliament; and, to that End, the said St. John had given

secret Assurances to the French Ministers, that her Majesty’s General in the Netherlands, though under the most solemn Engagements to act vigorously in Concert with the Allies, should not act against France; and had also engaged the said James Duke of Ormonde to concur in the said wicked Purpose: Which evil Practices of the said Henry St. John and others, when they were lirft suspected, giving the greatest Alarm to the Ministers of the Allies, the Parliament, and to the whole Kingdom; and being thereupon openly disavowed and denied by all the Conspirators in the most publick manner; he the said James Duke of Ormonde, in order to disguise and conceal from her said late Majesty, and the whole Kingdom, the said traiterous Designs then carrying on by the said Henry St. John, and other false Traitors to her Majesty and their Country, in Aid and Comfort of the French King, then in open War with, and an Enemy of, her said Majesty, did, by his Letter of the 2,f,th of May 1712, to the said Henry St. John, then her Maj city's Principal Secretary of State, called his publick Letter, because prepared, and intended to be read, before her said Majesty and her Council, wicked, fallly, and treacheroyfly, abuse and impose upon her said late Majesty and her Council, by affirming and declaring the rein, That, if he found an Opportunity to bring the Enemy to a Battle, he should not decline it; although, by a private Letter, writ by the said James Duke of Ormonde, of the same Date, and to the said Henry St. John, designed to be read by the said Henry St. John and the said Conspirators only, he the said James Duke of Ormonde did, on the contrary, wickedly promise and engage, that he would not attack or molest the French Army, or engage in any Siege against France.

Article the Third.

That he the said James Duke of Ormonde, in or about the Month of Jane 1712, being at that time General of her Majesty's Forces against France, and a Subject of her said Majesty, not considering the Duty of his Allegiance, but having altogether withdrawn the cordial Love and true Obedience which every faithful Subject otoed to her said Majesty, and devoting himself to (the Service of France, and designing to give Aid and Comfort to the French King and his Subjects, then in open War with, and Enemies to, her said late Majesty; in Violation of the many Treaties of Alliance between Great Britain and several other Princes and States for carrying on the War against France, and of the said late Queen’s Instructions to him, on or about the 7th of April 1712, under the Sign Manual in pursuance thereof, and of the solemn Declarations he had but lately before, by her said Majesty’s Command, and inber Name, made to the Penfiortary of Holland, and the Generals of the Confederate Army, to pufti on the War with all possible Vigour; and also in open and manifest Violation of the last Orders sent to him in a Letter from the said Henry St. John, on or about the 7th of June 1712, whereby he the said James Duke of Ormonde was directed to make no Cessation of Arms with the French, unless the Articles demanded by her Majesty, and expressly mentioned and let down in the said Letter, as the Conditions for the said Cessation, should be complied with by France, and whereby he the said James Duke of Ormonde was likewise furtherjexprefly directed and told. That in case the Conditions therein mentioned were not complied with by France, that then he was entirely free from Restraint, and at Liberty to take all reasonable Measures in his Power for annoying the Enemy, and at full Liberty of acting against France-, did, on or about the 25th of June aforesaid, fallly, maliciously, wickedly, and traiter-

Article the Fourth.

That he the said James Duke of Ormonde did not only wickedly and falsly affirm to the Generals of the Confederate Army, and the States Deputies, That his said Refu-fal to act any longer against France, and to cover the Siege of Quefnoy, was in pursuance of Instructions he had received for that Purpose; but also, to induce the said Generals of the Confederate Army, and the Stales Deputies, to comply with his Proposal to them to abandon the said Siege, he the said James Duke of Ormonde did wickedly represent their Compliance therein as the most effectual Way to induce her laid late Majesty to take care of the said Confederates Interest at the Peace; whereby he the said James Duke of Ormonde did, in effect, threaten her said Majesty’s good Friends and Allies, that, unlel's they would dishonourably abandon an Enterprize undertaken by common Consent, and thereby lave a strong Fortress, and a numerous Garison, of the Enemy, they were not to expect, that her Majesty would take care of their Interests at the general Peace.

Article the Fifth.

That he the said James Duke of having re-

ceived a Letter, dated on or about the 14th of July 1712, from the said Marechal Pillars, the French General, desiring to be informed what Troops remained with the Confederate Army, or whatTroops and Generals marched off from them with him the said Duke; and declaring at the same time, that the Reason of that Inquiry was, in order to fall upon and attack the said Confederate Army; he the said James Duke of Ormonde, on or about the 16th Day of July 1712, did traiterously and wickedly, contrary to the Duty of a true and faithful Subject, and contrary to his Allegiance, and the Laws and Statutes of this Realm, aid, help, assist, and adhere to, the said French King, and his Subjects, against her said late Majesty, and then in open War with, and Enemies to, her said late Majesty; and, in Execution of his said aiding, helping, assisting, and adhering, he the said James Duke of Ormonde, on or about the said 16th Day of July 1712, did traiterously fend

secret Intelligence to the said Marechal Villars the General of the French Army, of the Number of the Troops that had left the said Confederate Army, and also of the March the said Confederate Army had that Morning made.

Article the Sixth.

And whereas he the said James Duke of Ormonde had received Advice, that the States General, in or about the Month of October 1712, had formed a Design to surprise"

and take the Towns of Newport and Funtes, or one of them, then in the Possession of the French King; that he the said James Duke of Ormonde, intending to ftiiengthen the Hands of the common Enemy, by defeating the said Enterprize, did, on or about the 21st Day of October 1712, in a Letter to the said Henry St. John, then Viscount Bolingbroke, wickedly and basely suggest to and advise her said late Majesty to fend secret Intelligence -of, and to betray, the said Counsels and Designs of her good and faithful Allies the Statos General to the French King, then in War with, and an Enemy to, her Majesty; and did further, wickedly and shamefully, suggest the Means of putting the said Treachery in Execution, by giving private Intelligence of the Design to the said Marechal Pillars.

All which Crimes and Misdemeanors were committed and done by him the said James Duke of Ormonde against our late Sovereign Lady the Queen, her Crown and Dignity, the Peace and Interest of this Kingdom, and i« Breach of the several Trusts reposed in him the said Duke: And lie the said James Duke of Ormonde was General of her Majesty’s Forces in the Netherlands, and One of her Privy Council, during the time that all and every the Crimes before set forth were done and committed.

The first Article being read a Second time;

And the Question being put, That the said Article bfe one of the Articles of Impeachment against James Duke of Ormonde;

The house divided.

Mr. Liddall reported from the Committee, to w'hom America* the Petition of the Agent of Carolina, in America, and Colonies^ several Merchants trading thither, for and on behalf of themselves, and the miserable Inhabitants of that distressed Province, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Vf here the same was read; and is as follows; vis.

That the said Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of the House, met several times: And, upon.

Examination of the Matter of the said Petition, do find;

That the Dangers to which the Province of South Carolina is exposed, by the late Invasion of the Indians, are such as require a speedy and efteflual Relief; the Inhabitants fit to bear Arms not being Fifteen hundred or Two thousand Men; and the Indians are said to be upwards of Twelve thousand: That, the Proprietors not being able, at their own Charges, either to fend the necessary Succours for the prquent Relief of the said Province, or to support it under the like for the future, your Committee submit, in what manner it may be most proper to preserve and maintain this lb valuable a Province, which is a Frontier of the British Plantations' on the Continent:

But, unless some speedy, Supply of Men, Arms, and Ammunition, be sent for their Relief, the w hole Province must inevitably be ruined; to the great Prejudice of his MajestyVSubjects, and the Trade of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his.

Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to direct,

That such Relief may be lent to Carolina, as his Majesty shall judge uecessary for the Preservation of that Colony.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

Colonel Bladen reported, from the Committee, to whom Publick the Petitions of James Campbell Esquire, and of the Com- ?ebj® iiiiftioners of Equivalent, were referred, the Matter, as it bco an ‘ appeared to them; which lie read in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the fame, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, were read; and are as follow; vi

The. Committee having taken into Consideration the Matters of the said Petition of Campbell, of

London, Merchant, Agent lor the publick Creditors of Scotland

It appeared, That, by the Fifteenth Article of the Treaty of Union between England and Scotland, it is agreed. That all the publick Debts of the Kingdom of Scotland, as should be adjusted by that present Parliament, shall be paid out of the several Sums by the said Treaty payable to Scotland, by way of Incrcalcand Equivalents:

That, by an Act, of the last Parliament of Scotland, intituled, An Act concerning the publick Debts, the publick Debts of Scotland were adjusted.'

That, by an Act, of the First Parliament of Great Britain, intituled, An Act for further directing the Payment of the Equivalent-money, the Commissioners of Equivalent were impowered and directed to grant transferrable Debentures for the publick Debts, lb adjusted, to the several Persons intitled thereto, with Interest at the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum pet' Annum from the 24th of June 1708.

Sir Patrick Johnston, One of the Commissioners of Equivalent, attended the Committee; and, being examined, declared, That the said Commissioners of Equivalent had ifiucd out transferrable Debentures, beating

Interestat the Rate of Fire Pounds from the 34th of June 1708, pursuant to the aforesaid Act: That, by an Act of the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, an Act to acquit and discharge the Commissioners of Equivalent, 8$c. the publick Debts of Scotland, which, on the 24th of June 1714, remained

unsatisfied, and which were adjusted and certified, pursuant to the Direction of the several Acts of Parliament therein recited, are declared to amount to the Sum of 230,308/. 9*. 10 $d.;and the Commissioners of Equivalent are thereby directed and required to issue out new Debentures for the said Sum to the several Persons proportionally and respectively intitled thereto, with Ir>-terest at the Rate of Five Pounds per Cent, per Amwm from the said 24th of June 1714, payable out of the first and read left of the Monies which either are, or shall become due to Scotland by way of Equivalent, according to the Agreements in the Treaty of Union.

The said Sir Patrick Johnston acquainted the Committee, That the Commissioners of Equivalent have proceeded to issue out new Debentures, pursuant to the Direction of the said Act of Parliament, of the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty i And the Petitioner, James Campbell, also produced to the Committee several new Debentures, which have been issued by the Commissioners of Equivalent accordingly.

That, from the find Act of Parliament, of the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty, and from the Acknowledgment of the said Sir Patrick Johnston, who was examined to that Effect, it appeared to the Committee, That the publick Creditors of Scotland have not received any Part of the said principal Sum of 230,308/. 9 to^d. nor of the Intereli due thereupon.

That, by the 15th Article of the Treaty of Union, it is provided that the Commissioners of Equivalent (halt keep Rooks, containing Accounts of the Amount of the Equivalents; and how the same shall have been disposed of from time to time; which may be inspected by any of the Subjects who shall desire the fame.

The said Sir Patrick Johnston, and Patrick Campbell Esqulre, Treasurer to the Commissioners of Equivalent, being examined, acknowledged, That the said Commissioners had not kept such Books, with the Amounts of the Equivalents, to be inspected by the Creditors, or other Subjects of Scotland, as the Treaty of Union requires; because the said Commissioners themselves had not received the Accounts from the Officers of the Revenue, certifying the Equivalents growing due, as the said Act for further directing the Payment of the Equivalent-money appoints; whereby, only, proper Books might have been kept for that Purpose: And that,

U pon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioner, James Campbell Esquire, has fully proved the Allegations of his Petition, in behalf of the publick Creditors of Scotland.

After which, the Committee proceeded upon the Petition of the Commissioners of Equivalent, which was also referred to them: And,

It appeared to the Committee, upon reading the 15th Article of Union, with the Minutes of the Treaty, and Other Accounts thereto annexed, published by Authority;

That Scotland should have an Equivalent for what die Subjects thereof should he charged towards Payment of tire Debts of England, in all particulars whatsoever; viz. 398,085/. 10*. for such Parts of the Customs and Excifo, with which that Kingdom was to be charged upon the Union, as would be applicable to tire Payment of the said Debts of England, according to the Proportions which the then present Customs in Scotland, being 30,000l. per Annum, did bear to the Customs in England, computed at *>34!>559/- per Annum', and the then present Excises in Scotland, being 33,500l. per Annum, did bear to the Excises in England, computed at 947,602/. per Annum:

And, in regard the said Revenues would improve beyond the before-mentioned annual Values thereof, of

A. 1715.

which no Estimate could then be made, and for which a proportionable Equivalent ought to be asrfwered to Scotland; therefore, after the Union, there should ho an Account kept of the said Duties arising in Scotland, to the end it might appear what ought to be answered to Scotland as an Equivalent for such Proportion of the said Increase, as should be applicable to the Payment of the Debts of England:

That, for the more effectual answering the several Ends mentioned in this Article, after the Union, the whole Increase of the Revenues of Customs and Excise, over and above the annual Produce of the said respective Duties, as above stated, should go, and be applied, for the Terra of Seven Years, to the Uses hereafter mentioned; for Payment of the publick Debts of Scotland; and towards encouraging and promoting the Fisheries, and such other Manufactories and Improvements, in Scotland, as might most conduce to the general Good of the United Kingdom; and that, upon the said Account, there should be answered to Scotland annually, from the End of Sevea Years after the Union, an Equivalent in proportion to such Part of the said Increase, as should be applicable to the Debts of England: And generally,1

That an Equivalent should be answered to Scotland for such Parts of the English Debts as Scotland might there-. after become liable to pay, by reason of the Union, other than such, for which Appropriations had then been made by Parliament in England, of the Customs and Excise; in respect of which Debts, Equivalents are herein before provided:

That, at the time of the Treaty, certain Branches of the Customs and Excise of England were applicable for the Civil List; others appropriated to Perpetuity, or for a long Term of Years, for Payment of Debts; others were to continue for a short period of Time, for the same Purpose; and others were unappropriated, and applicable to the publick Service; the Value of all which respective Branches was taken from a Medium of the Produce in the Three Years immediately preceding the Treaty; and the Parts of the Scots Customs and Excise, applicable to the several Purposes aforesaid, were regulated by the Proportions above mentioned, as may appear by the aforesaid Minutes and Accounts of the Coonnissioners for the Treaty of Union.

A Petition of Stephen Locke, William Smith, John Insolveni Peachy, James Bodford, Edward Keddon, Philip Titcher, P«rfons Benjamin Maynard, John Marsh, Samuel Rout, Elias naud, Trijlram Roberts, Stephen Ftilford senior, Robert Creichton, John May, Stephen Ful/ord junior, John Ful-ford, Alexander Calder, John Hamond senior, John Ha-mondjunior, John Atwick, Joseph Fox, Benjamin , and Ralph Longland, Tradesmen and Inhabitants of and in the Borough of Gosport, in the County of Southampton, in behalf of themselves, and several Hundreds of other trading Persons and Inhabitants of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, for many Years past, very large Credit has been given by the trading Inhabitants of the said Borough to great Numbers of Seamen, as well Inhabitants as others, that have, from time to time, been employed in the Royal Navy, when they, the said Seamen, have been without Payment of their Wages for sundry Years; w ithout which Credit, neither they themselves, nor their Families, could have subsisted; and, by reason whereof, there is actually due, at this time, to the Petitioners, from Seamen, divers and ~ sundry Sums of Money, amounting to several Thousand.

Pounds: That such Credit has been ul’ually advanced by the Petitioners to Seamen, upon the Security of Assignments on their Pay and Wages due for their Service performed on board such Ships to which they did or do belong; that being the only Means and Power they have, of securing and discharging the Debts by them so contracted: That, even at this very time, the Families of several Hundred Seamen, now in his Majesty’s Ships abroad, are actually sup ported by the Petitioners, upon the bare Expectation of having Securities, in the manner before-mentioned, from the said Seamen, at their Return:

That if the Wages, 8$c. of such Seamen, w ho are indebted to the Petitioners, should be exempted from Payment of their Debts, by any Law to be made and enacted for that Purpose, it will not only destroy the Property, and utterly ruin the Petitioners, and many other Traders in these Parts; the major Part of whose Substance has been applied to those Uses; but will also very highly affect

Insolvent A Petition of Francis Benjamin

Armband Orlebar Fletcher, Jojhrn Green, and Samuel Green, w as

Navy.*1" presented to the House, and read, letting forth. That

the Petitioners having given large Credit to Officers in the Army, to supply them -with Necessaries, until l'uch time as their Pay became due; otherwise great Numbers of them could not in any manner have subsisted, who were to be paid as their Pay became due; several of the said Officers agreed with their Creditors to pay them by certain Sums each Muster-day; when they have been abroad, they have revoked that Agreement, and would allow nothing towards their Debts; should the Officers be relieved by the Bill now depending, from paying their just Debts, it tvould be a very great Hardship upon Persons that have credited them, to be Sufferers, whilst many of the said Officers are spending their Creditors Monies, in a very profligate manner: The many Difficulties and Hardships the trading Part of this Nation hath lain under, by bad Debts and large Taxes, during the late Wars: It is hoped they may not be Sufferers by the Persons they have helped to support, when there was never any Probability of their ever being paid, but out of their Pay; which they are as well able to comply with now, as when they came to be credited: And praying to take their same into Consideration, to prevent their being deprived of their just Debts; and that they may be beard against the said Bill, by themselves, or Counsel, before it passeth into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the Relief of insolvent Officers, Soldiers, and Seamen, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, before the Committee, thereupon, if they think fit.

The House proceeded, according to Order, to the fur- Taunton ther hearing the Merits of the Election for the Borough Heftnm, of Taunton:

And the Counsel on both Sides were called in:

And the Sitting Members Counsel examined several Witnesses, to justify several other of the Voters, which. the Petitioners Counsel had objected against; and also insisted, That all such Persons as were of that Part of the Parish of St.Mary Magdalen, in Taunton, which lies without the Borough, and come into the Borough, and boil a Pot, before the Teste oi the Writ for electing Members to serve in Parliament, have a Right to vote at such Elections; and examined several Witnesses touching the fame:

And the Petitioners Counsel examined Witnesses, in Contradiction thereof:

And the Counsel on both Sides were heard thereto.

And then they withdrew.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put.

That Persons living in that Part of the Parish of Mary Magdalen, in the Town of Taunton, which lies out of the Limits of the Borough of Taunton, who, at any time before the issuing Writs for calling a new Parliament, take a Room, and boil a Pot, within the said Borough of Taunton, do thereby acquire a Right of voting in the Election of Members, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough;

It passed in the Negative.

The Counsel were called in again; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the said Reiblution.

And the Sitting Members Counsel proceeded to examine Witnesses, to justify other Voters which the Petitioners Counsel had objected against.

And then the Counsel were directed to withdraw.

A PETITION of Richard Partridge, in behalf of the Inhabitants of the Colony of Rhode and ProvidencePlantation, in America, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That whereas there is a Bill for the Regulation of the Charter and Proprietary Governments in America, which, the Petitioner is informed, will affect the said Colony of Rhode Island (for which your Petitioner is concerned:) That thereby their Charter may become void: That the said Inhabitants having their Charter granted them by King Charles the Second, whereby they have the Privilege of choosing their Governor, Council, 8$c. and have defended the Colony ever since, at their own Expence, from the French and Indian Enemy, and always behaved themselves with great Submission to the Crown of Great Britain, and never in the least (that the Petitioner hath heard of) given any Suspicion of their abuling those Privileges they have been favoured with from their Sovereign: And praying, That a Clause may be admitted, to save the Rights of the said Government; or to hear the Petitioner, by Counsel, in their behalf.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for the better Regulation of the Charter and Proprietary Governments in America, and of his Majesty s Plantations, is committed: And that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the Committee, thereupon, if he think fit.

Mr. Walpole reported from the Committee of Secrecy, That the said Committee having, pursuant to their Orders and Powers given to them by this House, proceeded to examine Thomas Harley Esquire, who was sworn by such Members of the said Committee as are Justices of Peace for the County of Middle fax, and City of Westminster; and the Committee conceiving, that the said Mr. Harley had very much prevaricated in his Examination, the said Committee hacl directed, That some Extracts of Letters, relating to the said Mr. Harley, which gave Occasion to the said Examination; and likewise a Copy of the Depo-lition of Mr. Harley; should be laid before the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read: And the said Extracts of Letters, and Deposition, are as follows; viz.

Extract of a Letter from Mr. John, to the Lords Plenipotentiaries at Utrecht, 16° Februarii 1

THO’ I have a great deal more to say, in order to explain clearly to your Lordships the present Situation of the Queen’s domestick Affairs, and the Measures which lhe proposes your Lordships should pursue towards effecting your great Work, under all the Difficulties which are thrown in the Way, that can be contained in the Com-pals of a reasonable Letter; yet I should, by this Messenger, have entered into all that Detail, had not the Ile-solution been taken, of finally inlirufting Mr. Harley on Monday, in the View of dispatching him on

It were to be wished, that this Gentleman could have been lboner lent both to Utrecht and to Hanover; but the Hurry which we have been for some time in is inexpressible; and he was too useful to be spared, till the House of Commons wasperfeftly secured to the Queen’s Interest, and to the Measures of Peace: I think, I may say, that they are absolutely to now.

Your Lordships will have this Matter fully opened to you by Mr. Harley.

Extract of a Letter from the Lords Plenipotentiaries to Mr. Secretary St.John, 50 March 1712, N. S.

YOUR Favour, of the 16th pall, under your own Hand, give us Hopes of seeing Mr. Harley here very loon; and of receiving by him such’ Orders as may enable us to fix on something more certain than hitherto we could do.

Extra# of a Letter from Mr. St. John to Monfieurrfe Torcy Secretary of State to the French King, the 4th of March 17-^, O. S.

I should be ashamed, Sir, to have fb long deferred answering your Letters, if I did not believe I was able to allege, in my Justification, a good Reason; and which you will not disapprove: In a word, I was willing to write to you with Certainty; and, for that End, I was obliged to fray till the Ministers of the Emperor, and of the lte-publick of Holland, had more openly shewn their Game; till the necessary Dispositions were made among our People at home; and, in short, till the Queen had taken the only llesolution, which could bring us, in a little time, to a good and solid Peace.

I have now the Satisfaction to tell you, that this Resolution is taken; and that Mr. Harley will set out this Evening, or Tomorrow Morning, with the final I aft ructions of the Queen to her Plenipotentiaries.

You will give me Leave to refer myself to the Sieur Gaultier, to explain to you more at large the Subje# of this Gentleman's Commission; and what the Queen hopes his most Christian Majesty will do, to co-operate with her.

Extract of a Letter from Mr. St. John to the Lords Plenipotentiaries, 2b* March 1712.

Mr. Harley is, I make no Doubt, long before this, with your Lordships; and I hope he has fully explained the Queen's Defifes and Views to you; at least he is as amply instructed in them, as I am able to inform him: The Conduct of this Matter is in so good Hands, that I am hopeful an answerable Event may be expected.

Extra# of a Letter from the Lords Plenipotentiaries to Mr. St. John, 8° April 1712.

OUR lafi, of the 6th, acquainted you, that some People had been disappointed, that Day, in their Expectations of breaking this Congress; which we hope may be carried on, and produce the good Effects intended.

That Evening, after we had received ample Informations from Mr. Harley, and all’o spoken with Mr. Gaultier, we had a long Conference with the French Plenipotentiaries, upon the Project that was sent you the 22d; w hereof we again iuclofe a Copy, with such Remarks, as, after all we could urge, the French Ministers insisted on.

The Fifteen per Cent, they w ill by no means allow to extend to other Goods than l'uch as come into Spain, in order to be transported into America.

Mr. Harley thinks it may be requisite to let fall that whole Pretension, and settle Commerce on the Foot it stood in the time of King Charles the lid of and

that the only Use w-e need make of the Fifteen per Cent. is to get something for it another Way; which we shall be glad to hear from you; for, in that Cafe, our Work with the Dutch will become a good deal ealier.

Copy of the Examination of Thomas Harley Esquire, taken before the Right honourable Hugh Bofcawen Esquire, Comptroller of his Majesty’s Houshold, and one of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the County of Middltjejc, at the (Committee of Secrecy.

THE F.xaminant laith, That when he was first sent abroad, in or about March 1 ~x^-, he w-as lent by the Queen’s express commands, w ho was pleased to speak, herl'clf, very particularly to him: That her Majesty, ordered the Secretary of State to make such Powers . as were necessary to be given to him, but would make Vol. 18.

it ealy to him, and without any Formality: That di- Committee regions were given for full Powers, which this Exatni-nant left in the Office, where he thought they would be CondudL most fate: That he never received any Powers, nor ever few them; but, at his own Choice, went abroad without Powers: That the Queen ordered, That this Examinant should have an Account of the State of Affairs, to be communicated by him to such Persons as he was to discourse with abroad: That he received, from several Offices, several Papers, relating to the Revenue, and other Matters, touching the then Situation of Affairs; from which the Queen was pleased to order him to inform himself as well as he could, that he might be able to explain himself when he went; and in particular, when he came to die Hague, he was to give the Pensionary an Account of the State of Affairs, and to use the be it Arguments he could, to liaften the Peace: But he does not know whether, he has any of those Papers now by him; and does not remember, that he had any particular Instructions for himself, except from those Papers, but what he received from the Queen’s own Mouth; the Particulars whereof he cannot at present charge his Memory with, except as above-mentioned: That he did not produce, at the Hague, or at Utrecht, any credential Letters from the Queen, or any of her Ministers: That he had no Orders to transa# or negotiate any thing relating to the Peace, with any foreign Minister; and that he did not transact, in any manner, with any foreign Minister: That he did not, to his Knowledge, carry over any Plan, Proje#, or Scheme of a Peace; and that he did not traqfa# any thing at Utrecht with Abbot Gaultier, nor confer with him either there or before he went from England: That he does not remember he had any Orders from the Queen, or any of her Ministers, relating to the Fifteen Pounds per Cent.; and that he doth not remember, that he did signify any Orders to the Queen’s Plenipotentiaries concerning it; and that he does not remember any thing at all about the Fifteen Pounds per Cent.: That he staid in till he

had the Queen’s Order to go forward, signified by the Secretary of State: That he received several Letters whilst he was abroad; but from whom, in particular, he cannot remember; and that he wrote several Letters; but to whom he cannot remember; and that he doth not know', that he has cither Copies, or Originals, of any Letters that he either wrote or received: That he had no settled Allowance or Appointment; but, at his first going over the first time, he spent his own Money, which the Queen was afterward pleased to order should be allow ed him: That, the first time he went abroad, he received under Three thousand Pounds; and, in both Journies together, he received, in all, about Five thousand Five hundred Pounds; and that what he received, the Queen ordered for his Expences, and the Trouble he had been at: That nobody negotiated any Money for him upon the publick Account, but Mr. Decker', and that he does not remember, that he had any publick Money, but for his own Expence; which did not, in the Whole, exceed the Sum of Five thousand Five hundred Pounds.

T. Harley.

Jurat 21° Junii 1715°, coram me,

Hugh Boscawcn.

the Petition of several Bay and Say-weavers in Colchejla', in the County of Essex, in behalf of themselves, and several Hundreds of the same Trade; and to whom the Petition of many of the Baymakers of the said Borough, and all other Baymakers of the said Town, together with their Sons and Apprentices; were referred; the Matter of Fast, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Plate, and after-

times paid in Goods, instead of ready. Money; and that, he believed, ibme of the Weavers might live in the Bay-makers Houses; ami fewer Bays would be made, if the unlawful Helps were taken away; for that many Persons hath left off their Trade, and the Markets are over-stocked.

Mr. Abbot laid, he had been a Dealer in the Bay Trade 20 Years; and that he never knew any of the Weavers want Work, of one fort or another; and, since the Making of the By-law, the Trade has been much improved; for, often, a Baymaker has 40 or 50 Pounds with an Apprentice; which, if the Trade was open, would be loft: And, as another Instance, that there arc great Quantities of Bays made, more than the Markets can take off;

He further said. That the Weavers often leave out Three or Four Pound of Yarn out of a Bay; which occasions the Badness of their Goods; and is one chief Reason, why the Bays, made at a Place called Boching, within 12 Miles of Colchester are so good: But owned, that the

Weavers were paid sometimes in Goods, instead of ready Money; and that the Trade of Booking was open; but the Booking People dread an open Trade at Colchester, because their Men will run away from one Town to another: He further said. That he had often paid Two Shillings in a Bay more than other Places; because other People would take their Men away: He further said, Good Sums of Money were given with Apprentices, before the By-law was made.

The Committee asking some of the Witnesses, Whether there were not several of the said Baymakers, who had signed the Petition for the By-law to be continued, that came in by a free and open Trade; they all owned, That they had.

Mr. Dubourgh said, He had been a factor for the

Baymakers about Six or Seven Years; and that there is several Hundred Pieces of Bays in his Custody, more than the Markets can take off; and if the Trade should be open, and more Goods made, they must rot in the Hall.

That it appears to this Committee, That, till the Year 1707, the Trade of Baymaking was not reltrained to such Persons only as had served their Apprenticeship to Bay-makers; but was free to all who had served their Apprenticeship to any other Branch of the Woollen Manufacture there.

And that, upon the whole Matter, -the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of the said By-law of the Governors of the Dutch Bay-hall in Colchester, made in the Year 1707, as teftrains the Making of Bays to such as have served Apprenticeships to the Baymakers only, is highly detrimental to that Branch of the Woollen Manufacture.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, by means of the above-mentioned By-law, and by the ill Practices of some of the Baymakers in the said Town of Colchester, the poor Weavers have been grieve-oully oppressed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the said Weavers Relief, by giving free Liberty to all Persons, who had served their Apprenticeships to any Part of the Woollen Manufacture in Colchester, to work at their said Trades, and at the Making of Bays within the said Town; with proper Limitations and Restrictions relating to the said Dutch Bay-hall.

The Two First of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Weavers Relief, by giving free Liberty to the Persons who have served their Apprenticeships to any Part of the Woollen Manufacture in Colchester, to work at their said Trades, and at the Making of Bays, within the said Town; with proper Limitations and Restrictions relating to the Dutch Bay-hall: And that Sir Isaac Rcbow, Mr.

lieysham, Mr. Dockminicque, Mr. Ducane, and Mr.

Broderick do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Town and County of Southampton, and other trading Inhabitants of the fame, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Town of Southampton is a Sea Port Town; and that, during the last Ten Years of the late War with France, Brigadier Borrs Regiment of Marines was quartered there; and the Officers and Soldiers belonging to the fame, divers whereof became

Inhabitants there, and had Families, were trusted by the Petitioners with considerable Sums of Money, for the Support of themselves and Families, and other Necefl’aries:

That the find Regiment was broke in the said Town, soon after the Conclusion of the Peace; and then all Accounts between the said Officers, Soldiers, and the said Petitioners, were adjusted and settled, in the Presence of the Commissioners who disbanded the said Regiment; and, for the Repayment of the several and respective Sums due to the said Petitioners, amounting to several Thousand Pounds, the said Officers and Soldiers could give no other Securities, but Assignments on their Pay and Wages due for their Service in the said Regiment; which the Petitioners were forced to accept; That, by reason the said Town of Southampton being a Sea Port Town, it has been the Residence and Abode of divers Seamen, and their Families, who have had nothing to subsist, but their Pay and Wages for their Service in the Royal Navy; wherefore the Petitioners have trusted them with considerable Sums of Money, as well to fit themselves out to Sea, as to support and maintain their Wives and Children in their Absence; without which, they must have been reduced to the greatest Want; and, at their Return, all the Security they could give for the just Debts they then owed, was by Assignments of their Pay for their Service performed:

That, if the Pay and Wages of such Officers, Soldiers, and Seamen, who are indebted to the said Petitioners, should be exempted from the Payment of their just Debts by any Law to be made for that Purpose, it will not only bring the Petitioners to Poverty and Want, but also very highly affect the Trade of the said Town of,

and other Sea Port Towns, the major Part of whose Stock and Substance have been necessarily applied to the Uses before-mentioned: And praying, That we may be heard, by our Counsel, against the Bill for the Relief of insolvent Officers, Soldiers, and Seamen.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the Relief of insolvent Officers, Soldiers, and Seamen, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Insolv.n* Council of the City of Rochester, in the County of Kent, Perw>ns and of other Tradesmen and Inhabitants of the said City, and of the Towns of Chatham and Strood, and other adja-c:nt Places, on behalf of themselves, and several Hundred more of the Inhabitants and Tradesmen of the said City,

Towns, and Places, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners Trading and Dealing, during the late War, was chiefly with the Sea Officers and Seamen, and with the Marine Officers and Soldiers; and their Dealing and Trading still is very much with the Commission and Warrant Officers of die Navy, and other the Petty Officers and Seamen thereof; and, by reason of such Officers and Men being at Sea, and the Length of Time they have been unpaid, the Petitioners have been forced to credit them, and their Wives and Families, with all manner of Necessaries and Provisions; and by that means the said Officers, Soldiers, and Seamen, have contrafted great Debts with the Petitioners; iufomuch that all the Petitioners Substance is intrusted to them; and the Petitioners, and their Families, will be undone, should they lose their said Debts: That many of the said Officers, both by Land and Sea, have, by their profuse living abroad, wasted and (pent their Pay, which ought to have paid their just Debts at home contrafted; yet, by Frugality and good Management, may be in a Capacity of paying the same out of their future Pay, if not discharged from the same by the Bill for the Relief of insolvent Officers, Soldiers, and Seamen; which Bill, the Petitioners apprehend, will be greatly to their Prejudice, and tend to the utter Ruin of many of them, should the same pass into a Law: And praying, That they may be he heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, before it paifes.

Pozclet reported, That the Managers had been at the Conference: And that the Earl of Clarendon managed the same on the Part of the Lords; and acquainted the Managers on the Part of the Commons,' That the Lords have agreed to feme of the Amendments, made by this House, to the said Bill; and, as to One Amendment, that the Lords bad agreed to the lame, with an Amendment; to which Amendment they desire the Concurrence of this House; but that, as to the other Amendments, made by this House, to the said Bill, the Lords had disagreed to them; and they gave their Rea-fons for disagreeing to the same; which Realons the Lord William Powlctt read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

The Lords disagree to the Commons Amendment, Prese 15. line 31.;

Because they arc of Opinion, That the Word " only* answers the true Intent of the Bill; which is to bind only such Right as may be claimed under the Marriage Articles, mentioned in the Bill; and net such other Right as the Persons claiming under the Articles, or some of them, may possibly have by any other means not taken Notice of in the Bill.

The Lords disagree to the Amendment, Press 24.

Line 7.;

Because they are of Opinion, That the Words, " equally, Share and Share alike," will not agree with the Words following, in the Bill; viz. " in such Proportions, and " at such Times, as the said George and Robert

" Mitchell, or the Survivor of them, or the Executors " or Administrators of such Survivor, fit all think fit to *' appoint; which Words both Houses had agreed to.

The Lords disagree to the Amendment, in Lines 13, and 14.;

Because they are of Opinion, That the Words " equally,

" Share and Share alike," stand very properly in that Place, to prevent Disputes, and cause an equitable Division, among the Children, if in case Mr. Trenchard and Mr. Mitchell should not make any such Appointment as before-mentioned.

The Lords disagree to the Amendment, Press 27th,

Line 26th; which was the Addition of a Clause;

Because it does not' appear to their I,ordships, but that, if there is any such Sum as Fifty Pounds, with Interest, owing to the Poor of the said Parish, the same may be some way secured, preferable to the said Debts.

The Lords also disagree to the Amendment, in Line the 42d;

Because, the former Amendment being disagreed to, the Words " and the said Fifty Pounds, with Interest," will have Reference to no Part of the Bill.

An Act for encouraging all Superiors, Vassals, Land* lords, and Tenants, in Scotland, who do and shall continue in their Duty and Loyalty to his Majesty King Geoi'ge; and for discouraging all Superiors, Vassals, Landlords, and Tenants, there, who have been, or shall be, guilty of rebellious Practices against his said Majesty; and for. making void all fraudulent Entails, Tailzies, and Con- . veyances, made there, for barring or excluding the Effect of Forfeitures, that may have been, or shall he, in* curred there, on any such Account; as also, for calling any fiifpefted Person or Persons, whole Estates, or principal Residence, are in Scotland, to appear at Edinburgh, or where it shall be judged expedient, to find Bail for their good Behaviour; and for the better disarming dil*' affected Persons in Scotland:

An Act for building and endowing a Church upon the Site of the Castle of Leverpole, held by Lease from the Duchy of Lancaster; and for explaining a former Act for the building another Church there:

An Act for vesting the Estate of John Tanner Esquire, deceased, in Trullees, to be sold for Payment of his Debts:

An Act for confirming a Sale already made to Edmund Hummer Gentleman, of some Part, and for vesting other Part, of the Estate of John Bromfei Esquire, in the County of Southampton, oomprifed in the Articles made upon his Marriage with Anne his Wife, in Trustees, to be sold for the Payment of his Debts; and for settling the remaining Part thereof as near as may be to the Intent of the said Articles; and for making the reby, and by other means in the Act mentioned, some Provision for the said John Bromfeild and Anne his Wife, and their Issue.

Article the First.

He the said Thomas Earl of Strafford, being of her Majesty’s Privy Council, and her Ambafllidor Extraordinary to the States General, and appointed One of her Plenipotentiaries to treat with the Ministers of France of a good and general Peace, in Concert with the Ministers of her Majesty’s Allies, who, for that Purpotc, were atlembled, at Utrecht, with those of France, with full Powers to transact the same; having no Regard to the true Ends of his said Commissions and Powers; to the Honour or Safety of her Majesty, or her Kingdoms; to the many tblemn Engagements the was under to the old and faithful Allies of this Nation; or to the common Liberties of Europe; but, being devoted to the Interest and Service of the French King, the then Common Enemy; in Defiance of the Tenor of the several Treaties before-mentioned, or feme of them, as well as of the frequent Advices of Parliament, and the many Declarations of her Majesty from the Throne; but more'particularly in Defiance of the solemn and mutual Assurances, which had been so lately renewed, between her Majesty and the States General, to act in per-fest Concert with each other in making Peace as in making War, and of the several Irrftruftiops from her Majesty, under the Sign Manual, to him the said Earl, in pursuance thereof; was not only wanting in his Duty and Trust to her Majesty, by not advising against, and, as far as was in his fdwer, by not opposing, the going into any private, 17

separate, Negotiation with France; but on the contrary, when a separate, dishonourable, and destructive, Negotiation of Peace was entered into between the Ministers of Great Britain and France, without any Communication thereof to her Majesty’s Allies, according to their several Treaties, he the said Earl did not only take upon himself, and presume, from time to time, to advise and exhort; that the same should be continued and carried on; but did likewise frequently concert private and separate Measures with the Ministers or France, in order to impose upon, and deceive, her Majesty’s good Subjects, and her Allies; and, was instru mental in promoting the said separate Negotiation, exclusive of all the Allies, and to their manifest Prejudice and Detriment:

And, further, he the said Earl, when the Ministers of France, at Utrecht, refuted to anf.ver in Writing, a d, on many otiier Occasions, proceeded in a fallacious and un-justifiable manner in transacting the Negotiations of Peace* w-as not only wanting in his Duty, in not representing to her Majesty, and her Ministers, against the fame, and itt not supporting, in the manner he ought to have done, her Majesty’s good Allies in their reasonable Demands from France; but, on the contrary, commended the French Prudence in taking such Measures; and even suggested himself the Methods for France to make use of to create DitTentions amongst the Allies, and separate Negotiations betw een each of the Allies and , thereby to dissolve

the whole Confederacy:

By which wicked and treacherous Practices, he the said Earl prostituted the Honour of her Majesty, and the Imperial Crown of these Realms; and grossly violated his Powers and instructions, the many Treaties which her Majesty then stood engaged in to her Allies, and the repeated Assurances which the said Earl had, by her Majesty’s Order, and in her Name, given to the said Allies, to act in perfect Concert with them throughout the whole* Negotiations of Peace; thereby rendering the Design of the Confederacy, and the mutual Support expected from the same, altogether useless, and giving up the Affairs of Europe into the Hands of France.

Article the 2d.

Whereas the maintaining a perfect Union, and good Correspondence, betw een her late Majesty and the Illustrri-ous House of Hanover, was of the utmost Importance for preserving to tlielfe Kingdoms the invaluable BIdlings of their Religion, and Civil Liberties, by securing the Suc-celfion to the Crown to a Race of Protestant Princes, ever renowned for their great Justice and Clemency, and thereby defeating the traitorous Designs of the Pretender; and, for that Purpose, the great Wisdom of divers'Parliaments, which had fixed, and confirmed, the said Succession, had also laid the Obligation of an Oath upon the Subjects of these Realms, to support and maintain the same to the iitmost of their Power:

He the said Thomas Earl of Strafford, not regarding the many ill Consequences to her Majesty, and these Kingdoms, which would naturally ensue from a Disunion or Coolness of Affection, between Princes so nearly allied in Blood and Interest, instead of doing W’hat in him lay to prevent the fame, did, on the contrary, in his Letters, from Holland, to her Majesty’s Ministers of State in Great Britain, by divers false Representations, and scurrilous Reflections upon his present most Gracious Majesty, then Elector of Hanover, endeavour to alienate her Majesty’s Affeftious from his laid Electoral Highness, and to create, or widen, fatal Differences or Mifiinderstandings between them; and when, by the wicked and pernicious Advice of him the said Thomas Earl of Strafford, and divers other evil Counsellors, her late Majesty was at lait prevailed upon to make a fatal Cessation of Arms with the then common Enemy, without any Concert with his said Electoral Highness, and against the Consent, and contrary to the most earnest Representations, of all her Allies; for the Execution of which, he the said Earl w»as sent over to the Army in the Netherlands, where the Generals of the Auxiliaries paid by her Majesty, whole Honour and Conscien-ces would not permit them to abandon the Confederates,

Article the 3d.

Whereas, in the pernicious Negotiations of Peace carried on by him the said Earl, and other evil Counsellors, with the Ministers of France, the French King had pre-posed to acknowledge her Majesty’s Title to the Crown of these Realms, and the Protestant Succession in the Illustrious House of Hanover, when the Peace should be signed between Great Britain and France, and not before; whereupon the House of Lords, by an humble Address to her Majesty, on the 15th of February 1711, begged Leave to represent their just Indignation at that dishonourable Treatment of her Majesty; as also their utmost Refcntinent at the Terms of Peace offered to her Majesty, and her Allies, by the Plenipotentiaries of France; for which Addresses, her Majesty was pleated to return them her hearty Thanks for the Zeal they had therein expressed for her Honour:

He the said Earl was not only wanting in his Duty to her Majesty, and Zeal for the Protestant Succession, in not advising her Majesty against treating, with France upon such dishonourable Terms; but did himself, with other evil Counsellors, privately, wickedly, and treacheroully, concert and agree with the Ministers of France, that the said Proposals, lo derogatory to the Dignity of her Majesty, and dangerous to these Kingdoms, should be the Conditions, upon which France would agree to treat of a Peace with Great Britain:

And further, he the said Earl, in Contempt and Defiance of the Judgment of the House of Peers, which had received her Majesty s gracious Approbation, and afiting the Part of an Emissary of France, instead of a Plenipotentiary of Great Britain, being the reunto encouraged, and founding his Presumption on a Letter to the then said Bishop of Bristol, and him the said Earl, from Henry St: John Esquire, then principal Secretary of State, on the 16th of February 1711, the next Day after the said Act-dress of the House of Peers was made, and informing them of the Indignation expressed in Great Britain at the Offers of France; but that, by the Management of Mr. Thonuts Harley, then Secretary of the Treasury, the House of Commons was perfectly and absolutely secured to the Measures of Peace; did wickedly, deceitfully, and perfi-Vol. 18.

Whereby her Majesty, the Parliament, and the whole Nation, were most grolly and scandalously abused, and drawn into the said destrufitive Measures of Peace; to the great Dishonour of her Majesty, and these Kingdoms, and to the apparent Danger of the Protestant Succession.

That he the said Thomas Earl of in Defiance

Article the 5th.

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Parishioners, of the Church of St. Mary Wolnoth, London, was presented to the House, and read; lotting forth, That the said Parish Church was intirely burnt down by the late dreadful Lire in 1666; and, by an Act, made in the 2 2d Year of King Charles the Second, was included in the Fifty-one Churches, which, by the said Act, were to be rebuilt; all which, except the said Parish Church, have been rebuilt, out of the Monies appropriated by the said Act, and other subsequent Acts for that Purpose: That, soon after the said Fire, for the Conveniency of the Inhabitants, the said Church was only repaired; and the old Walls of the South Side, East and West Ends, and Tower, thereof, being since very much decayed, are become so weak and ruinous, that the Parishioners, from their Apprehensions of the dangerous Condition thereof, by the Advice of Surveyors, have fhoared Part of the Roof thereof, which is defective, as well as the Walls, which might Otherwise have fallen down, to secure them in their resorting to Divine Service: That, in order to their obtaining the Rebuilding thereof, the Petitioners applied to the honourable House of Commons; and, by an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty, for granting a longer Time to the Commissioners for building 50 Vof.; 18.

new Churches, therein letting forth, That there was a Necessity of rebuilding the said PariAi Church, it wa*

Enacted, That the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, Lc*4 Bishop of London, and Lord Mayor of London, or any Two of them, may appropriate, out of the Surplus of the Monies arising by the Duties and Impositions of Twelve Pence per Chalder, or Twelve Pence per Ton, on Coals, applicable for the Purposes in the Act of the First Year of the late King James the Second mentioned, after the Cathedral Church oiSt. Paul's be finished, and adorned, and other Charges upon the said Duties discharged, so much Money as shall be sufficient for rebuilding and finishing the said Parish Church, and Tower thereof: That the Petitioners, not having any Benefit thereby, applied, by Petition, to his Grace the Lord Archbishop of Lord Bishop of London, and Lord Mayor of London, for Rebuilding thereof; and his Grace was plealed, in the Month of July last, by Letter, to signify, for Answer,

That St. Paul's Church is not yet finished; and their Debts being very great, and the Coal Duty, out of which it is to be paid, being shortly to expire, the Petitioners must wait till those Obstructions are removed; as by his Grace’s Letter, may appear: That the Walls, of the said Church are now much more decayed, and cracked in several Places; and Parts thereof are continually dropping; so that, by the Apprehensions the Parishioners are under of its falling, most of them dare not resort thither: And praying, That, as, by his Grace’s said Answer, the pious Intentions of this honourable House, by the said Aftj seem to be ineffectual for rebuilding their laid Church,... will be plealed to take their same into Consideration; and, out of the Duties appropriated for building the Fifty new Churches, to order so much Money for Rebuilding and Finishing of their said Parish Church, and Tower; or to make such other Provision, for Rebuilding thereof, as to your great Wisdom shall seem meet.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for making Provision for the Ministers for the new Churches built, or to be built, in and about the Cities of London and Wtzstimnster, and Suburbs thereof, is committed, That they have Power to receive a Clause, to impower the Commissioners for Building the Fifty new Churches to apply Part of the Monies granted by the Act of the Ninth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, to the rebuilding the said Parish Church of St. Mary Wolnoth, to be repaid out of the Monies appropriated by the Act Of the Tenth Year of her said Majestys Reign, for the rebuilding the said Church.
