349

they could retake him, to murder him; and had before embrued their Hands in the Blood, of the Son of a neighbouring Gentleman: He never intended to have left his own Country; and, when some Gentlemen mentioned . coming into England, he opposed it: He was far from assisting, or encouraging, them in their Undertakings: He was not admitted into their Secrets, nor informed of their Designs; and was lo much a Stranger to their Proceedings, that, when they marched towards Northumberland, he was told, they were going along the Skirts of the Hills in Scotland, to avoid General; but after-

wards discovered they were in England, when it was too late; and to return alone into Scotland was too hazardous; which he did not attempt, because he had Reason to believe they would soon go back to Scotland.

Although he was constrained to keep the other Lords and Gentlemen Company, yet he never joined with them iu any Att of Hostility; nor assisted in taking any of the publick Money, or iu seizing any Guns, or other warlike . Instruments; or countenanced or abetted them therein: He did not at Preston, or elsewhere, fire a Pistol, offer Violence to any Person whatl'oever, or, in any other manner, fight against, or refilt, his Majesty’s Forces; but, with the rest, surrendered himself to General Wills.

The Honour of a Peer is more valuable than Life itself; and therefore he ought to be l'o much the more cautious, that it be not stained with the least Imputation of Guilt. The laid Earl knows his Innocence; and hopes your Lordships will excule him, if, in Justice to himself, and for the Preservation of his Honour, he does not take upon him the Guilt of Crimes, the very Thoughts of which were always Strangers to his Bread: And, therefore, in Answer to the Impeachment, he fays, That he is not guilty of the Treason, and other the Crimes and Mifde-meanors, mentioned in the said Articles, or any of them, in manner and Form as is therein alledged: And, for his Tryal, puts himself on your Lordships, who are his Peers; and begs your Lordships to believe, That this Answer proceeds from the Sense he has of the Truth of it, and not from Obstinacy, or any Inclination to give your Lordships, and the honourable House of Commons, any unnecessary Trouble, or from the least Doubt or Mistrust of his Majesty’s Clemency: But if, upon his Tryal, it shall appear, that he hath committed any Act, which, in the Rigour of the Law, may be cenflrued to amount to the Crime of High Treason, he hopes the Innocence of his Heart, and his Ignorance in the Law, will, by the Power of your Lordships Intercession, render him an Objefit of his Majesty’s Mercy, which he, and the rest, at the time of surrendering themselves, were encouraged, by his Majesty’s Officers, to depend upon. The said Earl submits his Cafe, thus circumstanced, to your Lordships great Wisdom and Judgment; and humbly prays your Lordships favourable Interpretation thereof, not doubting-but to make his Innocence appear to your Lordships Satisfaction.

A Petition of the Commissioners for railing Money by a Land Tax, who acted as such within the Palaces of Whitehall and St. James's,in the Year 1706, 1707, 1708, 1709, and 1710, or feme of those Years, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act of Parliament passed in the Year 1705, the said Palaces, which had formerly paid only the Sum of 10,686/. 5$. 4 d.to the 1 It. 2d, and 3d, Four Shillings Aid, were then charged with the further Sum of 20,068/. os. 11 d.amounting in the Whole to 30,754/. 6s. 3d.: That her late Majesty, considering the indigent Condition of a great Part of her Family, and of those who received Pensions from her, was pleased to declare lhe would pay Part of the said Tax: That the late Earl of Godolphin, then Lord High Treasurer, by Order from her laid late Majesty, directed the said Commissioners to consider what the Family was in a Condition to raise; telling them, That he would then receive her Majesty’s further Pleasure: That the said Commissioners, pursuant to those Directions, caused a new Assessment to be made, which amounted to the Sum of 19,403 /. 8 s. o and laid the same before the said Earl of Godolphin; who, feme time after, acquainted them, by Order from her Majesty, That her Majesty would supply the yearly Deficiency of 11,350/. 18 s. 3 d.;and that the said Commissioners were to pro-

ceed in making the Assessments accordingly: That her said late Majesty, according to her gracious Promise, was pleased, in the Year 1711, to pay the Sum of 21,000 /. and, in the Year 1714, to order a Warrant to be drawn for the remaining Part of the Deficiency, viz. the Sum of 47,105 /. 9$. 6d.; but lhe died before the same was per-

A Petition of Joseph Quilter, John Ellison, John Key, Fees ,pon and Andrew Vergez, in behalf of themselves, and great Lottery Or-Numbers of other Persons, both Natives and Foreigners, ders* concerned in the several Lotteries, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by the several Acts of Parliament relating to the Lotteries, it is Enacted, That, to encourage Persons to advance their Money, no Fee or Reward shall be taken, directly or indirectly, of any Adventurer in the said Lotteries, by any Officer of the Exchequer, or other Officer or Person whatsoever, but that the Crown shall satisfy all Persons any-ways employed therein out of the Money granted by Parliament; notwithstanding which, your Petitioners have been obliged to pay Fees to the Auditors of the Imprefts, before they could receive, out of his Majesty’s Exchequer, what was due upon several Lottery Orders, as the Petitioners are ready to make appear: That, in particular, the Petitioner Joseph Quilter, being impowered by one Robert Smethberd to receive Six Shillings, being Half a Year’s Interest due to the said Smethberd on a Ten Pound Lottery Order, the Petitioner was obliged to pay Three Shillings and Three Pence Half-peny at the Office of Mr. Auditor Foley, on the 3d . of December last, before the Petitioner could receive the said Six Shillings at the Exchequer; which said Sum was demanded of the said Quilter, as a’ Fee due to the Auditor, by the said Auditor’s Officers: That the Petitioner John Ellison being appointed Executor to Martha Taylour, and Guardian to Four Orphans, the Children of the said Taylour, and being, by her last Will, impowered to receive the Interest of One Lottery Order for the Use of the said Four Orphans, the Petitioner was obliged to pay Three Shillings and Four Pence, the Money of the said Orphans, on the 9th of November last, at the Office of Mr. Auditor Harley, before-the Petitioner could receive any interest at the Exchequer due to the said Orphans on the said Lottery Orders; which Sum was demanded, as the Auditor's Fee, by the Officers of the said Mr Harley:That the Petitioner John Key was obliged to pay, on the 10th of December last, at the Office of Mr. Auditor Harley, 3 4 for

MR. Pulteney acquainted the House, That he was Dutch

commanded by his Majesty to lay before this Troops. House, a Copy of the Treaty, made by Mr. Cadogan, with the States General, for a Body of Six thousand Men, taken into his Majesty's Service; with a Translation thereof:

And he presented the same to the House accordingly:

And the said Translation was read; and is as follows;

viz.

Treaty made between Mr. Cadogan, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of his Britannick Majesty, and Monsieur Geldermalfen, authorized for this Purpose by their Highnesses the Council of State of the United Provinces, according to the Resolution of the 30th Day of October 1715, concerning the Body of Six thousand Men, which their High and Mighti-nesses the States General fend into England.

-Art. I.

THAT such Part of the said Six thousand Men as do conlift of the National Troops of the States, shall be paid by his Britannick Majesty upon the same Foot with the British Troops; and the Swiss, according to their Ca-itulation made with their High and Mightinesse the tdtes General; and the said Troops shall enjoy the same Advantages, with regard to the Delivery of Bread, Forage, Tents, Waggons, Quarters, Hospitals, Recruiting-money, and other Benefits, as the National Troops

enjoy, and such as the Troops of their High and Mighti-nesses which served formerly in England did enjoy.

Art. II.

The Pay shall begin from the Day the Troops embark; and shall continue to the Day of their Landing in such Port as their High and Mightinesses shall please to appoint: Provided always, That the Forces which come to supply the Place of the said Six thousand Men, shall no longer be chargeable to their High and Mightinesse than from the Day on which this Body of Six thousand Men shall be embarked, to the Day on which they land.

Art. III.

His Britannick Majesty shall cause Two Months full Pay to be advanced to the said Troops, or so much left as shall be thought for the Good of the Troops: The same Advance shall be made to the General Officers, and others, that go over With the said Body; a List whereof is annexed at the End of this Treaty: And whereas several Non-commissioned Officers are wanting to this Body of Troops, besides One Serjeant, and OneDrum, to eachCom-pany, who are now to be raised, the Officers shall have an Allowance made, to enable them to bear that Expence.

Art IV.

This Body, with the General Officers, Etat Major, and all others included in the Lift hereunto annexed, shall take the Oaths to be faithful to his Britannick Majesty for the time they shall remain in his Service.

Art V.

The military Employments which shall become vacant^ in the said Body of Troops, whilst it is in the Pay of his Britannick Majesty, shall be filled up by their High and Mightinesse, or by the Provinces who have a Right to the fame.

4 X Art.

Dutch

'Troops*

28° Januard.' 1715-'

Art. VI.

The said Body shall have their own separate and parti* cylar Court Martial; and shall not be liable to be tried by any other.

Art. VII.

This Body, as well in Quarters as in the Field, shall not be divided, but when the Necessity of the King’s Affaifs, and the Service of the War, fha.Il require; and, in case they are separated, the said Regiments shall be quartered as near one another as possible: This to be done after having advised with, and taken the Opinion of, the General of the said Troops hereupon.

Art. VIII.

The Orders for the said Troops shall always be directed to the General of the States who commands them, at least as much as the Service of the War will permit.

Art. IX.

This Body shall be provisionally in the Service of his Britannick Majesty for the Space of Six Months, unless his Majesty should not have Occasion for them so long; when his Majesty shall be at Liberty to lend them back sooner; provided Notice thereof be given their High and Mightinefies a Month before hand; and the States General shall be at Liberty to recall the said Body of Troops sooner, if they should have need of them, for their own Defence against any foreign Enemies; in which same his Britannick Majesty shall be at Liberty to recall likewise the Body of Troops which he has caused to march fronj Germany, to supply their Place.

That the Affront offered by France, in acknowteging the Pretender King of Great Britain, though justly mentioned

by her late Majesty Queen Anne, of ever bieffed Memory, as one Cause of the War, which, in May 1702, was by her declared against France and Spam, could not be any In* ducement to the forming the Grand Alliance, as is fug-gefted in the Preamble to the said Articles; being subsequent to it, as most evidently appears; inasmuch as that Alliance was not only formed, but concluded and signed at the Hague, during the Life-time of die late King James the Second: And the said Earl admits, That the Emperor, and the States General, did also, about May 170s, declare War against France and Spain; and that other Kings, Princes, and States, of Eur&pe, loon after became Parties to the said Confederate War; which having been carried on, for many Years, at a vast Expence of Blood and Treasure, her said late Majesty, out of her tender Regard for the Good of her People, and from a sincere and real Design to prevent the further Effusion of Blood, and to ease her Subjects from the heavy Burthen of Taxes, which they had so long endured, did hearken to Overtures of Peace from France, after former Negotiations had been rendered fruitless, and give Instructions to the then Lord Privy Seal, now Bishop of London, and him the said Earl, to treat thereof at Utrecht, in Conjunction with the Ministers of her Allies, in order to bring the same to an happy Conclusion; and among such Instructions, several Clauses were interspersed to the Eflfeft in the said Preamble set forth; but, for more Certainty, refers to his original Instructions; which, together with all his other Papers relating to his Negotiations in the Low Countries, were taken from him in the Beginning of January left, and, he supposes, may continue in the Hands of One of his Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State: But the said Earl is t otally ignorant of any treacherous Correspondence with the Emiflrtries of France, or of any private or de-struftive Negotiation of Peace set on foot with the Intent to weaken, or dissolve, the Confederacy between her feid late Majesty and her Allies; And, for particular Answer to the several Matters wherewith he stands charged in the First Article, the said Earl faith, That, having been employed by his late Majesty King William in the Army, during his whole Reign, and likewise in his Court for several Years next before his Death, and having also had the Honour to be sent as his Majesty’s Minister to the King of Pruffk, he was so happy as to reconcile forne Differences, which had lately aril'en, between those Two Princes; and, upon his Return, received his Royal Matter’s Approbation; her late Majesty Queen Anne, soon after her Accession to the Throne, was pleated to command him to leave his Pott in the Army, and to go again to the said Court of Prujta, in the Year 1702, where he had the of her Ambassador Extraordinary; and continued in that Quality till April 17115 at which time her Majesty thought fit to appoint him her Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the States General; and, in June following, her Majesty was pleaded to honour him with the Title of One of her Privy Council; «nd, about December, in the same Year, to appoint him One of her Plenipotentiaries to treat, at Utrecht, with the Ministers of France, of a general Peace: And the said Earl thought it his Duty 'not to forople any Danger or Pains for her Service; believing his Zeal therein was the best Evidence he could give of his hearty Affection to 'his Country; and he conllantly did, with the utmost Sincerity, endeavour, according to his Abilities, to pvmitre the true Ends of his Commission, and Powere; to promote the Honour and Safety Of her Majesty, and her Kingdoms; to answer the Engagements the was under to her Allies; and to iectire the common Liberties of Europe: But he must, with the ntmost Detestation and Abhorrence, deny, that he was in the least devoted to the In-teFeft or Service of the French King; or that he ever acted in Defiance'of any of thfe feid Treaties, or of the Advice of Parliament; or of any-Declarations of her Majesty from tire Throne; or of her Assurances to the States General, to act in Concert with them in making Peace, as.

k» making War; or of her Instructions to him under ber Sign Manual: The feid Earl admits. That, as he was a Privy Counsellor, it was his Duty truly to have advised her Majesty in all Matters treated of in Council, whilst he was present; atwi had any thing, so treated of, appeared to him to have been to foe Dishonour of her Majesty, or to the Prejudice of her People, the said Earl would not have been wanting to advise against, and, with all Humility, to oppose the same: But, as he was her Majesty’s Ambassador and Plenipotentiary, he looked upon himself as a minifiedal Officer, whose Duty it was to pursue such Instructions as he shoukL from time to time, receive ;(and ftnee be could not doubt, but that all Orders, sent mm by her Majesty’s Diregions, had been first maturely weighed and digested, he humbly apprehends, your Lordships will think it had been too great a Presumption in him, to advise against, or oppose such Orders, which carried not in themselves any apparent Illegality, when he knew not the Springs or Reasons of them; and which, therefore, it became him to believe well warranted, and to have proceeded from just and proper Grounds and Motives: And the said Earl laith, He was so far from advising or exhorting, that any private, separate, dishonourable, or definitive, Negotiation of Peace should be continued, and carried on, between the Ministers of Great Britain and France, without Communication thereof to ber Majesty’s Allies, according to their Treaties; or from being in fir u mental in promoting any such Negotiation, as in the said Article is charged; that he did not know, or believe, that any such Negotiation was entered into: And, for a plain relation of the said Earl’s Proceeding in this Affair, he feith, That, about May 1711, being then her Majesty s Ambassador and Plenipotentiary to the States General, he received, from One of her Principal Secretaries of State, a Paper, supposed to be signed by Monsieur Torcy, containing some Propofols for setting on foot a Negotiation of Peace, with Orders to communicate the same to the Pensionary of Holland, that his Sentiments might be known thereupon; and to allure that Minister, and others of that Uepublick, that the Queen wasrefolved, in making Peace, as in make-ing War, to act in Concert with the States: In pursu-aoce of which Orders, he the said Earl did immediately coimnuuicate the said Propofols to the Penfioaary, and unto Two others of the States General, who had formerly been employed in the Negotiations at Gertrudyenberg, and whom the Penfioaary thought the most proper to be entrusted with that Matter; and they, having conffdered the said Propofols, did pray the said Earl to return her Majesty Thanks, in the Name of the States, for her Confidence in them; declared themselves weary of the War, and ready to join in any Measures her Majesty should think proper for obtaining a good Peace; and that they hoped her Majesty would bring the French to explain more particularly the several Points contained in the above-mentioned Propofols: Of this the said Earl sent an Account to her Majesty’s Secretary of State; and, soon after, received her Commands to repair to England; and, on his Arrival here, acquainted her Majesty with his Proceedings at the Hague; but being, by her gracious Permission, allowed to follow some private Affairs of his -own, he was often in the Country, and so much engaged, that be did not know of any of the Transactions with Monsieur Mefnager, or what was done in relation to the

Explications the States had defined her Majesty to procure (from Franee, upon the Points of Monsieur Torcy’s Propofol, till, m October following, he neoeived Instructions, dated the First of that Month; whereby he was required to return to Holland, and to communicate to the States dome Proportions, which had been signed by the said Mon-fieurA/e/wagerythe 2 7th day of September before, as a foundation for opening the Conferences of Peace with France; which he supposes to be the Instructions intended by those mentioned in the Preambleto the Articles, as dated the 21 ft Day of October; none of that Date appearing amongst the

Copies of his own Papers he has been permitted to take: But the said Earl never few Monsieur Mefnager till lie met

him at Utrecht, in January 171 f; nor, during all the time

of the said Minister s Stay in England, was in the least privy to, or made acquainted with, any Transaction between him and any of the Queen’s Ministers: The said Earl, having received his said Instructions, took his Journey for Holland; and, on his Arrival there, in pursuance thereof, imparted to the States General the said Proportions, and what had been communicated to him concerning any Transactions between Great Britain and France; and, at the same time, in further pursuance of his said Instructions, declared to them, That if they did not think those Proportions a sufficient Ground to open the Conferences, but were desirous to carry on the War, her Majesty was willing to concur with them; but could no longer bear that disproportionable Burthen which had been yearly increased on her Subjects; nor that Deficiency her Allies had been guilty of in every Part of the War; and that therefore it was incumbent on them, if the War continued, to furnish such Quotas of Ships, and Forces, for the future, as they had to that time been wanting in: That this was what her Majesty thought ihe might jufUy insist on, that they should comply with her in War, or ip Peace; since, in the former, lhe required nothing but what it belonged to them to perform, and what was necessary to the Succels of their Arms; and since, in the latter, lhe had done, and would continue to do, w hat was in her Power towards obtaining such a Peace as might be to the Satisfaction of her Allies: Soon after this, the States General lent Monsieur Buys to England, as their Plenipotentiary, to confer with her late Majesty s Ministers, and inform himself of the Circumstances of Affairs, and make Report thereof to his Masters; who having continued here some time, and transmitted to Holland an Account of the Pof-ture of Affairs, the States General contented to open the Conferences for Peace, and to invite the other Allies to lend their Ministers to Utrecht, the Place agreed on lor that Purpose; and, in order thereunto, granted Passports for the French Ministers to repair thither: And the said Earl is informed, that, amongst other Transactions by the said Monsieur Buys, whilst in England, he ligned a Treaty with her late Majesty’s Ministers, who were impowered for that Purpose dated the 18th Day of December 1711, O. S. for the carrying on the War, and the Negotiation of Peace, according to the mutual Engagements of former Treaties between England and Holland; which Treaty was ratified by her said late Majesty the Day after it w-as ligned, and was lent to Holland by the then Lord Privy Seal; but the States General, though their Ministers were often called upon, never ratified the fame: And the said Earl admits, That the said Lord Privy Seal, and himself, were appointed to be her Majesty’s Plenipotentiaries at the said Congrels at Utrecht; and he can, with great Truth affirm, that he afited, on all Occasions, with the highest and most disinterested Zeal, for procuring a general Peace, for the mutual Advantage of her Majesty’s Subjects, and Allies, in pursuance of the Powers and Instructions received for that Purpose; and is firmly persuadedhis Colleague did the same: The said Earl faith, That every one of the Confederates had their Ministers at Utrecht, w ho all agreed in the Method and Manner of proceeding in the said Negotiation; and had frequent Meetings and Conferences, to that End, among themselves, in order to lay down a general Scheme for their Conduct; and, for the better concerting these Measures, it was thought fit to have Two Conferences a Week with all the Allies, Two with the Dutch apart, and Two with all the Allies with the French; and, in those with the Dutch and the other Allies, what w as to be proposed on the Part of the Allies to the French was always previously settled: In the First general Conference with the French Ministers, they offered either to proceed to the Explanation of the general Points signed by Monsieur (which they acknowleged were binding only to and

not to the Allies), or that each of the Allies should make their Demands: On Deliberation, it was insisted by the Allies, That the Frenchfhould first give in a specifick Plan

of the Offers of the King their Maiter to all and each of

1715.

the Allies; and the French complied to give in such specifick Plan, in case the Allies would promise to return an Answer thereto, containing their several Demands; and, accordingly, the French Ministers did give in such Plan, in Write-ing; and the Allies, in Answer, delivered in their- Demands, also in Writing: The French, having thus given in their Concessions in Writing, and received the Demands of the Allies in like manner, thought fit to propose the entering into Debate upon the several Propositions mutually delivered in, agreeably to the Course of proceeding in former Treaties: But though some of the Allies thought there was no Necessity of infilling very much on any further written Answer; yet others pressed it more vehemently. To which the French replied, That both Sides having already explained themselves in Writing, it was agreeable to the Method of all Negotiations to proceed to debate Matters; and, in such Debates, specifick Anfivers to each Demand of the Allies would occur; and all the Allies agreed in this Principle, That the Method most expeditious and safe, whether by Writing or other wise, was fittest to be followed. Thus having given your Lordships a short Narrative of the Proceedings, which might render his Answers to the several Particulars charged in this Article more intelligible: As to that Part which mentions his frequently concertidg private and fep irate Measures with the Ministers of France, the said Earl doth acknowlege, that, when the settling any particular Interest of Great Britain might require it, he and his Colleague might confer with* the Ministers of France, in the same manner as the Ministers of each of the Allies conferred separately with those of France, touching their respefitive particular Interests; and the said Earl apprehends, they were justified therein by their express Orders from England for that Purpose; and sometimes the said Bishop and Earl had separate Conferences with the Ministers of France, at the Request, and, on the behalf, of one or other of the Allies, whose Regard to her Majesty made them often desire the Interposition of her Ministers, to support their several Pretensions; In Answer to the Fourth Article; the said Earl faith, That the Bishop of Bristol, and himself, being appointed her Majesty’s Plenipotentiaries, did, soon after their Arrival at Utrecht, pursuant to their Instructions, begin, by concerting with the Ministers of the Allies, in what manner it was most proper to open the Conferences, and what Method was to be observed in the Progress of the Treaty; and, if it had been thought proper to begin with the Dif-position of the Spanish Monarchy, the said Earl was ready to have infilled, as the said Instructions directed him to do in that Cafe; but, upon such Concert, it was thought most adviseable, and lb agreed, by all the Ministers of the Allies, that each of them mould, by a separate Instrument, make their respective Demands; with a general Clause to support each other s just and reasonable Pretensions; and this was looked upon as the most proper Method, and necessary to avoid that Confusion, which would otherwise ensue from the Contrariety of the Demands of the several Allies; it being then known, that many of them did and would inlist to have the same tiling for themselves, in Opposition to each other: The Imperial Ministers, as well as the rest, acquiesced in that Method; and, at a following Conference, it was further desired, that there should be added to such general Clause the Words " in Conformity " to their Alliances with which the said Bishop and Earl, as well as the reli, most readily complied; and those Words were accordingly added to the general Clause in each of the Allies Demands; which seemed to give a general Satisfaction; and there was nothing further at that time infilled on. In consequence of this Agreement, it was the general Expectation, that the Demand relating to and the West Indies, should be particularly mferted only in the Instrument to be given in by the Imperial Ministers; but, there having been a Day long before fixed for delivering in to the French all the Demands of the Allies, the Imperialists, the very Night preceding, at a Conference, proposed, That all the Allies should mention Spain, and the West Indies, likewise, in their several Demands: This caused a general Surprize; and none but the Ministers of Portugal concurred with them: Those of the States, in particular, declared the said Dominions ought to be demanded by them whom it did immediately concern; and that the Method Things had been put into could not suffer it to be otherwise; but, the next Morning, to give Content to the Imperialists, they yielded to make a verbal Declaration among the Allies, That they were refblved to make good all their Treaties on Occasion of this War, as well those that related to Spain, as those made with Portugal, Prussia, Savoy, and others: The British Plenipo-

tentiaries, to give the like SatislaClion, declared publickly at the Conferences the same Day, That, as her Majesty infilled for a just and reasonable Satisfaction for all her Allies, in Conformity to all her Alliances, those that might concern Spain, and the Indies, were understood thereby, as well as others that concerned the Interest of the rest of the Allies; wherewith the Austrian and Portugal Ministers seemed satisfied; nor did they request any thing further from the said Bishop and Earl on that Head; and therefore he humbly apprehends, that in the Negotiation he neither declined to infill, that Spain, and th Indies,

In Answer to the Fifth Article; the said Earl doth acknowlege, That her late Majesty, in her Speech from the Throne on the 7th Day of December 1711, having acquainted her Parliament, That both Time and Place were appointed for opening a Treaty of Peace, did, at the same time, remind them, that the best Way to make the Treaty effectual would be to make early Provision for the Campaign; and believes, Supplies were granted, and Magazines provided, for that End: But the said Earl faith,

That, at the time in the said Article for that Purpose meri-tioned, he was not informed of any reasonable Prospect tile Confederates then had of gaining new Conquests over the Army of France; nor doth he believe, that the Confederate Army, at that time, was the strongest that had been in the Service during the whole Course of the War; but, upon the Informatioa9 he received at the Hague, about the 19th-30th of April 1712; he understood, that the French were better posted than the Confederates, and their Army stronger; and that the Confederate Forces could not march to surprise the French in their Lines till they had green Forage, which would not be up in Three Weeks at soonest; and that the French had all their Troops, and the Confederates wanted great Part of theirs; especially the Imperialists, who, ’twas thought, could not, and in fact did not, join the Army till about a Month after:

In Answer to the Sixth Article; the said Earl, not admitting that he did advise, or procure, a Collation of Arms, or obtain for France any Separation of the Troops of Great Britain from the Confederate Army, or was otherwise concerned therein than as in his Answer to the preceding Article is set forth, denies, with a just Abhorrence, that he ever had any treacherous Purposes to advance or promote the Interests of France; or to render any future Correspondence, or Harmony, between her late Majesty and the States General, impracticable; or to weaken or distress the said States, or bring them under any Necessity of complying with, or submitting to, the Mea-lures of France; nor did or doth he know, or believe, that the taking Poliession of Ghent and Bruges by the British Troops was likely to produce any such Consequence; on the contrary, he conceives, that it was very much for the Advantage of the Allies, especially the States General, that the English Troops took Possession of those Towns, which would otherwise, in all Probability, have fallen into the Hands of the French: The said Earl doth acknowlege, That, when the British Troops were left by the other Forces w ho separated from them, and were under a Necessity of retiring to feme Place of Security, and it was reported, that the Dutch had given Orders to all the Commanders of the Towns in their Possession to refuse them Admittance, or Passage, he did not think the Resolution improper, which was taken by her Majesty’s General, to fend a Party of the Queen’s Troops to march through some 14

Part of those Towns, to make Experiment whether they would refuse them Passage; for, if Passage should not be refused them, the Dutch would be vindicated from the Report which had been given out, so highly reflecting on their Honour, and so repugnant to the repeated Professions and Assurances of the Good-will and Friendship they had so constantly declared for Great Britain; and, if such Passage should be refused, it would demonstrate the Necessity the English Troops were under of relucting to Ghent and Bruges: However, the said Earl doth not admit, that he did advise therein; much less had he any such Hopes, or treacherous Designs, as in the said Article are mentioned; nor did he seek any Pretence to put in Execution any Design, or Resolution, concerted with the Ministers of France; nor was any such Design, or Resolution, to his Knowlege, or Belief, concerted: The said Earl doth believe, that a Party of the Queen’s Troops, being sent with Intentions to obtain Admittance into feme of the Towns in Flanders, where some of the English Magazines and Hospitals were, or, at least, to obtain Passage through them to some other Places of Security, were refused by the Dutch Commanders, although those Towns had been conquered chiefly by British Blood and Treasure: But the States General disavowed their giving any Orders for that Purpose; and thereby relcued themselves from the Reproach of an Usage, that might have been-thought inhumane to Confederate Troops, who had speot their Blood for their Service, and had done no Act of Hostility, nor given any just Reason to the States to apprehend any ill Consequences from such Passage or Admittance: The said Earl doth acknowlege, that, after this Refusal of the Dutch Commanders to receive any of the Queen’s Troops into, or permit them to pals through, the Towns in their Possession, they retired into Ghent and Bt'uges; the former having been their usual Quarters, and the Citadel thereof having been garifoned by them from the beginning of the Campaign: But the said Earl does not know, or lielieve, there was any treacherous or destructive Design in the Marching of those Troops into, or taking Possession of those Towns; nor doth he know, or believe, it was done in Concert with any of the Ministers of France, who, he is confident, were not privy to, or knew any thing of it, till after it was executed: Nor doth the said Earl difeern how it contributed to the Prejudice of the Confederates, or Advantage of the French Army; but, on the contrary, the said Earl is very well assured, that it proved greatly to the Advantage and Security of the former, whole Convoys were thereby protected, and the Communication between Holland and the Confederate Army kept open; and the Advantages thereby to the common Cause were lb notorious and visible, that the Allies frequently expressed their Satisfaction, that those important Places had been so well secured; by which means, the Allies had all the Advantages of those Towns, without being at the Expence of Garisons, the Furnishing of which would have obliged them to make such Detachments from their Army, as would have rendered it difficult for them to have kept the Field: And, on the other hand, the French Ministers frequently complained of the great Diladvantages occasioned there-by to the Arms of their Matter, whom they thought not well treated by her Majesty on that account: And the said Earl apprehends, that the British Troops had equal Right with those of the States to enter into Ghent and Bruges, or any other Place of the Law Countries, which, by Agreement, were under the joint Government of the Queen and the States General; and this happened, at that time, to be of the greater Importance, since the Queen’s. Troops were thereby enabled to maintain a Communication with Dunkirk and England, and was afterwards found likewise very useful towards obtaining the Removal of the unjustifiable Impositions laid by the Dutch upon the British Merchandize in the new Conquests in the Netherlands; which they themselves had many Months owned to be a Grievance j but had not before thought lit to redress.

The said Earl humbly hopes he has fully answered the several Articles exhibited against him; and he doubts not but your Lordships will, in your great Wisdom, maturely

weigh

2 Geo. I.

a8%~31 ° Jamarii.

3*S

weigh the Nature of the Charge, which is chiefly founded on his Transactions abroad with the Ministers of foreign Princes and States; whose Testimony, though never so material towards clearing his Innocence, it will be impossible for him to produce: He allures himself, your Lordships will have a due Regard to the wide Extent, the great Length and Intricacy, of the Negotiations, wherein he was engaged by his late Sovereign’s express Commands;. to which he did the more chearfully submit, being joined in the most considerable Parts thereof with a Reverend Prelate, whose long Residence abroad and Experience in the Methods of treating with foreign Princes and States, had abundantly qualified him for the Difenarge of so important a Trull: However, the said Earl, on his Part, may in any respect, have been unequal to the Province assigned him; yet sure he is, that he alway s endeavoured to acquit himself therein with the utmost Integrity; and cannot but express a just Detestation of the many evil Intentions wherewith he is loaded by the said Articles: And as he humbly apprehends, the several Facts, mentioned in the Articles, if they could be proved, will not appear criminal, abstracted from the ill Motives and Designs from which they are supposed to proceed; so he is fully persuaded, your Lordships will distinguish between the Actions themselves, and the Intentions wherewith they are charged to be done; and he allures himself, that your Lordships will judge of the Sincerity of his Intentions by the Tenor of all his Letters and Papers, and not by any particular Passages selected from them; and is secure in your Lordships Justice, that no strained Construction of any such Passages will be made by your Lordships to his Prejudice: He cannot but think himself extremely unfortunate in falling under the Displeasure of the honourable. House of Commons; nor could he receive the first Inti- mation of it without the greatest Surprize: Not being con-fcious to himself that he had transgressed any known Law', he was not without Hopes, having spent the best and greatest Part of his Life abroad in the Army, and in fevered Embassies, always endeavouring to promote the Welfare of his Country, that he might, at his Return, have met with its Approbation, as a Recompence for his long and faithful Services: However, he comforts himself with this Reflection, That every Step of his Proceedings in the late Negotiation was laid before her Majesty, and received her Royal Approbation: Nor will it, he conceives, be judged improper, if he observes to your Lord-fiiips, That the States General, in their Letter to her Ma-a little before the signing the Peace, acknowleged they could not enough commend her Plenipotentiaries for the Assistance they had given them in their Treaty with France; and that all the Allies gave frequent Marks of their Esteem for the said Earl, and his Colleague, on account of the many Services they had received from them. The said Earl is confident it will appear to your Lordships, that although lie did, with the utmost Application, pursue the Good of his own Country preferably to that of any other Nation whatsoever; yet he was never wanting to promote- the Advantage of the Allies, particularly of the States General, where it did not interfere with the Interest of Great Britain. A separate Treaty of Peace was lb far from his Thoughts, that, on the contrary, he was truly zealous to make it general; and he had the Ilappi-ness to succeed therein in as great a Degree as was ever known, when lb many Confederates were concerned: Nor was the said Earl less zealous in supporting, to the utmost of his Abilities, the Honour and Reputation of his late Royal Mistress; which was so far from being profti-tuted, or suffering any Diminution, by his Negotiations, that her Majesty did, through the whole Course of those Negotiations, and to the very Hour of her Death, maintain as great and glorious a Character as any of her Royal Predecessors, or as she herself had done in any former Part of her Reign.

And as to all other Matters and Things in the said Articles contained, and not herein before particularly answered, the faicLEarl faith, He is not guilty of them, or any of them, in the Manner and Form as the same are charged Voj.. 18.

upon him in and by the said Articles; and humbly fub-mits himself to your Lordships Judgment.

Strafford.

William Cowper, Clcr. Parliamentor.

That, the Price of Cochineal having been very high for feme time past, which hath been a great Loss to the Petitioners; the Merchants, for that Reason, not having bought the usual Quantities of Cloths: the Petitioners were, notwithstanding, encouraged to continue their Trade, upon the Hopes that Cochineal would soon be very cheap;

A Petition of the Trustees appointed by Act of Parliament, for amending the Road from Shoreditch to the furthermost Part of Enfeild, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That since the Palling of the said Act of Parliament, there has been laid out, over and above all the Toll produced by the Turnpikes, above 3,5001. occasioned by the Roads being gone so very much to Ruin and Decay, and by the great Length thereof, the same being 12 Miles from London, or thereabout; and, upon, a Computation made, most, if not all, the Toll, for the Term to come in the said Act, ought to be laid out in the Highway; whereby the Money borrowed cannot be repaid; for, if it should, the Road mult, of Necessity, go to Decay again: And notwithstanding the re was at first advanced and lent 3,000l. for a Year, without Interest; and although the Trustees have always borne their own Expences in the Execution of the said Act, yet they find, if 4hey should pay off any of the principal Money borrowed, the said Road cannot be effectually mended: And there being several Clauses wanting in the said Act, to prevent the evading the Toll to be collected at the Turnpikes; and for the more effectually obliging the several Inhabitants to do their Statute-work, ana keep their Ditches and Watercourses scoured and cleansed: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for lengthening the Time of the said Act of Parliament, with such other Clauses for the more effectually mending the said Road, as to this honourable House shall seem fit and' redson-able.

Richard Sand ford,

Isaac Newton.

And that afterwards his Majesty was pleased to command the Lord Chancellor to declare, in his Majesty’s Name and Words, the Causes of his coming to his Parliament at this time, besides the passing the Bills which were ready for the Royal Assent; as they were contained in a Speech,- which his Majesty delivered to the Lord Chancellor from the Throne: Which Speech the Lord Chancellor read to both Houses; and of which, Mr. Speaker laid, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I TAKE this Opportunity of acquainting you, That my Forces have obliged the Pretender to fly out of Scotland -, and he is since, as I am informed, landed near Gravelines: But I don’t know yet, whether any Country in Amity with us w ill give him Protection, after baring fopublickly invaded our Kingdom.

The Dangers, to which the Nation was exposed, made me determine, that neither the extraordinary Rigour of the Season, nor any fallacious Proposal of the Rebels, should divert me. from using all possible Endeavours towards putting a speedy and effectual End to this unnatural Rebellion.

Sabbatiy 18* di Februarii;

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I mull return you my Thanks for the great Progress you have made in the Supplies. The necessaryDispositions are made for raising additional Forces; but, as I shall always consult the Ease of my People, as far as it is con-filtent with their owm Security, I shall not make use of the Confidence you have placed in me, unless the restless Malice of our Enemies should make it necessary to go 'on with those Levies.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I promise myself, from the Zeal and Wisdom of this Parliament, that the future Happinelsand Tranquillity of my Subjefits will be established on a solid Foundation; and such Measures taken, as may deprive our Enemies at home of the Power, since that alone can deprive them of the Inclination, again to attempt the Disturbance of my Government: This, therefore, is what I think myself obliged to recommend to you, as a Deliberation of the Vol. 18.

Mr. Comptroller reported from the Committee appointed to draw up an Address, to be presented to his Majesty, upon the Resolution of Yesterday, That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had di-refited him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

WE your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjefits the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, do, with Hearts full of Gratitude, return your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne j and do beg Leave most heartily to congratulate with your Majesty upon the Succeis with which it has pleased Almighty God lb far to blefe your Arms, as to force the Pretender out of your Majesty’s Dominions.

We are willing to hope, that no Prince or State in Amity with your Majesty will give Refuge, Countenance, or Protection, to a Person who, in so notorious a manner, has disturbed the Peace of your Kingdoms: But the Dangers to which your Majesty’s Sacred Person, and Government, the Religion, Laws, and Liberties, of our Country, have been once exposed, by this vile Attempt, would leave your Commons without Excuse to those they represent, if they should fee, with Patience, the Nation exposed to the like Hazard for the future, by the Pretender to your Majesty’s Crown being Iheltered in your Neighbourhood: We do therefore make it our humble Request to your Majesty, That you will use the most earnest and pressing Instances with all Princes and States in Amity with your Majesty, That he may not be harboured in their Territories': And we beg Leave to give your Majesty the Itrongeft Assurances, That we will, to the utmost of our Power, contribute whatever shall, by your Majesty, be judged necessary to render those Instances effectual.

The tender Regard which your Majesty expresses for the Ease of your People, in declining to put the Nation to any farther Ex|>ence, at present, for additional Forces, does, if possible, heighten that Confidence which we so justly had repoled in you: But we beseech your Majesty, that, in settling the Proportion of Forces to be maintained this Year by Sea and I^rnd, your Majesty will have such a regard to the Disposition and Preparations of our Neighbours, from time to time, as to provide effectually for the Security of your Kingdoms against any Power that shall presume to countenance or abet the Pretender.

Your Commons cannot sufficiently express the just Sense they have of your Majesty’s consummate Wisdom, and firm Resolution, not to be diverted or amused by any Difficulties of the Season, or any specious Artifices, from pursuing the Rebels in Scotland to their faveral Retreats; since that Method alone could restore, and secure with Honour, Peace and Tranquillity to that Part of your Dominions.

It is with the utmost Concern we observe, that the Malice and Inveteracy of our Enemies at home is so great, that they want not the Inclination to disturb your Majesty’s Government; but your faithful Commons, in Duty

to your Majesty, and Love for their Country, will endeavour to deprive them of the Power, by taking such prudent and necessary Measures, as may most effectually secure the future Safety, Ease, and Prosperity, of your People.

The said Address was read a Second time.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be- presented to his Majesty.

Sir John Ward reported from the Committee, to importing whom the Petitions of several Merchants of London, in Cochineal, behalf of themselves, and others, Exporters of the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom; of the principal Traders, and others concerned in the Woollen Manufactory, of the City of New Sarimi; of the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester} of the Company of Worsted Weavers of the City of Norwich, and County of Norfolk;and of the Clothiers of the County of Wilts;were referred; That they bad examined the Matter contained in the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the same to the House, with their Resolutions thereupon; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and the said Report and Resolutions are as follows; viz.

That the Committee have taken the said Petitions into their Consideration: And, having, according to the Order of the House, heard the Commffioners of the Customs; and upon Examination of the Matters

a Geo. I. 20° Febrilarii. 383

ters of Fad; it appeared to the Committee, upon hearing the Commissioners of the Customs, in relation to the Importation of Cochineal;

That, by a Medium, the Importation of Cochineal has been annually about 59,836/. Weight, and the Exportation has been about 9,797 /. Weight; and, from thence, the annual Remainder, for the Home-consumption, appears to be about 49,439 /. Weight.

That Cochineal has, in an Average of Seven Years, from 1708 to 1714, been at between 19 and 20 Shillings per Pound:

That the present Price here is about 43 Shillings per Pound:

That the Price in Holland is now about 63 Skellins; which, being reduced, will bring it to about 36 Shillings Sterling here:

That the annual Consumptionufed to be about 50,000l. Weight:

That there may be better than 3,000l. Weight now in London for Sale:

That there are 30 Bags, containing about 7>500^ Weight, soon expected from ;which were lent

from Holland:

That, should Permission be granted for a free Importation from all Parts, it would not lessen the Price above Five Shill, per Pound:

That about 120 Bags are bought up abroad:

That it is probable there may be considerable Quantity saved out of the Flotilla; all the Sloops and Vessels belonging to Jamaica being gone on that Expedition; and, if any Cochineal is saved, the same will be carried directly to Carolina, New England, or New York; from whence it may be brought hither in about Six Weeks or Two Months:

That fonie may be expected from the Canaries That the Price in Spain is now about 27 Shillings and Six Pence per Pound; and there may be there about Two Ton, which is about4,000l. Weight:

That the South Sea Company has sent a Ship to the Spanish West Indies, which failed from the Dozvnes the Second of the last Month.; and Ihe may probably be here in about Eight or Nine Months.

That, upon the Examination of several Merchants, and others, concerned in the Woollen Manufactory, it was alleged,

That, admitting 50,000l. Weight of Cochineal to be the annual Consumption; and that there should be about 3,000l. Weight in hand; there would then be wanting above 40,000 /.; But, by the strictest Inquiry and Examination that they were able to make, they can hear of but One Bag in the First Hand; viz. one Mr. , a

Merchant; and that there might be about 200l. Weight in the Salters Hands:

That there is Ten Pound per Cent. Difference in the Weight between Holland and England; which reduces the Price to 33 Shillings Sterling j so the Difference is Ten Shillings per Pound Weight, admitting it to be 63 Skellins in Holland, and 43 Shillings per Pound Weight here:

That the lead Quantity of Cochineal allowed for dyeing a Cloth into Sclarlet, or other Grain Colours, is Five Pound; and many Cloths that cost under Nine Pound per Cloth, white, have so much bellowed on them:

That of long Bays, which may cost, white, about 7 /. lor. per Bay, many are dyed into Grain Colours; and the leall Allowance of Cochineal for doing it, is Three Pound per Bay; so, in Holland, they can lave 2/. 10*. Sterling per Cloth, and 1/. 10#. Sterling Bay, in the Article of Cochineal only,. besides what they lave in the Labourj being much cheaper in Holland than England: That, not above a Year and a Half ago, the Price for dying Grain Colours here was but 7 /. 1 os. and now 14/. per Cloth, by reason of the Scarcity of Cochineal.:

- That the Bay of Biscay is a very troublesome Sea, and the Bar of Bilboa very dangerous; and that the Ships from Holland going to Bilboa lose Four Months time; and the Spring-time is the only Season for Dyeing:

Vet. 18.

That there are. great Quantities of white Cloths, which at present lie at Blackwell-hall, and in the Factors Hands, undisposed of: That one particular Factor Had' above 800 Cloths lying upon hand, for want of Cochineal; and that if the Price was fallen upon Cochineal, he could fell 500 Cloths immediately:

That the Price here upon white Cloths was much fallen: And several Instances were given of the Charge being at present considerable left in dyeing white Cloths in Holland than in England \ but, if Cochineal was cheaper, they should not.fend their Cloth thither:

That all that was desired, was, That they might be put upon an equal Foot with their Neighbours that Permission for a free Importation might be granted for feme short time, in order to lessen the Price of Cochineal, which must otherwise unavoidably increase j that our neighbouring Nations may not under-fell us in foreign Markets, to the Detriment of our Woollen Manufactory.

That, upon Consideration of the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Senna. The House being informed, That some of the Commissioners of the Customs attended;

Certificates of Druggists, and others, about the Use of Senna: And allb,

An Account of the Quantity of Senna imported for Three Years, to Christmas last.

And then they withdrew.

And the Titles of the said Accounts and Certificates were read.

The said Accounts and Certificates arc as follow; viz.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

In Obedience to his Majesty's Commands, signified to us by the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, pursuant to an Addrefe of this honourable

House to his Majesty, we have caused an Account to be prepared by the proper Officers, shewing how Senna was rated, or charged, before the Act passed in the 3d Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, wherein it is mentioned to be used in Dyeing; and how it has been rated, or charged, since the Making thereof: Which Account we herewith humbly lay before this honourable House, in the Paper annexed, dumber I.

And, in further Obedience to his Majesty’s Commands,' by the annexed Certificate, N* II. of several eminent Salters, Drugfters, Dyers, and Apothecaries, which we caused to be procured, it appears, that the Drug, called by the Name of Senna, is made use of in Physick, and not in Dyeing: the Commodity used in Dyeing being only bastard Senna, or Plantain;

We have likewise caused an Account to be prepared of the Quantity of Senna imported for Three Years, to Christmas last; which we take Leave humbly to lay before this honourable House, in a Paper, N* III.

And to observe, That, by a Medium thereof, the Difference of the present net Duties from what the same would have amounted to, in case Senna had not l>een mentioned in the said Act to be for Dyers Use, appears to I. upwards of 1,300l. per Annum.

All which is humbly submitted to the Consideration of this honourable House.

Custom-house, London, J. , Walter,

THESE may certify whom it may concern. That I never fold the Drug Senna; nor do I believe it proper for Dyers Use. I have fold a Commodity, called Plantain, and sometimes Senna, imported from France; which I never knew valued at more than Thirty Shillings per Hundred Weight; which Commodity, 1 am informed, is not at all medicinal. Witness my Hand, this 17th Day of February 1715. Law. Parker,

Witness, Tho. Peirce. Dry Salter.

THESE are to certify whom it may concern, That we, who have hereunto affixed our Hands, never fold any Senna but to Persons whom we believe did design to use or fell it as Physick: Nor do we know, or ever heard, that it was proper for any other Use, We have not Vox- 18.

known it of less Value thart Eighteen Pence per Pound; and believe it always is imported from Turkey, or Leghorn. Witness our Hands, this 18* Day of February 1715.

Witness, Thomas Hollinworth, John Caresby, James Eyton. Tho. Brortifeild.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Seven hundred and Two Pounds Eight Shillings and Seven Pence, be granted to his Majesty, to discharge One Year’s Interest, after the Rate of Six Pounds per Centum per Annum, of the Sum of Sixty-one thousand Seven hundred Seven Pounds Three Shillings and Two Pence, or thereabouts, remaining due and un&tisfied of the Sum, not exceeding Seven hundred thousiuid Pounds, which was borrowed on an Act, made in the 3d Year of the Reign ofher late Majesty Queen Anne, of blessed Memory, for laying Duties upon Low Wines, and other things therein mentioned: and towards the Repayment whereof another Act passed in the Sixth Year of her laid late Majesty’s Reign, charging Coffee, and other Merchandizes, for the Term of Four Years; which expired on or about the 23d Day of One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eighteen thousand Eight hundred Fifty-three Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to his Majesty, to discharge One Year’s Interest, after the Rate of Six Pounds per Cent, per Annum, of the Sum of 314,219/. 11 s. or thereabouts, remaining due and unsatisfied of the principal Sum, not exceeding Five hundred thousand Pounds, which was borrowed on the Act of Parliament of the Eighth Year of the Reign ofher late Majesty Queen Anne, of blessed Memory, for laying Duties upon Candles, and other Duties, for Five Years; which expired on the lft Day of May 1715.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-two thousand Six hundred Sixty-five Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Six Pence, he granted to his Majesty, for supplying the Deficiency of the Fund of 168,003 /. per Annum, to make good the Payments to the Ten Pound Lottery of 1712, for the Two several Years ended at Michaelmas One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen.

A Petition of the Gentry, Merchants, Owners of Ships, Bridlington Freeholders, and others, inhabiting in and near the Town Piera-of Bridlington, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Bay of Bridlington aforesaid is a spacious and safe Place, as well for his Majesty s as other Ships and Vessels to anchor in stormy Weather; That the Harbour, or Quay, there, while the Piers were in good Repair, was a Place of great Security, as well as very commodious for supplying them with fresh Water and Provisions: That the Town of Bridlington hath long been, and still is, by the Advantage of its Situation, very considerable for its Traffick; in which very great Numbers of Men and Ships are employed, to the great Benefit and Improvement of Navigation:

That, upon Decay of the said Piers, an Act of Parliament formerly passed, granting § Duty upon Coal water-borne towards the Repairs thereof; but the Profits ariting thereby being all expended, and having proved insufficient to perfect that Work, notwithstanding great Sums of Money have been also laid out by the Town in Aid thereof, the said Piers are again by the Impetuosity of the Weather, and Violence of the Seas, shaken, disjointed, and, if not timely prevented, in imminent Danger of being destroyed:

The Repairs of those Piers will be so vastly chargeable and expensive, that it cannot be eftefted without the Assistance of this House: And praying, That Leave may be

The Order of the Second of February last being read’ requiring LewisPryfe Esquire, to surrender himself into

the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House by that Day Month, at farthest;

The Serjeant was called upon, to know whether he had heard from the said Mr. Pryfe; and he acquainted the House, That he had not heard from him.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had received a Letter from the said Mr. Pryfe; and he deliver^ cd the same to the Clerk, to be read: And the same was read accordingly; and is as follows; viz.

Sir,

T1S with Pleafere that I embrace every Opportunity of returning you my Acknowlegements for the good Offices you have done me, as often as the same of my unavoidable Absence has come under Debate in the House: The repeated Experience I have had of your Friendship in this Point, encourages me to hope for the Continuance of them; which I shall not offer to desire longer than the Reasonableness of my same shall appear to deserve them.

I beg Leave once more to represent it to you; and, through your Assistance, to the honourable House; whose Displeasure, as it is a very sensible Affliction to me, I should be glad, by any means in my Pow er, to remove: That as it is impracticable for me to attend by the Time appointed, because of a very severe Fit of the Gout which I am now afflicted with, and thereby give Satisfaction to the House in the Method they have insisted on; I hope they will accept of such as is in my Power; and give me a favourable Hearing, when I represent to them, That I was chose Knight of the Shire of Cardigan when I was at ioo Miles distant from it, and had been absent thence for jo Months before the time of my Election: which I was fb far from seeking, that I never aiked a Vote for it, and was chose even against my Inclinations.

I know not how far a Man is obliged to Hand to the Choice a County makes of him: Sure I am, that I have Reason to complain of a Force that has administred the Occasion of my difbbliging the honourable House, by an Absence caused by Infirmities, under which I laboured at the time of my Choice, and wffiich have continued upon me ever since, with the greatest Severity, and with little or no Intermission.

In these Circumstances, I would fain hope, that the honourable House will rather blame the Country’s Choice, than him who has been unwillingly forced into a Post,

V Ola 18.

and lies under the Misfortune (for t Matter myself ’twill not be thought a Crime) of not being able to attend the Business of it; and will therefore lay aside their Dif-pleafme, and remit the Sentence ordered again(1 me:

And I am the rather encouraged to hope this, because Mr. Prynne, in his Comment on the 4th Book of Sir Edward Coke's Institutes, (hews, from various Records, That incurable Distempers have been constantly allowed by the House for a just Excule of Non-attendance; and, upon Debates in such Cases, no other Punishment has been inflicted than excusing the Service of the Member, and ordering a new Writ for electing a Person duly qualified, and capable of attending the Business of the House:

This being the Course of Parliamentary Proceedings in such Cases as mine, which I have now truly represented to you, and can produce Hundreds of Witnesses to con- ' firm, 1 hope, that the unhappy Incapacity I am under of attending the Service of the House, will be thought to deserve no severer Treatment than has been usual in the like Cafes; and that my ready Submission to the honourable House’s Pleasure in this Point, will be a Means to restore me to their. favourable Opinion, and engage you to promote the Request of

Your most obliged and A be rilefenny, Feb. obedient humble Servant,.

i8° 1715.

I know not how far the House, in their last Order about me, might be influenced by any Report of the Messenger who came down to my House; but, to prevent Misrepresentation, I think it proper to assure you, that, within Three Days after a very dangerous Fit of the Gout fullered me to come down Stairs, I came from thence hitherto my Father-in-Law’s, 18 Miles in my Way to London: But the Motion of even so small a Journey brought another Fit upon me immediately; with which I have been laid up here ever since; not having been yet so much as able to return to my own House.

Poors an Mr. Molesworth, according to Order, reported from

IUte»n8*r ^ie Committee appointed to inspect the Poors Rates, and Scavengers Rates, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Weekly Bills of Mortality, the Matter, as it appeared to them, relating to the Poor of the Parish of St. Martin in the Fields; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, finding it a Work of insuperable Difficulty to perule, within any competent time, all the Books and Accounts of the said Parishes, in such manner as is necessary for the thorough Information of this House, have thought it more for the public Service to apply their Endeavours principally to those that relate to the Maintenance of the Poor:

And because the Parish of St. Martins in the Fields has been represented to the Committee as the most free r ora Frauds and Abuses, and averred to be under the bell

Regulation of any Parish in London, in respect to the Government of the Poor, the Committee, rather willing to propose a good Example for the Imitation of others, than desirous of finding Fault, have chose to begio with that Parish: And, that they might be able to set such Matters as relate to the Poor in as true a Light as the Shortnels of the Time would permit, they have perused several Volumes of Accounts; and have likewise endeavoured to get the best Informations, viva voce, from Persons understanding, and well acquainted with, that Parish; which may hereafter be of some Use for Proceedings in other Parishes, when it shall be thought proper and fealbnable to go through with a Work of this Nature: But, because the immediate Interposition of this House seems necessary to redress such inveterate Evils as have been complained of even in this Parish, though represented to be under the bell Regulation, as aforesaid, the Committee, in pursuance of the Order of Thursday last, have prepared a Report, as far as they have proceeded; which they have directed to be made as followeth; viz.

That the Committee finds, That the Maintenance ap pointed for the Poor in the aforesaid Parish, orifes from the several Funds following; Part whereof are under the Management of the Churchwardens, and the rest under that of the Overseers of the Poor; viz.

Rates on Houses, commonly called The Poors Rates:

The Royal Bounty, and Contributions on extraordinary Occasions:

The Fines:

The Collections at the Church and Chapel Doors;

The Composition for Bastards:

The Annuities and Legacies:

The Parish Estate:

The Altar or Offertory-money at the Church and Chapels:

The Conviction-money of Swearers, 8$c.;

The Rents of the Pews:

The Burying-money:

Monies arising from Petitions to Persons of Quality at

Christmas:

The Sales of Goods of poor People deceased; and several other small Receipts.

It is not denied, That Part of the Monies arising from some of the aforesaid Heads is applicable to the Use of the Church, as to Repairs, when necessary, and several incident Charges; but, the principal and original Intention of these Charities and Funds being the Maintenance of the Poor, it may justly be expected, that far the greater Part should be applied tofo necessary and pious a Use: But the Committee find the Accounts of the Distribution of these Sums, in the Books, as to the Charities and Expences, so mixed and confused between the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor, that ’tis a Work of some time, and Pains, to dillinguith them: (However,)

which, taking for granted the Truth of the Books and Reckonings delivered in, they find to stand thus:

The ObservatSons which the Committee made on thele Accounts werethefe;

1. That there are very great Sums of Money rated and collected yearly, in this Parish, for the Use of the Poor.

2. That, the Books being filled with great Multitudes of Names, and of Sums distributed at feverat Times to Persons carrying those Names, it was impossible to distinguish which were fictitious, and which were real j but die most Part most be taken upon Trutl.

3. Several material Objections were made to the Largencfs of the Sums in the Articles of the Orphans, and pensionary Poor; but, as to that of the casual Poor, it appears, that it amounts yearly to near One-third above what is distributed to the known or Standing Poor: And it is in this Article, principally, that the Committee is of Opinion the Publick may be more than ordinarily imposed on; Several fraall Articles being blended into this, under the Name of Extraordinaries, to make it appear die greater.

4- That the Purchases of Houses or Land, called Part of the Parish Estate, which is thought to belong more immediately to the Repairs of the Church, arc made with the Poors Money; and uioft of the extraordinary Expences of the Patiih are deduced out of the said Money.

5. That the Arrears of the Poors Hates, amounting yearly to a great Sum, and, in these afore-mentioned Three Years, te 1,187/. ]4*- are given in as defpe-rate, and totally loft to the Parish; whereas, upon Perusal of the Books of Arrears by the Committee, it appeared, that many Persons named therein were very sufficient, and of Quality and Reputation; and that from fouie of them the Arrears had been demanded; so that the Committee has Grounds to believe several of them may have been collected, though never brought to Account, afterwards.

What confirmed the Committee in this Opinion is, That, they having summoned Peter , formerly an Oveiicer of the Poor in the said Parish; he, being examined by the Committee, testiiied.

That, in the Year .1698, there was a Surplus of 300l. in the Overseers Hands, for that Year, aliove what maintained the Poor; and which, as the Law directs, ought to have been paid into the Hands of the subsequent Over-leors; but was, by a Majority of St. Martins Vestry, voted to be paid into their Hands: And that, in the Year 1 699, the said Hill being then one of the Overseers, there did likewise remain, in his and his Partner's Hands, an Overplus of about 220/.; which he the said Hill would have paid over to the succeeding Overseers; but his Partner opposing the lame, and the Vestry, taking Cognizance of their Dispute, did, notwithstanding all the Opposition he could make to so illegal a Practice, by a Majority of Voices oblige him to pay the said 220/. to them, and not to the luccceding Overseers as he hath been since informed he might by Law have done, without their Content or Approbation:

And the said Hill further laid, That he being afterwards, in the Year 170.5, required to pay his Proportion of the Arrears of an additional Assessment, made in the said Parish for the Maintenance of the Poor for Four or Five Years before, and refuting to pay the same, because that additional Charge was unnecessarily laid; he knowing of the aforesaid great Surplusages, which would have saved the said additional Assessment, if those Sums had been applied as the Law directs; Mr. Price, Mr. Vincent, and Air . It hell, the then Churchwardens and Vestrymen

of St, Martins Parish, with aConstable, Two Collectors, and a lleadle, of a diitant Ward, did distrain a Silver Pepper Box out of his House, and detained the lame, till jjg had paid his Proportion to the said additional AlTeff-

ment: Also, that several of his Neighbours were frightened into Payment of the said Assessments, under the Apprehension of the like Distrefics; being summoned to the Vestryj and there threatened to have their Goods seized, if they did not pay; by which means great Sums were raised out of the Deficiencies of the Poors Rates for several Years after the Books were delivered up, wherein they returned such as insolvent.

6. That although the French Inhabitants, and some Dxffenters from the Church of England, pay their Share of the Poors Rates and other Collections; yet they receive nothing out of it towards the Maintenance of their own Poor; but do it themselves.

As to the Altar or Offertory Money, the Committee cannot but observe, that the Methods uled iu St. tins Parish for collecting Sacrament-money, is such as is liable to great Frauds; being without Cheque or Controul, and, according to the Confession of the Churchwardens themselves, wholly left to the Discretion of such as col left it, and those they pretend sometimes toaccountto: Whereby there is Reason to believe, this great and signal Piece of Christian Charity, offered to God for the foie L’fe of the Poor, at the Times of the most solemn Devotion, is, notwithstanding the Directions given by the Rubrick (which orders, That the Money given at the Offertory shall be disposed of to such pious and charitable Uses as the Ministers and Churchwarden shall think fit; wherein if they disagree, it shall be disposed of as the Ordinary shall appoint), diverted from its primitive Use and Delig-nation, and turns to the private Profit of those who ought to be most exemplary to others for Piety and Charity.

8. The Committee further takes notice, That, con-

fidering the Multitude of Communicants at St. Martini Church, upon the score of qualifying themselves for Employments, and the Frequency of Sacraments there (being every Sunday), the Account given in of the Oftertory-money does not seem to rife in a just Proportion; and they are confirmed the rather in this Opinion, because Charles Medlycot Esquire, a Justice of the Peace, and

Vestryinan of the said Parish, avers, and is ready to tef-tify upon Oath, That Jeremiah Rose, Churchwarden for the Year 1714, did allure him, the said Charles Medlycot, upon his Inquiry, That the Offertory-money for St. Martins Church alone, exclusive of the Chapel, amounted that Year to above 400l.: And One of th*

Vestrymen, and formerly Church warden, of the said Parish, affirmed to the Committee, That the said Jeremiah, Rose had, at another time, confessed to him. That the Offertory-money of SainitMor/m’s Church, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen, amounted to 400l.; notwithstanding which, the said , forgetting himself, has, in the Accounts now delivered in, reckoned the Offertory-money, of the Year 1714, to amount to no more than than 344/. 6s. 3d.

9. That the Money arising from the Rents of the Pews in Trinity Chapel do fully maintain the said Chapel, in every respect; and, as to the Offertory-money, it was disposed of without Controul, as at St. Martin's Church; and that all other Emoluments whatsoever, arising from the Easter Offerings, Chiiftenings, Marriages, and Burials, there, as well as the Balances of the Offertory-money, are paid to the Vicar.

10. That there is 30 I. per Annum charged as Rent paid for Oxendon Chapel; which the Committee conceives, might, and ought to be paid out of the Rent of the Pews; several of which are not lett, by reason of the high Rent demanded lor them.

12. The Committee, having carefully examined the said Eddridge what those casual Poor were, on whom fitch great Sums were yearly expended, could get no good Account from him of them: Sometime he said, They were the like as settled Poor, though not entered upon the Pensions; sometimes, that they were such as had received feme Misfortune accidentally in the Parish: And, being further demanded, Whether he had the Warrants from Justices of the Peace for relieving such Poor, according to the Statute; he said, He had: But when his Books were produced, to that Intent, he could not shew so.muchasone single instance satisfactory to the Committee: That the said Eddridge, over and above his Handing Salary, raised, in the said Three Years, great Sums out of the said Poors and Parish Money, amounting to above 832/. exclusive of what he receives upon Account of the Surveyors and Scavengers j which, upon Perufel of several particular Accounts of his, did clearly appear to the Committee to be unreasonable, if not fraudulent; which Accounts are ready to be produced to this House, whenever they Dial I be called for; whereby it may appear how necessary a person this said Eddridge is to the governing Part of the said Parish, when such Accounts shall be suffered to pals.

13. That the Vestry of St. Martins Parish, at least the acting Part of it, is composed of lucn as have been Churchwardens themselves; it being the Custom, when a Churchwarden goes out of his Office, to elect him a Veltrvman: These state the Accounts ot all succeeding Churchwardens and Overseers, and elect all Vestrymen; so that, should once any Corruption get in, ’tis scarce possible it can otherwise be remedied than by the Authority of this House:

That whatever is wanting for the Use of the Church supposing the Accounts of Quantities and Qualities to be fairly given in, is bought at the worst Haind, and paid for at extravagant Rates; because the Persons who furnish their Goods, or their Work, are, for the most part, such as have been Churchwardens and Vestrymen; of which the Committee had several Infiances produced.
