15. The Committee finds, upon Examination, That the Ex peaces and Disbursements of the Churchwardens and Overseers, given in for the Three afore-mentioned Years, exclusive of all Charities to the Poor, amount to 5,448/. io s. 4 \d.being altnoft One whole Year’s Revenue of the Parish, in Three Years time; whereof, the Committee conceives, £ds might be saved.

Mr. GriJ'dale, Clerk of St.Martina Church, being sent

for, and his Books of Burials being perused for the Three last Years, the Committee observed, That the Proportion of Children buried far exceeds that of Men and Women; and, being examined touching the fame, said. That one Year with another, there was about 1,200 Christenings; and that above -J-s of those die every year; which he could not attribute to any thing, unless the Air of St. Martina Parish was more unwholsome than that of other Parishes:

He further took notice, That the Burials in the Months of December and January last, being the most rigorous Part of the Winter, were twice as many as was usual in other Months; and according to the Lilt given in, amount to 97 of the casual Poor, not reckoning others.

16. The Committee have taken these Accounts of Collections and Distributions De bene according as they were delivered in; but, should either of these prove un fair, the Abuses complained of will be much the greater; find, by several Instances already discovered, the Committee finds Reason to doubt of the Truth of many of

11.cm.

17. The Petitioners, or settled Poor, are given in at between 1,200l. and 1,300l. per Annum, for the last Three Years; and Multitudes of Names are entered in the Books, which the Committee could find no Method of comptrolling; much left that other vast Article of the casual Poor, amounting to between 1,800l. and 1,900l. per Annum: notwithstanding all which real or pretended Distributions, the begging Poor about the Streets, in this Parish, are observed to be as numerous as ever.

18. The Orphans are given in in a distinct Article from that of Parish Nurse Children, and Bastards, which are comprehended under that of casual Poor j and amounts to a great Sum yearly; namely, to 800 /.

The Committee has had no time to inquire into the Particulars of other Parishes; but has received the following Informations in generul;

lft. That in many Parishes, notwithstanding that the Poors Rates amount to a very great Tax; yet, under Pretences that there is not sufficient levied for the Poors Ule in the Four Quarters, they raise more Money; which, improperly, they call Five, Six, nay, even to Seven, Quarters, some Years; which comes to near as much as a Land Tax at 2 s. per Pound.

2d. That the Money lately collected by voluntary Contributions, upon account of the excessive cold Winter, in order to the immediate Relief of the Poor, has not been distributed in purliiance of the said charitable Intention; but, in many rarillies, remains undillributed to this Day; ferae being carried into the Chamber of London, from whence it is not ealily to be retrieved within any competent time; so that Multitudes of Poor, which ought to have been relieved, have starved to Death during this most rigorous Winter; and this may appear by the large Increase in the Bills of Mortality about that time.

3d. That a great many poor Infants, and exposed Bastard Children, are inhumanly fettered to die by the 20

Barbarity of Nurses, especially Parish Nurses, who are a fort of People void of Commiseration, or Religion; hired by the Churchwardens to take off a Burthen from the Parish at the cheapest and ealieft Rates they can; and these know the Manner of doing it effectually, as by the Burial Books may evidently appear, according to'Mr. Grifdales own Observatiom.

4. That the Increase of strange Beggars, Cripples, lusty idle Men and Women, Vagabonds, blind People, pretended and real Mad-folks, and sech-like, is altogether owing to the Negligence of those that should remedy it, and of the Parish Officers, who take no due Care to purge their several Parishes of such fort of Vagrants; but connive at them, on purpose that such appearing Objects of Charity may give a fair Pretence to these yearly exorbitant Collections of all kinds; this kind of Beggars receive little or no settled Parish Alms, but live upon what they can extort by their Cries and Importunities in the Streets, and at Coach-tides; and what they thus get, they are generally obliged to ipend at feme Tipling house kept by the Beadles, who have good Salaries allowed them, or their Friends and Relations, who fell unwholsome Spirits, which carry off Multitudes of them every Year.

5. The Committee observed several ftaferes in the Pu-rish Books delivered in to them; as also, that some Books of Accounts are freshly written; but cannot lay this was done to any sinister Intent.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee cannot induce themselves to be of Opinion, that much above One-half of the great Sums aforesaid, which are collected by, and paid to, the Churchwardens and Overseers yearly, are really expended on that pious and charitable Work of relieving the Poor; but that, in consequence of the present Methods taken, the Poor are rather increased in this great City, of late, than diminished; and those of them which are relieved, are not done lb in the manner they ought to be; but that many very miserably perish for Want.

A Petition of the Tanners, Curriers, Leather-fellers, Shoemakers, and Spanish Leather dressers, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, since the laying on the Duties upon Hides and Skins, several Branches of the Leather Trade is mightily fallen to Decay, chiefly occasioned by the using of Ticking, Canvass, fc. to cover the upper Part of Shoes with, instead of Leather; by reason of which, both Tanners, Curriers, and other Dealers in Leather, find a very great Decay in the Drefiing and Selling of Calves Skins, and all other Sorts of thin Leather: The Drefiing of Spanish Leather, being, a Manufacture that hath been

attained to in this Kingdom, hath proved a good Livelihood to many Families; and the Crown receives considerable Duties upon importing Goat Skins, and other Commodities used in that Trade; the said Trade being very much declined by the using of other Things, as aforesaid: likewise Turkey and Morocco Leather, which, upon Importation, pays a very high Duty to the Crown, is, in a

geat measure become ufold's: And praying to take their afe into Consideration, how injurious it is to the Revenue, as welt as to the Petitioners; and grant them such Relief as in your great Wifdoni shall seem meet.

Dagenham A Petition of Dominick Donnelly Gentleman, was pre-B reach. fented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the

Petitioner, at the Request of One of the Trustees appointed by Act of Parliament to receive Proposals for the speedy and effectual preserving the Navigation of the River of Thames, by (lopping the Breach in the Levels of Havering and Dagenham, did, at a considerable Expence, provide Boats, Hands, and other Necessaries, to survey and take a Plan of, the fame: That the Petitioner, after he had spent above Two Months in taking the several Soundings, and in making such Observations and Experiments as were necessary to find the Pulh of the Water at the Mouth of the said Breach, and the Nature of the Earth at the Bottom thereof, did actually survey, and take an ex-aft Plan, both of the Breach, and the Levels overflowed thereby: That, on the Petitioner’s Return to London, he made Models of the several Machines he had contrived to stop the said Breach; and then delivered in his Proposals to the Trustees; and offered to undertake, and perfect, the same for 15,000l.; But Mr. being a prior

Propofcr, was employed, notwithstanding the Petitioner did then assign undeniable Reasons to convince both

15

well, and his Friends, that his Method was impracticable:

After the Lois of a whole Year, and Seven thousand Pounds Expence, BofweWs Works blew up; and the flopping the said Breach is thereby rendered more difficult, and the Sand Bank at the Mouth thereof very much increased:

Upon the first Notice in the Gazette for receiving new Proposals, the Petitioner did again deliver in his Proposals for (lopping the said Breach, and demanded only 16,300l.; but the Trustees then infilled upon Security for Ten thousand Pounds Forfeiture, in case his Method did not succeed: But, on the Petitioner’s representing die Hardships of such Resolution, they reduced the Forfeiture to 6,000l.; but then allowed him Two Days only to get such Security: A Committee being appointed to inspect the several Schemes, of which Notice was agreed to be lent to each Propoler, the Petitioner was prepared with his Plans and Models; but had no Notice till after the Committee had met, and agreed in favour of Mr. Perry, One of the Propoiers; since which, the Petitioner could never prevail to have his Scheme examined; the Trustees have agreed to pay to the said Mr. Perry 25,000 /. and to advance what Money he shall have Occasion for in the Undertaking; notwithstanding the Petitioner proposed topei> fest the same for 16,300l. .* That several able Mathematicians, who have considered Mr. s Scheme, have

declared it as their Opinion, That the said Scheme will be found to be impracticable: And praying this House, to prevent any further Misapplication of publick Money, and the great Damages that may arise, by future Miscarriages, to the Navigation of the River of T, and the Trade of this Kingdom, to appoint a Committee to examine the several Schemes of the Petitioner and Mr. Perry.

Palatines A Petition of John Champante Esquire, Agent of the fctded in Province of New York, for and on the behalf of Brigadier Araenca. General Robert Hunter, his Majesty’s Governor in Chief of the said Province, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, the Precarioufiiefs of the Trade of Great Britain with the Northern Crowns for Naval Stores having occasioned great Difficulties, the Lords Commissioners for Trade and the Plantations, in the Year 1709, laid a Proposal before the late Queen in Council, That Three thousand of the Palatines, then lately arrived here, might be employed, to the very great Advantage of this Kingdom, in the Province of Nezo York, on the Production and Manufacture of Naval Stores; which Proposal her said Majesty was pleased to approve of, and to charge the said Governor with the Care and Execution thereof: That the Charge of making such a Settlement of the said Palatines was computed to amount to Thirty thousand Pounds; which the said Governor had Assurances should be made good to him; and, pursuant thereto, had the Sum of Eight thousand Pounds issued to him, towards their Transportation, and to answer other Charges on their Account; and, as to the Remainder of the said Thirty thousand Pounds, he had Directions to draw, Quarterly, Bills of Exchange on the Treasury for proportionable Parts of the fame; which accordingly he has been necessitated to do; but none of his Bills, except Two of One thousand Pounds each, have been ever accepted, or paid; which has turned not only to his very great Damage, but to the Prejudice too of the public Credit, upon tire Faith of which the several Sums of Money he drew for were advanced: And praying, That this House would take the said Governor’s same into Consideration, in relation to the Monies due on the said Bills of Exchange, which were drawn pursuant to her late Majesty’s Instructions, and the Directions of the Treasury; and to cause, that Provision may be made for the Paymertt thereof.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Merchants trading to, and residing in, New England, in behalf of themselves, and others, is referred.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into Consideratioti the State of that Part of Great called Scotland:

And Mr. Secretary Stanhope delivered in at the Clerk's Table.a Letter to the Duke of Argyle, dated the 15U1 February 1716.

Which Letter was read; and is as follows; viz.

May it please your Grace,

THE unfortunate Circunoltances our Country is reduced to, by our late Divisions, are such as mult move the Pity and Compassion of any true-born;

and we have just Grouud to expect, that the Generality, which every Man allows tolhine lb bright in your Grace’s Churafter, will make it very disagreeable to you to fee your Country in that Situation.

The many and great Hardships we groaned under since the late Union, were not the least Motives of making us take Arms; and, however our Judgments may have been millaken in the Way of procuring Redress, our Intentions mull, we think, be allowed to be honourable, and what became a People who have, for so many Ages, preserved their Independency.

Whatever Hardships, and unexpected Accidents, have attended our Undertaking, we are the more ealy under them, that we always were resolved to bear the worst, and were willing to hazard our Lives in a Cause which appeared to us so just: But were our Lives our only Consideration, we would not have given your Grace the Trouble of this Letter: That which touches more fenfi-bly is, the melancholy View we have of so many old and worthy Families as mult fall with us; which makes ns wish, for the Good of our Country, that Peace and Tranquillity were restored; and that once more we should all return to that Love and Affection to one another, that ought to be the Entertainment of so many People link’t together by Blood and Relation.

This Reflection, we are confident, will touch your Grace as much as it does us, and make you use your Endeavours to obtain so happy an End; which would be belt effectuated, could we expect the Government would grant an Indemnity to such as are willing to live peaceably at home, and Liberty for those to go abroad who are desirous to pass the rest of their Lives beyond Seas.

It may not, perhaps, be unworthy the Government to accept the Acknowlegements of so many Noblemen and Gentlemen as have appeared here in Anns; and the Experience of all Ages shews what a Body of Men, reduced to Despair, may do; and we should consider it as the greatest Hardfkip that can be imposed on us, were we forced to act a Part of that Nature, which must prove so fatal, iq our Country.

Your Grace has now an Opportunity offered you of shewing your Affection to it, and, at the same time, doing a considerable Service to the Government, by securing the Obedience of lo many Noblemen and Gentlemen by the Ties of Gratitude, which must be considered very strong by Men of Honour; and, we hope, these Motives will prevail with your Grace to give us a speedy Answer, and let us know what are the Rel'olutions of the Government concerning us; and whether we may expect an Indemnity for what is pait, and Protection for our Lives and Fortunes in Time coining; which we consider the only Means of obtaining the End we now aim at, the Peace and Welfare of our Country, by preserving so many honourable Families as are engaged in this Affair.

We

Ways and Means.

Supply.

Where toe Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follows; viz.,

Upon the Petitions of Sir Wm. Baronet, and

Hugh Bethel Esquire; and oiChristopher and others, Burgesses of toe Borough of PonteJraR, in the County of York.-,complaining of an undue Election and Return of the honourable John Downey and Robert Frank Esquires, for the said Borough:

The Committee examined the Merits of this1 Elec1-tion:

That it was agreed, That this was a Borough by.Pro* icription; and that the Right of Election is in Persons having a Freehold of Burgage-tenure, paying a Burgage-rent.

The Poll was,

For Mr. Daumey, 149: For Sir Wm. Lawther, 122:/

Mr. Frank, 145: Mr. Bethel, 11 i

That the Petitioners Counsel complained of Partiality in the Mayor, Recorder, and Town Clerk; and alleged they should add 41 to their Poll, and take off 38 from the Sitting Members.

It appeared by the Poll, That Two voted twice for the Sitting Members.

And, by the Evidence of Wm. Lee, it appeared, That Three Quakers tendered their Votes for the Petitioners; and were refused, because they would not take the Abjd-ration Oath; though they offered to take the Affirariation to the Eflfeft thereof:

That the Mayor was governed in the Poll by the Recorder, and Mr. Edmund Abbot the Town Clerk; who was an Agent for the Sitting Members, and took several Votes for them, w ho had no Right; and refused several for the Petitioners, who had a Right: And that Abbot who has the making up of the Fee-farm Book every Year for the Mqyor, wherein the different Tenures should be distinguUhed, and all toe Burgages truly entered, had marked therein several as Burgage-tenants, who were not so; and omitted the marking others, who were; winch Partiality run in favour of the Sitting Members; and that Disputes upon the Poll had been frequently determined by this Book:

That Twelve Persons, who, by Conveyances from Sir William Lawther, dated January 2d, 1713, and proved by Mr. Lee, claimed Twelve BuFgages, Part of an Estate formerly Wakefield’s, and which pay Burgage-rent, and were purchased by Sir Wm. Lowthe in 1711, tendered their Votes for the Petitioners; but were refused; although most of them, or their Predecessors, had been admitted at former Elections, when they voted in a contrary Interest.

The Petitioners Counsel proceeded to add Eleven, who,

by Conveyances from SieWm. Lawther and Mr. Bethed, dated January5th, 1714, claimed Eleven Burgages, Part of an Estate formerly EngliJKs, and which pay Burgage-rent, and were purchased by Sir Wm. Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That the Meflen-ger who went, pursuant to the Order of the Seventh instant, to bring Lewis Pryfe Esquire, up in Custody, was returned:

Whereupon he was called in; and, at the Bar, gave the House an Account what he had done pursuant to that Order; viz.

That he had been at Aberllefer where he had heard

Mr. Pryfe was; but did not find him there; and that he had been at Mr. Pryfe's House in Cardiganshire, and had

searched that and several other Houses for him, but could not find him: But that one Dr. Pugh, Mr. Pryfe & Physician, delivered a Letter to him from Mr. Pryfe, dated the 12th instant at Aberlqferry; which he delivered in; and it was read; and is as follows; viz.

Mr. Kingham, Aberlleferry, March is* 1714-

HAVING had feme Intelligence of your coming here,

I thought it more adviseable to be removed out of the Way, Sian to make myself a Prisoner, in this sickly Condition that I am now in; the Consequences of which would be fatal to me, if I should be required to undertake a London Journey, as my Physician, and the whole Counby, can inform you. Im

Your Friend and Servant,

Le. Pryfe.

Resolved, That Lewis Pryfe Esquire, a Member of this House, havinjg been sent for in Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, the 8th Day of August last, for not attending the Service of this House; and having never qualified himself as a Member of this House, by taking the Oaths at the Table; and having been, on the 2d of February lad, summoned to surrender himself into Custody of the Serjeant at Arms, upon pain of being proceeded against with the utmost Severity; and he having absconded, and peremptorily refused to surrender himself into Custody; be, for the said Contempt, expelled this House.

A Petition of the Three French Regiments of Foot, late under the Command of Major General Brigadier Belcastell, and the Right [honourable the Lord Lifford, formerly Brigadier Ducambon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, being all French Proteuant Refugees, and having served, the former War, in Ireland and Flanders, with a Zeal suitable to the Gratitude they owe for the Protection they have received from the English Nation, this House, out of a more particular Care for them, did, by a Refo-Jution, of the lft of March 1698, appropriate, for Payment of their Arrears, the Sum of 32,551/. gs. 5</. Part of the 800,000l. then granted by Parliament for Payment of the Arrears due to the Forces in;

which passed i_the Royal Assent on the lft February before; notwithstanding which, and contrary to the said Resolution, above One-third part of that Money was withheld from them, and diverted to other Purposes: That this House, upon their Application in the Years 1705, 1706, 1707, 1708, and 1709, being very sensible of the Grievance they had sustained, of the Justness of their Demands, and the great Zeal they have likewise shewn, during the last War in Flanders, Spain and caused

V01..I8.

several Bills, at several times, to be brought in for their Relief; but it appearing that their Accounts required too much time to have them settled, the Petitioners obtained an Address to her Majesty, to command the Auditors of the Imprest to state their Accounts; which, on the lothr March 1708, were, by the said Auditors, laid before this House: That the Petitioners found themselves aggrieved, in several respects, in their Accounts, as dated by the Auditors of the Imprest; made, in the Year 1710, their Application to this House; praying. That, as the Sums due to them were of the same Nature with the Deficiencies, the Payment thereof was by a Bill then depending, assigned on the South Sea Stock, their Payment, bout Principal and Interest, might likewise be assigned to them on the said Stock; seeing all these Deficiencies had been equally made good, and, upon pressing State Exigencies, applied by the Government to other Uses than they had been intended for: That the Petitioners, notwithstanding their earnest Solicitations, had the Misfortune not to be comprehended in the said Bill, which Wes’ passed into an Act: That the Petitioners are ready to prove several Errors in the Accounts passed by the Auditors of the Imprest: And praying this House to refer them to the Commissioners appointed for taking and stating the Debts due to the Army, that they may examine what is lawfully due to them on the Balance of their Accounts, and give in a true State thereof; to the End that the Petitioners may be paid in such Manner as shall be judged most proper and convenient.

Resolved, That the said Petition be rejected.

A Petition of Robert Ludga of the Parish of Saviour's, Southzeark, was presented to the House, and

read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, upon Notice in the Gazette about Three Months ago. That the Trustees appointed, by A fit of Parliament, for Hopping the Breach in the Levels of Havering and Dagenham, would meet at Guildhall, to receive Proposals for stopping the said Breach, laid a Scheme, and Proposals, for that Purpose, before the said Trustees; which Scheme had been viewed and approved by some of the Ikilfulleft Men in the Kingdom; and when the Question was asked in Court by One of the Trustees, Whether the Petitioner’s Scheme would do, not One of the Trustees could say it would not: notwithstanding which, the said Trustees were pleased to prefer Captain John Ferry's Scheme; though the Petitioner proposed to do the Works for 5,000 /. leis than they agreed to allow the said Captain John Ferry; and notwithstanding the Petitioner offered to bring up the Works to Low-water mark, at his own Charge, before he touched a Peny of the publick Money: And praying, That his Scheme, and Proposals, may be referred to the Committee appointed to look into the Schemes and Proposals of Mr. Dominick Donelly, and the said Mr. Perry; not in the least doubting but the Publick, and the Petitioner, will have Justice from this House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of Dominick Donelly is referred.

Mr. John Chetwynd reported from the Committee, to

whom it Mas referred to inquire into the Abuses practised in the manufacturing Tobacco, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the iloufe; and he read the same in his Place; which he afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the same was read; and is as follows;

That the Committee had inquired into the said Abuses, and examined several Witnesses for that Purpose; and find the Matter to be as follows;

Edward Willis said, That he had spent much Time and Labour, in order to discover the Frauds and Abuses committed in the Manufacturing, and Selling; of Tobacco: That he knows great Quantities of Walnut-tree Leaves, Hop Leaves, and Chesnut-tree Leaves, have been gathered, upon the Fall of the Leaf, at Cashalton, in Surrey, and other Places; which Leaves have been dried, stripped, cut, and mixed with Tobacco, and many times fold for Tobacco unmixed; and that Two Persons may gather a Ton of such Leaves in a Day:

That John Sheffeild has a Work-house, or Cutting-house, at Lambeth; where he employs several Persons in

the Manufacturing of 1'uch Leaves, instead of Tobacco; of which he has fold great Quantities to divers Persons, as Sheffeild told him: That Sheffeild employed, all last Winter, Half a Dozen Men, who might easily manufacture about 20 Hundred Weight of such lham Tobacco in a Week:

That, to discover this ill Practice, he went to an Ale-house near the said Cutting-house, and sent for the said Sheffeild', but, he not being the re, Clerk, One of the Cutters, came to him; of whom he asked the lowest Prices of the several Sorts; who told him, they were sold at gd. 10 d.and 11 d. per Pound; but recommended him

to Thomas Sharpies, who was then at Work with one Mr. Horton, a Tobacconist in Queen-street, for his better Information; but neither Clark nor Sharpies shewed him any Samples: That, afterwards Willis met with Sheffeild at the Pye Bull, in Thames-street; but he produced no Samples, although he left a Note with for that Purpose; presuming that Sheffeild suspected Willis came as a Spy, in order to discover the Fraud; but yet Sheff'eild appointed another Meeting, saying, the lowest Prices of the several Sorts was 8 \d. gd. and to Pound, and asked Willis what Quantity he wanted; who answered,' 1,000 Pound Weight, if he liked the Goods, and they could agree.

That Abel Lee informing Willis, That Sheffeild told him, he had fold 10 or 11 Hundredweight of such Leaves, mixed with Tobacco, to one Burley, a Tobacconist at Shadwell Dock, at i o d.per Pound, Willis afterward went to Burley's, and asked a Woman, then in the Shop, for a Pound of ordinary Tobacco; w ho said. She had none under 12 d.per Pound , of which he bought a Pound, and w ent to a neighbouring Alehouse, where Abel Lee waited for him; and there he opened the Pound he bought at Burley's, and, comparing it with the Samples which Lee had from Sheffeild, found it to be of the same ibrt with One of the Samples:

That on Lady-day last.be was at Lambeth, and there farw the aforesaid Work-house as full as it could hold of the said Leaf cuttings; but what Quantity it might contain, he knows not:

That Sheffeild has also a Warehouse in Green lane, in Camion-street; wherein he keeps great Quantities of the said cut Leaves for Sale; which sometimes are mixed with Tobacco; whereof there is not above One-fourth Part.

Abel Lee, Tobacconist, said, That he knows the said John Sheffeild has employed several Men in gathering, and cutting, great Quantities of Walnut-tree Leaves, Chesnut Leaves, and Hop Leaves; which be fells instead of Tobacco; and sometimes mixes a final! Quantity of Tobacco with such leaves; which he fells at different Prices; and has been told, that several other Persons use the like Practices: That Lee went to Sheffeild, in Order to know the Price of the several Sorts of such manufactured Leaves, and VoL. 18.

Tobacco; telling Sheffeild, he should have Occasion for 2,000 W; and Sheffeild said, The lowest Prices were, for Hop Leaves only, 84- d. Pound; mixed with Spanish Tobacco, g\d. per Pound; and mixed with Oronoko Tobacco, 1 o d. per Pound; but Sheffeild theu shewed him no Samples: That, the next Day, he met Sheffeild again, expecting to fee Samples of the several Sorts aforesaid; but Sheffeild told him, he had not brought the Keys of his Warehouse; nor then produced any Sample; but, on Monday the 19th of March last, he met Sheffeild, and then he produced Three Samples;

One of Hop Leaves only, another mixed with Spanish, and the Third with Oronoko, Tobacco; saying. He had fold great Quantities of those Sorts to several Persons; and particularly named one Burley, living at Shadu ell Dock; who had bought 10 or 11 Hundred Weight of him, at 10 d.per Pound:

That, afterwards, Lee and went to the said

Burley's; and Willis bought a Pound of Tobacco at Burley's, which colt him 12 and, upon comparing it with One of the Samples he had from Sheffeild, found it to be of the same Sort; which Pound he produced to the Committee:

That Sheffeild has a Cutting-house at Lambeth, w here he employs several Men in the manufacturing the said Leaves; who work privately,' and convey them from thence by Night; and that, on Lady Day last, he fuw there about Four Tons of them, as near as he could guels; and produced several Samples of the said Leaf-cuttings, which he had from Sheffeild's Work-house at Lambeth.

Sheffeild has also a Warehouse in Canon-street, w here he keeps great Quantities of the said Cuttings for Sale, and there likewise he saw, some time the Week before Lady-day Nine or Ten Stands, of about or ,500* Weight each; and several Hags, which might contaiu near the like Quantity.

Fra. Palmer, of Westminster, said, That he knows great Quantities of Hop Leaves have been gathered up at Dartjord, in Kent, and Earn ham, and Walnut-tree Leaves at Cashalton, in Surry, for the Use of John Shes-Jeild, who has a Cutting-house at Lambeth, where, he manufactures the said Leaves in Likenels of Tobacco, and fells them sometimes mixed' with Tobacco, and sometimes un-mixed: That he has seen Sheffeild’s Men at Work at Lambeth; and knows all or most of them; viz. Sharpiefs, and his Brother, Clark, and and this Practice

was first begun about Three Years since:

That Walnut-tree Leaves have also been gathered up in Hyde Park, for the Use of Mr. Carter, Tobacconist, Katharine Street, and one Snell, in Spittle-Jields, as he has been told:

That he has disposed of considerable Quantities of loch manufactured Leaves, mixed with Tobacco, sometimes I, of> and 4, of Tobacco, from g\d. to 1 id. per Pound, for Mr. Sheffeild; in the Whole, amounting to about 2.5 Hundred Weight; but believes the Buyer generally knew the Tobacco was mixed with something, though they knew "hot w hat; and believes, that the same was fold for the Home Consumption; but does not know, that any was exported.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent Frauds in manufacturing Tobacco: And that Mr. John Chetzrynd, Mr. Lowndes, and Mr. IJey/ham, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That an bumble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he w’ill be graciously pleased to direct the Attorney General to prosecute John Sheffeild, and others, who have been concerned in Frauds relating to the Manufacturing of Tobacco.

The House being acquainted, That the Commissioners for the Salt Duties attended

They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House a particular Account of the several Allowances made on the' Exportation of Fish, and what Quantities of Salt arc used in curing- the fame, respectively; and of Frauds discovered concerning the same.

And then they withdrew.

The Title of the said Account was read.

The laid Account is as follows;

A particular Account of the several Allowances made on Exportation of Fish, and what Quantities of Salt are used in curing the fame, relpefitively; and of Frauds discovered concerning the same.

For every Calk or Vessel of Pilchards containing 50 Gallons, there is allowed, for Drawback, 4ojh,; which is the full Duty of Six Bushels of foreign Salt; and that, computed at 84/. to the Buftiel, is alter the Rate of 72 Gallons of Salt to 50 Gallons of Fish:

We consider the Drawback, in this Article, upon the Duty of foreign Salt only; no other being proper for well curing of Pilchards for foreign Markets; and we are allured, by the general Observation of our most experienced Officers, that Two-thirds of the above-mentioned Quantity of Salt allowed, is not really used in curing the same: But we must further observe, That, in case the Traders in Pilchards shall use English Salt, a greater Advantage will yet arise by the Drawback; Forty Shillings being the Duty on twelve Bushels of English Salt, which is at Fifty-six Pounds to the Bushel, and the Fish so cured will not be fit for distant Markets; though the Law, as it now Hands, leaves the Trader at Liberty to use either.

It is also observable, that there has been a very great Increase of the Winter Fishery for Four or Five Years last pad; and that though it be known, by common Experience, that Fish will not receive lo much Salt in Curing in W inter, as it will in the Summer; yet the Law has given the same Allowance, without any Exception to the Season; which Itill makes the Drawback the more extraordinary.

For every Barrel of White Herrings there is allowed, for Drawback, Ten Shillings and Five Pence; which is more than the Duty of Three Bushels of English Salt; that being the Salt with which they are cured:

In curing a Barrel of White Herrings, a Bushel and Half of English Salt is the most that is really used:

For every Barrel of Red Herrings^ the Drawback allowed is Six Shillings and Eight Pence; which is the full Duty of two Bushels of Salt; they being

generally cured with English Salt.

In

Earl Maris-chtill's c. Attainder.

Salt used in curing Fiflu

6ftlt uffd in curing Fish.

424 18° — 190 A. 171

In the Curing of Herrings that are in part felted at Sea, when first taken, and afterwards re-salted in the Merchants Store-houses, there is a Bushel of Salt

afed to a Barrel; but lets serves for those that are salted in the Warehouses only; which is Nine Parts in Ten of what, is taken; and there is not more than Half a Bushel nfed to cure shotten Herrings; though they draw back as much as the other.

The Duty on a Bushel of Salt is Three Shillings and Fourpence; but Three Pence is abated out of it, for Dil'count on prompt Payment; and Three Pence for Waite, though there be scarce any wasted; lb that they really pay but Two Shillings and Ten Pence Bushel Duty:

For every Barrel of Salmon there is allowed, for Drawback, Sixteen Shillings and Eight Pence; which is the* Duty of Two Bushels and an Half of foreign Salt:

There i3 not above Half that Quantity of foreign Salt used in curing a Barrel of Salmon; that being the Salt with which that Sort of Fish is cured.

For every Hundred of wet Cod, Fish, Ling, or Hake, w;hich shall contain in Length 24 Inches, and upwards, from the Bone in the Fin to the Third Joint in the Tail of such Fish, there is allowed, for Drawback, Two Pounds Ten Shillings; which is',the full Duty of 15 Bushels of English Salt; they being generally cured with that Salt.

For every Hundred of wet Cod Fish, Ling, or Hake, which shall be of the Length of 18 Inches, or more, and under the Size of 24 Inches, from the Bone in the Fin to the Third Joint in the Tail of such Fish, there is allowed, for Drawback, 1 /. 5 s;which is the full Duty of Seven Bushels and an Half of English Salt:

So that, upon a Medium; there is Eleven Bushels and a Quarter of English Salt allowed for the Curing of an Hundred of wet Cod Fish, taking one with another; whereas there is not above Five Bushels of English. Salt used in curing an Hundred of such Fish; they being generally cured promiscuously:

For every Hundred of dried Cod Fish, Ling, or Hake, commonly called Haberdines, there is one Moiety of the Allowance which is on wet Cod Fish, Ling, and Hake, of the same Dimensions.

One Moiety of the Salt used in curing an Hundred of w et Cod Fish, will cure an Hundred of dry, of the same Dimensions:

For every Last of dried Red Sprats there is allowed Six Shillings and Eight Pence; which is the full Duty of Two Bushels of English Salt; they being generally cured with that Salt:

No more than a Quarter of a Bushel of English Salt is tiled in curing a Last of Sprats; their Method being only to sprinkle a little Salt upon them, and then hang them of to dry.

We have great Reason to believe, that there are Frauds committed in running foreign Salt; particularly upon the Coast of Cormval, whither the French Barks come from the Coast of Brittany, Guernsey, and Jersey, and supply

the Fishing Boats with Salt, in the Night; by which means, great Quantities of foreign Salt are run; and the many Creeks and Coves on that Coast make it impossible to be intirely prevented by the greatest Diligence of our Officers: Thus the Fishermen are fumished with Salt, for which no Duty has been paid, and yet receive the Drawback; there being no Proof required of them, that the Fish, flopped for Exportation, is cured with no other Salt than such for which his Majesty’s Duties have been paid, and not drawn back; except White Herrings, for which such Proof is required, upon Exportation.

Great Quantities of unmerchantable Fish are offered to our Officers: for Exportation; which they have refused; and, we are w'ell afliired, have afterwards been packed up, in the Middle of Calks, amongst good Fish, in order to pass unobserved in some other Port; which can’t be effectually prevented, unless Power be given to destroy all such bad Fish as shall be tendered for Exportation.

It is principally owing to these extraordinary Allowances

on the Exportation of the several Species of Fish before-mentioned, the Over-allowances for Waste, the running Salt from the French Coast, and the fraudulent Package of Fish, that we find fb great an Abatement on our net Produce in this Branch of the Revenue; whereby our annual Payments into the Exchequer fall so much short of the Funds for which they were given, notwithstanding the great Increase of the gross Produce; and, if these growing Evils are not reltrained by Parliament, must every Year grow left and left.

B. Mildway,

Salt Office, T. Woodcock,

13th April 1716. James Cardonnel,

Cha. Dent,

A. Ingram.

A Petition of Charles Empson, of Lowden, in the County of York, Gentleman, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, in 1713, being encouraged by the Commissioners that were appointed to take, and examine into, such Proposals as should be laid before them for improving and cultivating such Lands as were drowned by the Inundation of the River of Thames at the Breach thereof at Dagenham, in the County of Eff'ex, did, on their Promile to allow him loo/, per Annum, for his Trouble therein, at their Request, go down with some of them to view the Stoppage of the said Breach, and the Grounds adjacent: That the Petitioner, finding the said Breach, then newly flopped, to be very defective, by reason of the improper Materials used therein, and of the Want of Judgment in the Undertakers, told the Commissioners then present, That it would not hold many Days, unless such Materials as the Petitioner then directed were used to fortify , the same against the Force of the Waters: That although the Commissioners gave immediate Orders for the Materials directed, and uled great Diligence to hasten the same thither, yet they came too late; for, in Four Days after, the said Works were quite ruined, and carried off, as the Petitioner had foretold them: That the Petitioner, some time after, hearing that Engineers were at Work to flop the said Breach, went thither; and, observing their Method and Proceedings to be wrong, told them thereof; and offered to direct them therein: but they, confident in their own Skill, and being deceived in pursuing a curious Model, rejected his Advice: But the Undertaker, in about Six Weeks after, finding his Works to fail, and being convinced, that the Petitioner had made a true Judgment therein, applied to him for his Assistance and Direction; but the Petitioner, finding him not provided with proper Materials, and the Season of the Year then too far advanced, declined to intermeddle therewith at that time: That the said Works being again destroyed, and new Proposals made for flopping the same before Commissioners at Guildhall, London, the Petitioner applied himself to those Commissioners; and, finding that none of the Models proposed would answer the End, offered a Scheme of his own for effecting the Work in Half the Time, and much less Charge, than any other body had proposed; notwithstanding which, and although the Petitioner offered to make a Demonstration otthe Certainly of his Method, but being a Stranger ift , little re-

gard was had to him, the Commissioners being too much atnufed with fine Models, Engines, Plans, Sc.: And praying. That he may have Leave tt> lay before the Committee appointed by this House a Draught, or Scheme, for the l'peedy and effectual Performance of this Work; and that the Petitioner may have Leave to demonstrate the same to them; and may have such Encouragement for his Skill and Pains taken therein, and the vast Expence of Money which he shall save to the Publick thereby, according to his Performance thereof, as to this

1 O

House shall feerri most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the Committee, to whom the Petition

of Dominick Donnelly, and the other Petitions relating to the Breach at Dagenham, are referred, do make their Report to the House upon this Day Scvennight.

A Petition of the Mayor and Commonalty of the Town and Port of Hasting, in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, by the Laws and Constitution of this Kingdom, no Parliament is to continue longer than three Years; and, under the Protection of that Law, which we look upon as one of our greatest and most valuable Privileges, we elected our last Members of Parliament, and thought proper to entrust them, for Three Years, as our Representatives, if his Majesty thought proper to continue them so long: That hearing a Bill is prepared, and now depending before the House of Peers, for altering the Laws now in being relating to Parliaments; and for continuing this present Parliament for a longer time: And praying to take the same into Consideration, and prevent the said Bill passing into a Law; for we cannot but look upon it as overturning out present Constitution, and an Infringement of our Liberties, by making Representatives for us for a longer Time than we entrusted them.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council, and Freemen, of the Corporation of Cambridge, was presented to tie House, and read; setting forth, That, by the ancient Constitution of this Kingdom, the frequent Calling of new Parliaments has always been uled, and esteemed a Security to the Crown, and also to the Liber-Vol. 18.

A PETITION of the Bailiffs, Aldermen, capital and other Burgesses of the ancient Borough of Car-diffe, in the County of Glamorgan, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of King aild Queen

Mary, it was Enacted, That, after the Dissolution of that Parliament, no Parliament, for the future, should have a longer Continuance than for Three Years; and that legal Writs should, for the future, issue for calling and allem-bling anew Parliament every Three Years at the farthest; which Act has continued for about Twenty Years in full Force, and never has been attempted to be repealed, or suspended: That the Petitioners being informed, That a Bill is brought into the House of Lords, for repealing, or suspending, the said Act: And praying, That your Honours will not consent to a Repealing, or Suspension, of the said Act; which, by fb long Experience, has been found to be of the greatest Advantage and Security to the Liberties and Properties of all the Commons of Great Britain. Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Aprilis: 4$ f

Christopher Potter Gentleman, and Phyllis his Wife, Sarah Burrowes, and Martha Burrowes, Spinsters; which said John, Elizabeth, Phyllis, Sarah, and Martha, were Brother, and Sifters, and Legatees, of George Burrowes, of London, Merchant, deceased; Creditors of the said Sir Alexander Rigby; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Sir Alexander Rigby, of London, Knight, now a Prisoner in the Fleet, stands indebted to the Petitioners, by Bond under his Hand and Seal, dated the 24th October 1698, of the Penalty of 2,100l. conditioned for the Payment of 1,051 I. 4 on the ill of November 1699: That the said Sir is charged

in Execution in the said Prison, by virtue of a Judgment Obtained on the said Bond; but hath not paid One Peny, Principal, Interest, or Charge contrafted, or due, on the said Bond: That the Petitioners, being informed Sir Alexander is about procuring an Act to be released of his Confinement, humbly presume to lay before this House the State of their Cafe; viz.That George Burrowes, of London, Merchant, died in the Year 1693; by his last Will did leave his Effects, after his Debts, Funeral Expences, and feme small Legacies, paid, to be divided among the Petitioners, in such Manner and Proportions as in his said Will are mentioned; and appointed his Father George Burrowes foie Executor of his said Will; who duly proved the fame: That, the greatest Part of the Testator’s Effects lying in the Hands of his Partner in Italy, the said Executor did impower the said S\v to demand, and receive, the fame, on the behalf of the said Executor, in order to be divided amongst the Petitioners, according to the Purport of the said Will: That the said Sir accordingly received the said Money; for which the said Bond was given, as aforesaid, to the said Executor, for the Petitioners Use; being the Balance due, after all he demanded for his Trouble and Expences were deducted: That the said Debt was not contrafted in Trade with the ‘said Sir Alexander, whereby any Profit might have accrued to the Petitioners, but all Money paid into his Hands: That the said Sir Alexander, about 17 Years ago, and soon after he entered into the said Bond, failed; and hath had all this time to pay such of his Creditors as he pleased, and to spend, dispose of, or intricate, his Estate, at his Pleasure; and now pretends to surrender up his Estate to his Creditors: That the Principal, and Interest due on the said Bond, amounts to a large Sum, and is a great Part of the Petitioners Substance: And praying this House to take their same into Consideration; and to afford them such Relief therein, as to your Honours shall seem most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause, That the Discharge of Sir Alexander Rigby shall not be a Discharge of any one that was a Partner in Trade with him; nor of any one that is bound jointly with him for any Debt; any further than the Creditors shall receive Satisfaction out of the said Sir Alexander Rigby's Estate.

Mr. Hampden reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Complaint of the Breach of Privilege committed against the Right honourable the Lord Coningsby, a Member of this House, by John Ensor and Job Beardsly, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterw ards delivered the said Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report, and Resolutions, were read; and are as follows; viz.

That the Committee examined the Matter of the said Complaint; and heard Counsel, and Witnesses, on both Sides, thereupon:

That it appeared to the Committee, That John , as Plaintiff, did, at the last Assizes for the County wick, by Job Beardsley his Attorney, bring on to Tryal an ACtton of Trespass against Edward Terry, a menial Servant to the Lord Coningsby.

Edward Terry, being called, said, That there had been, to his Knowlege, great Waite and S|>oil committed upon the Lord Coningsby s Woods and Grounds, at Aldcot, in

Warwickfnre', and that he was, upon the 5th Day of September last, hired by Mr. Thomas Harris, his Lordship’s Chief Steward, to be his Lordship’s Bailiff, to look after thofeWoods and Grounds, and prevent such Waste and Spoil for the future, and give Notice thereof: That thereupon he did, on the Tenth Day of the same Vo 1.18.

her, acquaint the Tenants and Townfinen of where he lives, with his having been lb hired into his Lordship’s Service: That the like Notice thereof, pursuant to a Letter from Mr. Harris, was also given to them; and particularly to the said Plaintiff Ensor, and to Beardsley his Attorney; and that, upon such Notice, they both treated his Lordship with very abusive Language, and spoke of his Lordship’s Privilege with great Contempt; Ensor expressing himself to tills Purpose; viz. That the Lord Coningsby was a Rogue, and a Rascal; and many an honester Man would be hanged; that he hoped the Times would change between that and Christ-rnas; and then his Lordship w ould be no more than a Boy to dry Shoes; and Beardsley expressed himself to this Purpose: viz.That he did not value any Steward, Bailiff, or other Servant, of the Lord Coningsby; that his Lordlliip was a very Rogue, and many ah honester Man was hanged; and that they would cut down the Woods at Aldcot, and, with the Money, Law with his Lordlliip for them: And Beardsley added, That he would make Terry quit the Town; and threatened to ruin him with Actions at Law, at every Assize, if he continued in his Lordship’s Service: And that he did afterwards, at another time, viz.about Michaelmas last, at Tamcorth, acquaint Beardsley with his Privilege, as Lord Conihgaby’s Servant; to which Beardsley answ ered, He did not value any Privilege which any Servant of his Lordship had: And that Beardsley was again acquainted, in open Court, by Mr. Harris, and by Terry's Counsel, at the Tryal, before the Verdict w as brought in That his Lordship did insist upon his Privilege.

HumfryWoodcock said, He was present at Tamrcorth, about Michaelmas last, when Terry acquainted Beardsley with his being a hired Servant to the Lord Coningsby, td look after his Lordship’s Woods: To which BeardjleJ answered, That lie w ould go on with the Law against him notwithstanding.

Mr. Tho. Collins said rHe was present at the Tryals of Two Actions against Terry, at the last Warwick Assize: one of which was the Action belore mentioned, wherein Ensor was Plaintiff; and that, before either Cause came on, both the Counsel and Solicitor for Teny acquainted Beardsley, the Plaintiff Ensor $ At;orney, That the Defendant Terry was privileged, and protected by the Lord Coningsby; and that, if he proceeded, he must expect td bear of it in the House of Commons: To which Beardsley made a slighting Answer; saying, That he did not value the Lord Coningsby, or to that EfflCt; and then brought on the other Cause first j and, after that this of s. That, on behalf of the Parties complained against, it appeared, by the Evidence of Mr. Wm. Robinson, and Humfry Webb, That this, and the other^ Action, tried against Terry, at the last Warwick Assize, had depended above a Year; and had been several times entered for Tryal, but were put off upon a Reference; which coming to nothing, the Defendant, and his Attorney, without mentioning any thing of Privilege, gave Notice to the Plaintiff, and his Attorney, That, if the Plaintiff would not proceed, the Defendant w'ould bring on the Cause by Provilb.

Fisher Littleton and Edward Taylor Esquires, being called to the Reputation of Terry, gave him an ill Character, in general Terms; and spoke of him as a Person not credited in the Country where he lives, and unfit to be employed by the Lord Coningsby, or any one else:

And Mr. Taylor added, That he was present at the Tryal, and remembered it was then said by Terry's Counsel, That the Lord Coningsby would protect Terry; but did not remember it was laid, That lie was then actually protected.

A Petition of Ralph Harwood, John Scott, and Beitja-min Coker, in behalf of themselves, and many others of the Cow-keepers, residing in several Parishes and Places within the Weekly Bills of Mortality, in the County of Middlesex, was prefen ted to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by the late Mortality among Cattle, sustained very great Losses, almost to their utter Ruin; and, if it had not been for his Majesty’s great Bounty and Clemency, they had not been able to follow their Employments: That the Petitioners are likely to be aggrieved by feme Clauses in a Bill, now depending, for better regulating Select Vestries within the Cities of London and Westminster, Borough of Sou tine ark, and Bills of Mortality; and for preventing any Misapplication of such Sums as shall be raised, or given by charitable Persons at the Sacrament, or otherwise, for the Maintenance of the Poor; and particularly by a Clause, which obliges the new Vestries to tax by a Pound Rate lor Relief of die Poor; and if the said Bill should pass, as it is now drawn, it will be a great Prejudice to the Petitioners; they paying very great Rents, without any Allowance from their Landlords for parochial Taxes: And praying to permit them to be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, what they have to offer against the said Bill; or otherwise to relieve them, as this House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Bill.

A Petition of the Deputies of the States of the Islands

Vol. 18.

of Jersey and Guernsey, in behalf of the Inhabitants of the said Islands, and of the Inhabitants of the Islands of Alderney and Sark, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the chief Subsistence of the greatest Part of the Inhabitants of the said Islands consists in the Manufacturing of Wool, transported thither from England, under the Restrictions of several Acts of Parliament, made for the Benefit of the Inhabitants of the said Islands; without which Manufacture they could not subsist there: That the Petitioners are informed, there is a Bill depending in this House, for the better Encouragement of the Woollen Manufactures; wherein are contained divers Clauses, impracticable and impossible to be put in Execution in the said Islands, without the utter Ruin of the Inhabitants thereof; who have, on all Occasions, distinguillied themselves, by their steady Zeal, and inviolable Fidelity, for the Protestant Succession, in Times of the most imminent Danger: And praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against so much of the said Bill as relates to the Islands aforesaid, in such manner as this House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better Encouragement of the Woollen Manufactures is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the Committee, thereupon, if they think fit.

And the said Report, and Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Petitioner had lpent above Two Months in surveying, and taking a Plan of, the Breach, and the Levels overflowed thereby; and contrived Models of the Machines he proposed to make use of in flopping the fame; and, before any conclusive Agreement was made with Boswell, he delivered in his Proposal to the Trustees,

for perfecting the same for 15,000 I. as appears by their Journal; and, for his Trouble and Diligence, the Thanks of the Board were given him by the Lord Mayor, then in the Chair; and that he did assign Reasons to why his Scheme could not succeed, about the ti ^e the Agreement was made with Boswell for 16,300l.:

That, after Boswell's Works blew up, the Petitioner again delivered in his 2d Proposal: Mr. acquaint-

ed him, That the Trustees gave him then Two Days only to get his Security: But it appears, on Colonel Coole's Application to the Board, and by the Trustees Journal, he Had longer Time allowed him:

That, on the 26th January, which was the Day appointed to examine and view Proposers Schemes, be attended at Guild-hall-, and like wife brought his Plan and Models, to remove all Objections; and endeavoured to be called in; but was not; neither was his Scheme examined.

Colonel Armstrong said, That Captain Perry proposed to stop the Breach by Dovetail Piles: That he had seen all the Schemes, and was of Opinion, that Captain Perrys was the most practicable; that, if it could not be done by Dovetail Piles, it could not be done at all; but, if you fire for stopping the Breach that Way, you will have it to patch and mend for ever; but, by railing a Wall, or Bank, so high as to let the Water flow gently and gradually through the Creek, the Breach w ill never affect the Navigation; and the same Sum that is offered for one, will do the other: But said, He made no such Proposal to the Trustees, being never asked.

Brigadier Richards affirmed, That Perry's Scheme did appear to him to be the most practicable.

Mr. Ach-.worthsaid, That nothing appeared to him

more practicable than Perry's Scheme: That he had not seen Donnellys, but as it lay upon the Table as he came in; but saw enough of it to know it would not do.

Captain Perry said, He had brought his Scheme, and Description of his Method, for flopping the Breach; and was ready to shew, and explain, his Reasons, in Writing, after what true and effectual manner he shall carry on his Works, with several Affidavits thereto annexed: That he has always practised the same Method, with Success, in the flopping and turning the Course of Rivers in foreign Parts: But, as the Art and Skill he has attained to in performing Works of this Nature has been acquired by the Study and Industry of his Labour, and the greatest Part of his Life; so he humbly begged the Justice of the Committee, as he formerly insisted to the Trustees at Guildhall, that he may not be obliged to discover the Secret of his Knowledge and Skill of putting his Method in Execution to any Persons, but w hom this honourable Committee shall think proper Judges as to the Art and Workman-ship that is required for carrying on the fame, and who have practised, or have seen, some Works of such Nature; and likewise desired, that such Persons, to whom he shall be obliged to divulge, and explain, his Method, may not make use of, or discover, the same to his Disadvantage; for as there are some tilings of his own Invention, and Improvement, particularly in the fixing of the foundation, and Placing of Sluices, after a much more effectual manner than has been hitherto used in England, and in the proper Applying of Dovetail Piles for the Damming up of Rivers, which has been acknowleged by those Persons, to whom he had already dil'covered his Scheme; and it being the general Content of Mankind to allow every Man the Right of his own Invention, which thp Trustees at Guild-hall did assure him should be preserved to him; so, in Justice, now hopes this honourable Committee will have the same regard, and take the same care of him; and he shall, very gladly and w illingly, comply with what is desired of him to do: And he laid his Plan for flopping the Breach before the Committee, and like-wife his Description of his Method of working, in Writing; and the same was read; and immediately delivered back to him again.

The Reverend Mr. Defaguliers said, He was no-ways concerned with Mr. Donnelly, as to Profit or Loss; and that he had not seen Mr. Perry's Scheme; but that he heard it was by driving Dovetail Piles: That, since he first attended the Committee, he had been down at the Breach at Dagenham, and taken the Soundings thereof; and Vo l. 18.

found, that the Difference from Side to Side, where Mr. Dagenham Donnellyproposes to fink his Machines, is not above Two Breach. Foot: And then he gave his Opinion of Donnelly ’ s Scheme, and of Perry's, to the Committee; and they desired him to reduce the same into Writing; as also Doctor Harris,

Captain John Macarrell, the Reverend Mr. Hort, Mr.

George Ball, Mr. Leoni, and Mr. Billingsley; who fe-

verally delivered their Opinions, and Reasons, in Writing; which here follows;

An Abstract of the Opinions of Dr. John Harris, Mathematician and Mechanick; Mr. J. T. Defaguliers, Mathematician, Mechanick, Experimental Philosopher, and F. R. S.; Mr. Josiah Hort, Mathematician; Mr. James Leoni, Architect and Engineer; Captain John Macarrell, and Mr. George Ball, Practical Engineers and Me-chanicks; Mr. Hear it. Mill- wright, and Director of the Works at Londm Bridge; Mr. same Billingsley, Mathematician and Mechanick; which, by Order of the Committee, they did severally deliver in Writing; wherein they declare their several Reasons, why Captain Perry's Scheme for flopping the Breach in the Levels of Havering and Dagenham is impracticable; and why the Method, proposed by Mr. Donnelly, may succeed:

i ft, The loose Sand and Moor-log at the Bottom of the Breach is very improper to hold the Three Rows of Piles, which Captain Perry intends to drive.

2dly, These Piles being made of Fir, which is specifically much lighter than Water, the vast Quantity , of Water that goes in and out of the said Breach every rlide, especially upon great Land-floods, Nor-weft Winds, and every Full and New Moon, ebbs and flows with that Force and Rapidity, that the Earth at the Bottom ot hi?

Piles will unavoidably be washed away, and his Piles set afloat, though he should drive them 16 Foot into such a Bottom.

3dly, The Canal and Sluice he proposes to make, will ease but One 17th of the Puffage he streightens; and, consequently, will not prevent the Force and Weight of the Water from breaking his Dovetails, or the Grooves that contain them.

4thly, In former Attempts to stop this Breach by Driving of Piles, i( has been found, that, when the Works are come near to a Close, the Strength of the Water has been so much increased thereby, that it has gullied and tore away the Bottom, and made it 30 Foot deeper than it was before at Low-water Mark.

5thly, The Foundation he intends to make being no less than 100 Foot, will require Time to bring it up to Low-water Mark; and the great Fall of the Water in the Flood, but especially in the Ebb Tides, occasioned by the Resistance of his Piles, will cause such strong Whirls and Eddies between them, as will spew them up long before his Foundation can be finished.

6thly, Part of the Bottom of the Breach, where Captain Perry is now w orking, is a hard Gravel; and the Drive-ing of Dovetail Piles, of so great a Length as will be here required, will be exceeding difficult, if not impossible; for, if the least Stone or Gravel gets betwixt his Grooves, they can never be driven home Besides, every Second Pile he drives will loosen the Fiift, and make it apt to Hart.

ythly, His Three Rows of Piles, which he intends to cross the Breach from each Side, and close them in the Middle, were it possible to do, which it is not, would never be able to sustain the Weight and Velocity of the Water, which will push against them in right Angles every high Tide.

8thly, That driving Dovetail, or other, Piles, unless in small Works, where there is a good Bottom, and no great Flux or Reflux of Water, has been always found unsuccessful; and therefore justly exploded both by the Ancients, and the Moderns.

gthly, The Breach at Dagenham has been formerly attempted to be flopped by Driving of Dovetail Piles; but without Success; the Fall of the Water, when by such Works the Passage has been straightened, being much greater than at London Bridge; and the Force and Velo-

city of it, especially in its Return from the Lands, has pressed with that Violence, that no Pile Works hitherto made use of has been able to sustain the Weight of it; but have been blown up, and set adrift.

Reaions humbly offered, why Mr. s Scheme

may be attended with Success.

The Machines are so well contrived, as to answer, in a more certain manner, all the Designs of flopping Breaches which have been proposed by others; as by Chest-work, sinking Ships, Piling of any fort, making Banks and Dams, cutting Canals, and Sluices, to carry off Part of the Back-water:

lft, That the Machines, while floating, can be managed with great Ease; and, by the Help of Tackles, can be united and fattened together without any Difficulty.

fidly, WThen this is done, the whole Machine, being happily contrived, so as to have all the Upper Part in Sluices, by opening them, and by the Use of Instrutnents, will fink uniformly and equally in a few Minutes; and close so exactly to the Bottom, which is near to a Level, as to binder the Water from pressing under.

3dly, For making this more effectual, a strong Work of Stone and Cement, whole Nature is to harden in Water, being raised in his Machines to Low-water Mark, shall, by its great Weight, press the false Keels into the Soil, and compress and settle into the Bottom, so as to hinder any Water from oufing under them; which Danger will be also further prevented, by spreading ori the Ground, from the Bottom, double-quilted Canvass, loaded with Lead at the outer Edge, like a Casting-net; over which he can easily form a Tallue, or Slope, both on the Outside and Inside of his Machines, and occasion even the Water itself to make his Ground good, by catting the Ooz, Slubb, 8$c. continually upon it; which will lodge in the Slope made of Faggots, Brush-wood, 8$c.\ and, in a little time, make all firm round the Machine to Low-water Mark.

4thly, As the Machines, when funk, will project in Two great Angles, the one towards the , or

Flowing Water, the other towards the Ebbing or Back Water, as the Sterlings of London B^dge, it will refill the Impression of each so effectually, that, the more they press upon it, the firmer it will be.

5thly, Captain Mackarell has f«en, in the several Moles run out a great Way into the Sea; and were built upon the same Principles with Mr. s Ma-

171

chines; and the Genovees have built a Cattle upon such Machines, funk in the open Sea, where it was above 60 Foot deep, upon which they planted Guns, to defend the City from a Second Bombarding by Sea, as it was in 1684, by the French; and, though the Seas are very violent in those Parts, yet the said Cattle and Moles are immoveable as a Rock.

6thly, Several of them have been very conversant in Works of this Nature, and ground their Judgments on the Observations they have made on the Moles in the Streights, and several Bridges, ancient and modern; as also several Breaches of this Nature, in which One of them was particularly concerned; and are of Opinion, as the present Enterprize requires more curious Application than any of the above-mentioned, so the Machines prepared by Mr. Donnelly are so contrived, by being truncated Pry-feins, and most part in Sluices, as to take off a more extraordinary Force of the Water, and make it serviceable, in adding a great Weight to keep them down, and press them with all that Force on the Foundation; and answer all other Intentions necessary for such a great Work.

7thly, The Sluices, which are ranged quite thorough the Machine from one End to the other, and from Low to High-water Mark, giving him great Command over the Water, so that it shall pals freely through, without doing any Damage to the Works; and, by keeping the Water near a Level within and without, and between, the Machine, will take off the Force occasioned by Waters of unequal Heights; as also preserve the Foundation, and secure it from being dug up and ruined; and prevent such dangerous Falls and Eddies as will attend all other Ways of flopping this Breach.

8thly, The truncated Pyramid, made by the Inside of the Four Machines, may be easily filled with proper Materials, that Mr. Donnelly may not only build a Wall on it quite across, but, if it be required, a Fortification.

I should be as glad of 1,000l. as any- Man; but you know my Circumstances are such, that I can advance no Money: Bennet answered, That he should have it without his advancing One Farthing; you shall not be brought into any Inconveniency; you shall know further, if you meet me on Monday Night at Mr. Ward's House: That, at the General Meeting, he acquainted the Board of this Matter; and said. Resolved, That it does not appear to this Committee, upon the Examination of the Petition of Dominick Donnelly, That there has been any Misapplication of the publick Monies by the Trustees for stopping the Breach of Dagenham.

The Committee have, according to a subsequent Order of the House, of Monday last, taken into their Examination, the State of the Breach at Dagenham; how far it affects the Navigation of the River of Thames: And, upon examining the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Trinity house, they find,

That the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants, do believe, That the Navigation is very much damaged by the said Breach: That Ships cannot pals so well as formerly, by reason of the Shelf, or Sand-bank, which is grown up near the Mouth of the said Breach, and is increasing, and growing over the River; and that the said Shelf can proceed no other Way than from the said Breach:

That, on the North Shore, where there was a deep Vol. IS.

Mail. 443

Water, there is now no coming; and that where there was 20 Foot of Water, the Year before the Breach was, it is now dry; and that the Men of War could formerly ride there at low Water:

That, in the belt of the Chanel, there is now Four Foot of Water left than there was before the Breach:

That, in the Year 1676, the Swan Man of War rid at Anchor where the Shelf now is:

That the Breach does not prevent the Tides rising lb high as formerly; and that they believe it not visible, if it does; and that there has been as high Tides lately, as ever:

That they have had Pilots at the Breach very lately; and they confirmed to them what they now say.

The Trinity-house Report, dated the 4th May 1714,

was read:

And the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants, affirmed, That they are now of the same Opinion as they were at that time.

And, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution viz.

Piefolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Breach in the Levels of titroering and Dagenham is prejudicial to the Navigation of the River of Thames.

Colonel Coote produced a printed same of BoJJwelC s, relating to Dagenham Breach; and read the following Clauses out of it; viz.

That one Parmey, who lived on the Premises, and was concerned for the former Undertakers, cut down the Booms and Flood-gates of BoJJivell, which was made to carry off the Back-water

That several of his Servants refused to work at such times as he had the greatest Occasion for them:

There is some Reasons to believe. That a Relation of Mr. Perry's corrupted and seduced One of BofweWs Master Workmen; and that, in consequence of such Corruption, the said Master Workman drove several Piles, which he never fattened contrary to the known Methods of the said Works; and that such Piles, for that Reason, were of no Use.

Sarah Sish said, That she lived with Mr. Parmey, and overheard him say to his Wife, That he had cut down BoJJwell's Booms, and hoped, that the Flood-gates would be gone by the next Morning:

That Parmey was out in his Boat, and came home late that Night, when he said this to his Wife; and told her,-Thathe had done BojwelVs Business for him:

A PETITION of the poor distrefiM Prisoners for Debt, and Damages, in the Cattle of Norwich, being the common Gaol for the County of in

behalf of themselves, and many others in the said Prison, was pretented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by reason of great Losses and Misfortunes incident to Trade, and otherwise, are thereby uncapable of paying their Creditors their respective Debts; but the Petitioners, are ready and willing to make them the utmost Satisfaction they are capable of, by delivering unto them, or their life, upon Oath, all the Petitioners Substance and Effects, so as they may be discharged from their Confinements, and be it Liberty to exercise their respective Trades, for the Subsistence of themselves, and their poor Families: And praying this House will be pleased to assist in passing an Act for so pious and compassionate an End.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Petitioners Counsel objected to Six of the Sitting Members Voters, for Non-residency;

It was proved they were not refient; but were, several Years ago, sworn Burgesses, had voted in former Elections, and were objected to in 1710, as being honorary Burgesses; and that One of them had served in Parliament for this City.

The Sitting Members Couniel insisted, That the Right of Election is in the Community, or Select Body, and not in the Commonalty; to be of which Community, it is necessary to take the common Burgesses Oath, according to the ancient and constant Usage as well before as since the Charter:

To prove the Antiquity of swearing the Burgesses, and that it did not come in with the Charter; the Form of their Oath is recorded in the Town-books, in the Reigns of Queen Mary, Queen Elizabeth, and King James the First.

The Sitting Members Counsel alleged. That Admission into any of the Companies within this Town gives a Freedom to exercise Trade there; but that a Biirgeship carries with it farther Privileges, and, peculiarly, Exemptions from inferior Offices; for which they anciently paid Fines; and, by the Constitution, cannot have Burgeship, but by Admission at the Convocations, or General Assemblies, of Mayor, Masters, and Burgesses, in Common Council: And several ancient Entries were read in the Town-books, of Admissions at such Convocations, and Gifts given, and Fines paid, for the Burgeship, in the Reigns of Queen Mary, Queen Eliz. King James the First, and in subsequent lleigns: And it appeared, That Freedom had been once refuted; and in several Instances, was granted, upon a Second or Third Petition for it:

And it was alleged by the Counsel, That if this ancient and uninterrupted Usage be inverted, this Town will be in the utmost Confusion, and want Persons to serve inferior Offices.

And it was proved by Wm. Sage, and Mr. Jo. the Town Clerk, the First of which spoke to 40 Years U sage, and the other to 15; That, in all their time, none ever voted but the Mayor, Masters, and sworn Burgesses; and that the common and constant Reputation has always been, That no others have any Right of voting; and that no others ever pretended to vote till lately: And,

Mr. Gutch added, That, according to the Constitution of the Town, and in all his time, all Admissions to Burgeship must be, and have been, at the Common Hall, by Vote of the Majority of their Convocations, or Assemblies, of Mayor, Masters, and Burgesses being of the Common Council; and that, out of such Convocation, or at any other Assembly, or by the Mayor alone, none can be, or ever have been, admitted in his time:

He farther laid, That the Petition for Burgeship, signed by the Persons before-mentioned, was not preferred at any such Convocation, but at a Quarter Session; which is an Assembly of a different Nature from their Convo-. cations: And said, He never knew any such Petition offered at any such Session before.

That the Sitting Members Counsel infilled on the ancient Usage of the Tow n, and the last Determination in Parliament: And called,

Simon Finch, Wm. Gandy, Win. Grover, Tho. Holloway, and Edward Lewis: Who spoke for Thirty and Forty Years past; and said. That, before the Determination of the House, in 1708, all Housekeepers, and alj Freemen, and the eldest Sons of Freemen, being of Age, were always allowed to vote; none were ever objected to, though they received Alms; and the common Reputation was, That they all had a Right of voting.

In 1708, the House determined the Right of Election to be in the Freemen and Inhabitants; such Freemen not receiving Alms, and such Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot.

The Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Reading, in the County of Berks, is in the Inhabitants only, paying Scotland Lot.

Mr. Cholmley reported, from the Committee, who were Cenduft of appointed to inquire into the Causes of the unusual Li- Serjeant at berty that has been allowed of late to Persons committed Arm8‘ to the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House; whereby they have had Opportunity to make their Escapes; the Matter, as it appeared to the Committee; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have examined several Witnesses j and find the Fact as follows; viz.

Mr. Nicholas Ryal said, That, soon after the Resolution, in 1688, he was a Deputy to Mr. Topham, then Serjeant at Arms of the House of Commons; and so continued till the time of his Death; and that he took several Persons into Custody during that time: That Mr.

Topham was a Housekeeper in Bartlett's where

he kept Four or Five Prisoners in Custody at a time; and when he had not room at home, he used to fend them to One of his Messengers Houses, and not otherwise; and that the Prisoners never went abroad without Leave of the House; except in the same of Two Maltmen, who were great Dealers, and committed upon the Complaint of Sir JVm. Whitlock, a Member of this House; and then the Speaker, upon their Application to him, gave them Leave to go out about their Business; but Ryal always went with them; and they returned the same Night in Custody:

Mr. Ryal further said, That Sir John Parsons, Alderman Sturt, and Mr. Fane, Commissioners of the Victualing, being ordered into Custody, upon their Petition to the House of Coihmons, Leave was given them to be confined at their own Houses, which were within the Bounds of the Victualing Office; and that Ryal lay at One of their Houses every Night, and, every Morning, reported to the Serjeant, That he had leen his Prisoners:

And, except in the Instances above-mentioned, he knew of no other Enlargement to the Confinement of any other Persons in Custody.

Daniel Kingham said, He was a Messenger in the Convention Parliament, under Mr. Topham; who kept his Prisoners at home, and never let them go abroad without a Messenger.

John Hollingjhead said, That he was a Messenger under Mr. Serjeant Topham about 27 Years ago, when he lived

in Bartlett's Buildings: That Mr. Topham used to order his Prisoners to a Messenger’s House; but does not know he ever gave Liberty for any to go abroad without a Mefe fenger to attend them; and cannot remember, that Mr.
