A Petition of Frances St. John, the Wife of Henry late Viscount Bolingbroke, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner’s said Husband was, by an Act of tills present Session, attainted of High Treason: And that the Petitioner brought him a very good Fortune, contifting of a real Estate in Land, as well as Money; and the Petitioner, to supply her said f lulband’s ()ecafions, did not only consent to fell great Part of her own real Estate, but did likewil'e join with him in felling Part of her Jointure: And the Petitioner, upon her Iiuf-band’s said Attainder, did represent her deplorable Condition to his Majesty, to grant her the remaining Part of her said Husband's real and personal Estate for her Support: And his Majesty was pleased to give Direction, that proper Instruments should be prepared for that Purpose: And, by a Clause in a Bill now depending, intituled, An Act for appointing Commissioners to inquire of the Estates of certain Traitors, Sc. the Petitioner’s said Husband's Estate will be vested in his Majesty, for the Use of the Publick: And praying, That a Clause may be inserted in the said Bill, to enable his Majesty to pursue his gracious Intentions for the Petitioner’s Relief, in such manner as to his Majesty shall seem meet.

H E Orders of the Day being read;

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petitions of several Merchants trading to, and residing in, New England and New York, were referred:

And the said Report was read; and is as follows;

viz.

Upon the Petition of several Merchants trading to, and residing in, New England and New York, on account of Monies lent by the said Merchants to the Government, for the Service of the Expedition to Canada:

That the Committee have taken into Consideration the Matters contained in the said Petitions.

It appeared, That the Petitioners did fumish the Government with very considerable Sums of Money for the Expedition to Canada; and received Bills of Exchange for the fame, drawn by General Nich

Governor of New York, Sir Hovendon Walker, and others, Agents and Ministers for the Crown, on the Treasury Board, and other Offices, pursuant to her late Majesty s Instructions to them for that Purpose.

It appeared, that her late Majesty, in her Letter of Credit, did promise punctual Payment of the said Bills; but the Petitioners have not as yet received any more than a Part of some of the said Bills, and of others no Part at all, after a long and tedious Attendance; having been near Five Years out of their said Money.

That the Committee, being desirous to come to a full Understanding of the Cafe, and being acquainted, That Mr. Banister could inform the Committee in feme Fa61s relating to the Bills of Exchange, lent for him: And he, appearing, said,

That he was in New England at the time when General Hill, and Admiral Walker, were there: That the General Court, or Assembly, made a Loan to the Merchants of 40,000 /. free of Interest, for Two or Three Years; which Money they paid for the Bills of Exchange they received for the Government here; l’o that the Merchants were nothing in Disburse:

That the Rate of Exchange was settled by the General Court at 401, per Cent. Advance; and their own Members subscribed 18,000 /. towards the Supply which was demanded; and the rest was subscribed in Six Hours time, without giving any publick Notice, that the Subscription was open; at which the Merchants in general were much difoufted:

That, afterwards, General applied to the General Assembly for 10,000l. more for carrying on the Expedition; and publick Notice was given of this new Subscrip-Vol. 18.

tion; and he has heard, that betwixt 50 and 100,000l. Was subscribed to the fame:

That 40 per Cent, was below the Value of the Exchange; which was, at that time, from 55 to 60 per Cent, among Merchants; and these publick Bills preferable to private ones, in Consideration that no Money was to be paid for them till after Three Years.

Mr. Hummer, who appeared for the Government and Merchants of New England, replied, That the Loan made by the Government of New England to the Merchants, was at first but 40,000 /.; when that Sum was found to be insufficient for the Ends proposed, they did, at the Desire of General Hill, and Colonel Nicholson, add 10,000l. more:

That the Loan was given at first only for Two Years; and that, though the Time of Payment was prolonged for One Year more, it was not done till the Merchants had first paid in Half their Money; and had set forth, in a Petition, That they had been paid but Tw'o-t birds of any of their Bills, and of some no Part at all; and that 5 /. per Cent, had been struck off from others; and that their Correspondents in England had been at great Charge in soliciting the same:

That the Merchants had since paid in a Sixth-part more of their Debt; and believed all was paid before tins time: Said, That if no Part of the Loan had been paid in, yet it could not be said, that the Merchants had advanced no Money, because the Loan was but 50,000 /.; whereas the Draughts were for above 75,000 /.

In Answer to what wfas alleged in relation to the Aflem-bly. That they took the Advantage of the Loan to themselves, without allowing the Merchants their equal Share, Mr. Dummer produced an attested Lift of all the Persons

w’bo had the Benefit of the Loan; by which it appeared there were but Eleven of the Assembly, out of Seventy-four, that were concerned in it:

That the 18,000 /. was not subscribed by the Members of the General Court singly, but in Company with other Merchants of the Place, as appeared by die aforesaid Lift:

lie further called several Merchants, to whom the Bills for the 18,000l. were indorsed; who gave an Account, That abotit 12,000 /. of it were for Account of other Persons; viz. the Merchants in New England and here; so that the Merchants neither Mere, nor could be, disgusted at the Assembly, in relation to the Loan, as was pretended:

He further said, That the Merchants, having advanced Money for the Expedition to Annapolis , the Year before; and they having no Advice of their Bills being paid; were unw illing, and many of them unable, to trufc the Government on a new Score; especially when so large a Credit was demanded: Others declared, If they did. trust the Government, they would allow but 20/. per Cent, for the Exchange of Money: And that, for the Encouragement of the Merchants, as well as to raise the Value of the Bills, the Government of New England came into this Loan.

Mr. Dummer also produced a Letter, wrote by Brigadier Hunter to the Lord Treasurer; giving an Account of what publick Service the Loan in New England was; and that he, for want of such a Help in his Government of Nero York, could get but 30 /. per Cent, for his Bills.

As to the other Objection, That the Bills were drawn at an inferior Exchange, he undertook to prove, by the Merchants then present, That publick Bills were then at % 40 /. per Cent.; and had been so both before and since: That private Bills were no higher than 50 /. per Cent.; which were at least 10/. per Cent, better than the Publick: As to the publick Bills, he instanced in those drawn by Colonel Nicholson, for the Expedition to Annapolis Royal, the Year before; which were drawn at 40/. per Cent, and so accepted, and paid. They likewise produced a large Lift of Bills of Exchange on the Navy, Victualing, and Board of Ordnance, since the Expedition, at 35, 40, and 45, per Cent.

A Petition of Edward Berington, a Prisoner in the Privilege — Gatehouse, was presented to the House, and read; setting a Person In forth, That the Petitioner being Printer of a Paper called Custody The Evening Post; in which Paper he printed a Letter, i^Laree. which had been printed and published by other Persons; but contained some Reflections; by which means, the Petitioner fell under the Censure of this House; and being ordered to be taken into Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for the fame: That the Petitioner is very poor, and has a great Family, and nothing but his Labour to support them: And that the Petitioner never before fell under the Displeasure of the Government, although he has followed the Trade in the Reign of King William to this present Time; and that he is very sorry that he hath incurred the Censure of this House: And praying, in regard of his Circumstances, and his numerous Family, That he may be discharged out of Custody.

Purpose; and no other Customs or Duties ware ever demanded for the said Goods during the said Trade; and that the Petitioners, and others concerned in the said separate Trade, fold the said Goods by the Candle; in which Sale,. had always a special regard to the Duties paid for the same, those being the Measure or Standard of their Profit or Loss; and, after such Sales, according to the Measure of those Duties, from time to time, paid and balanced all the net Produce of their respective Traders, and Dealings amongst all Persons interested: That Sir Edward Nerthey, his Majesty’s Attorney General, in or

about February 1714, upon an Information by him exhi-. bited against the East India Company, their Accounts being then open, and not adjusted with his Majesty, or the late Queen, in relation to the Duties before-mentioned, and on Suggestion of some Fraud committed in the Payment of the said Duties, obtained a Decree in the Court of Exchequer, against the said East India Company, for a new Way of computing and paying those Duties in the alge-braick Way, according to a Scheme then approved of by. the said Court; but the said Decree was not to extend to private Persons, or separate Traders, licensed as aforesaid: That long after the Expiration of the said separate Trade, viz.in Easter Term last, the said Attorney General hath exhibited a great many Informations in the said Court of Exchequer, against the Petitioners, and others, to compel them to pay greater Sums of Money than they all along paid during the said separate Trade, on account of the Duties of the said unrated East India Goods, pursuant to the said new algebraick Method of Computation; although the Petitioners had long before that time, paid the Duties demanded of them for the said Goods, in Discharge of the Securities by them given for the fame: And the Petitioners were mostly Agents for other Persons in . entering the said unrated Goods; and their Correspondents, and Dealers in the said separate Trade, being many of them dead, and others become insolvent, and others have withdrawn themselves into Places remote; so that, if such Prosecutions should be carried on, and Recoveries had, against the Petitioners, and many others, for those new-demanded Customs, during the Continuance of the said separate Trade, the Petitioners, and many more Families, must inevitably be ruined; there being no Probability that the Petitioners, after such a Length of Time, could ever be reimbursed, or have any Recompence of the Parties then interested; and which, if it were possible, would be the Occasion of innumerable and endless Suits of Law: And praying to take the Premises into Consideration.

A Petition of Sir George Mathew Knight, Sir Richard Houblon Knight, Bartholomew Swartz, John Stafford, Peter Hambly, and Thomas Clarke, of London, Merchants, in behalf of themselves, and great Numbers of other Merchants, late separate Traders to East India by Licence, pursuant to several Acts of Parliament in that behalf made, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the separate Trade to East India was established by several Acts of Parliament; particularly by One Act of the Second of Queen Anne, which separate Trade expired at Michaelmas 1714, and was always exclusive, and independent of the East India Company: That during the said separate Trade, great Quantities of East India Goods, as well rated as unrated, were imported into this Kingdom; and the same were entered at the Custom-house by the Petitioners, and others, and Securities given for the Payment of the Customs and Duties of the fame, as usual; which were afterwards duly paid as they were required, and adjusted by the proper Officers of the Customs according to the ancient Method used for that Vot. 18.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended his Majesty, in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to declare, That he had commanded the Lord Chancellor to declare the Causes of his Majesty’s meeting his People in Parliament at this time, as they were contained in a Speech, which his Majesty delivered into the Lord Chancellor’s Hands from the Throne; and his Lordship read the same to both Houses: And that, to prevent any Mistakes, Mr. Speaker laid, he had obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth;

Vol. 18.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I was in Hopes, that the Success which it pleased God to give us, in defeating the late Rebellion, might have secured to the Nation Peace, Plenty, and Tranquillity.

My Endeavours have not been wanting, during your Rccels, to improve the happy Prolpeft which was in View, by entering into such Negotiations, as I judged most conducive to those good Ends j and ’tis with Pleasure I can acquaint you. That many Defects in the Treaties of Utrecht, which very nearly aftefted the Trade, and even the Security, of these Kingdoms, have been remedied by subsequent Conventions; the happy Consequences of which have already very sensibly appeared, by the flourishing Condition of our Trade and Credit

By the Alliance lately concluded with , and the

States General, we are soon to be eased of all future Apprehensions from Dunkirk and Mardyke: The Pretender is actually removed beyond the Alpshis Adherents are deprived of all Hopes of Support and Countenance from France; and even the Assistance of that Crown is ftipu-lated to us, in case of Exigency.

It seemed reasonable to expect, that such a Situation of Affairs, at home and abroad, should have recovered from their Delusion all such of our Subjects as had unhappily been seduced by the Craft and Wickednels of desperate and ill-designing Men; and thereby have afforded me the Opportunity, which I desired, of following the natural Bent of my own Inclinations to Lenity, by opening this Session with an Act of Grace: But such is the obstinate and inveterate Rancour of a Fastion amongst us, that it hath again prompted them to animate and stir up foreign Powers to disturb the Peace of their native Country: They will choose rather to make Britain a Scene of Blood and Confusion, and to venture even the putting this Kingdom

6 E under

Designed Invasion by Sweden.

Addrtfs on the King'* Speech.

474

2oB — 21° Februafit. A'. 1715.

under a foreign Yoke, than give over their darling Design of imposing a Popish Pretender.

I have ordered to be laid before you Copies of Letters, which have passed between the Ministers on this

Occasion; which contain a certain Account of the projected Invasion: And I promise myself, from your experienced Zeal and Acte&ion to my Person and Government, that you will come to such Resolutions, as will enable me, by the Bleiing of God, to defeat all the Designs of our Enemies against us.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I did hope, the putting an End to the late Rebellion would have so far secured the Peace and Tranquillity of the Nation, that I might, confidently with the Safety of my People, have made a considerable Reduction of the Forces: But the Preparations which are making from abroad to invade us, oblige me to aik such Supplies, as you shall find absolutely necessary for the Defence of the Kingdom.

You are all sensible of the insupportable Weight of the National Debts, which the Public became engaged for, from the Necessity of the Times; the Pressures of a long and expensive War, and the languishing State of publick Credit: But the Scene being now fb happily changed, if no new Disturbances shall plunge us again into Streights and Difficulties, the general Expectation seems to require of you, that you should turn your Thoughts towards feme Method of extricating yourselves, by reducing, by degrees, the Debts of the Nation.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have an intire Confidence in you; and have therefore nothing to ask, but that you would take such Measures as will bed secure your Religion and Liberties: While you preserve those inestimable Blessings, I shall fit easy and safe on my Throne; having no other View but the Happi-nefe and Prosperity of my People.

After which, Mr. Secretary Stanhope acquainted the House, That his Majesty had commanded him to lay before this House Copies of Letters which paired between Count Gyllenberg, the Baron Gortz, Sparr, and others,

relating to the Design of railing a Rebellion in his Majesty’s Dominions, to be supported by a Force from Sweden;

And he presented the same to the House accordingly.

And the said Copies were read; and are bound up with other Papers of this Session.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return him the Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne: To congratulate his Majesty upon his safe and happy Return to his Kingdoms; and upon the prudent Administration of the Government by his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, under his Majesty; and the great Care his Royal Highness took of the reace and Security of the Kingdom during his Majesty’s Absence: To acknowlege his Majesty’s Goodnels and tender Regard to his People, in remedying the fetal Defects of the Treaties at; and in so fe t-

fonably discovering the traiterous Designs that are again set on foot against his Sacred Person, and Government:

To express the higheftRefentment and Indignation at this desperate Attempt: And to allure his Majesty, That this House will stand by and support, his Majesty against all his Enemies at home and abroad, who shall, in any manner, aid and abet the Pretender to his Crown; and will most chearfully contribute such Supplies as shall be found necessary for the Safety of his ltoyal Person, and the Defence of his Kingdoms; and will apply themselves, with all possible Diligence and Attention, to the great and necessary Work of reducing the National Debts.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw up an Address, to be presented to his Majesty, upon the said Resolution:

Usual Orders: Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right

to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, as a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting.

Ordered, That the Back-uoor of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day be-| fore the Door is locket! up.

Resolved, That; notwithstanding the Oath taken by any Candidate at or after any Election, his Qualification may be afterwards examined into.

Resolved, That the Person, whole Qualification is expressly objected to in any Petition relating to his Election; shall, within Fifteen Days after the Petition read;'give to the Clerk of the House of Commons a Paper, signed by himself, containing a Rental of Particular of the Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, w’hereby he makes out his Qualification; of which any Person concerned may have a Copy.

Resolved, That if any fitting Member shall think fit to question the Qualification of a Petitioner, he shall, within Fifteen Days after the Petition read, leave Notice thereof in Writing with the Clerk of the House of Commons; and the Petitioner shall, in such Case, within Fifteen Days after such Notice, leave with the said Clerk of the House the like Account, in Writing, of his Qualification, as is required from a Sitting Member.

GEORGE, by the Grace of God, King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, 8$c. To our trusty and well-beloved Lieutenant General George Carpenter, Greeting: We; repofitig especial Trust and Confidence in your Loyalty, Courage, and Experience iri Military Affairs, do, by tlicfe Presents, constitute and appoint you to be Governor of the Island of Minorca, and the Town and Garison of Port Mahon, and the Castle, Forts, and all other Military Works and Fortifications thereunto belonging, or elsewhere situated in the said Island: Yod are therefore to take the said Island, Town, and Garison; with the Castle, Forts, and other the Fortifications thereof; into your Care and Charge; and carefully and diligently td discharge the Duty of Governor thereof by doing and performing all and all manner of Things thereunto belonging: And we do hereby strictly charge and command all our Officers and Soldiers, who now are, or hereafter shall be, in Garison in the said Island, Town, Castle, or any other the Fortifications there, and all other our Ministers, Officers, and loving Subjects, whom it may concern, to obey you as our Governor thereof; And you are to observe and follow such Orders and Instructions, from time to time, as you shall receive from us, according to the Rules and Discipline of War, in pursuance of the Trust we hereby repose in you. And the Instructions to him, as Governor of Minorcat Sfc. were also produced, and read; a Copy whereof is as follows; viz.

By his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, Guardian of Great Britain, &c.

Instructions to George Carpenter Esquire, Governor of his Majesty’s Island of Minorca, George, P. C. R. given at the Court at HamptonCourt, the 4th Day of August 1716, in the Third Year of his Majesty’s Reign.

HIS Majesty having appointed you Governor of his Island of Minorca, you will apply yourself in the Discharge of that Trust, and in the Execution of such Orders as you shall receive, with that Zeal which his Majesty’s Service, and the Interest -and Prosperity of his Subjects in those Parts, do require,

In case of your necessary Absence from the Island, it is his Majesty s Pleasure, That the Lieutenant Governor shall command in Chief; and, in case of his Absence, the Lieutenant Governor of Fort Philip shall command; and, in case of his Absence, That the Command shall devolve on the eldest Officer in the Island.

When any Vacancy shall happen in a Military Employment, you shall acquaint his Majesty with it, and receive his Directions for supplying the same; and, in case of your Absence, the Officer commanding in Chief on the Island is to acquaint you with it, that you may lay it before his Majesty, and know his Pleasure therein.

You are to give Orders, That no Officer have Leave to be absent from the Island, without your Knowledge and Allowance.

You are to take care, that, upon no Pretence whatsoever, the Paymasters of the Regiments do receive Pay for any absent Officers; but that such Pay be left in the Deputy Paymaster General’s Hands on the Island, till such time as the Officer returns to his Post: You are to give Orders, That none be inuftered but the Effectives; and

that

3 Geo. I. at* — 22

that the non-effective Money be applied towards recruiting, by proper Warrants.

► You are to take care, that the State of the Accounts of

j each Regiment be made up every Two Months, and delivered in to yourself; or, in your Absence, to the Commander in Chief.

You are to give Orders, That no Serjeant, Corporal, Drum, or private Soldier, be discharged, without Leave from the Commanding Officer of the Regiment to which they belong; nor are they to receive any corporal Punish-raent, except Confinement, but by the Determination of a Court Martial.

P. C. R.

Addrefe on Mr. Onjlaw reported from the Committee appointed uc King's Yesterday to draw up an humble Addrefe, to be pre-

" c fented to his Majesty, That they had drawn up an Act-

dress accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

YOUR Majesty’s dutiful and loyal Subjecfe, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty their humblest Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Your Majesty’s safe and happy Return into your Kingdoms gave an universal Joy to all your People; and as the prudent Administration of the Government by his Royal Highness the Prince of , under your Majesty, did, in some degree, make the Want of your Royal Presence more ealy to us, we beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty upon the Peace and Security, that, during your Majesty’s Absence, was, by the great Care of his Royal Highness, preserved in the Kingdom, to the general Satisfaction of all your Subjects.

We can never sufficiently acknowledge the repeated Instances of your Majesty’s Goodness, and unwearied Concern for the W elfare of your Kingdoms: We fee, with Admiration, many of the fatal Defects of the Treaties at Utrecht, and the great Difiidvantages that were imposed upon this Nation, at the Head of a victorious Army, and powerful Confederacy, happily remedied by your Majesty, even in the midst ofintestine Dangers and Troubles: Your consummate Wisdom has renewed those Alliances that were basely betrayed and dissolved, and concluded such new Treaties, as may render the Peace safe and lasting; and we are at a Loss to determine, whether, in future Ages, the suffering the Demolition of the Port of Dunkirk to be scandalously evaded, will be a greater Reproach, or the procuring the Destruction of the Sluices of Mardyke, a greater Honour to the British Nation.

We cannot, at the same time, but with the highest Re-fentment and Indignation, look upon the obstinate and inveterate Rancour of those, who are again endeavouring to embroil their native Country in Blood and Confusion: It is astonishing to find, that any, who call themselves Protestants, can be so indexible and restless in their Endeavours to impose upon us a Popish Pretender; and rather venture to subjectthe Kingdom to a foreign Yoke, than depart from their darling and avowed Design of altering and fiibverling the present happy Eftahlifhtnent in the Protestant Succession. We adore the watchful Eye of Heaven, that has so wonderfully guarded and protected your Sacred Person; and cannot too much extol the Wisdom and Vigilance that has been uled, in so early and sea-fonably discovering this desperate Attempt: And, in order most effectually to defeat it, your faithful Commons, with Hearts sincerely zealous in the Cause of their King and Country, allure your Majesty, That they will, to the ut-teoft, mind by and support your Majesty against all your

Yoi. 1ft.

' Feb'ruarii. 477

Enemies at home and abroad, that shall, in, any manner, presume to aid or abet the Pretender to your Crown; and will most chearfully grant to your Majesty such Supplies as shall be found necesiary for the Safety of your Royal Person, and the Defence of the Kingdom.

We are all but too sensible of the infuppoi table Weight of the National Debts; and therefore will not neglect to apply ourselves with all possible Diligence and Attention to the great and necessary Work of reducing and lessening, by degrees, this heavy Burthen; which may prove the most effectual Means of preserving to the publick Funds a real and certain Security.

Gentlemen,

THE Duty and Zeal which you express, in this loyal Address, to my Person and Government; your Affectionate Concern for the Welfare of your Country; your Promiles of an effectual Support against all our Enemies at home and abroad; and your resolution of applying yourselves to case My People, by reducing gradually the heavy Load of the publick Debts, deserve my hearty Thanks: You shall never have cause to repent of the Confidence you repole in me; the Honour, Welfare, and Prosperity of this Nation being what I have chiefly at Heart.

Ltominster A Petition of several of the oppressed Inhabitants of the Election. ancient Borough of Leominjle in the County of Hereford, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Borough is a Borough by Prescription, and have lent Members to Parliament Time immemorial: That it was an open Town until the DiiTolution of Monasteries, and the happy Reformation thereupon: That the Petitioners Predecessors, during those Times of Popery atul Superstition, were influenced by the Prior and Monks of a great Priory within the said Town, and w ho were ngt only Lords of it, but several of the adjacent Parishes; That, towards the latter End of the Reign of Edward the Sixth, a Charter of Incorporation was granted for better

14

Government of the said Town; but not sealed, by reason of the Demile of the said King; and during the lhoit Continuance of that Reign, the ancient Privileges of the Petitioners Predecessors were rather retrieved and enlarged, than lessened and destroyed thereby; but, a stop being put to the blessed Reformation by the Accession of Queen Mary to the Throne, several persons who, upon that unfortunate Turn, had expressed a furious Zeal for the Support of that bloody Government, obtained as a Reward, a more enlarged Charter, and themselves to be made Governors of the said Borough, by the Names of a Bailiff, High Steward, Recorder, and Twenty-four Capital Burgesses: That the Petitioners Predecessors, who professed the Protestant Religion in those early Times, and in this then bigotted Place, whilst the popish Reign lasted, could not, Burning for Conscience-fake excepted, lie under heavier Oppressions than the Petitioners have done for several Years last past: And, as if the Inhabitants of Leominster were always destined, whenever Popery prevailed, and the Protestant Interest was in Danger of being subverted, that their Privileges as Englishmen should be, amongst the first, in Hazard of being invaded; the Petitioners do, in the most humble manner, representto this honourable House, That, when the glorious King William, of immortal Memory, the great Preserver, under God, of the Protestant Interest, and Liberties of Europe, arrived, to relieve us from King James's Popery, and arbitrary Power, this an-

cient Borough was restored to their just Rights and Privileges in the Choice of their Members to serve in Parliament j and do, because they may with truth, and without Vanity, affirm, That no Corporation, for the Space of near Sixteen Years, in this Kingdom made use of that great Trull reposed in them freer from Corruptions and Bribery, and in all other respects with greater Regard to the true Interest of their Country, than the now abused Petitioners did; butfince those Men have had any Power, w'ho our glorious King, in his Royal Proclamation for summoning this present Parliament, mentions to have been diffaffefited to his happy Accession to the Throne, and to have left this Kingdom not only under the greatest Difficulties in respect of its Trade and Navigation, but have, as his sacred Majesty is pleased further to declare, to his great Surprize, very much increased, even since the Conclusion of the last War, the publick Debts of the Nation, wc the Petitioners have laboured under great Difficulties, by means of the unjust and arbitrary Proceedings of the Three following Receivers of the publick Money, who are all Inhabitants of our Town, and Two of them capital Burgesses of our Corporation; viz. Caleb Powell Esquire, our present Bailiff, and Receiver General for the publick Taxes in the Shires of Brecon, Radnor, and Montgomery; James Ca/wall Esquire, likewiscaCapital Burgcfe of the said Borough, and Receiver General for the publick Taxes of the Counties of Monmouth, and Three more other Counties in the extreme Parts of North Wales; and Samuel Clarke Esquire, Receiver General for the publick Taxes in the County of Hereford: That, since the Three said publick Officers have had the Command of so much publick Money (for before they had none to spare from carrying on their respefitive Trades; the One being a Tanner, the other a Glover, and the Third a Mercer), they have, in Combination and Confederacy with Mr. Thomas Price, Attorney at Law, another Capital Burgess of the said Borough, and Town Clerk of the fame, and several of the Magistrates of the said Corporation, at several past Elections, but more especially at the last, for choosing Members for this present Parliament, in order to force us to elett Edxcard Harley Esquire, Recorder of the said Borough, One of the Auditors of the Imprefts, and Brother to the late Lord Treasurer the Earl of Oxford, to whose Favour Caleb Powell and James aforesaid owe

their Employments, by the illegal, arbitrary, and unjust. Proceedings following, as far as in them lay, endeavoured to sob us of our invaluable Privileges; to invert the Method of our Elections; and not only to usurp to themselves the foie Government of the Body Corporate, but so bring into the Members thereof the Power, at least of

directing,.

dire filing, in an arbitrary manner, the Inhabitants of this ancient Borough by Prescription who they shall trust with all that is dear to them in this World; and more particularly they, by themselves, Servants, Agents, or Accomplices, have, by their lending lo many, and such great, Sums, either of the Publick or the said Mr. Harley's Money, to so many of the poorer or most indigent Sort of Voters of, and Inhabitants within, the said Borough, and upon such Securities as they the said Voters could not obtain any Money elsewhere, and have since broke Ibme of the said Voters, got such an Influence upon so many of the Voters of the said Borough, that, by their arbitrary, illegal, and unjust, Proceedings, and by their Threats of suing the said Voters, and forcing them to pay what they are not able, their said Debtors are compelled to comply, and vote in Elefilions for Members of Parliament, as they are direfiled by the aforesaid Magistrates, Town Clerk, and Receivers, or their or some of their Agents and Accomplices, contrary to their own Inclinations and Opinions, as many of them declare; and which, being so great a Number, makes the Petitioners find the hard Effects of such arbitrary and illegal Proceedings; And moreover, to carry on such indirefcl Proceedings, the present Bailiff, and the Magistrates, as living within the said Borough, have, for many Years last past, by indirect Contrivances, kept the Bailiwick, the Magiltracy, and Government, of the said Borough in their own Power, and amongst their own Party; for that the present Bailiff hath been Three times Bailiff of the said Borough, Two Years of which have been within the Space of Ten Years last past; and the said James Cajwell hath been Four times Bailiff of the said Borough; and hath been, within the Space of Seven Years last past, Bailiff of the said Borough for Three Years successively; and his Father-in-law Bangham Esquire,

One of the Justices of the Peace of the said Borough, hath been Three times Bailiff of the said Borough, and ended his last Year’s Bailiwick at Michaelmas last; and, for the Continuance of such their Management, and keeping up the Number of their Party in the Chamber, there are but Nineteen Persons, besides the Bailiff, in that Community, which ought to consist of Twenty-four, besides the Bailiff: And the said Bailiff, and his Accomplices, neglect to fill up the said Chamber with other proper and fit Persons; because those who are most proper and fit to be chosen for capital Burgesses of the said Borough are in a contrary Interest, and opposite to then), and who will not willingly join in such indirefit Practices as are used in the said Chamber, who haye divers Houses, Lands, and Tenements, belonging to the said Chamber lying within the said Borough, and are demised to many of the Inhabitants and Voters of the said Borough for Lives, under yearly Rents and Fines; which Fines are arbitrary; but, where the Tenants are in the Interest of the now and late Years prevailing Bailiff and Magistrates, and their Associatcs, their Fines are much easier than their Opposers are forced to undergo *, and, as an Instance in this Matter, the aforesaid Mr. Edward Bangham, and Mr. Thomas Price, who hold the Two Messuages, they respectively live in, and lying within the said Borough, by Lease under the said Chamber, by their Friendftnp amongst their Brethren, obtained, each of them a Lease of their respefifive Houses for Three Lives; with a Covenant, that each of them should, upon the Death of any One Life mentioned in their respefilive Leases, be admitted to add a Third Life, at One Year’s Value, at such a Rate as they then put upon their respefilive Houses; whereas none other of the Tenants of the said Chamber ever had any such Covenant allowed them: And the said Bailiff and Magistrates, and several others of their Party in the said Chamber, being Commissioners, and having the executive Pow er of directing and levying all the Taxes within the said Borough, they have, for many Years last past, extremely ealed themselves, and the Persons in their Party, in all or most of their respefilive Taxes; and loaded their Opposites with Stock in Trade, Money at Interest, and other heavy Burthens, contrary to the Rules of common Justice; 'but the Receivers, who have each of them several Thousands of Pounds at Interest, not Vot. 18.

charged for the fame: And, as an undeniable Instance of their Injustice to the Government, there is not, nor hath been, One House lying within the said Borough charged at Thirty Shillings per Annum for Light Money, according to the A fit of Parliament, since the same was made; though there are near Forty Houses within the said Borough that ought to be charged therewith; and in such Method are theirs, and all their Votaries, Houses, underrated, or totally omitted to be rated: And, for the further carrying on of their Oppression in the like Nature, all Persons who will engage with them, and vote in their Interest, are admitted to be Inhabitants, and vote in the said Borough, without giving any, or, at least, no sufficient Security to indemnify the Town from their Charge; and by which means some Families are now-, and more like to become, a Charge to this Borough for the Support of them; but, if any Persons who are their Opposites come to live within the said BoFough, they are forced to give undeniable Security; nor will that be accepted but at Will and Pleasure; and also all such, and likewise such other Persons who are their Opposites, living within the said Borough, are loaded with Offices, forced to serve upon unprofitable Juries, irnpoverithed by the Inequality of Taxes, and terrified by the Frowns and Threats of the Magistrates, and governing Part of the Town; and such as are Publick-house Keepers and Voters, if they will not join with the said Magistrates in voting for Members of Parliament as they please, are threatened they shall have no Licences to sell Ale; but such as will comply with them shall be licensed, or have Leave to sell Ale without Licence; by reason w hereof, there are this present time Forty Publick-houses that sell Ale within this final! Borough: Under all which Aggrievances, the oppressed Petitioners have laboured for several Years last past; and therefore have just Reason now to complain; which they would have avoided, had not the ill Prafiiices, unjust and corrupt Proceedings, in the last Elcfilion for Members to serve for the said Borough in this present Parliament, given them just Occasion to represent to this honourable House, That after the aforesaid Caleb Powell Esquire, the present Bailiff of this Borough, had received the Mandate from the Sheriff of the County of Hereford, for the defiling Two Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament, for this Borough, by the Advice of his aforesaid Town Clerk, and, as is believed, by the Approbation, if not Direction, of the aforesaid Mr. Harley the Recorder, after Sunset, on Friday the Twenty-eighth Day of January last past, did cause publick Notice to be affixed on several Places in the said Town, That he the said Bailiff intended to proceed to elefil Two Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough, by Nine of the Clock on the Tuef-dayMorning following, being the First Day of February initant; which was but Three Days Notice, and contrary to the Act of Parliament in that same made and provided, which requires Four Days Notice, at least, to be given of such Elefilions: And notwithstanding the said Bailiff1 was then informed, that such Notice was not according to Law; yet the said Bailiff would not alter what he had di-refiled; nor did he take care, that the Town Clerk should publish the Proclamation for difiolving the last Parliament: And the Petitioners further sheweth, That, from the time that the aforesaid publick Notice was given, even to the very Hour of the Elefition, and during the fame, such Bribery, arbitrary and corrupt Proceedings, by Menaces, Threats, Force, and Locking up of Voters the Night before the Elefilion, were used and prafilifed within the said Borough, for and on the behalf of the said Edward Harley, by the said Receivers, Magistrates, their Agents or Accomplices, or some of them, as----- want Words to express,

by forcing Men to vote contrary to their Inclinations and faithful Promises, and by filling them so with Drink, that many of the Voters, when they passed their Votes, did not rightly understand who they voted for; and which had so lamentable an Effefil upon One of the said Voters, formerly a very sober Man, that, as soon as he was led home from voting, he was laid down upon his Bed in his Clothes, and declared he was prevailed with to vote against his

Mr. Harley, to be duly elected Members to serve for the said Borough in the next Parliament; and that he would, and accordingly did, return the fame; and notwithstanding the said Mr. Gorges' Agent did then, on the behalf of the said Mr. Gorges, tender One Indenture to the said Bailiff, ready ingrossed, and required the said Bailiff' to return the said Mr. Gorges, he being a Member, had Justice been done him, duly and legally chosen; but the said Bailiff positively refused to do the fame; and the said Bailiff, the Morning after the said Election, turned One of the Searchers and Sealers of Leather for the said Borough, being a Place of some Profit, out of his Office, for no other Reason as can be known, than that he voted at the - " said Election against the said Mr. Harley: All which Actings and Doings, and many more of the same Nature, are express, contrary to the Rules of Justice, and are arbitrary, illegal, and unjust; and which Practices and Proceedings not only tend to the Ruin and Destruction of the Rights and Privileges of the Petitioners, and this Borough, in choosing their Representatives in Parliament; but also, if pra&iied in other Cities and Boroughs, will end in the Extirpation of our truly happy, if qot abused, Constitution and Government: And praying to be relieved against all these Oppressions.

letting forth. That the Right of electing Members of Parliament for the City of Bristol is vested in the Freemen and Freeholders of the same City; and that the Petitioners, together with Sir William Dairies, and Joseph Earle Esquire, stood Candidates; and that, after, the Election was ended, an Indenture was made between the said Sheriffs and the Freemen and Freeholders of the said City, importing, That the said Petitioners were duly elected; which Indenture was executed by many of the Freemen and Freeholders, and by Mr. Taylor, One of the said Sheriff's, who attended the whole Poll (but the other Sheriff" was absent during the greatest Part of the Time); the said Indenture wa3, by the said Mr. Taylor, fattened and sealed to the Writ; but the said Sheriffs have unduly and falsly returned the said Sir William Daines, and Joseph Earle, Members for the said City; and, by undue Practice, fevered the Writ from the said Indenture: And praying Relief therein.

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Table: Where they were read and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Ten thousand Men be allowed for the Sea Service for the Year One thousand Seven hundred Seventeen, beginning from the First Day of January One thousand Seven hundred Sixteen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Ten thousand Men for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred twenty-six thousand Seven hundred Ninety-nine Pounds Five Shillings Three Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred Seventeen, including Half Pay.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Nine hundred fifty-nine thousand Nine hundred Forty-three Pounds One Shilling 19 r

Ten Pence Halfpeny, be granted to his Majesty for maintaining Guards, Garilbns, and other his Majesty s I^ind Forces, in Great Britain, Jersey, and for the Year One thousand Seven hundred Seventeen.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That wholocver shall

advance or lend any Sum, not exceeding Six hundred thousand Pounds, for the Services of the Publick by Sea or Land, shall be repaid the same with interest at Four Pounds per Cent, out of the First Aid to be granted this Session of Parliament.

A Question being proposed, That this House will, on all Occasions, maintain, in the most strict and inviolable manner, all Parliamentary Engagements;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out " on all Occasions maintain, in the mott strict " and inviolable njanner," and to insert " effectually make " good the Deficiencies of

And the Question being put, That the Words proposed to be left out do stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the Question being put, That the Words " efe " fectually make good the Deficiencies of," be inserted, instead thereof;

The same was agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That this House will effectually make good the Deficiencies of all Parliamentary Engagements.

.by themselves and Agents, and by Bribery, and other indirect Practices, procured themselves to be returned; and that the find Charles Mason was not qualified as the Law requires; his Estate being under Extent to the Crown for a great Sum of Money appropriated by Act of Parliament: And praying Relief therein.

A Petition of the said Edward Harley Esquire, commonly called Lord Harley, w-as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was a Candidate at the last Election for the Borough of New Radnor, and the other Boroughs in that County; and that a very great Majority of the legal Voters did appear, and tendered their Votes for the Petitioner; but Mr. Samuel Bur-Ion, Builiflf of the said Borough, refused to admit them, and returned Thomas Leans Esquire, junior, who is not qualified as the Law requires; and the said Thomas Lewis, and others, by Menaces, Bribes, and other illegal Practices, endeavoured to influence the Electors to give their Votes against the Petitioner: And praying Relief therein.

Ship, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, in the Town of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, ,on behalf of themselves, and of several other Inhabitants of the said Township, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Town of Sunderland is situate on the River Wear, and is a Town of great Trade, and very populous; and that a great Quantity of Coals, Salt, ana other Merchandizes, are yearly shipped from thence, and sent to divers Places; to the great Increase of the publick Revenue: But the said River and Harbour has been of late much prejudiced, and choked in its Chanels, and the Depth of Water exceedingly lessened by Sands thrown up by the Sea; and other gross Matters waihed or brought down by Land Floods, is a Lessening of the Trade on the said River, and in the said Port: That the amending the Abuses and Inconveniences aforesaid, and making the said Chanel deep, and more navigable, will be a Means of keeping low the Price of Coals j and much tend to the Preservtion of the said Port, and Increase of Trade: And praying, Thatlfeave may be given to bring in a Rill for the amending the Abuses and Inconveniences; and for the Purposes aforesaid.

Mr. Edwards said, That he knows the Gravel, and other Materials, within the said Parishes, for repairing the said Roads, are exhausted and he, as Surveyor of the Highways, was obliged last Year to fetch 2,000 Load of Gravel for that Purpose as far as Newington; for which was paid 2 s.per Load, and 3 s.for Carriage.

That, upon Consideration of the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their said Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for repairing and amending the said Roads, according to the Prayer of foe said Petition.

A Petition of Thomas Duke of Norfolk, Francis Viscount Montague, Henry Lord Hugh Lord Clif-

ford, Charles Lord Dormer, James Lord I Valter Lord Aston, Sir fVitliam Goring, Sir H Gage, Baronets, William Stafford

Henry Charles Howard, Edward Blount, and Ed-

ward Gage, Esquires, for and on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by the late Act, which obliges Papilts to register their Names, and real Estates, the Petitioners are, upon Default of taking the Oaths before the Twentieth of January, bound to register their Names within Six Months after: That the Time being lb very short, and several having (mail Estates very remote, and in different Counties, cannot be furnished with such exact Particulars thereof as are necessary; nor can they command their Deeds, or Settlements, out of the Trustees or Mortgagees Hands, in order to let forth their Estates and Interests, which the said Act requires: That several of the Petitioners Estates conlilt of many Farms, and finall Tenements, and those again divided, and subdivided, in the Hands of Undertenants, and their Assigns; whereby the Possessors cannot be so soon ascertained as the Act requires; so that the Want of Time will render the Registry not only imper-fest, but impracticable: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for explaining the said Act; and inlarging the Time for Papilts to register their Names, and real Estates.

Wear A PETITION of the Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriff Navigation. and the rest of the Common Council, of the Town

and County of Nervcastle Tyne, on behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of poor People inhabiting in and about the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Town is a very ancient Corporation, principally supportedby Navigation; and is the chief Nursery^or Seamen employed in his Majesty’s Service; and that, over and above all other common Duties laid upon Coals, Salt, and other Merchandizes, there is a Duty of Twelve Pence Chalder, payable for ever to the Crown for every Chalder of Coals exported out of the River Tyne to the City of London, or Coastwise; which is not payable for any Coals exported out of the Port at Sunderland; and the Petitioners perceiving the re is a Bill brought in for Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, they humbly conceive, that, if the said Bill should pals into an Act, it will not only be very prejudicial to his Majesty’s Revenue, and the publick Good, but also to the said ancient Corporation, and will ruin many Hundreds of poor Families: And praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Bill do pals.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for the Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, before the Committee, by their Counsel, if they think fit.

Mr. Secretary Stanhope presented to the House, pursuant to their Address to his Majesty, the Treaties with the Bishop of Munster, and the Duke of Saxe Gotha, for Six Battalions of their Troops taken into his Majesty’s Pay; with Translations of them:

And the Titles of the Translations of the said Treaties were read:

And the Translations are as followeth; viz.

FRANCIS Arnold, by the Grace of God, Bishop of Munster and Paderborn, Burggraff of Stromberg, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, Count of Lord of Borkeloh and Werth: We hereby declare, and make known, That whereas a Treaty between the most Serene and most Potent Prince George Lewis King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, 8gc. Duke of Brunswick Lunenburg, Arch Treasurer and

Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, and ourselves, relating to our furnishing of Four Battalions of Foot, has been concluded by the Ministers authorized for that Purpose on each Side, dated at Munster the 23d of December last. Word for Word, as follows:

The Treaty.

Whereas his Royal Majesty of Great Britain, out of the particular Confidence he has in his Highness the Bishop of Paderborn and Munster, has caused Overtures to be made to him for furnishing some of his Infantry to replace those Troops, which, during the present Troubles in Great Britain, may be drawn out of the Garisons of the States of the United Provinces, to be lent thither; and whereas his Highness has readily taken this Opportunity of shewing his particular Regard for his Majesty, and how willing he is to serve him; the following Agreement has been made, and concluded, in order to its being ratified:

I.

His Highness engages himself to furnish Four Battalions of Foot, of 525 Men each, exclusive of the Staff Officers, consisting of Seven Companies, of 73 Men each, with prime Plan, according to the annexed Lift, marked Lit. A; and his Highness agrees to fend with these Four Battalions no Officers of a higher Rank than such as receive Colonels Pay.

II.

And whereas the said Four Battalions are to be employed in the Dutch Garisons, in the room of those which the States General may yet send to his Royal Majesty, into Great Britain; it is agreed, That during the time of their Service there they are to take an Oath of Fidelity to the States General.

III.

The Troops are to be received in this Country by the King’s Commissary; and are to enjoy their full Pay and Subsistence, according to the Dutch Establishment,

Vol. 18.

B; by which the Regiments have been paid during th last War: They shall be provided with Carriages, and other Necessaries, in their March to the Netherlands, as well as their Return; and his Majesty, or his Electoral Regency at Hanover, shall fend requilitorial Letters for that Purpose.

IV.

The said Pay and Subsistence is to begin the 15th of January, N. S. 1716; and to be continued as long as his Royal Majesty shall make use of the Troops to the above-mentioned Purpose: When his Majesty shall stand in no further Need of them, or in case there should be no Need of them at all, Three Months Notice shall be given of it to his Highness the Bishop of Paderborn and;

after which Term the Pay and Subsistence of these Troops shall cease: But it having been represented, That his Highness would be at nofmall Expence by the complete-ing the said Battalions, and the clothing and furnishing them with all Necessaries for their March, his Royal Majesty, upon this Consideration, pursuant to the annexed Establishment, Lit. B, consents to pay One long Dutch Month, of Six Weeks, more, after the Three Months that Notice has been given are expired; and this in any Case, whether the Troops serve a long, or a short, time, or if they should not serve at all.

V.

As to the ordinary Recruits, each Company shall be allowed the same Douceurs the States of the United Provinces allow their own Troops: But if the Troops shall happen to diminish very sensibly by any contagious Distemper, or other Accident; in that same due and sufficient Satisfaction shall be given, according to what the States have observed hitherto in the like Cafes, and what other Troops have enjoyed.

VI.

His Highness expects the Payment of the monthly Subsistence from his Majesty only, without being obliged to solicit, or to put himself to any other Expence, for it; and his Royal Majesty does accordingly engage for the punctual and prompt Payment of the fame.

VII.

The Troops may either furnish themselves with Provisions in the Garisons; or, if they choose to have it out of the Magazines, they are to pay for it out of their own Pay, as the Dutch Troops themselves do; and, as to what

relates to Physick, and Hospital Expences, they shall be allowed what the Troops of the States enjoy, and what the Troops of Paderborn and Minister have formerly enjoyed in the States Service.

VIII.

If, in the said Battalions, any should be found that have been formerly in the Service of his Royal Majesty, or the States General, or any other Prince, and have deserted, they shall be pardoned, and not be delivered up.

IX.

The Naming and appointing of all the Officers, as likewise the Military Jurisdiction over the said Four Battalions, are reserved to his Highness.

X.

As these several Articles have been agreed upon, in order to their being ratified; and as the Ratification of his Royal Majesty of Great Britain has been promised to be exchanged here, with all possible Speed, for that of his Highness the Bishop of Paderborn and Munster; fb the Electoral Regency at Hanover engages, in the meantime, for the procuring the fame. In Witness whereof, Two Instruments, of the same Tenor, have been drawn of this Treaty, signed and sealed by his Royal Majesty, and his Royal Highness’s Ministers, authorized for this Purpose; One of which has been delivered to each Party.

Given at Munster the 23d of December 1715.

(L. S.) Marquis of Numis. (L. S.) B. B. of Mengo^fen.

FREDERICK, by the Grace of God, Duke of Saxony, Juliers, Cleoe, and Berg, also of Engria and Westphalia, Landgrave in Thuringia, Margrave of Mif-nia, Prince and Count of Henneberg, Count of the Marck and Ravensberg, Lord of Ravenstein and Sonna We

hereby make known, and declare, That whereas we have caused a Negociation to be carried on with his Royal Majesty of Great Britain for Two Battalions; which we are to furnish his Majesty with: And whereas a Treaty has been signed by the Plenipotentiaries on each Side, Word for Word, of the following Tenor:

"Whereas his Royal Majesty of Great Britain, out of the particular Confidence he has in his Serene Highnefe the Duke of Saxe Gotha, has caused Overtures to be made to him for furnishiag feme of his Infantry, to replace those Troops, which, during the present Troubles in England, may be drawn out of the Garisons of the States of the United Provinces, to be sent thither; and whereas his Serene Hig'nness has readily taken this Opportunity of 22

shewing his particular Regard for his Majesty, and how willing he is to serve him; the following Agreement has been made, and concluded, in order to its being ratified:

I.

His Serene Highnefe engages himself to fornish unto his Majesty Two Battalions of Foot, consisting of 500 Men only at present; but his Highnefe will augment them, by the 15th of January 1716, to the Number of 640 Men each, exclusive of the Staff, that they may con-fist of Eight Companies each, with the prime Plan of 80 Men, according to the annexed Lift, A; and no Officers of higher Rank shall be sent with these Battalions than Colonels.

n. /

And whereas the said Two Battalions are to be employed in the Dutch Garisons, in the room of those which the States General may yet send to his Royal Majesty into Great Britain, they are, for the Time of their Service there, to take an Oath of Fidelity to the States General.

III.

The Troops are to be received in this Country by the King’s Commissary; and are to enjoy their full Pay and Subsistence, according to the Dutch Establishment, Lit. B; by which, during the last War, the Regiments of Saxe Gotha have been paid: They shall be provided with Carriages, and other Necessaries, in their March, as well as

their Return; and his Majesty, or his Electoral Regency at Hanover, shall fend requisitorial Letters for that Purpose.

IV.

The said Pay and Subsistence is to begin the 15th of January 1716, N. S. and to be continued as long as his Royal Majesty shall make use of these Troops to the above-mentioned Purpose: When his Majesty shall stand in no further need of them, or in case there should be no Need of them at all, Three Months Notice shall be given of it to his Serene Highness the Duke of Saxe;

after which Term, the Payment and Subsistence of the said Tloops shall cease: But it having been represented, That his Serene Highness would he at no small Expence by increasing the said Battalions to the number speciti Art. I. and by the clothing and furnilliing them with all Necessaries for their March; and that the said Troops, upon their Return out of the Dutch Garisons to the Territories of his Highness the Duke of Saxe Gotha, must needs be obliged to a long, uneasy, and expensive, March; his Royal Majesty, upon Consideration of this, pursuant to the annexed Establishment, Lit. B. contents to pay Two short marching Months more, after the Three Months that Notice has been given are expired; and this in any case, whether the Troops are kept in Service a long, or a short, time, or if they should not serve at all.

V.

As to the ordinary Recruits, each Company shall be allow ed the same Money which the States of the United Provinces allowed their own Troops: But if, by any contagious Distemper, or other Accident, the Troops should happen to diminish very lenfibly; in that Cafe, due and sufficient Satisfaction shall be given, according to what the States have observed hitherto in the like Cafes, and what other Troops have enjoyed.

VL

His Serene Highness expects the Payment of the monthly Subsistence from his Majesty only, without being obliged to solicit, or to put himself to any other Expence, for it; and his Royal Majesty accordingly answers for the prompt Payment of the fame.

VII.

The Troops in the Garisons may either furnifti themselves with Provisions; or, if they choose to have it out of the Magazines, they are to pay for it out of their own Pay, as Dutch Troops themselves do; and, as to what relates to Physic, and Hospital Expences, they shall enjoy what other Troops are allowed by the States, and what the Troops of Saxe Gotha have formerly enjoyed in that Service.

vm.

If, in the said Battalions, any should be found that have been formerly in the Service of his Royal Majesty, or the States General, or any other Prince, and have deserted, they shall be pardoned, and not delivered up.

IX.

The appointing the several Officers, as likewise the Military Jurisdiction over the Two Battalions, are reserved to his Serene Highness, in the same manner as has been observed of late by the Regiments of Saxe Gotha lish or Dutch Pay.

X.

And whereas his Royal Majesty has likewise desired the Liberty of transporting the said Troops into England, in case he should find it necessary to employ them there; his Serene Highness, out of his particular Affection to his Majesty, and several other Considerations, willingly con-fents to it: And, in this Cafe, the said Battalions shall take an Oath of Fidelity to his Majesty during that time: They are then to receive English Pay from the Day of their being embarked to the Day of their landing again on this Side; from which time, and till they reach the Territories of Saxe Gotha, they are to be paid upon the Dutch Foot again: His Serene Highness, in the mean time, expects, that in case, as aforesaid, his Royal Majesty ntends to employ these Battalions in Great Britain, y ol.is.

Copies Of the English Establishment shall be delivered to him, that he may know what Allowances are to oe made for extraordinary Recruits, and Lolfes either in the Field, or by contagious Distempers, or in any other Cafe, that so his Serene Highness may agree with his Royal Majesty about these Articles: His Highness, however, promises not to flop the March of the Troops out of his Dominions upon this Account,

XL

In case his Majesty should farther1 want any moreTroops, his Serene High&efs, to shew his particular Affection, promises to serve his Majesty in it as much as possible; being persuaded, that his Royal Majesty, on his Side, will continue the good Correspondence which has always been between their most Serene Predecessors.

XII.

As these several Articles have been agreed upon, in order to their being ratified; and as the Ratification of his Royal Majesty of Great Britain is to be exchanged, with all possible Speed, here at Gotha, for that of his Serene Highness; lb the Electoral Regency of Brunswick Luncnberg engages, in the mean while, for the procuring the fame. 2d, It appears, That although Mr. Howell, late Receiver of South Wales, hath not passed his Accounts, yet, when the Allowances reported due are made good to him, his Balance will be overpaid; and that Mr. Brougham, the Receiver for the Counties of Cumberland and Westmorland, and Mr. Farran, formerly Receiver for the County of Oxford, have not passed their Accounts; but their Allowances already reported, and the further Claims they have to make, will very near balance the fame.

Mr. Thomas Lloyd, late Receiver for Chester and North Wales, Mr. Bradgate for Leicestershire, and Mr. Broom for Part of Norfolk', appear to be indebted to the Government, over and above the Allowances reported to be due to them; and that Mr. Dixon, Receiver for Somer-fetshire, who has absconded for some Years, is indebted a great Sum, which the Government is in Danger of losing, through the Insolvency of him, and his Securities.

The Committee do further represent, That there are several of the Petitioners, and others, Receivers General, who have not petitioned, or had any Reports for Allowances for several Years in which they have been employed; so the Committee could not examine their Claims; But, upon Inquiry, do find, they have cleared their Accounts to the End of the Year 1714, except as before excepted; and many of them ought, in Justice, to have proper Allowances, when they shall make Application for the fame.

Allowance TV /I R- Lawson reported from the Committee, to whom

That they had considered the said Petition; and had directed him to report to the House the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Fanners, Gardeners, Stage Coachmen, Carriers, Waggoners, Higlers, and others, who frequent and pals the said Highways; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Highways contain the greatest Part of the Road which leads to his Majesty’s several Royal Palaces; and, being the great Western Road to and from London, they are, by reason of many heavy Carriages, become very ruinous, and in many Parts thereof so bad, that, in the Winter-season, the same are dangerous to his Majesty, and the Royal Family, and such who are obliged to attend them, and also to all others who have Occasion to travel through the said Highways; and the Inhabitants of the said Towns and Parishes, in which the same lie, have, from time to time, been at great Expences in repairing the said Highways; yet they are so very bad, they cannot, by the Laws now in Force, be kept in good Repair: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repairing and amending the said Highways.

all Sorts of brown and white Linen Cloths, being the proper Manufacture of the said Kingdom; and, by an Act of the First of his present Majesty, the said Liberty of exporting Irish Linen was continued to them: That, unless some Provision be made, that the Merchants of Great Britain be put upon an equal Foot with the Traders of Ireland, it is much feared a great Part of the Trade will centre in that Kingdom, by the many Advantages they have already gained: And praying, That the Rnglish Merchants may be put upon the same Foot with the Inhabitants of Ireland.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole Floufe, to whom the Bill for continuing the Liberty of exporting Linen

Cloth to the British Plantations, is committed.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for continuing the Liberty of exporting Irish Linen Cloth to the British Plantations, is committed.

who, by virtue of the said Act, shall and may sue for, and recover, the fame, besides Cost of Suit, by Action of Debt, or of the Cafe, as is before mentioned; any thing in the said Act, or any other Act, Law, Usage, or Custom, to the contrary notwithstanding: That this Clause may be of very fatal Consequence, not only to the present, but former, Adventures of the Company; and the Adventurers, and their Heirs, being ever liable to a Prosecution for Dividends they have received: That, during the time the Company was limited to a short Term of Years, the Dangers from this Clause were not great; but now the Fears are most justly grounded, since the Company is made perpetual by the Act of Parliament of the Tenth of Queen Anne: And praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and so explain and qualify the Clause aforesaid, that the private Adventurers, and their Heirs, may not be exposed to chargeable and vexatious Lau’-suits.

Resolved, That the said Petition be rejected.

It was insisted on by the Petitioners Counsel, That the Election of free Burgesses, or Burgesses at large, was entirely governed by the By-laws made pursuant to the Charter; the Charter being silent as to such free Burgesses: And,

The Petitioners Counsel, in order to disqualify upon their Objections, produced,

Dat. 21 September 1680, a By-law, signed by the Mayor, and eight chief Burgesses, assembled in Common Council, That no chief or free Burgess should be elected, or sworn, without the Mayor, and major Part, were then present of the chief Burgesses; that is to say, Six chief Burgesses, besides the Mayor; under a Penalty of Ten Pounds upon the Mayor: And,

Dat. 21 September 1698, another By-law’, signed by the Mayor, and Ten chief Burgesses, assembled in Common Council, That no chief or free Burgess shall be chosen without the Mayor, and Six chief Burgesses be present, and contenting; and, if any be chol'en by a less Number, such Election to be ipso faRo void; and the Mayor to forfeit Fifty Pounds for every such Offence.

Which By-laws were vacated, and declared void, at a Common Council holden the Fifth Day of by the Mayor, and Six chief Burgesses present: But,

The Petitioners Counsel insisted, That, until they were so repealed, these By-laws governed the Elections of the Burgesses:

And, on this Head, they objected to Colonel Henry Holmes, and William Bowrcman Esquire, That, during the time these By-laws were in force, they were elected chief Burgesses by a less Number than such By-laws made requisite.

Dat. 21 September 1670, another By-law was produced, made by a Mayor, and Five chief Burgesses, assembled in Common Council, That, for the time to come, no chief Burgess, or Burgess at large, otherwise called free Burgess, should be made, unless the Mayor, and Five chief Burgesses, be present, and give their consent, at the Election; upon Pain of Forfeiture of Ten Pound for every Burgess that shall he made contrary to this Law.

That, in Answer to what had been offered, the Sitting Members Counsel insisted,

That the Objections made to the chief Burgesses and free Burgesses before named were not sufficient to make void either the Offices of such chief Burgesses, or their Votes, or the Votes of the free Burgesses elected under them:

And they argued, That the Common Council could not, as they had done by the By-laws of 1670, 1680, and 1698, appoint the Power of Election of chief Burgesses to be executed by a greater Number than the Charter required, which is a Mayor, and the rest of the surviving chief Burgesses, or the major Part of them:

That Colonel Hbknes, and the other Two chief Burgesses objected to, had many Years continued in Office; and all along acted and voted without Interruption or Objection: That Colonel j Bowreman, another of the Three,

has, in 1698, unanimously elected Mayor by a Mayor, and Ten chief Burgesses, the whole Number then in being; who, by this Choice, took him to be a good chief Burgess, by choosing him Mayor, as the Charter requires him to be umm de Jeipjis: That Colonel Holmes had been also Mayor; and both acted in their several Mayoralties without any Objection; which Facts were admitted by the Petitioners Counsel:

That if the Offices of the Three chief Burgesses objected to thou Id be avoided; yet, as free Burgesses, they liad a Right of voting:

That, supposing the y were not originally well elected chief Burgesses, yet, having so many Years acted as such without Interruption, they were at lead to be looked upon as chief Burgesses de facto;and, as such, their Acts would be good till their Offices should be avoided; consequently, that the free Burgesses, who were elected by the Mayor, and chief Burgesses, when these chief Burgesses made the Quorum, were well elected: And farther, as to the free Burgesses, that the By-laws of 1670, and 1680, did not declare the Elections of free Burgesses, made contrary thereto, to be void; but only laid a Penalty upon the Mayor in Cafes of such Elections.

The Sitting Members Counsel also infilled, and it was admitted by the Petitioners Counsel, That, anciently, before the making any of theft By-laws, the Elections of free Burgesses were by a leis Number than any of those By-laws make requisite; and that several of the chief Burgesses, who voted for the Petitioners, joined, in 1706, in the Repeal of the By-law’s of 1680, and 1698. And,

The Sitting Members Counsel produced Instances, in the Years 1672, 1673, and 1674, of Elections both of chief Burgesses and free Burgesses, contrary to the Bylaws then in being: One Instance, by a Mayor and Twq chief Burgesses; another, by a Mayor, and One chief Burgess; and another, by a Mayor, and Four chief Burgesses: From whence they inferred, That the By-laws did not, in the Opinion of the Burgesses, vitiate any Election; and that the an ient Usage in the Borough, to which these Instances were agreeable, justilied the Elections of the Burgesses objected to:

They also ffiewed, by the Town-books, That Five of the Petitioners Voters were elected, w hen Colonel Holmes, who was objected to, made up the Quorum of chief Bur-

fesses; and that, in 1671, a Deputy Mayor, with only

"our chief Burgesses, elected the succeeding Mayor; whereas there is no Power in the Charter to appoint a Deputy Mayor: Which Facts were admitted by the Counsel for the Petitioners, and were offered by the Sitting Members Counsel, not to avoid such Elections of Burgesses, but to shew, that, if the Petitioners Objections prevailed, all the Acts done in this Corporation, for many Years past, would be void; and the Corporation might be found to be dissolved, for want of a due Succession of Mayors and Burgesses: And,

They shewed, by the Town-book, That Eight of the free Burgesses, before objected to by the Petitioners Counsel; viz. Captain John Wood, and the Seven others elected with him the.23th of September 1710; were confirmed and allowed the 9th o (.Octoberfollowing, at a Common Council holden by a Mayor, and Six chief Burgesses; whereof Colonel Holmes, before objected to, was One:

And that Thomas Sanders and Jonathan Combes, Two of the Petitioners Voters, were, on the 16th of October 1693, elected chief Burgesses by a Mayor, and Six chief Burgesses; whereof Colonel Holmes was One; and if he was not good, as was urged for the Petitioners, there was hot a Quorum, according to the By-law of 1680; which was then in being, and required Six chief Burgesses, bc-fides the Mayor, to be present.

Being cross-examined, he said, He had never denied to Robert Thomas, John Read, or James , his having

Robert Thomas, John Read, and James being called on the Petitioner's Part, they averred, That this Bartlet was asked by Thomas and Read, what he had for his Vote for the Petitioner; and that he solemnly denied he ever had any thing; and swore to it; but owned, he had borrowed Three Guineas of O.rley, and had given his Note for it; and Harvey added, That Ganfeild had averred to him solemnly, That, as he hoped for Salvation, he never received a Farthing of any Body for his Vote.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the Twenty-ninth of March last, have exa- . mined the Matter of the said Petition; and find, upon Examination of several Justices of Peace, Gentlemen, and Surveyors of the Highways, of the several Parishes in which the Roads aforesaid lie; and several other Persons; viz. That the said Roads are, as far as the Extents of Heston a Parish, in the said County, so extremely bad, that many Parts thereof have several Holes therein, and are very dangerous to Passengers:

That many Waggons and Coaches have been stuck, and several overturned, in the said Roads; and several Passengers on Horseback thrown off their Horses, by the Badnels of the Roads; by which great Milchiets have been done;
