That the Justices of Peace, living in or near the said Road, acquainted the Committee, That, in regard the Roads were so very ruinous, they had looked into the Accounts of the several Surveyors of the Highways; and, having examined the same very narrowly, found, that they had done their Duty, according to the Laws relating to the Highways; and that the Rates had been equally laid, and duly collected, except from same poor People; who, by reaibn of their Poverty, were not able to pay their Rates:

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Corporation of , in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read: setting forth, That the Privileges granted to the Trish in the Linen-trade, by a free Exportation to the Plantations, the several Makers and Manufacturers of Linens of this Corporation, and Parts adjoining, have found

Seat Discouragements in their Manufactures, to the great ecay of many Hundred Families, being forced to use great Quantities of Ir\JhLinen Yarn, which pays a Duty upon its Importation into Great Britain; and, when manufactured here, has no Drawback allowed upon its being exported: That, unless some Provision be made, whereby the Trade of Ireland may be kept on an equal Foot with the Mauufeftures of Great Britain, they, in time, will gain the wholePlantation trade: And praying, That the Irish Linen-trade may be upon the same Foundation as formerly.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom die Bill for continuing the Liberty of exporting Irish Linen Cloth into the British Plantations is committed.

Chancellor to acquaint both Houses of Parliament with the Reasons of his meeting his Parliament at this time, as they were contained in a Speech, which his Majesty was pleased to deliver, from the Throne, into the Lord Chancellor’s Hands , who read the same to both Houses; and of which, to prevent any Mistake, Mr. Speaker laid, he had obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followed); viz.

9

My Lords and Gentlemen,

IT is with great Satisfaction, that, after this short Reeds, I can acquaint you with the certain Advice I have received, that my Fleet is lately arrived in the Sound; which, by the Blessing of Almighty God, will secure these Kingdoms against any immediate Danger of an Invasion.

I have by this means an Opportunity, which is very acceptable to me, of making a considerable Reduction in our Land Forces; having established it as a Rule with myself, to consult the F.afe of my People in every thing, lb far as is consistent with their Safety: And, for my own Part, as I shall always place my Greatness in the Prolperity of my Subjects, so I shall always desire, that my Power may be founded in their Aflfeftions.

It is upon these Considerations that I have given Orders for the immediate Reducing of Ten thousand Men.

That nothing may be wanting in me to quiet the Minds of all my Subjects, I have like wife given Directions to prepare an Act of Grace; and, however it may be received by those who are obstinately bent on the Ruin of their Country, I promise myself, that it will raise a due Sense of Gratitude in all such as have been artfully mifled into treasonable Practices against my Person and Government, and preserve them from Handing in need of the like Mercy for the future, when such an I nftance of Clemency may not be lb expedient for the publick Welfare, as it would be agreeable to my own Inclinations.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I thank you for your Readinels to suppott me in the present Juncture of Affairs; and for the Supplies which you have given; and do promise you, that they iha.ll be employed for the Uses for which you deligned them.

I shall order such faithful Accounts to be laid before you the next Session, as will make it appear, there was no other View in asking any particular Supply, than to prevent a much greater Expence, which the Nation must have unavoidably incurred without it.

I mult recommend to you, as I did at the Beginning of the Session, to take all proper Methods for reducing the publick Debts, with a just regard to Parliamentary Credit.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Year being so far advanced, I hope you’ll go through the publick Business with all possible Dispatch and Unanimity; it being my Intention to meet you early the next Winter, that the Sitting of Parliament may be brought into the more usual and convenient Season.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Address

be presented to his Majesty, returning the humble Thanks of this House, in the most dutiful and affectionate manner, for his many gracious Declarations in his Speech from the Throne: That the Directions his Majesty has been pleafrd to give for reducing such a Body of Land Forces is the most acceptable Pledge he could give his People of his Tender-ness for them; and is such an Instance of his Wisdom and Goodness, as must for ever endear him to all his Subjects: That his gracious Intentions of Mercy give great Satisfaction to this House, as being highly conducive to the Tranquillity of the Kingdom: That this House has a grateful Sense of his Majesty’s gracious Intentions to lay before them an Account of die Application of the Supplies granted by the Commons: That this House will carry on the great and necessary Work of reducing the publick Debts, with a just regard to Parliamentary Credit; and are resolved, by the Unanimity of their Proceedings, to convince the World, that they are inviolably engaged in Duty and Affection to his Majesty’s Person and Government, on the Support of which the Welfare of these Kingdoms, under God, intirely depends.

full of Gratitude to your Majesty for the many gracious Declarations you have been pleased to make to us from the Throne.

Our Duty to your Majesty, and our Concern for the Security of your Kingdoms, at a time, when the Nation was threatened with a desperate Invasion, obliged us to make Provision for keeping up such a Body of Land Forces, as might shew that we were in a Posture of Defence; but your Majesty having Grounds to hope, on the Arrival of your Fleet in the Sound, that, by the Blessing of God, a Check will be put to that Design, we must for ever acknowlege, that the early Directions you have been pleased to give for reducing such a Body of those Land Forces is the most acceptable Pledge you could give your People for your Tendernels for them; and that your Majesty has nothing lb much at Heart as their present and future Welfare; and is such an Instance of your great Wisdom and Goodueis, as must for ever endear your Majesty to all your Subjects.

We are bound to express our just Satisfaction in your gracious Intentions of Mercy, as being highly conducive to the Tranquillity of the Kingdom, and a convincing Proof of your Majesty’s Desire to reign in the Affections of all your Subjects.

We have so often experienced the happy Effects of the Confidence we have repoled in your Majesty, that we can never entertain any Doubt of the due Application of any Supplies granted by us; and do receive, in the most dutiful and affectionate manner, your Majesty’s Promise to lay the Accounts of such Application before us, as a great Instance of your Justice to the Nation.

We are truly sensible how much the Eale and Prospe-rity of your Subjects depend on the accomplishine that great and necessary Work of reducing the publick Debts; and are resolved to carry it on in the most effectual manner, with just regard to Parliamentary Credit.

We are likewise resolved, by the Dispatch and Unanimity of our Proceedings, to convince the World, that we are inviolably engaged m Duty and Affection to your uieft Sacred Per Ion and Government; on the Support of which the Welfare and Happiness of these Kingdoms, under God, intirely depend.

That it appeared to the Committee, that, when fds of these Bills w'ere ordered to be paid, there was a Minute made in the Treasury, That the remaining Third-part should be paid as soon as it should appear, who were to be charged with the Monies taken up for the Service, that it might regularly be accounted for; and that an Account of this Resolution wasfent to the Governor of New England, for the Encouragement of the Merchants there, by the I>ord Dartmouth, then One of her Majesty s Principal Secretaries of State:

Air. Speaker reported, That the House did attend his Answer to Majesty Yesterday, and presented to him their Address; Address.° and that his Majesty was plealed to give this most gracious Answer;

Gentlemen,

IT is with great Pleasure that I find the Directions I have given to make a Reduction in the Army, and my Intentions to grant an Act of Grace, are so much to the Satisfaction of my faithful Commons.

I thank you for the hearty Assurances you give me of your Affections to my Person and Government; and shall always make such an Ule of the Confidence you repose on me, as may be most for the Advantage of my People.

The Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Supply. Aiorning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Aiornisg, Nine of the Clock.

A PETITION of Richard Weales Matter, Thomas Regulating Pafcall, Henry Pafcall, Samuel Orbell, Thomas Pilots.

Thompson, and Thomas Appleby, Wardens of the Society and Fellowship of Pilots of the Trinity-house of Dover,

Deal, and the Isle of Thanet, on behalf of themselves, and the Fellowship, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That, Time out of mind, the Peti-» tJoners, and Predecessors, have been a Society of Pilots for Conducting of Ships and Vessels up the Rivers of Thames and Medway.; and to examine and swear all such Persons as (horrid offer themselves for Pilots, for Con-dufting of Ships and Vessels up the said Rivers, in Conjunction with the Lord Warden, or his Deputy; and they have also constantly held Courts of Load-Manage at Dover\; at which Courts the Petitioners, the said Matter and Wardens for the Time being, do fit to rectify all Misdemeanors: That several Persons, not Pilots, have taken the Charge of conducting Ships and Vessels up the said Rivers; to the great Prejudice of Merchants: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill to enable them effectually to prevent the same for the future.

A Petition of several Merchants in the City of London, Ditto, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Fellowship of Pilots, long established in the Cinque Ports, is very useful to the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom:

That, by ignorant Persons presuming to conduct Ships to the Port of London, without having undergone any Examination into their Abilities for that Service, tend to the manifest Hazard and Danger of Ships, and their Car- -goes: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for securing the said Fellowship, and remedying the said Mischiefs, by such Methods as shall be thought fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petitions: And that Admiral Aylmer, Sir John Norris, and Mr. Heysham, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of Sir John Trevelyan Baronet, and James Minehead Milner Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Election, setting forth. That at the last Election of Members for ... Borough of Minehead, in the County of the

Petitioners, and Samuel Edwin md Thomas Gage Esquires, flood Candidates: That, according to the ancient Usage of the said Borough, the Right of Execution and Return of the Precept is In the Constables of the said Borough; but Joseph Brown Esquire, Sheriff of Somerset, in Prejudice of the Petitioners, directed his Precept burgenjibus et ele&oribus burgi de Minhead; however took care to deliver the said Precept unto One of the Constables, and infilled upon his Return: That the Petitioners were duly chosen by a Majority of legal Votes, and so declared by the Constables; and notwithstanding Indentures, duly executed by the said Constables, and the Majority of the said Burgesses and Electors, were tendered to the said Sheriff, yet he refuted to receive the same, or to return the Petitioners; but the Sheriff, in Prejudice to the Petitioners, affixed an Indenture, prepared by some few of the Burgesses and Electors, whereby Mr. Edwin and Mr. Gage are mentioned to be elected for the said Borough: And praying, That the Indentures so affixed to the said Writ may be taken off from the same; and that the Indentures.

"by which the Petitioners were returned, may, infleaa thereof, be affixed thereto.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That John Browning, of Shepton Mallet, do attend this House upon Wednesday next, when the High Sheriff and Under Sheriff of the County of Somerset are to attend this House.

and the Community of the said City, was referred, the Matter of Fast, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read iu his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, the 13th of May instant, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find,

That, in the Year 1693, the publick Debt of the City of Edinburgh amounted to the Sum of 82,913/. 16$. gftf.; and that, by an Act of Parliament passed in Scotland, the 13th June 1693, a Duty of Two Penies Scots is laid upon every Pint of Ale and Beer brewed, brought in, vended, tapped, and fold, within the Town of , Suburbs

and Liberties thereof, to be paid to the Magistrates, for a Term not exceeding Thirty Years, to commence on the ift Day of July 1693; which Duty is appropriated for Payment as well of the Interest of the Debt aforesaid, as of the principal Sum due from the said Town, for the Term of Three Years j and, after the Expiration of the Term of Three Years, the same is appropriated for the Payment of the principal Debt only; and then the Interest of the said Debt, by that Act, is directed to be paid out of the other Revenues of the Town, and not out of the Duty arising by the said Act:

And, out of the said Duty, the Sum of Two thousand Marks Scots per Annum is, by that A Cl, to be paid to the French Ministers, during the Perfection, and

Continuance of the said Duty, and no longer

That, by an Account produced to the Committee, it appeared, that the gross Produce of the Duty arising by the said A Cl, between the ift of July 1693, and the ift July 1710, amounted only to the Sum of 7(1,511 0;

and that the Duty, arising during the remaining 13 Years of the said Term, was farmed towards discharging a Debt 45,5831- 6$. 8 d.with the Interest due, and growing due, for the same:

That the said Act, restraining the Magistrates of the Town from applying any more of that Duty towards discharging the Interest of the said Debt of 82,913/. 165. than what should ariie in die Three First Years, did put the Town under a Necessity of borrowing Money to discharge such Into eft as should become due for the said Debt after the lirft Three Years; the whole Produce of that Duty not being equal to the annual Interest of the First Debt.

That, by another Account produced to the Committee, it appeared, that the whole Revenue of the Town, exclusive of the Duty aforesaid, between Michaelmas 1699 and Michaelmas £. s. d. 1706, amounted to- - 43,772 4 1

And, between Michaelmas 1706 and Michaelmas 1713, to ... 38,760 14 1

And, in the Years 1713, 1714, amounted to - - - 10,330 4 10

So, upon comparing the Accounts, it appears, That there has been a gradual Decrealc of the Revenue of the Town since the Union; and that the Difference between the annual Revenue at the Union, and in the Year 1715, hath been ----- 1,088 1 i{

That the Committee called Mr. George Irvin: Who said, He had examined the Accounts produced to the Committee; and that the fume w ere true, and ligned by. the Accountant General: He further said, That the publick Works, in regard they had been much neglected many Years, would cost a very considerable Sum of Money to repair them as they ought to be; and that it was abl’olutely necessary to inlarge the Harbour of Leith, and deepen the Chanel thereof; and also to build and endow Two new Churches, and a Work-house for the Poor of the said Town.

That it also appeared to the Committee, That the Trade of the City, and its Suburbs, is very much decayed since the Year 1707, the Time of the Union, for want of the

of England, and others, their Heirs and Assigns, the Province of Carolina, as a County Palatine, in common Soc-cage, under the yearly Rent of Twenty Marks; and di<i thereby constitute them absolute Proprietors of the said Province; with Powers to build Forts, and raise and exercise armed Men, to defend themselves against the barbarous Nation of the Indians: That, upon the Encouragement given in the said Charters, divCrs Families of Merchants, and others, trailIported themselves to the said Province, and there settled, and expended great Sums of

Money in planting and strengthening the said.....and have carried on a great Trade from thence to Great Britain; to the great Improvement of his Majesty’s Customs and Revenues: That, about Two Years since, the Indians came down, in great Multitudes, upon his Majesty s Subjects inhabiting in the said Colony, and invaded the fame, and killed great N umbers of the Planters, and other Inhabitants thereof.; and have, ever since that time, by the Instigation of the French and Spaniards, continued a barbarous and bloody War against the Inhabitants thereof:

A Petition of the Magistrates, and remanent Members, of the Town Council of Dumfries in Scotland, for themselves, and in the Name of the whole Inhabitants of the fame, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, from their hearty Affection to the Government during the Time of the unnatural Rebellion, have been at great Charge in procuring and giving Intelligence to and from the South and North Parts of the Kingdom; in fortifying this Town, and providing great Quantities of Arms and Ammunition; besides what they have been at by a great many extraordinary Contingences; whereby the publick Stock of this borough is very much funk: That this Borough hath but One Church, wherein not above Half of the Parishioners can be accommodated the time of Divine Worship, and they altogether unable to build another: That they a long time endeavoured, with great Industry, to carry on a good Trade, notwithstanding the Want of any convenient Harbour: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling them to pay the Debts contrasted for his Majesty’s Service; to build a Church; and to make a convenient Harbour, or Dock, at Dumfries, for the Encouragement of Trade.

Dufy on Mr. Norris reported, from the Committee, to whom Loft Salt, the Petition of John Fletcher was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That, the Committee having examined the Allegations of the Petition, it appeared, That the Petitioner did, on or about lOthDayof November 1712, put on board the Ship called the Salmon of Belfast, 1,040 Buthels of white Salt; and, in the said Voyage, the said Ship and Cargo, and all the Crew, except one Man and a Boy, were loft in a violent Storm; and the Exporter, not having Notice Vol. 18.

thereof in due time, could not make Proof of the Lots of the said Salt within the Time limited by an Act of the Fourth and Fifth Years of the Reign of her late Majesty; which enacted, where any Salt, or Rock-salt, ffiip-ped in order for Exportation to Ireland, and the same should perish by Sinking; in l'uch case, the Exporter of such Salt so perilliing, or loft, should, upon Proof made of the Loss of such Salt, receive a Certificate from the Justices of Peace; and, upon producing such Certificate to the Officer of the Place where the said Duty should have been paid, or secured, such Security should be discharged; or so much Money as was actually paid for the Duty of such Salt, should be repaid, upon Demand; provided such Proof be made within Six Months after such Lots:

That the Commissioners for managing the Salt-duties attended the Committee; and said, That the Petitioner did make Application to their Board, in order to be relieved for to much Duty as had been paid, or secured, for the Salt so loft; but the Commissioners had no Power to give the Petitioner any Relief, because the Petitioner had elapsed the Time limited by the said Act of Parliament; which provides. That the Proof of such Loss be made within Six Months: But they had no other Objection against the Petitioner’s being relieved, by giving him a further Time of Six Months, to make legal Proof of the Loss of the said Salt.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for Sheriffs the better enabling Sheriff's to sue out their Patents, and Patent®» &c* pals their Accounts: And that Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Mr. Jessop, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Upon the Petition of several of the Inhabitants of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks, in behalf of fheinlelves, and several others, who have Right of Election for Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough: And also,

P Upon the Petition of Joseph Gray, and other Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot within the said Borough; severally complaining of an undue Election and Return of George Bruere Esquire, and the Right honourable the Lord Shelburne of the Kingdom of Ireland, to serve for the said Borough:

That Counsel on both Sides attended the Committee:

That the Counsel for the Petitioners against Mr. Bruere, objected to him as unqualified, with respect to a Particular mentioned in the Rental given in by him for his Qualification; which Rental amounts to 334/. 10s. Annum.

The Particular objected to is mentioned in the said Rental, to be a Messuage, Tenement, Farm, and Lands, with the Appurtenances, called the Home Farm, and Bryan's Farm, and a Parcel of I.ands or Warren, called Whiteley-hill, in the Parish of , in the County of Sussex, in the Tenure of Mary Ryce, of the yearly Value of Forty-four Pounds.

And the Petitioners Counsel called.

Geo. Ryce: Who said, He did not? know any Farm called Home Farm, or Bryan's Farm; but that he rents a Farm called Whiteley-hill, which is all Warren-land, except about Seven or Eight Pounds a Year: That he pays his Rent, which is 44/. per Annum, to Mr. Gale; and never heard of any Interest Mr. Bruere had:

That, on Mr. Bruere's Part, a Conveyance to him for his Life, by Leafeand Iteleafe, dated i* 8$ 3d* July 1713, from Leonard Gale Esquire, of Part of Two Farms, therein called by the Names of Home Farm, and Bryans Farm, a Warren called Whiteley-hill, and other Premises therein mentioned, was produced, and proved to be duly executed; and the Consideration-money, being 1,000l. bona fide paid by Mr. Bruere. And,

Mr. Gale said, That he did, by the said Deeds, actually convey those Farms and Premises to Mr. Bruere, for his Life; and, bona fide, received the Consideration-money: That he had, indeed, received the Rent since the Conveyance, but it was for Mr. Bruere'& Use; and for no other Reason than because himself lived in that County, and Mr. Bruere lived Fifty Miles off; and that he bona fide, annually accounted for, and paid, the same to Mr. Bruere.

That the Counsel for the Petitioners against the Lord Shelburne acquainted the Committee, That they did not infill upon their Petition.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Rejoiced^ That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That George Bruere Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right honourable Henry Lord Viscount Shelburne, of the Kingdom of Ireland, is duly elected a

Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Great Marlow.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Hampden reported, from the Committee of Pri- Shaftesbury vileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, Ele"ion‘ touching the Election for the Borough of Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report, and Resolutions, were read; and are as follow;

Upon the Petition of William Hearst Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Edward Nicholas Esquire, to serve for the Borough of Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset:

The Counsel on both Sides attended the Committee.

The Petitioner’s Counsel alleged, That their material Witnesses, whereof Mr. Long, One of the Overseers of the Poor, was the principal, were taken ill upon the Road, and lay sick at Salisbury; which they offered to prove; and said, They had not any material Witness in Town, and could not therefore proceed to the Merits of the Election; but desired farther Time to bring up their Witnesses:

To which the Sitting Member’s Counsel answered, That this was only a Pretence: That, if the same had been so, the House ought to have been acquainted therewith before the Committee met to hear the lyierits of the Election; and Notice should have been given to the Sitting Member; neither of which had been done: That the Merits of this Election were originally appointed to be heard on the Two-and-twentieth of April last; and the Hearing would have come bn before now, had not the Committee been sometimes adjourned: That it came on now in course, and the Petitioner had time enough to bring up any Witnesses he thought fit: That there was another Overseer in the Town besides Long; and he might have lent up any Poors Rates he had, if he could not have attended himself:

That the Sitting Member, having had no Notice of this Pretence, had brought up his Witnesses; been at great Expence; was ready to justify his Election; and ought to be discharged of this Petition, if the Counsel for the Petitioner did not think fit to’ call any Witnesses to make out the Matter of his Petition:

Which the Petitioner’s Counsel not doing, nor making it appear to the Committee, That the Petitioner had ever summoned any Witnesses to attend;

And the Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Edward Nicholas Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

John Hearing: Who said. That he has voted at former Elections: That all the Candidates at this Election asked his Vote; and that Captain Welling gave him Twenty Guineas as a free Gift; but never asked his Vote:

That he and several other Voters, in Number Forty, met Mr. John Cafwall, the Sitting Members Brother, and Captain Welling: That the Sitting Member eame once into the Room, and drank tome Ale with them; they drank his Health; for which he thanked them; anil said. He hoped they would vote for him; and went away, without saying any thing more to them: They all agreed not to vote on either Side under Twenty Guineas a Man; and, Mr. John Cafwall offering that Sum, thereupon they all put down their Names in a Paper, that they would vote for General Gotges and Mr. That the Captain gave him his Twenty Guineas; and, he believes, all the rest had the lame; but he saw none paid, except his own: That the Sitting Member never gave, nor offered, him any thing: That he voted for Mr.

K'all; but, without the Twenty Guineas, should have voted for Captain Gorges:

Being cross-exainined, he said. That, before Mr. wallcame down, Mr. Bangham the Receiver General of the County, had asked Votes for General Gorges; acted as his Agent; and gave the Witness Seven Guineas as a free Gift; but did not alk his Vote when he gave the Money; and that Mr. Batch had also, before this, bid Ten or Eleven Guineas apiece for Votes for General Gorges; but the Witness did not know he gave any thing:

This Witness, being asked, Whether he was not to give his Vote for the Twenty Guineas, which he called a free Gift, answered, That he did not suppose they were given him for nothing.

Thomas Caldecot said, That William Spencer gave him Ten Guineas as a free Gift, and never asked his Vote, nor said what he was to do for them: He voted for Mr. Cafwall; and, without the Ten Guineas, should have voted for General Gorges:

Being cross-examined, he said, That Mr. Bangham, the Receiver-General, had, before this, given him Seven Pounds; which the Witness paid him back again, after he had received the Ten G uineas; and Mr. Bangham told him, He would give him the Seven Pounds clean, if he would vote for them: That it was reported, Mr. Bangham asked Votes for General Gorges, and Spencer for Mr. Cafwall.

Mr. Samuel Burton said, That he happened to be at Leominster at the Time of the Election; and, meeting with the Sitting Member there, took Notice to him of the Report how liberal he was for his Election: To which the Sitting Member answered, That he might be chose elsewhere; but here he was born, and he would be a Member of Parliament for that Place, whatever it cost him; and said, He had brought down with him the Sinews of an Election:

Being cross-examined, this Witness said, He is Receiver General for Radnorshire, and has been so Two Years: That he is Agent for General Gorges; and is sure the General never gave any thing to any Man alive for his Vote.

John Kcdward said, That he voted for Mr.;

and was One of the Forty who let their Hands to the Paper, to vote for Twenty Guineas a Man: That Captain Welling gave him Twenty Guineas: but gave it as a free Token: That, he believed, the rest of the Forty bad their Twenty Guineas apiece also; for he few them come out of the Room with nothing but Gold in their Hands; though he did not fee any paid, bot his own; for Mr. John Cafwall, the Sitting Member’s Brother, and Captain Welling, who paid the Money, called them all out of one Room into another, one by one; but the Sitting Member was not there when the Money was paid;

This Witness, being cross-examined, laid. That before this, Mr. Bangham, the Receiver General, asked his

Vote; and, at the same time, gave him Six Guineas to Leomiatte vote for General Goiges; and that he paid the Six Gui* fcltetion. neas back again to Mr. Bangham, before the Election:

That the Witness telling John Bourn, who voted for General Gorges, what he had for his Vote, Bourn said,

He had Ten Pounds; and that it was all in Shillings and Sixpences; and not one Half Crown among them.

Mr. John Colt junior said, That Francis Steel, who voted for the Sitting Member, told the Witness, He owed the Sitting Member's Brother, upon Bond, Thirty Pounds, which he borrowed of him when he was Receiver General; and was afraid he should be thrown into Gaol, if he did not vote for Mr. Cafioall.

Katherine Halfpenny said, That Mr. Thomas Price, the Town Clerk, went up and down lbliciting Votes for the Sitting Member; and the heard him declare publickly, in the open Street, to about Twenty Persons, most of which were Voters, That whatever Money was given on the other Side, they would double it, to carry the Election:

But the Sitting Member was not present when this Declaration was made.

The Sitting Member’s Counsel infilled, That no Credit ought to be given to the Witnesses produced, who had confessed themselves to be corrupt on all Sides: That, if such Witnesses were in any fort to be credited, their Evidence only affeCled feme particular Voters, who did not appear, by any Poll produced, to have voted for the Sitting Member: That, should all those they had impeached be taken off the Poll, the Sitting Member would yet have a great M ajority against every other Candidate: That no Candidate pretended to dispute the Poll, or the Right to fit: That the Witnesses produced had declared the Sitting Member never gave, or offered, any thing; nor was he ever present when any thing was offered, or given; nor did it appear, that any thing was offered, or given, by his Direr ion; and therefore they thought it not necessary to produce any Evidence on his behalf, the Evidence produced not affecting him, nor pretending to take away his Majority.

to which the Petitioner’s Counsel replied, That although the Majority was not disputed; yet the Sitting Member having procured his Election by Bribery and Corruption his Election is void.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to this Resolution:

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That George Cafwall Esquire is not duly elected a Burgefe to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Leominster, in the County of Hereford.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A PETITION of the poor distressed Prisoners for . Debtor, Debt in the Sheriff’s Prison, or Ward, in the Parish Petition*, of Saint Thomas the Apostle, in and for the County of

Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they are a great Number of Prisoners, in moll fad, miserable, and starving Conditions, as well as their Families; most of them having not wherewithal tp make the least Satisfaction of their Debts; and they that have any thing, are willing to surrender their All for Ihtir Liberty and Releasement: And praying, That an Act of Parliament may pais for their Relief Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the poor Prisoners for Debt in his Majesty’s Prisons of the King's Bench and Fleet, w as presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the Petitioners have been reduced, by the frequent Losses and Casualties in Trade, and other unavoidable Misfortunes, so as to be rendered utterly uncapable of paying their Creditors their foil Debts: That the Petitioners suffer the greeted of Miseries, Confinement; and, whilst they are starving in the Prison, their Wives and Children are perishing out of it: That perpetual Imprilbiiment of poor insolvent Debtors deprives his Majesty, and the Nation, of the Service of many useful and faithful subjects, and renders great Numbers of their Families a Burthen to the Publick: That there are several Accidents of Life, which no human Prudence can foresee, or prevent; l'uch as Losses at Sea, by Fire, 8$c.; and the Sufferers are always accounted Objects of Compassion, and not of Punishment: That the Petitioners, and those in the same Circumstances, are the only unfortunate Persons rendered uncapable of reaping the least Benefit from the Blessings of his Majesty’s Reign; and it is no small Addition to their Affliction, that their same admits of nothing but Mourning, when the rest of their Fellow Subjects have so many just Occasions to rejoice: That the Petitioners are willing to deliver up their All, under the fe-vereft Penalties, to their Creditors; which they cannot expect, if their little Substance is wasted in a Prison:

And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for their Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Thomas Gage and Samuel Edwin Esquires Minehead was presented to the House, and read; setting, forth, Election. That at the last Election of Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Min the County of Somerset, the Petitioners, and Sir Trevelyan, and James Milner Esquire, stood Candidates: That, at the said Election, John Jones and George James pretended to act as Constables of the said Borough; and, as such, to preside at the said Election, as the Returning Officers; which they had no Right to do; and the Aftings and Doings of the said John Jones and George James were contrary to the ancient Rights and Usage of the said Borough: That, notwithstanding the Petitioners had a Majority of legal Votes, yet the said Sir John Trevelyan, and Mr. Milner, although not qualified within the late Act for securing the Freedom of Parliament, by the farther Qualifying of Members to fit in the House of Commons, by Bribery, and other indirect Practices, procured themselves to be returned; in Wrong to the Petitioners:

And praying to be relieved therein.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, whereby his Majesty may be enabled to grant the Petitioner such Settlements as the Petitioner would have been entitled to, in case her said Husband w'ere naturally dead.

To the honourable (he Commons of Britain in Parliament aflem bled.

THE Governor and Company of Merchants of Great Britain trading to the South Seas, and other Parts of America; and for encouraging the Fishery; having under their Consideration, how they may be most serviceable to his Majesty and his Government; and to shew their Zeal and Readinels to concur in the great and honourable Designof reducing the National Debts, in such manner as may be consistent with, and for the Support Parliamentary Credit; do humbly propose,

lft, That they will be content, and do submit, that their present Capital Stock of Ten Millions be increased to the Sum of Twelve Millions, either by Subscription or otherwise, as by their General Court shall be thought most expedient:

2dly, That the Two Millions, so to be advanced, shall be paid into his Majesty’s Exchequer by Four equal Payments; the last whereof to be on or before the 24th December next; and shall be employed towards redeeming the Principal and Interest charged on the Four Lottery Acts of 1711 and 1712, and the Annuities of Three Pounds per Cent, payable for the Bankers Debt contracted in the Reign of King Charles the Second; and not otherwise:

3dly, That the present annual Sums of 600,0001, and 8,000l. payable to the Company, be continued to them, for and in respect of their laid Ten Millions, until the 24th June 1718; and that, for the Two Millions, to be advanced as aforesaid, there be allowed to the Company an Annuity after the Rate of Five Pounds per Cent, per Annum, from the respective Times of Payment thereof into the Exchequer until the said 24th of June 1718: 4tbly, That, from and after the said 24th June 1718, there be payable to the Company, by weekly Payments, as the Funds shall produce, an annual Sum of 600,0001. being after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, for the whole Twelve Millions; together with their present Allowance of 8,0001, per Annum; to continue until redeemed by Parliament, as herein after is mentioned:

5thly, That the present Duties and Revenues, chargeable with the Payment of the present annual Sums of 600,000l. and 8,000l. together with such Duties and Revenues as shall be redeemed by the said Two Millions, to be advanced as aforesaid, shall be continued, and made the Fund for, and chargeable with, the Payment of the several Annuities, which; pursuant to this Proposition, shall become due and payable to the Company, and with all Arrears thereof incurred, and to be incurred; and that the Surplus of all the said Duties and Revenues, after such Payment to the Company, as aforesaid, shall be applied and appropriated for and towards paying and discharging feme other of the present National Debts.

6thly, That the Sums unpaid, charged on the General Mortgage 1710, which is Part of the Company’s present Funds, be paid out of the Aggregate Fund, to arise out of the Savings of the several Funds which shall be redeemed) or reduced, this Section:

7thly, That all Transfers of the Company’s present and increased Capital Stock shall be free and exempt from any further Duties than the Transfers are at present subject to by Parliament; and that their present and increased Capital, and Stock in Trade, be exempt from all Taxes and Impositions whatsoever:

8thly, The Company do submit, That the said annual Sum of 600,000 /. for the said Twelve Millions, and the said annual Sum of 8,000l. may be redeemable by Parliament, upon a Year’s Notice, to be given by Authority of Parliament, on any of the Four usual Quarterly Feast-days in the Year, after the 24th June, *7 25, and upon Payment to the said Governor and Company of the said Vol. 18.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

THE Governor and Company of the Bank of England, having understood the Resolutions of this honourable Hoofe, in a Committee of Ways and Means, on the and and 34th of this inilant; and having observed the several Particulars wherein the said Resolutions do differ from the Proposal laid before this honourable House by the said Governor and Company, on the 17th of this Month; do content to the several Alterations; except, That, in Consideration of their past Services; the many Difficulties they have struggled with, in supporting publick Credit; their chearful Concurrence in redeeming their own Funds; and their Assistance in discharging other Debts of the Nation;

They do humbly insist, That they may have as long a Term of Time allowed them for the future Redemption of their Funds, as shall be granted to any other Corporation this Session of Parliament:

And that the Annuities, to be established for paying off the Lotteries, and other redeemable Funds, may be made transferrable, and payable, in the Bank; which Service the said Governor and Company are willing to undertake, without any Charge to the Publick, other than Salary for Clerks, and Fees in passing the Accounts: And that all such Privileges and Clauses, as Hi all be thought necessary and reasonable to enable the Bank to perform the respective Services proposed, be inserted in the Bill to pals on this Occasion; and that no further Duties or Taxes may be laid on their present or increased Stock; nor on any Transfer of the lame; nor on any Bonds or Bills to be issued by the Bank for Support of their Credit

ill, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present annual Sums of 600,0001, and 8,000l. payable to the South Sea Company, be continued to them, for and in respect of their Capital Stock of Ten Millions, until the 24th Day of June 1718, inclusive.

2d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the said 24th Day of June 1718, there be payable to the said Company, by weekly Payments, an annual Sum of 500,000l.; being after the Rate of Five Pounds per Cent, per Annum, for the said Ten Millions; together with their present Allowance of 8,000l. per Annum, to be continued until redeemed by Parliament.

3d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present Duties and Revenues, chargeable with the Payment of the present annual Sums of 600,0001. and 8,000l. shall be continued, and made the Fund for, and chargeable with the Payment of, the said Annuities of 500,000l. and 8,000l. as the same shall become due and payable to the Company; and with all Arrears thereof incurred, and to be incurred; and that the Surplus of all the Duties and Revenues, after such Payment to the Company, as aforesaid, shall attend the lurther Dif- of Parliament.

5th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Transfers of the said Company’s Stock shall be free and exempt from any further Duties than the Transfers are at present subjefit toby Parliament; and that their Capital, and Stock in Trade, be exempt from all Taxes and Impositions whatsoever.

further Sums lb to be advanced, be secured as well upon the Surplus of the said Duties and Revenues to arise over and above the said Annuities, payable for the said Ten Millions; as also upon the Duties and Revenues to be redeemed with the said Sums, not exceeding Two Millions, to be further advanced, as aforesaid.

Mr. Hampden reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of William Hartley, and others, Creditors for Work done, and Materials found, for amending the Road between Hockley, in the County of Bedford, and Stony Stratford, in the County of Bucks, on the behalf of themselves, and divers other like Creditors, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which Report he read in his Place, and afterw ards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: and is as follows; viz. That, the Committee having examined the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared,

That by an Act of the Fifth Year of the late Queen Attne, for repairing the said Road, several Powers are granted to the Trustees therein named, for railing Money to be laid out in amending the said Roads:

That the Trustees, in the Act named, contrafted with the Petitioners, for the Carriage of Stone, Gravel, and other Materials, from several Places remote from the said Road; whereby there is a considerable Debt due to them for the same; amounting to the Sum of 6,000 I. and upwards:

That the Monies, arising by the said Toll, amounting to no more than about Four hundred Pounds per Annum, communibus Annis, were not sufficient to discharge the said Debts; whereupon another Act passed in the Eighth Year, of the said Queen, for making more effectual the aforesaid Act, by granting a longer Term of Years for col-left ing the said Toll:

That the Petitioners also complained of some Defects in the former Act of Parliament; particularly in relation to the Toll upon Oxen, Sheep, and Hogs; by which it is Enacted, That there shall be paid, for every Score of Oxen, Six Pence; for every Score of Sheep or Lambs, One Peny; and, for every Score of Hogs, Three Pence; and so in proportion for any Number exceeding Five: But that the Drovers, to avoid the Duty, always take care to separate their Oxen, Sheep, and Hogs, into finall Parcels, under the Number of Five in a Parcel; by means whereof the Law is evaded, and the Duty loft: That it appeared also to the Committee, That great Numbers of Persons, travelling the said Road, do avoid the Turnpike, by going with their Waggons into private Persons Grounds:

That the former Act of Parliament directs, That a Turnpike, or Turnpikes, shall be erected between Forn-hill and Stony Stratford’, by means whereof, several Persons avoid paying the Toll, by going a By-road near Stratford Bridge; whereas the Turnpike ought to have been set up at Stratford Bridge, or any Part thereof; but, as the Act now uands, they have not sufficient Power so to do:

That the Petitioners allege, That, in the former Act, they have not a Power to dig for Stone, Gravel, or other Materials, necessary for amending the Roads, into waste or other Grounds, as is in all other Acts of the like Nature.

That, upon the whole Matter, it appeared. That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition; and, unless they have the Aid of an Act of Parliament, to remove the before-mentioned Impediments, and to explain the former Acts, the Roads, which are Eleven Miles in Length, cannot be kept in good Repaid, nor the Creditors paid their just Debt, so long Handing out; which will tend to the Ruin of them, and their Families.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, and making more effectual, the Acts of the Fifth and Eighth Years of her late Majesty’s Reign, for amending the Roads between Hockley, in the County of Bedford, and Stony Stratford, in the County of Bucks, And that Mr. Hampden and Mr. Denton do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

<» A P ETITI ON of the Mayor, capital Burgesses, and Soap, Sec. f\. Assistants, of the Town and Borough of Tiverton,

in the County of Devon, and of the Merchants, Fullers, Serge-makers, and others, trading and dealing in the Woollen Manufactures in the said Town and Borough, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the Woollen Manufactures within the said Town have been, for Ages past, the principal Support of the poorer of the Inhabitants; and, in case the said Manufactures are not encouraged, the Poor will become too burthensome for the said Town: That vast Quantities of Soap and Candles are daily spent in the working and fulling the said Manufactures; and the Duty on Soap and Candles being so very high, it is a great Clog to the said Manufactures; by Means whereof , the Traders are incapacitated of carrying on their Trades:

And praying to be relieved in such manner as this honourable House shall think fit

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants, Clothiers, Serge-makers, Duties on Fullers, and others, trading and dealing in the Woollen So!*1’’ Manufacture, in and near the Town of , in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the Woollen Manufactures within the said Town have been the principal Support of the poorer Sort of People; and, in case the said Manufactures be not encouraged, the Poor will become a Burthen greater than the said Town can bear: That there are vast Quantities of Soap weekly used in working and fulling the said Manufactures; and the Duties, payable on Soap, being lb very considerable, renders it very difficult to dispose of their Goods, in foreign Parts, at a Market-price, and uncapable of carrying on their Trades, unless proper Methods are taken to retrieve the fame: And praying to be relieved therein.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Salt ofed for Mr. Cunningham reported, from the Committee, to curing Fith. whom the Petition of the Merchants and Dealers in Fish on the Coast of Fife, and other Places in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, in pursuance of the Order of the , House of the Third of June instant, have examined

the Allegations of the said Petition; and do find the Matter of Fast to be as follows; viz.

That by an Act of the Parliament of Scotland, intituled, An Act for advancing and establishing the Fishing-trade in and about this Kingdom, bearing Date the 21 ft of September 1705, it is Ordained and Enacted, That all White Fish, and Herrings, to be exported, shall bepyned, cured, and packed, from the Bottom to the Top, with foreign Salt allenarly:

And by another Act of the Parliament of Scotland, of the same Date, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Exportation of Beef and Pork, it is Statute and ordained. That all Beef and Pork to be salted for Exportation be made and packed with foreign Salt:

And by the Eighth Article of the Union it is agreed, That, from and after the Union, the Laws' and Acts of Parliament in Scotland for Pyning, Curing, and Packing, of Herrings, White Fish, and Salmon, for Exportation, with foreign Salt only, without any Mixture of or

Vol. 18.

Irijli Salt; and for preventing of Frauds in Curing and Packing of Fish; be continued in Scotland, subject to such Alterations as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain.

That, by the Tenor of the Laws of England, there is no manner of Restraint upon home-made Salt; but that it may be used in curing either Fillies or Fleflies.

And that, upon Examination of the Secretary and Deputy Comptroller of the Salt Office, it appeared to the Committee, That there is no Restraint in England as to home-made Salt; and that the Exporters of Fishes and Fleshes make no Affidavit whether their Fishes or Fleflies for Exportation are cured with foreign or home-made Salt; but that the Drawbacks, in both Cafes, are the fame:

And that, by an Act of the First of Queen Ann, the smallest Size of Fish, for which a Drawback is allowed on Exportation, must contain in Length 18 Inches from the Cone in the Fin to the Third Joint in the Tail of such Fish.

And it appeared to the Committee, upon Examination of Colonel Erskine, and others, That Co^-fish under the Size of 18 Inches, especially those taken in the West of Scotland, are a valuable, vendible, Commodity, in foreign Markets.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Carter reported, from the Committee appointed to search Precedents in relation to the Proceedings of the Commons in Prosecutions of Impeachments, the Matters they had directed him to report to the House; fthich he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee appointed to search Precedents, in relation to the Proceedings of the Commons in Prosecutions of Impeachments, have inspected the Journals of both Houses of Parliament; and are of Opinion, That it is the undoubted Right of the Commons to impeach a Lord, either for High Treason, or for High Crimes and Misdemeanors; or, if they fee Occasion, to mix both the one and the other in the same Accusation:

That the Impeachment preferred against Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer is one continued Accuse-

tion, consisting of High Crimes and Misdemeanors, and also of Charges of High Treason: The Fasts on which the Articles preceding those of High Treason are grounded, are laid together in Order of Time, and follow one another successively in the manner they were committed.

As the Commons thought this the most natural Method for exhibiting, the several Articles against the said Earl, they were of Opinion, that they ftmuld proceed in the

Proof of these several Fasts after the same Method; fmee it is manifest, that, in laying open the Course of such a wicked Administration, the preceding Parts of it give Light to those which follow; and that the Proof of several of the Articles of High Crimes and Misdemeanors would naturally lead to the Proof of those of High Treason.

The Lords received these several Articles of Impeachment without making any Exception against the Form in which they were exhibited.: The said Earl made his Answer to them in the same Order j and has no-w here infilled to be tried in any other Method; so that the Com- . mittee are surprised to find a Stop put to the Prosecution of the Commons, by an Objection which has never been darted by the said Earl, and which the Lords' had given them so little Reason to expect.

To this your Committee mull add, That as the Commons only are Matters of the Evidence; and as, upon that account, they are best able to determine what to charge first, and what next; so they are most proper to determine in what Method to proceed for the Advantage of the Prosecution; in the Event of which, all the Commons of Great Britain are so highly concerned:

To which they mull further add, That they fee no Reason but that the Lords may as well invert the whole Order of the Articles, as prescribe to the Commons those particular Articles on which they are first to proceed; which will necessarily produce such a Condition both in the Fast&and Evidence, as is by no means confident with that Cleamels and Perspicuity in which the Committee think this Affair ought to appear.

Your Committee, upon examining Precedents, do fiud divers Precedents of Impeachments for High Treason, and other High Crimes and Misdemeanors, in the same Accusation; and do not find, that the Lords ever ob-jested to such Proceeding, or ever gave Judgment upon any particular Article of an Impeachment, before the Commons had gone through, and concluded, their Evidence upon all the Articles, or so many of them as they thought fit: And your Committee are at a Lois to conceive what Arguments, or Precedents, can be brought to support the Kesolution of their Lordships to give Judgment upon one Part of the same Accusation, referring the other Part for a subsequent Tryal; as they are to know what' their Lordships mean, by admitting the Commons to proceed upon the Articles for High Crimes and Mifde-meanprs, after Judgment is given upon the Articles for High Treason, supposing the Judgment proper for High Treason should be given against the said Earl.

Resolved, That a Conference be desired with the Lords, relating to Proceeding in the Prosecutions of Impeach-'ments.

Ordered, That the Committee appointed to make good the Articles of Impeachment against Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer, and to whom it was referred to search Precedents in relation to the Proceedings of the Commons in the Prosecution of Impeachments; do draw up what is proper to be offered to the Lords at the said Conference: And that they do withdraw immediately into the Speaker’s Chamber, to draw up the fame.

Ordered, That the said Report from the said Committee be referred back to the said Committee.

And the Committee withdrew accordingly.

and after your Lordships have, on your Parts, also desired a Conference upon the same Subject: -

That free Conferences are the most ancient and established Methods for adjusting the Differences that have at any time arisen between the Two Houses; and, as the Commons conceive, the only Method to preserve a good Correspondence between them on such Occasions; which, at this time, is of the highest Importance; because a Misunderstanding on this Account would tend to defeat the Tryat of the Impeachment of the Commons:

That the Commons conceive clearly, that the Subject-matter of the last Conference is not a Point of Judicature, but a Point relating only to the Prosecution of the Commons; it having arisen before any Matter of Judgment had come before your Lordships upon the Tryal:

For which reasons, the Commons conceive, that your Lordships ought not to have denied them a free Conference upon the Subject-matter of the last Conference.

Ordered, That Mr. Craggs do go to the Lords, and desire the said Conference.

Address to The Lord Castlecomer reported from the Committee except Karl who were appointed to draw up an Address to be pre-5-5°f<r’OUt to his Majesty, upon the Resolution of the House

t o race, yesterday, That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and is as follows;

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty s most faithful Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, do most humbly representto your Majesty, That, in our Impeachment exhibited against Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer, we did set forth, That he, the said Earl, did traitcrously adhere to, aid, and abet, the late French King, then an Enemy to her late Majesty; and did begin, and carry on, a clandestine and separate Correspondence and Negotiation with the Ministers of the said French King; in consequence of which, it is evident, that great Part of the Forces, maintained at the Expence of so much Treasure, in order to reduce the Power of France; as likewise great Part of the Subsidies granted by Parliament to foreign Princes, for the same End; were, in Reality, made subservient and instrumental to awe the good Allies of her Majesty into a Compliance with the hard Terms dilated by France; the unhappy Catalans were abandoned; the Emperor, Empire, and King of Portugal, were left to treat for themselves; the Kingdom of Sicily was given to the Duke of Savoy, as an Inducement, and Reward, to him for quitting the Common Cause; in direct Defiance and Violation of the Grand Alliance, and of the declared Sense of most of our good Allies, and especially the Dutch, who, to this Day, have never af-

lcnted to that Condition of the Treaty of Utrecht; a

7

shameful and dishonourable Treaty of Peace was at last concluded; by which, impracticable Terms of Trade were imposed on Great Britain; the Demolition of Dunkirk; which had been addressed for by Parliament, was eluded by a treacherous Connivance at the Making of a new Canal at Mardyke; and the Security which was proposed, by removing the Pretender out of Ftmice, was in the like manner evaded, by a treacherous Connivance at his residing in Lor rain.

It is owing to your Majesty’s unwearied Endeavours for the Good of your Subjects, and that just Regard which is paid to your Majesty by foreign Princes and States, that we fee ourselves delivered, in a great Degree, from the Effects of these pernicious Measures, which might other wise have proved fatal to your Kingdoms.

Vol. 18.

ceffes of a long and glorious War had put them into a Condition of gaining the most beneficial Terms from the Enemy.

Your faithful Commons did likewise exhibit several other Charges against the said Earl; representing him, in many notorious Instances, as a Person who had abused the Trust and Confidence which her late Majesty had reposed in him; and sacrificed the Honour of his Sovereign, and the Good of her People, to private Views of Intcrelt and Ambition.

Your faithful Commons have not been wanting in their Endeavours to bring the said Earl to Justice; but, by reason of the unhappy Differences that have, in this Proceeding, ariten between the Two Houses, we have fomld ourselves disappointed of our just; Expectation, and reduced to the Necessity either of giving up Rights and Privileges of the highest Importance to all the Commons of Great Britain, or seeing this great Offender escape with Impunity for the present.

For these Rcalbns, we do most humbly bGfeech your Majesty, That your Majesty will be pleased to except Robert Earl of O.ijord and Earl Mortimer out of the Act of Grace, which your Majesty has been graciously pleased to promise from the Throne; to the end the Commons may be at Liberty to proceed against the said Earl in a Parliamentary Wa v.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council do wait upon his Majesty, humbly to know his Pleasure when he will be attended by this House.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

It appeared by Cox’s Lease, That he is obliged to pay all Rates and Taxes. And,

William Raymond said, Cox is an Inhabitant, and a Housekeeper; and paid him the Poor Rate last Year.

Joseph Raymond laid, John Sprint is a Housekeeper, and an Inhabitant; has a House and Land worth Twelve Pounds a Year; was struck out of the Rate Three Years ago, contrary to his own Desire; and the Sub-bailiff has refuted him out of Antipathy. And,

It appeared to the Committee, That, in February last, he made a Purchase of Four Acres of Land at Milbourn Port, which colt him Fifty-three Pounds; and that he had several times defiled to be put into the Rate, but was refused, though his Land was formerly assessed, and paid the Rates.

William Raymond said, Richard Willmoth rents Land to the Value of Twenty Pounds a Year; which Land is rated, and lie pays the Rate.; though his Brother’s Name, of whom he rents the Land, is in the Book.

It was proved, on the Petitioner’s Part, and admitted on the other Side, That Mr. Medlycot is One of the capital Bailiffs; which capital Bailiffs are by Tenure in Right of their Estates; and that Mr. Medlycot purchased his capital Bailiwick, and has the Latids by which he claims to be such capital Bailiff.

John Wilkins said, William Chamberlain has a House

at Milbourn Port; Part of which he has lett, and other Part is reserved to himself: That he has Goods there, and is rated, and pays the Rates: And,

That Joshua Barret has a House there; and is rated, and pays the Rates.

MttGrandy said, George Baynton has Land of Inheritance at Milbourn Port, of Seven Pounds a Year, and is rated, and pays Scotland Lot, for it.

That William Chamberlain pays Scotland Lot at Mil-bourn Port; but has lett his House there to Two Tenants, and himself lives at Sherbourne:

That George Baynt on works Journey work at Milbourn Port, at weekly Wages; and never was upon the Poor Rate.

The Sitting Members Counsel objected, That Four of the Petitioner’s Voters; viz.Thomas Travell Esquire, Robert Everet, William A court, and George Man; who voted as capital Bailiffs; bad no Right to vote as such:

And called,

John Noalce: Who said, That neither of those Four Persons had any of the capital Bailiwick Lands; but that all those Lands are in Sir Thomas Travell, and Mr. Med-lycott; and that George Man is kept by Charity.

That the Sitting Member’s Counsel also called,

William Brook: Who said, Colonel Stanhope's Servant offered him Eight Guineas to vote for the Petitioner; but that he voted for the Sitting Member.

John Noake said, That Robert , who voted for the Sitting Member, told him, That Colonel Stanhope gave him Money to vote for the Petitioner; and he said, He would petition, if he had but Two Votes: And,

That Benjamin Co.xf, who voted for the Sitting Member, told him, He had Six Guineas to vote for the Petitioner.

Robert Baynton, who voted for the Sitting Member, said, He was offered Seven Guineas, by the Petitioner’s Brother, to vote for the Petitioner.

Henry HaUett laid, He was present when lett asked his Sen-in-Law, William Baynton, to vote for the Petitioner; and Baynton answering, That he had promised Mr. Harvey, and would be as good as his Word, Sumuel Hallett replied, That the Esquire would lay down a Hundred Gaineas upon the Table, and he should take what he would for his Vote: But Baynton voted for the Sitting Member.

That the Petitioner’s Qualification was objected to:

The Particular given in for such Qualification amounts to 346/. 13$. Ad. per Annum:

To which the Sitting Member’s Counsel objefited, That 21 61. 13$. A^. per Annum, at in

and a Rent-charge of 120 per Annum issuing out of Lands in Nottinghamshire, are mentioned to be purchased by the Petitioner for his Life, 31 ft of May last, for 2,5051.; which they took to be not a valable Consideration; and therefore suspected the Purchase: They also urged, That such a Rent-charge could be no Part of a Qualification, within the Meaning of the Act of Parliament, which requires a landed Interest; and that the Estate charged therewith might be subjefit to other Reprizes and Incumbrances:

And, as to the Wandsworth Estate, they called,

Samuel Welden, One of the Tenants thereof, at 12 a Year: By whole Evidence it appeared, That, since Mid-Jiimmer last, he had Notice to get ready his Midsummer Rent, because Mr. Brand had fold that Estate to the Petitioner; which Notice came from the Person to whom he had always paid his Rent for Mr. s Use.

In Answer to which, the Petitioner’s Counsel called,

Mr. Frewen, who lent that Notice: And he said, That Mr. Brand had acquainted him with his having fold that Estate at Wandsworth to the Petitioner; and that the Petitioner was to receive the Rents from Lady-day last; and that the Petitioner had desired him to continue to receive those Rents for him, as he bad before done for Mr. Brand; and that he had accordingly made of his Accounts, to Mr. Brand, to Lady-day.

The Petitioner's Counsel infilled, That the Purchase-money was a full and valuable Consideration; the Purchase being for Life only, and confining chiefly in old Houses; and that there could be no Objection to the Rent-charge.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Michael IJai-cey Esquire, is not duly elected a Bur-

gefs to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Milbourn Port, in the County of Somerset.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Charles Stanhope Esquire, is duly elefited a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of MUbourn Port.

The laid Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the Clerk of the Crown do attend this House upon Monday Morning, to amend the Return for the Borough of Milbourn Port, in the County of Somerset, by r&sing out the Name of Michael Harvey Esquire, and inserting the Name of Charles Stanhope Esquire, instead thereof.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Press 2. L. 24. Leave out from " Seventeen" to "and," in the 35 Line of the Third Press, and insert Clause marked A:

Clause A: " And be it further Enabled, by the Authority aforesaid, That no Action or Suit for any Penalty, or Forfeiture, contained in this or the said former Act, for wilfully neglecting, or refuting, to register, or for committing Fraud in such Registry, shall " be commenced or brought after Two Years after the Offence committed, against any Person offending therein, who shall, before the Commencement of such " Action or Suit, have duly registered, according to the Purport of this and the said former Act; which Re- giftry such Person is hereby authorized to make, notwithstanding the Time prescribed by the said Statutes, or " either of them, for making such Registry, be elapsed:

" And that every Person, offending in any of the Matters aforesaid, shall be liable to be feed, or prosecuted,

" for such Offence at any time before such Registry " made; this, or any other Law or Statute to the contrary, notwithstanding

Press 4. L. 6. Leave out from " Aft" to " and, " in the 28th Line of the same Press:

Press 5. L. 22'. Leave out the Word " openly

L. 25. After " Incapacity," insert " and have " entered such Claim, in open Court at the General Session of the Peace for the County, City, Riding, or " Division, wherein such Manors, Messuages, Lands,

" Tenements, or Hereditaments, lie, or arise

L. 29. Leave out from " notwithstanding" to the End of the Bill, and insert Clauses marked B and C: Clause B: " Provided nevertheless, That whereas it " was, amongst other things, enacted by the said Act of Voj,. 18.

" Parliament, made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years u of the Reign of the late Ring William the Third, That, " from and after the Tenth Dhy of April which should " be in the Year of our Lord One thouserid Seven hundred, every Papist, or Person making Profession of the " Popish Religion, should be difebled, and was thereby " made incapable, to purchase, either in his or her own " Name, or in the Name of any other Person or Persons " to his or her use, or in Trust for him or her, any Manors, " Lands, Profits out of Lands, Tenements, Rents, " Terms, or Hereditaments, within the Kingdom of " England, Dominion of Wales, and Town of Berwick " upon Tweed; and that all and Angular Estates, Terms,

" and any other Interests or Profits whatsoever, out of " Lands, from and after the said Tenth Day of April, to *( be made, suffered, or done, to or for the Use or Behoof of any such Person or Persons, or upon any Trull " or Confidence immediately, or immediately to or for " the Benefit or Relief of any such Person or Persons, " should be utterly void, and of no Effect, to all Intents, " Constructions, and Purposes, whatsoever; it is hereby " Declared and Enacted, That the said recited Part of the " said Act of Parliament shall not be hereby altered or " repealed; but the same shall be and remain in full " Force, as if this Act had never been made

Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy reported from the said Committee, That they had searched Precedents, and prepared Reasons to be offered to the Lords at the said Conference; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read, and agreed unto by the House; and are as follow, viz.

The Commons, having this Day received a Message from your Lordships, in these Words, "That the Lords " have accepted and passed a Bill, intituled, An Act " for the King’s most gracious, general, and free Pardon, Nemine contradicente.-, and have sent it down to Vol. 18.

" this House; " have desired this Conference to acquaint your Lordships, That this Message is not according to the usual Way of transmitting Bills between the Two Houses; for that neither House does acquaint the other by what Number any Bill before them doth pass; and the introducing any Alteration in the usual Method of Proceedings may be of dangerous Consequence.

Ordered, That a Conference be desired with the Lords Conference upon the Subject-matter of their Lordships Message to Wllh Lords, this House with the Bill, intituled, An Act for the King’s most gracious, general, and free, Pardon.

Ordered, That Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy do go to the Lords, and desire the said Conference.

Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy reported to the House,

That he had, according their Order, been at the Lords, and desired the said Conference, and that the Lords do agree to a Conference, and appoint the same immediately in the Painted Chamber.

Ordered, That the Committee, who were appointed to draw’ up Reasons to be offered at the said Conference, do manage the Conference.

And the Managers went to the Conference.

And, being returned;

A Message from the Lords, by Sir Thomas Gery, and Lords desire Mr. Bennett: a Conference

Mr. Speaker,

We are commanded by the Lords to acquaint this House, That the Lords desire a present Conference with this House in the Painted Chamber, upon the Subject-nntter of the last Conference.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Resolved, That the House doth agreed to meet the Lords at a present Conference.

And the Messengers w’ere called in again; and Mr.

Speaker acquainted them therewith.

Ordered, That the Managers who managed the last Conference do manage this Conference.

And the Managers went to the Conference.

And, being returned;

Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy reported, That the Managers appointed had met the Lords at the Conference; and that the same was managed, on the Part of the Lords, by the Lord Privy Seal; who acquainted the Managers,

That their Lordships, in order to preserve a good Correspondence with the House of Commons, which they shall always endeavour to do as far as lies in their Power, have desired this Conference upon the Subject-matter of the last Conference; and have commanded us to acquaint you,

That the Lords, upon Perusal of their Journal of the 20th of May 1690, do find, that the like Message was then sent down from the Lords to the Commons, upon the same Occasion, with the Words Nemine contradicente, to which the Commons now seem to object; and their Lordships do not find, that any Notice was then taken thereof by the Commons, nor at any other time; although the said Mel-sage was sent to the Commons on the said 20th Day of May, and the Bill was not returned till the 23d of the same Month, and the House of Lords continued fitting on the intermediate Days: And the Lords are of Opinion, that, the passing of Bills of this Nature differing so materially in many Circumstances from the Forms of passing other Bills, no Argument can be drawn from those Forms to support the Objection made by the Commons to the Mef-sage sent by the Lords with the Bill, intituled, An Act for the King’s most gracious, general, and free, Pardon.

Ordered, That the said Report be now taken into Consideration.

The said Report was read.

Ordered, That the Committee who managed the last Conference do search Precedents, and prepare Reasons to be offered to the Lords at a Conference, upon the Subject-matter of the last Conference: And they are to withdraw immediately into the Speaker’s Chamber; and make their Report with all convenient Speed.

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS our Parliament {lands prorogued to the Ninth Day of this instant October: We, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Ninth Day of this Instant,

toThurfday the One-and-twentieth Day of November next: And we have given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same accordingly: And we do hereby further declare our Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said One-

and-twentieth Day of November, be held, and fit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty, and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal; and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners of Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons; are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance accordingly, at Westminster, on the said One-and-twentieth Day of November next.

Given at our Court at Hampton Court, the Eighth Day of October 1717, in the Fourth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the King.
