AM E S S A G E from his Majesty, by Sir William Oldes, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And, being returned;

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Law s made for that Purpose.-

Then a Bill for the more effectual preventing, and punching, the" Stealing, or unlawful Killing, of Cattle, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty was pleased to declare, That he had commanded the Lord Chancellor to declare the Causes of his Majesty’s meeting his People in Parliament at this time, as they were contained in a Speech which his Majesty delivered into the Lord Chancellor’s hands from the Throne;

And his Lordship read the same to both Houses; of which Mr. Speaker laid he had, to prevent any Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as folio, weth j

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I AM very glad I have been able to bring the Sitting of Parliament into a more proper and usual Season of the Year: I hope such an early Meeting will not only be a Benefit to the Publick, but a Convenience to your private Affairs.

As I have always had at Heart the Security and ease of my People, so I never kept up any Troops but for their Protection; and (have taken every Opportunity to disband as many as I thought consistent with their Safety: I have reduced the Army to very near One-half finee the Beginning of the last Session of Parliament; and lessened them to such a Number as will neither be a Burthen to my good Subjects, nor an Encouragement to our Enemies to insult them.

You cannot but be sensible of the many Attempts which have been set on foot to disturb the Peace of Europe, and of these Kingdoms: They only pretend not to fee, who are not afraid of them: But as no Application has been wanting on my Part to preserve the publick Tranquillity, I have the Pleasure to find my good Offices have not been altogether unsuccessful; and have Reason to hope they will, in 'the End, have their full and desired Effect. Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I question not but you are very well pleased to find, that your Endeavours for lessening the National Debts have, at the same time, raised the publick Credit; and that Vol. 18.

whatever was proposed for that End is actually and completely effected: This Succeis must chiefly be attributed to that just and prudent Regard you have shewn to Parliamentary Engagements.

It was with the View of procuring and settling a lasting Tranquillity, that I demanded the extraordinary Supply which you granted me last Session: The Credit which this Confidence reposed in me hath given us abroad, has already been so far effectual, that I can acquaint you, we have a much better Prospect than we had: I have ordered an Account to be laid before you of the very small Part of that Supply, which, as yet, has been expended: Any further Issues that may be made of it shall be also laid before you; and you may be assured, that every Part of it shall either be employed for your Service, or saved to the Publick.

I have ordered to be laid before you a State of the Deficiencies of the present Year, and the fevfcral Estimates for the Service of the next; which you will find considerably diminished: I rely upon your making the necessary Provision for them; not doubting of the Continuance of that Zeal for the Good of your Country, which hath been so eminently conspicuous in every Session of this Parliament. /

I cannot in Justice avoid putting you in mind, that several Arrears of Pay and Subsidy, incurred before my Accession to the Crown, are claimed by foreign Princes and States: I shall order them to be laid before you, to the End you may put them in a Method to be examined, and stated; which will very much tend to the Honour and Credit of the Nation.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I could heartily with, that, at a time when the common Enemies of our Religion are, by all manner of Artifices, endeavouring to undermine and weaken it both at home and abroad, all those who are Friends to our present happy Establishment might unanimously concur in feme proper Methods for the greater strengthening the Protestant Interest; of which as the Church of England is unquestionably the main Support and Bulwark, so will {he reap the principal Benefit of every Advantage accruing by the Union, and mutual Charity, of all Protestants.

As none can recommend themselves more effectually to my Favour and Countenance than by a sincere Zeal for the jult Rights of the Crown, and the Liberties of the People; so I am determined to encourage all those who act agreeably to the Constitution of these my Kingdoms; and consequently, to the Principles on which my Government is founded.

The eyes of all Europe are upon you at this critical Juncture: It is your Interest, for which Reaibn I think it mine, that my Endeavours for procuring the Peace and Quiet of Christendom should take Effect: Nothing can so much contribute-to this desirable End as the Unanimity,

Dispatch, and Vigour, of your Resolutions for the Support of my Government.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Ad- Address or dress be presented to his Majesty, returning the humble King's Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from sPeech*

Humfreys: And they are to meet upon Wednesd next, at Five of the Clock in the Afternoon, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and to fit every Friday, Monday, and Wednesday, in the Afternoon: And all that come are to have Voices: And they are to take into Consideration all such Alatters as shall or may come in question touching Returns, Elections, and Privileges; and to proceed upon Double Returns, in the First Place; and to report their Proceedings, with their Opinion therein, to the House, from time to time: And all Persons that will question Returns are to do it in Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in: And the Committee are to have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records, for their Information: And all Members who are returned for Two or more Places are to make their Election by this Day Three Weeks for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place: And if any thing shall come in question touching the Return, Election, or Alatter of Privilege, of any Alember, he is to withdraw during the time the Matter is in Debate: And that all Members returned upon Double Returns to withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Alember to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Perl’on petitioned against.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned as a Alember of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, That any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in rdpect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Alifdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given , false Evidence, in any Case, before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain for any Lord of Parliament, or anyj-ord Lieutenant of any . County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House; and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him;' and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day before the Door is locked up.

I’fual Order*. _ Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning to Four in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar and be

kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Resolved, That, notwithstanding the Oath taken by any Candidate at, or after, any Election, his Qualification may afterwards be examined into.

Resolved, That the Person whose Qualification is expressly objected to in any Petition relating to his Election shall, within Fifteen Days after the Petition read,.give to the Clerk of the House of Commons a Paper, signed by himself, containing a Rental, or Particular, of the Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, whereby he makes out his Qualification; of which any Person concerned may have a Copy.

Resolved, That of such Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, whereof the Party hath not been in Possession for Three Years before the EleCHon, he shall also insert in the same Paper from what Person, and by what Conveyance or Act in Law, he claims and derives the same; and also the Corisideration, if any, paid; and the Names, and Elaces of Abode, of the Witnesses to such Conveyance and Payment.

Resolved, That, if any Sitting Member shall think fit to question the Qualification of a Petitioner, he shall, within Fifteen Days after the Petition read, leave Notice thereof, in Writing, with the Clerk of the House of Commons; and the Petitioner shall, in such case, within Fifteen Days after such Notice, leave with the said Clerk of the House the like Account, in Writing, of his Qualification, as is required from a Sitting Member.

Resolved, That the Four last of the said Refutations be

declared to be Standing Orders of the House.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, crave Leave to express our Gratitude to your Majesty for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Our Minds are filled with the most lively Sense of your Majesty’s Regard to your People, in bringing the Sitting of Parliament into a more proper and usual Season of the Year; and, as your Majesty has been graciously pleased to consider the Convenience of our private Affairs in this early Meeting, we shall endeavour to answer your Majesty’s gracious Intentions, by improving it, as much as we are able, to the Benefit of the Publicfo

We are highly sensible of the Concern your Majesty has shewn for the Welfare of your People, by the Reductions you have been pleased to make, from time to time, of the Land Forces, so loon as the Posture of Affairs rendered it safe to these your Kingdoms: It is our peculiar Happiness to fee ourtelves governed by a Sovereign who is not influenced by any Notions of Greatness that are incon-fillent with the Prosperity of his Subjefits; and who proposes to himself the Ease of his People, as the chief Glory of his Reign.

We acknowledge, with Hearts full of Duty and Gratitude, your Majesty’s unwearied Endeavours to prevent the many Attempts which have been set on foot to disturb the Peace of Europe, and the Quiet of these Kingdoms; and have the more Reason to apprehend the ill Consequences of such Attempts, since there are those, who, as they would be thought to fee no Dauger in them, give us llcafon to believe, that they would not be troubled at their Success: We are therefore firmly resolved, in the most effectual manner, to support your Majesty in such Mea-hires as your Majesty, in your great Wisdom, shall judge necessary to procure the Establishment of the Tranquillity of Europe.

We receive with the greatest Satisfaction your Majesty’s gracious Expressions and Assurances, touching, the extraordinary Supply granted last Year; and will chearfully

Debtor* - A PETITION of the insolvent Debtors in Hereford Petition. County Gaol, in behalf of themselves, and many

Thousands more in tike respective Gaols in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That, by reason of those numerous and heavy Taxes occasioned by the late War, and other Misfortunes, the Petitioners are reduced, and brought under Confinement; whereby they suffer under unspeakable Calamities and Miseries, through which they are subject to daily Wants, and not in a Capacity to make Satisfaction to their Creditors: That this House, in their Three last Sessions, was pleased to demonstrate a compassionate Intention towards the Relief of the distressed Petitioners, by ordering a Bill to be brought

in for that Purpose; which, though read twice, proved abortive, by reason of the more weighty Affairs of the Publick: That his Majesty hath also been pleased to grant an Act of Pardon to his rebellious Subjects, and set them at Liberty; and also, since, upon a Petition lately presented to his Majesty by the Petitioners Fellow-sufferers in the King's Bench Prison, was graciously pleased to commi-ferate the deplorable Condition of such Objects, by giving his Royal Word and Promise to the said Petitioners, alluring them, that his Majesty would recommend their same to the House: And praying such Relief as to the House, in their great Wisdom, shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And then the Commissioners withdrew.

And the Titles of the said Accounts were read; viz.

An Account of the prohibited East India Goods remaining in the Warehouses at Leaden-hall at Michaelmas One tlioufend Seven hundred Sixteen; what brought in since that time, what exported, aS also what remained at Michaelmas One thousand Seven hundred Seventeen: And also,

An Account of the prohibited East India Goods remaining in the respective Warehouses of the Out-ports at Michaelmas One thousand Seven hundred Sixteen; what brought in since that time; what exported; as also, what remained at Michaelmas One thousand Seven hundred Seventeen; And also,

An Account of Naval Stores imported from Russia into the Port of London from Michaelmas One thousand Seven hundred Sixteen to Michaelmas One thoulaud Seven hundred Seventeen: And also,

An Account of the Naval Stores imported from Russia into the Ports commonly called the Out-ports from Michaelmas One thousand Seven hundred Sixteen to Michaelmas One thousand Seven hundred Seventeen.

Cock*rmouth A Petition of the Lord Percy Seymour was presented to JLUdion. the House, and read; setting forth, That a Writ, upon the Vacancy of Nicolas Esquire, for the Borough

of Cocliermouth, in the County of Cumberland, was duly VOL.T8.

issued: That such Writ was not lent by a proper Messenger; but, by indirect Means, concealed, and unduly delayed, for several Days before it w as delivered to the Sheriff of the said County; yet the Petitioner was fairly and duly -elected by a Majority of legal and undoubted Votes; and w'as returned; notwithstanding which, Sir Wilfred Lawson Baronet, a Minor, under the Age of Twenty-

one Years, and (incapable of being elected, or returned, did, by many indirect Practices, procure several Persons to vote for him; and did likewise prevail with the Bailiff, contrary to Law, and the Statute in that behalf made, to return the said Sir Wilfred Laws by another Indenture,

as duly elected by a Majority; the said Bailiff refuting to' allow the Petitioner a Scrutiny, though several times demanded: And praying to be relieved.

very kindly.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Cockemoouth A Petition of Sir Wilf red Larofon Baronet, was pre-ElelHon. fented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, at the late Election of a Burgefe for the Borough of Cockermouth, in the County of Cumberland, the Petitioner, and the Lord Peircy Seymour, stood Candidates: That the Petitioner had an undoubted Majority of legal Votes, who voted for the Petitioner; and were allowed by Thomas France, Bailiff of the said Borough; notwithstanding which, and although the said Lord Peircy Seymour, by himself, his Agents and Servants, was guilty of notorious Bribery, and undue Practices, in the said Election; yet the said Bailiff thought fit to make a Double Return of the Petitioner, and the Lord Peircy Seymour, for the said borough; to the manifest Injury of the Petitioner: And praying Relief therein.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be also heard, at the Bar of this House, upon Thursday the Sixteenth Day of January next.

The Order of the Day being read;

Supply. Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

AP ETIT IO N of Thomas Gage and Samuel Edwin Esquires was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That at the last Election of Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Minehead, in the County of Somerset, the Petitioners, and Sir John Trevelyan, and James Milner Esquire, stood Candidates: That, at the said Election, John Jones and George James pretended to act as Constables of the said Borough; and, as such, preside at the said Elen ion as the Returning Officers; which they had no Right to do; and their Actings and Doings were contrary to, and in Violation of, the ancient Rights and Usage of the said Borough: That notwithstanding the Petitioners had a Majority of legal Votes, yet the said Sir John Trevelyan, and Mr. , although

not qualified within the late Act, made in the Ninth Year of the late Queen Anne, for securing the Freedom of Parliament, by the farther qualifying of Members to lit in the House of Commons; by Bribery, and other indirect Practices, having procured the Votes of several of the Burgesses, got themselves to be returned; in Wrong of the Petitioners: And praying Relief therein.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Ten thousand Men be allowed for Sea-Service for the Year One thousand Seven hundred Eighteen; beginning from the First Day of January One thousand Seven hundred Seventeen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Month, be allowed for maintaining the Ten thousand Men for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred twenty-four thousand Eight hundred Fifty-leven Pounds Fourteen Shillings Eleven Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Vou Hfe

Ordinary of the Navy for the Year One thousand Seven hundred Eighteen, including Half-pay.

A Petition of Edward Harley Esquire, commonly called Lord Harley, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was a Candidate at the last Election for a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Bishop's Castle, in the County of Salop; had a Majority of legal Votes; but that Charles Mason and Richard Harneage Esquires did, by themselves, and their

Agents, John Homes, of HiJJington, Witting-

ham, Edmund Morris, John Jones, Moris Pugh, Richard Colehach, and Humphry Thomas, by Bribes, and other indirect and illegal Practices, procure themselves to be returned: That the said Charles Mason was not qualified, at the time of the Election, as the Law requires, to be elected a Member; his Estate, at the time of his Election, being under Extent to the Crown, and liable to . other great Incumbrances: And praying such Relief as to the House shall seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter of the said Petition; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of the said Edward Harley Esquire, commonly called Lord Harley, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was a Candidate at the last Election for a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of New Radnor, and the other Boroughs in that County: That a great Majority of the legal Voters appeared, and tendered their Votes for the Petitioner; but Mr., Samuel Burton, Bailiff of the said Borough, refused to admit them, and returned Thomas I^ervis Esquire, junior; who is not qualified, as the Law requires, to serve for a Borough; and that the said Mr. Burton, Thomas Lewis senior, Esquire, and William James, of Ccven Keecc, have pretended to make feme Hundreds of illegal Burgesses, and polled them for Mr. Letvis, contrary to the known Practice and Usage of the said Borough; declaring, at the time of making the said Burgesses, it was to exclude the Petitioner: That the said Bailiff did not give Four Days Notice of the Election, as the Law requires: That Mr. Burton, Thomas Lewis senior, Esquire, Mfr.

berlenn, Deputy Sheriff, and One of the Coroners of the said County, and others their Agents, by Menaces, Bribes, and Threats, have endeavoured to influence the Electors to give their Votes against the Petitioner: And praying such Relief as to the House shall seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter of the said Petition; and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of Phillip Freke and Thomas Edwards junior, Esquires, was presented to the House, and read j setting forth, That the Right of Election of Members of Parliament for the City of Bristol is veiled-in the Freemen and Freeholders of the same City: That the Petitioners, together with Sir William Dairies, and Joseph Esquire, were Candidates at the last Election there: That the Petitioners were duly chosen by a great Majority, which the Sheriffs did declare on calling up the Poll Books: That, after the said Election, an Indenture, importing that the Petitioners were duly elected, was, by Mr. Taylor, One of the Sheriffs, fattened and sealed to the Writ for the Electing of Members there; notwithstanding all which, the -laid Sheriffs have, unduly and maliciouffy, returned the said Sir William Daines, and Joseph Earle j the Indenture before-mentioned having, by undue Practice, been fevered from the said Writ: And praying such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter of the said Petition; and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors now in the common Gaol for the County of Hertford, on behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of their differing Brethren in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by Loffe; and Misfortunes incident to Mankind, are brought under Confinement; and, having no Allowance from the Gaol, rely only on the Charity of well-disposed Christians: And praying such Relief in the Premises as to the House, in their great Wisdom, shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several poor insolvent Debtors, Prisoners in Nonvich Castle, in the Name of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by reason of their long Confinement, and having neither Friends, nor other Support, but the County Allowance, are utterly ruined by the Law executed on them: And praying such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

and the same were entered at the Custom-house by themselves, or Agents; and Securities given for the Payment of the Customs and Dudes of the lame, as usual; which were afterwards duly paid as they were required, according to the constant and ancient Method used and pra&iled for that Purpose: That all Persons concerned in the said separate Trade fold the said Goods at the Candle; To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury.

May it please your Lordships,

IN Obedience to your Lordships Order of Reference of August 12th, that I should lay before your Lordships a State of the Gold and Stiver Coin9 of this Kingdom in Weight and Finenefe, and the Value of Gold in proportion to Silver, with my Observations and Opinion; and what Method may be best for preventing the Melting down of the Silver Coin; I humbly represent, That a Pound Weight Troy of Gold, Eleven Ounces fine, and One Ounce Allay, is cut into44L Guineas; and a Pound Weight of Silver, Eleven Ounces Two Peny Weight fine, and Eighteen Peny Weight Allay, is cut into 62 Shillings; and according to this Rate, a Pound Weight of fine Gold is worth Fifteen Pounds Weight Six Ounces Seventeen Peny Weight and Five Grains of fine Silver, reckoning a Guinea at 1/. is. 6d. in Silver-money; but Silver in Bullion, exportable, is usually worth 2 or 3d. per Ounce more than in Coin; and if, at a Medium, such Bullion of Standard-allay, lie valued at 5*. 4id. per Ounce, a Pound Weight of fine Gold will be worth but 14 lb.wt. 11 oz. 12 diet. 9 gr. of fine Silver in Bullion;

and, at this Rate, a Guinea is worth but so much Silver as would make 20j. 8r/. When Ships are lading for the East Indies, the Demand of Silver for Exportation railes the Price to 5 s.6d. or 5 s.8 per Ounce, or above; but I consider not tliofc extraordinary Cafes.

A Spanish Pistole was coined for 32 Rials, or Four Pieces of Eight Rials, usually called Pieces'of Eight, and is of equal Allay, and the Sixteenth-part of the Weight thereof; and a Doppio Moeda of Portugal was coined for Ten Crufados. of Silver, and is of equal Allay, and the Sixteenth part of the Weight thereof: Gold is therefore in Spain and Portugal of Sixteen times more value than

Silver of equal Weight and Allay, according to the Standard of those Kingdoms; at which Rate, a Guinea is worth 22 s.id.: But this high Price keeps their Gold at home in good Plenty, and carries away the Spanish Silver into all Europe', so that at home they make their Payments in Gold, and will not pay in Silver without a Premium: Upon the Coining in of a Plate Fleet the Premium ceases, or is but finall; but as their Silver goes away, and becomes scarce, the Premium increases, and is most commonly about Six per Cent.', which being abated, a Guinea becomes worth about 10s. §d. in Spain and Portugal.

In France, a Pound Weight of fine Gold is reckoned worth Fifteen Pounds Weight of fine Silver: In raising or falling the ir'Money, their King’s Edicts have sometimes varied a little from this Proportion in Excefe, or Defect; but the Variations have been lb little, that I do not here consider them: By the Exlift of May 1709, a new Pistole was coined for Four new Lewifies, and is of equal Allay, and the Fifteenth-part of the Weight thereof, except the Errors of their Mints: and, by the same Edict, fine Gold is valued at Fifteen times its Weight of fine Silver; and, at this Rate, a Guinea is worth <los. 8 I consider not here the Confusion made in the Monies in France by frequent Edicts to fend them to the Mint, and give the King a Tax out of them; I consider only the Value of Gold and Silver in proportion to one another.

The Ducats of Holland and Hungary, and the Em-

?ire, were lately current in Holland among the common 'eople, in their Markets, and ordinary Affairs, at Five Guilders in Specie, and Five Stivers; and commonly changed for so much Silver-monies in Three Guilder-pieces and Guilder-pieces, as Guineas are with us lor 21 6d.

Sterling; at which Rate, a Guinea is worth 20 7 According to the Rates of Gold to Silver in Italy, many, Poland, Denmark, and Sweden, a Guinea is worth

about

4 Geo. I. 210 Decembris. 5

about 20 s.and yd. 6d. 5d. or 4; for the Proportion

varies a little within the several Governments in those Countries: In Sweden, Gold is lowest in proportion to Silver; and this hath made that Kingdom, which formerly was content with Copper Money, abound of late with Silver, sent thither, I suspect, for Naval Stores.

In the End of King William’s Reign, and the First Year of the late Queen, when foreign Coins abounded in England, I caused a great many of them to be allayed in the Mint; and found by the Allays, that fine Gold was to fine Silver in Spain, Portugal, France, Holland, Italy, Germany, and the Northern Kingdoms, in the Proportions above-mentioned; Errors of the Mints excepted.

In China and Japan, One Pound Weight of fine Gold is worth but Nine or Ten Pounds Weight of fine Silver; and in East India it may be worth Twelve; and this low Price of Gold in proportion to Silver carries away the Silver from all Europe.

So then, by the Course of Trade and Exchange between Nation and Nation in all Europe, fine Gold is to fine Silver as 14$, or 15, to One; and a Guinea at the same Rate, is worth between 20 s.5 and 2or. except

in extraordinary Cafes, as when a Plate Fleet is just arrived in Spain, or Ships are lading here for the East Indies; which Cafes I do not here consider: And it appears by Experience, as well as by Reason, that Silver flows from those Places where its Value is lowest in proportion to Gold, as from Spain to all Europe, and from all Europe to the East Indies, China, and Japan; and that Gold is most plentiful in those Places in which its Value is highest in proportion to Silver, as in Spain and England.

It is the Demand for Exportation which hath raised the Price of exportable Silver about 2d. or 3c?. in the Ounce above that of Silver in Coin; and hath thereby created a Temptation to export, or melt down, the Silver Coin, rather than give 2d. or 3 d.more for foreign Silver; and the Demand for Exportation ariles from the higher Price of Silver in other Places than in England in proportion to Gold; that is, from the higher Price of Gold in England than in other Places in proportion to Silver; and therefore may be diminiffied, by lowering the Value of Gold in proportion to Silver: If Gold in England, or Silver in East India, could be brought down so low as to bear the same Proportion to one another in both Places, there would be here no greater Demand for Silver, than for Gold to be exported to India; and if Gold were lowered only so as to have the same Proportion to the Silver-money in England which it hath to Silver in the rest of Europe, there would be no Temptation to export Silver rather than Gold to any other Part of Europe: And to compass this last, there seems nothing more requisite than to take off about 10 d.or 12 from the Guinea; so that Gold may bear the same Proportion to the Silver Money in England, which it ought to do by the Course of Trade and Exchange in Europe; but if only 6d. were taken off at present, it would diminish the Temptation to export, or melt down, the Silver Coin; and, by the Effects, would thew hereafter, better than can. appear at present, what further Reduction would be most convenient for the Publick.

In the last Year of King William, the Dollars of Scotland, worth about 4?. 6%d. were put away in the North of England for 5s. and at this Price began to flow in upon us: I gave notice thereof to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury; and they ordered the Collectors of Taxes to forbear taking the m; and thereby put a Stop to the Mischief.

At the same time, the Lewidors of France, which were worth but Seventeen Shillings and Three Farthings apiece, passed in England at 17 s.6d.: I gave notice thereof to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury; and his late Majesty put out a Proclamation, That they should go but at 17s.; and thereupon they came to the Mint; and 1,400,000l. were coined out of them: And if the Advantage of s,\d. in a Lewidor sufficed at that time to bring into England so great a Quantity of French Money,

and the Advantage of Three Farthings in a Lewidor to Vol. 18.

bring it to the Mint, the Advantage of gid. in a Guinea, Gold and or above, may have been sufficient to bring in the great Silv*r Coin*. Quantity of Gold which hath been coined in these last Fifteen Years, without any foreign Silver.

Some Years ago, the Portugal Moedors were received in the West of England at 285. apiece: Upon Notice from the Mint that they were worth only about 27 yd. the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury ordered their Receivers of Taxes to take them at no more than 27 6d.:

Afterwards, many Gentlemen in the West sent up to the Treasury a Petition, that the Receivers might take them again at 28s. and promised to get Returns for this Money at that Rate; alleging, that w’hen they went at 285. their Country was foil of Gold, which they wanted very much: But the Commissioners of the Treasury, considering, that at 28 s.the Nation would lose 5 apiece, rejected the Petition: And if an Advantage to the Merchant of 5 d. in 28^. did pour that Money in upon us, much more hath an Advantage to the Merchant of 9 in a Guinea, or above, been able to bring into the Mint great Quantities of Gold, without any foreign Silver; and may be able to do it {till, till the Cause be removed.

If Things be let alone till Silver Money be a little scarcer, the Gold will fall of itself; for People are already backward to give Silver for Gold, and will, in a little time, refuse to make Payments in Silver without a Premium, as they do in Spain; and this Premium w ill be an Abatement in the Value of the Gold; and so the Question is, Whether Gold shall be lowered by the Government, or let alone till it falls of itself, by the Want of Silver Money.

It may be said, that there are great Quantities of Silver in Plate; and if the Plate were coined, there would be no Want of Silver Money: But I reckon, that Silver is safer from Exportation in the Form of Plate than in the Form of Money, because of the greater Value of the Silver and Fashion together; and therefore I am not for coining the Plate, till the Temptation to export the Silver Money, which is a Profit of 2d. or 3 an Ounce, be diminiffied, for as often as Men are necessitated to fond away Money for answering Debts abroad, there will be a Temptation to fend away Silver rather than Gold, because of the Profit, which is almost Four per Cent.; and, for the same Reason, Foreigners will choose to fend hither their Gold rather than their Silver.

Wisdom.

Isaac Newton.

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury.

May it please your Lordships,

IN Obedience to your Lordships Order of Reference of the 19th Instant, That an Account be laid before your Lordships of all the Gold and Silver coined in the last Fifteen Years; and how much thereof hath been coined out of Plate upon publick Encouragements; and what Copper Money hath been newly coined; it is humbly represented, that since Christmas 170^ to the loth Instant, there hath been coined in Gold 7,127,835 Pounds in Tale, reckoning 44i Guineas to a Pound WeightTroy, and 2li. 6d. to a Guinea; and in Silver 223,380 Pounds Sterling, reckoning 31. 2 to a Pound Weight Troy; and that Part of this Silver, amounting to 143,086 Pounds Sterling, was coined out of English Plate, imported upon publick Encouragement in the Years 1709 and 1711; and another Part, amounting to 13,342/. was coined out of Vigo Plate in the Year 1703 and 1704; and another Part, amounting to 45,732/. w'as coined from Silver extracted from our own Lead-ore; and the rest, amounting to 21,220/. was coined chiefly out of old Plate melted down by Goldsmiths; and some of it out of Pieces of Eight.

The Graver of the Mint hath been hard at Work, ever since the last Session of Parliament, in making the EnibolT-ments and Puncheons for the Halfpence and Farthings,

Mr. Lowndes, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolution, which they had directed to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, which, by former Acts of Parliament, have Continuance to the Twenty-fourth Day of June 1718, be further continued, and charged upon all Malt which shall be made, and all Mum which shall be made, or imported, and all Cyder and Perry which shall be made for Sale within the Kingdom of Great Britain, from the Twenty-third Day of June 17*8, to the Twenty-fourth Day of June 1719.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That, towards the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, which, by former Acts of Parliament, have Continuance to the Twenty-fourth Day of June 1718, be further continued, and charged upon all Malt which shall be made, and all Mum which shall be made, or imported, and all Cyder and Perry which shall be made for Sale, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, from the Twenty-third Day of June 1718, to the Twenty-fourth Day of June 1719.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders in the City of Bristol was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, from this and divers other Ports, great Quantities of Cyder are yearly exported, and the Produce thereof returned in such Merchandizes as pay considerable Duty; and greatly encourage the Navigation of this Kingdom: That there is a Duty of Six Shillings and Eight Pence per Hogshead, by former Laws to be paid by the Retailer; and, for feme Years past, a further Duty of Four Shillings per Hogshead on all made for Sale within Vol. 18.

Great Britain, to be paid by the First Buyer, or Retailer

thereof: That the Petitioners apprehended, by the said Laws, it was not intended the Exporters should be chargeable with any Duty; but, of late, several Prosecutions have been brought against divers Persons, in the Name of the Attorney General, for the said Duties; although the Cyder was actually exported; which if it had been entered, and the said Duties paid, the Persons exporting ought to have a Debenture, or Drawback, for the whole Duty; but are refused any Debenture for the Duty of Four Shillings per Hogshead; the not Allowing of which is* great Discouragement to Trade in general: And praying to be relieved, by taking off the Discouragements to Exportation.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for continuing the Duties on Malt, Mum,

Mr. Cadogan reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the High Sheriff, Justices of Peace, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the County of Berks; and of the several Coachmen, Waggoners, and other subscribing Persons, tiling and travelling the Roads between Maidenhead, and the Towns of Reading and , in the County of Oxon; was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 20th of December last, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find, upon the Examination of several Witnesses, That the said Roads are very bad, and, in many Places, are impassable in the Winter feafbn; and that, by the Badneis and Narrownels thereof, great Mischiefs have happened:

That the Parishes, in which the said Roads lie, have been indicted, on account of the Badness of the said Roads; but the Justices, upon Examination of the Mutter, finding the Inhabitants had done their Duty, thought fit to discharge the said Indictments: And it appeared also to the Committee, that the said Parishes have constantly done their Statute-work; and feme Inhabitants much more than they were obliged to do; notwithstanding which, by reason of the many heavy Carriages that pass and repals through the said Roads, many Parts of which lying very low, and Materials lying at a great Distance from feme of the said Parishes, the said Roads are so bad and ruinous during the Winter-season especially, that they cannot, by the Laws now in Force, be effectually amended by the said Parishes.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for re-pairing the Highways from Maidenhead Bridge to lane End, in the Road to Reading, in the County of Berks; and from the said Bridge to Henley upon , in the County of Oxon: Ann that Mr. Cadogan and Mr. Neville, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That this honourable House, in their Two last Sessions, was pleased to demonstrate a compassionate Intention towards the Relief of the distressed Petitioners, by ordering a Bill to be brought in for that Purpose; which, though twice read, proved abortive, by reason, as it is presumed, of the more weighty Affairs of the Publick: That his Majesty hath been graciously pleased, from the Throne, to manifest and declare. In this Manner has the Trade to the East Indies been carried on for Twelve Years pad.

But, upon further looking back, and comparing the Exports of the Bullion in these Twelve Years with the Exports of the Bullion in Five Years from Christmas 1698 to Christmas 1703, it is very observable, that the Old and New Companies, before and after their Union, exported Gold and Silver, in the said Five Years, for East India, to the Value of

£'3,159,607 12 6 from London:

And - 193,189 14 — from Cadiz:

In all 3,352,797 6 6

That is, communibus annis, £.634,733. 7 11 which

was left than was in those Years exported in Bullion by the Companies.

When the Custom-house Books are brought up, we shall take the Liberty to lay before your Majesty an Account of our Home-consumption; and shall then be better able to judge, how they interfere with our own Manufactures.

We mult further add, that we find, in our Office, a Representation made to his late Majesty King by the Levant Company; wherein they set forth, That they lol'e the Vent of 9,000 Cloths per , in Turky for

Persia, by the East India Company being obliged, by their Charter, to export £.100,000 per Annum in English Manufactures and Products for , which are chiefly sent to Persia, and consumed there.

Upon this, as the Trade to Turky has ever since lain under the same Difficulty, we shall only state the Account thereof; and submit the Whole to your Majesty’s Consideration.

Of these, the Two last Articles, amounting to 35,778! Cloths, are the Exports which the Levant Company assert are prejudicial to their Trade; the Medium whereof, for One Year, is Cloths 2,981!.

They compute, that about One-half Part of the Cloth sent to Surat jmay. proceed to Persia; but admitting the Whole to be carried thither, and that their Allegation is true, the Nation loses the Export of 6,018! Cloths per Atmum; which, at a Time when that particular Manufacture lies under the greatest Discouragement, the Exportation thereof being decreased, since the Year 1712, at least One-fourth Part, seems to require an effectual Redress.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of this House, of the 21st instaut, have taken the said Petition into their Consideration; and do tind the Matter of Fact to be as follows; viz.

That, by the Examination of Richard Marriot, and others, the Manufacture of English Bone-lace, hath, by the Industry of the Petitioners, and others, been greatly improved of late Years; whereby many thousands of poor Persons have been, and are, employed; and those of very tender years are enabled to get their Livings:

'lhat some of the Petitioners have been put to great Expences, and hindered from carrying on their Trades, and others are daily threatened to be disturbed therein, by several Persons, who have, of late, taken upon themselves to prosecute and inform against them before some of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace, on the Pretence; that they ought to have Licences, according to an Act of the 9th and i oth King William the Third, for licensing Hawkers and Pedlars.

That it appears, upon reading the said Act, That the said Petitioners are not within the Meaning of the same, or liable to any the Penalties thereby to be inflicted; and ought not to be deemed Hawkers and Pedlars:

Which is farther made evident by a Resolution of this House, upon a Report, made the Sixth of 1699, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Edward and others, Bone-lace-makers, was referred; viz. That the Workers of Bone-lace, his, her, or their, Children, Apprentices, Servants, or Agents, and all Wholesale Dealers in the said Manufacture, though they go from Shop to Shop to any their Customers who fell the same «tgain by Retail, shall not be deemed Hawkers and Pedlars by the Act made in the 9th and 10th King the Third.

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and St.Micharfi Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Michael,

London, was presented to the House, and read; setting urc forth, That, by an Order made in the Year 1704, by the then Archbishop of Canterbury, Bishop of London, and Lord Mayor of London, the Tower of the said Church was appointed to be rebuilt out of the Monies arising by die Duty on Coals, appropriated for building of Parochial Churches by several Statutes; but the said Petitioners could not get the said Order complied with: That by another Order, in 1715, the said Tower, being dangerous to the Neighbourhood, was taken down; and is rebuilt about Twenty Foot high; but the Monies arising on the said Duty on Coals was so far expended in the other great Incumbrances on the said Duty, that there was not Money sufficient to go on with, and finish, the said Tower:

That in regard the said Tower hath been, in part, rebuilt by the Monies arising out of the Fund given for that Purpose, and was intended to have been fiiiished thereby, and ought so to be, before the same Duty be applied to other new Uses; and for that the Work is not carried up aboye half way to the Roof of the Church; and will cost Six thousand Pounds to finish it: And praying.

That Provision may be made for the finishing the said Tower by the Duty granted by the Statute, of the 9th of the late Queen, for Building of Fifty new Churches.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Grand Jury, and other Gentlemen and Freeholders, in the County of Gloucester, assembled at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace held for the said County; the Fourteenth Day of January 1717; and also of the Grand Jury of the City of Gloucester, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace held for the said City, the Seventeenth of January 1717: was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, several Years past, great Quantities of Cyder and Perry have been made and brought into this and other Counties for Exportation into foreign Parts; to the great Advantage of the Petitioners j who have been thereby encouraged to increase their Plantations of those Fruits: That the Exportation thereof is of great Advantage to the Nation, by improving the Trade and Navigation, and Increase of his Majesty’s Revenues; but hath been greatly discouraged by several Prosecutions lately commenced in the Court of Exchequer for a Duty of Four Shillings per Hogshead against the Exporters thereof: That the Discouragement to the Exportation of Cyder and Perry will be a great Prejudice and Loss to the Petitioners, by lessening the Value of their Estates, and the Revenues of his Majesty: And praying such Relief as to the Floufe shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for continuing the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, for the Service of the Year 1718, is committed.

A Petition and Representation of the Mayor, Jurats, Dov*r and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Port of Do- N«r. ver, for repairing the said Harbour, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Parliament, in 1700, having had a true State laid before them of the then dangerous Condition of Dover Harbour, and of the great Usefulness of it when in Repair, did pass an Act for its Repair, by laying a small Duty on Tonage, only on such Ships as passed by, to, or from, the said Harbour, as were capable of being secured by it: In few Years after, the Produce of the said Act made for Nine Years, was found to fall short of what it was computed at; thereupon a liibsequent Act was made, enlarging the Time Nine Years more; and although the Money arising by the said Acts hath been constantly applied for the Care of Dover Harbour, yet the Wars havelo considerably lessened even the Sum proposed as necessary, that the Money raised, and already expended towards making this a commodious Harbour, will be finely loft, unless the said Duties, which expire in May next, be furl her continued, or other provision made for the Completing and Preserving of it;

And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill either to continue the present Duties, or otherwise to provide for the effectual Repair and Preservation of a Harbour lo necessary for the Security of Trade, and Benefit of the whole Kingdom.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person shall be intitled to Half-pay, who was a Minor, under the Age of Sixteen Years, at the time when the Regiment, Troop, or Company, in which he served, was reduced.

Refclvcd, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person shall be intitled to Half-pay, except such Persons who did actual Service in some Regiment, Troop, or Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person having any other Place or Employment of Profit, Civil or Military, under his Majesty, shall be intitled to Half-pay.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Chaplain of any Garison or Regiment, who has any Ecclesiastical Benefice, or other Preferment in Great Britain or Ireland, shall be intitled to Half-pay.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person shall be intitled to Half-pay, who hath religned his Commission, and has had no Commission since.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Half-pay shall be allowed to any Person, by virtue of any Warrant or Appointment, except to such Persons who would have been other wile intitled to the same as reduced Officers.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Half-pay shall not be allowed to any of the Officers of the Five Regiments of Dragoons, and Eight Regiments of Foot, lately difoanded in Ireland, except to such as were taken off the Establishment of Half-pay in Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ninety-four thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, for Half-pay, for the Year 1718, upon Account, to the reduced Officers of his Majesty s Land Forces, and Marines.

Cloth Mr. Booth reported from the Committee, to whom

Button* and the Petition of the Taylors, Buttonsellers, Throwfters, B«tton-hol . Twiders, Dyers, Spinners, Buttonmakers, and others, living in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, Borough of Southwark, and Places adjacent, concerned in the Manufactures of raw Silk, and Mohair Yarn, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of others employed therein, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That by an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for employing the Manufacturers of raw Silk and Mohair Yarn, it is Enacted, That no Taylor, or other Person, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, shall make, fell, or set on any Cloaths, or wearing Garments whatsoever, any Button or Button-holes made of Serge, Drugget, or any other Stuffs, of which Cloaths, or wearing Garments, are usually made of, under the Forfeiture of Five Pounds for every Doaen of Button or Button- holes, so made, fold, or set on; and in like Proportion for a lesser Quantity; one Moiety to - Von. 18.

her Majesty, the other to the Prosecutor; to be recovered by Action of Debt, Bill, Plaint, or Information , or upon Complaint to any Two Justices of the Peace, who are to summon and examine Witnesses upon Oath.

That the Petitioners produced Witnesses to prove tire Deficiency of the said Act, and' the Difficulties and' Hardships they suffer thereby: And, fird,

John Baker, an Attorney, said, That he had been employed by the Buttonmakers in Eight several Actions against Taylors, for making Cloth, Serge, or other Buttons and Button-holes, contrary to the said Act; but could never convict more than one Person; and then the Jury gave a Verdict but for Fifteen Pounds, though the Action. was for One hundred Pounds; which was proved at the Tryal; and was often nonsuited for want of Witnesses, who were either bought off, or absconded; so as not to be found when the Cause should be heard.

Mr. John Metcalf, Attorney, said, He has been employed by the Buttonmakers in prosecuting several Offenders against the said Act, before the Justices of the Peace; but could not get Two of them together; and very few care to act therein: That he applied himself to Mr. Justice Con* Clerk for a Warrant against an Offender, having his Witnesses ready; and the Clerk said, His Master would not grant his Warrant, nor act in Affairs of that Nature.

Mr. Newman, a Wholesale Buttonseller, said, He attended Mr. Justice Hungerford and Mr. Justice Sanders Three or Four Months, in order to put the said Act in Execution; and Mr. Hungerford offered his Assistance; yet he could not get the Two Justices together; and very few will act therein: That he has also prosecuted at Law. upon the said Act; but, before he could come to Tryal, his Witnesses could not be found.

Then the Petitioners proceeded to prove the Loss of their Trades.

Mr. Edward Keep, Buttonseller, said, That he had followed that Trade for 25 Years, and employed abundance of Persons in making of Needle-wrought Buttons, and the Materials of Silk and Mohair wherewith they are made: That, for Two Years lad pad, he has not fold Half the Quantity of Buttons he used to do; so that he has been forced to turn off Half the Work-folks he before employed} and can impute this Loss of Trade to no other Cause than a Practice Taylors have newly taken up of making Cloth and Drugget Buttons and Button-holes, contrary to the said Act.

Mr. Newman affirmed what Mr. Keep had said.

And there were several other Buttonsellers, and Buttonmakers, attended the Committee, who gave the like Evidence. t

Tho. Pickering, Taylor, said, He has loft near Half his Trade, because he will not make Cloth and Drugget Button-holes, contrary to the said Act; which others do privately: That he used to employ 16 or 20 Men about this time of the Year; and now Eight do his Work.

Lawrence Anderton, Taylor, said, That, in March lad, he was so ill, that he could not follow his Bufinefe; and gave Orders to his Foreman not to make any Cloaths contrary to the said Act; yet he made several Suits privately for himself, and thereby got many of s

bed Customers from him, though he paid him Wages at the same time.

Tho. Bolton, Taylor, said. That lad Week, Cloth was fetched from his House, because he would not make Cloth Buttons; and that he saw the same on his Customer’s Back with Cloth Buttons the next Day.

Edward Keep said, That George Halstead and Dixon, Taylors, have removed into the Fleet; and these carry on the Trade of making Cloaths with Cloth Buttons and Button-holes.

Peter Johnson, Taylor, said, That Benjamin Badger, a

Taylor, now living in the Mintold him, He kept 16 Men at Work} and feme of Badger's Men, who have since wrought with Johrfon, told him, Badger's Work chiefly was in making Cloaths with Cloth Buttons and" Button-holes.

Mr. Morice reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of divers Merchants, and other Proprietors in the subscribed Lottery Annuities', and diher Ari(unties established by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them;- which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read} and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, upon Examination of several Witnesses, d» find,

That the Transfer-books of the South Sea Company have continued shut, to prepare for a Dividend, usually Seven Weeks, but sometime Eight:

That the Proprietors of that Stock are supposed to be above 6,000 to 7,000 Persons:

That the Dividends on South Sea Stock are made hall-yearly:

That the Proprietors of Lottery Annuity Stock arc above 13,000 to 14,000 Persons:

If therefore Seven Weeks are necessary for preparing the Dividend Warrants on the South Stock, twice that time is necessary for that Purpose on the Lottery Annuity Stock; lb that no time at all remains for transferring, on this Supposition, if the Dividends continue to be made quarterly:

But, supposing it possible to prepare the Lottery Annuity Warrants in Ten Weeks tinfe, there will then remain but Three Weeks time in each Quarter for Transfers; which is exceeding short, considering the great Number of Proprietors:

That the Proportion of Capital Stock, being the Produce of Tallies of Sol, which, when completed, will amount to upwards of 900,000l. more; and also the Produce of the unsubscribed Orders, amounting to upwards of 300,0001, more> are not allowed for in the aforegoing Scheme; the said Scheme being made only upon the Proportion of Capital, being the Produce of subscribed Lottery Orders, and Bankers Assignments.

St. Gyle*’ in A Petition oiDr.William Baker, Rector, Henry Wright, the Fields and Edward Liney, Churchwardens, as also of the Church. Vestry and Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Gyles's in the Fields, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Parish Church was built with Brick; and is now become very old and ruinous; and, by the Computation of Workmen, will cost Three thousand Pounds to put it into Repair: That, the Ground all about being higher, the Church lies lower than the Street by several Feet; and is thereby very damp and unwholsome; and this Inconvenience would remain, although the said Sum of 3,000l. should be laid out upon it; and can no-way be remedied, but by an intire new Building: That the said Parish pays annually, towards maintaining their Poor, 3,300l. at lead; so are in no Condition to repair, or rebuild, their said Church:

And praying, That their said Church may be One of the Fifty Churches appointed to be built by Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Michael, ComhiU, London, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Drawback A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Community, on Leather. Qf Shoemakers within the City of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Duty upon Leather is of very pernicious Consequence to the Manufacturer; and the Poor are in a very deplorable Condition for want of Employ; and chiefly for want of Leather, it being bought up by the Merchants to fend abroad; and, by reason of the Drawback that is allowed to them, they have great Encouragement to fend away great Quantities of Leather, which they wet, and pack up close for Exportation; which commonly makes it weigh One-fifth Part more than when it is brought dry from the Tanner; the King defrauded of his Duty; and foreign Countries supplied with our bed Leather at cheaper Rates than us: And praying, That the Drawback allowed upon Leather exported may be taken off; and Irish Hides and Calvcs-lkins may be allowed to be brought in.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

unto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That, in the petty Towns and Villages in the Neighbourhood of Bridport, there are several Persons that make great Quantities of Malt for Sale; and feme of them make weekly, for Sale, as much Malt, or more, as any of the Petitioners do; and, by reason the Malt they so make is not so conilantly and carefully forveyed and gauged as the Petitioners Malt is, or for some other Rea-fons, unknown to the Petitioners, they are enabled to under-fell, and do under-fell, their Malt, and at lower: Rates and Prices than the Petitioners can afford to fell; to the neat Decay and Hurt of their Trade; and to the

That the said Church was built with Brick, and is now become very, old and ruinous; and cannot be repaired under the Expence of Three thousand Pounds at least: That the Ground whereon the said Church doth stand lies about Seven or Eight Feet lower than the Street; which is very unwholesome to the Parishioners, by reason of the great Dampoefs which is occasioned by the low Situation of the said Church; and that this Inconvenience is no-ways to he remedied but by an entire new Building of it:

That, the said Parish being very large and extensive, the Charge of maintaining their Poor amounts, nibus minis, to Three thousand Three hundred Pounds, and upwards; by reason whereof, and of other their Taxes, the Parishioners are in no Condition to rebuild their said Church.

It likewise appeared to the Committee, That there is no Waste-graund, or Site, within the said Parish, to be purchased to build a new Church, without pulling down many Houses; which will occasion a very great Expence; and that the Commissioners have not contracted for any Site, or Ground, to build any other Church than what is now building; and that the said Parish Church, when rebuilt, together with the Church now building, will be sufficient to contain all the Inhabitants of the said Parish.

Sir William Pole reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Portreeve, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Saint Germans, in the County of Cornu all; and several other Petitions, relating to the importation of Irish Yarn; was referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of several Witnesses, That the Petitioners labour under the greatest Difficulties, by reason of the continual Importation of very great Quantities of Irish Worsteds, which are entered in the Custom-house Books under the Denomination of Bay-yarn; and thereby pays no further Duty than Q#. 6d. per hundred Weight; the same being valued, in the Hook of Rates, to be worth only 31. 6 s.

8 d.; whereas the Worsted, which is thus imported under the Denomination of Bay-yarn, is really worth from 11 I. to 16/. per hundred Weight; which Practices have already greatly impoverished vast Numbers of poor Spinners, Woolcombers, and others employed in the Woollen Manufacture; since this Irish Worsted is, by this means, rendered 4 d.per pound Weight cheaper than ’tis possible to be made by our poor Labourers here in England.

John Thomas, Woolcomber and Weaver, declared, That he has, for many Years, dealt in Irish Worsted; and hath known the same manufactured up into Stuffs of different Sorts; which Irish worsted can and hath been sold by the Importer at Bristol, at least, 4 per Pound Weight chea|>er than English Worsted of the same Fineness can be afforded:

He produced Two Samples of Irish Worsted; one of which cost 2 s. per Pound Weight, and the other 2 s.

11 d. per Pound Weight; and said, That the former was bought cheaper by, at least, 4 d. per Pound Weight, and the latter, being a finer Sort, by, at least, 6d. than Eng-l\jh Worsted of the same Goodness can be bought:

Being ctked w hat difference there was between Irish Bay-yarn and Worsted, lie answered, That the Worsted w as made of the fine Wool combed, and the Bay-yarn of Vol. 18,

the Dross of such Wool Carded; and that the Worsted was at Three times the Value of the Bay-yarn.

William Alford, Woolcomber and Weaver, declared,.

That he has been an Agent, or Factor, to receive great Quantities of Irish Worsted from on board several Ships; which have imported the same to: That such

Worsted was worth from 2 s. to 3s. per Pound Weight; and that the same was entered at the Custom-house under* the Denomination of Bay or Woollen Yarn, and paid Duties as such; and that Bay or Woollen Yam is worth but about One-third Part of the Value of Worsted; and that great Quantities of Irish Worsted are wrought up into Shalloons, and other Stuffs, without the least Mixture of Bay or Woollen Yarn: That he has manufactured great Quantities of English Worsted; and assured the Committee, that it cannot be afforded so cheap as Irish Worsted of the same Goodness, by, at least, 4 Pound Weight for some, and 6 d.for the finest Sort.

That the Committee, being desirous to be informed from the Commissioners of the Customs, what Quantities of Worsted, Bay and W oollen Yarn, had been imported for Three Years last past, ending at 1717, in

order to compare the same with an Account in the Journals of this House of the same Species of Goods imported in the Years 1706, 1707, and 1708, find, by the Commissioners Report to their Order, and comparing the same with the former Account, That the Importation of Woollen or Bay-yarn had increased exceedingly; inso much that, in the last Year, there is entered above double the Quantity that was imported in the Year 1706; which, in that Year, was only 696,565 Pounds Weight; and the last Year it role to 1,478,005 Pounds Weight; and it does not appear, that any Worsted has been entered at the Custom-houl'e by the said Report; although it was made evident by several Witnesses, that very great Quantities have been imported.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

MR. Craggs presented to the House, pursuant to their Articles of Address to his Majesty for that Purpose, Rules w*r< and Articles for the better Government of his Majesty a Land Forces:

And the same were read; and are as feUow; viz.

GEORGE R.

RULES and Articles for the better Government 06 his Majesty’s Land Forces:

Article ill.

All Officers and Soldiers, not having just; Impediment,

shall diligently frequent Divine Service, and Sermon, in such Places as shall be appointed for the Regiment,

Troop, or Company, to which they belong; and such' as either wilfully or negligently absent themselves from Divine Service, or Sermon, or else, being present, dot behave themselves indecently or irreverently during the same, if they be Officers, they shall be severely represended at a Court Martial; but, if private Soldiers, they shall, for every such First Offence, forfeit each Man Twelve Pence, to be deducted out of their next Pay; and, for the Second Offence, forfeit Twelve Pence, and be laid in Irons fa Twelve Hours; and, for every like Offence afterwards, shall foflfer, and pay in like manner: And the Money, to forfeited, shall be applied to the Relief of the lick Soldiers of such 'l'roop or Company, to which the Offender does belong.

Article 2d.

If any Sutller in any of our Ports, Garisons, Camps,

Barracks,

4 Geo. I.

4° Februarit.

709

Barracks, or Guards, shall, during Divine Service, or Sermon, presume to fell any Beer, Brandy, Wine, or other Liquors, or any Kind of Victuals, or other Merchandize; he shall be delivered over to the Civil Magistrate, to be punished according to Law.

Article 3d.

Whosoever shall use any unlawful Oath or Execration, whether Officer or Soldier, shall incur the Penalty expressed in the First Article.

Article 4th.

If any Officer, or Soldier, shall presume to blaspheme the Holy and Undivided Trinity, or the Persons of God the Father, God the Son, or God the Holy Ghost; or shall presume to speak against any known Article of the Christian Faith; he shall be delivered over by the Commanding Officer to the Civil Magistrate, to be punished according to Law.

Article 5th.

If any Officer, or Soldier, shall abuse or profane any Place dedicated to the Worship of God; or Dial! offer Violence to any Chaplain of the Army, or any other Minister of God’s Word; he shall receive such corporal Punishment as shall be inflifited on him by a Court Martial.

Article 6th.

If any Officer, or Soldier, shall presume to use any traitorous or difrefpefitful Words against the Sacred Person of his Majesty, his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, or any of the Royal Family; or shall behave himself with Contempt or Dillefpefit towards the General, or ether Commander in Chief, of the Forces; or speak Words tending to his Hurt or Diffionour; he shall be punished according to the Nature of his Offence by the Judgment of a Regimental or General Court Martial.

Article 7th.

Whatever Officer, or Soldier, without Leave of his Majesty, the General, or Commander in Chief, for the Time being, shall hold Correspondence with any Rebel, or Enemy of his Majesty, or give them Advice or Intelligence by letters, Messages, Signs, or Tokens, or in any manner of Way whatsoever, shall suffer Death, or such other Punishment as shall be inflifited by a Court Martial.

And whatever Regiment, Troop, or Company in Field, Garilbn, or on Part)', shall treat with such Rebels or Enemies, or enter into any Conditions with them, without being reduced to the utrnoft Extremity, or Leave had, as aforesaid; every Officer, and Soldier, who shall knowingly consent thereto, and shall be convicted thereof before a Court Martial, shall likewise suffer Death, or such other Punishment as by a Court Martial shall be inflifited:

And whatever Officer, or Soldier, shall advise, encourage, or persuade, any other Officer, ’or Soldier, to hold any such traiterous Correspondence, or enter into such Conditions, shall, upon Conviction thereof, suffer Death, or such other Punishment as a Court Martial shall think fit:

But whatever Officer, or Soldier, can prove, that lie did his utmost to resist and avoid such Treaty, he shall not go only unpunished; but be rewarded for his good Behaviour and Fidelity.

Article 8th.

If any Officer, or Soldier, shall excite, cause, or join in, any Mutiny, or Sedition, in the Company, Troop, or Regiment, to which he belongs, or in any other Company, Troop, or Regiment, in his Majesty’s Service; or on any Party or Poll where the Duty is done by Detachment from several Regiments, or otherwise, in the Army; he shall suffer death, or such other Punishment as a Court Martial shall inflifit:

And-if any Officer, Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, shall hear any Words tending to Mutiny or Sedition; or, being any way privy thereto, do not immediately use their utrnoft Endeavours to suppress the fame, as also to discover it to their Superiors; if an Officer, he shall be cashiered; and, if a Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, V«l. L8.

he shall be severely punished, at the Discretion of a Court Martial.

Article 9th.

If any Officer, or Soldier, shall refuse to obey the military Orders of his superior Officer, he shall suffer Death, or such other Punishment as shall be inflicted by a Court Martial.

Article 10th.

If any Officer, or Soldier, shall presume to resist any Officer in the Execution of his Office; or shall strike, draw, or offer to draw, or shall lift up, any Weapon against, his superior Officer, on any Pretence whatsoever; he shall be punished with Death, or such other Punishment as a Court Martial shall inflifit.

Article 11 th.

And to the Intent that no Officer, commanding aTroop, or Company, may pretend Ignorance of what he ought to pay to every Non-commission Officer and Soldier in our Service, we do hereby command them Unfitly to observe such Regulations as are, or shall be, direfited by us under our Royal Sign Mapual, pursuant to the Afit of Parliament now in Force.

Article 12th.

All Officers and Soldiers, who have received Pay, or have been duly lilted in our Service, and shall desert the fame, either in the Field, upon a March, in Quarters, or in Garison, < and be convifiied thereof before a Court Martial, shall suffer Death, or such other Punishment as by the said Court Martial shall be inflifited.

Article 13th.

No Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, shall leave his Troop, or Company, and inlist himself in any other Regiment, Troop, or Company, without a Discharge from the Commanding Officer of the Regiment in which he last served, under Pain of being reputed a Deserter, and differing Death for it, or such other Punishment as a Court Martial shall inflifit:

And in case any Officer shall knowingly receive, or entertain, any such Non-commission Officer, or Soldier; upon Proof made thereof before a General Court Martial, he shall be cashiered:

Nor shall any Discharge granted to any Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, be allowed of as sufficient, unless signed by a Field Officer of the Regiment, whence such Soldier was difmiifed.

Article 14th.

If any Officer, or Soldier, shall persuade, or advise, any other Officer, or Soldier, to desert, he shall suffer Death, or such other Punishment as shall be inflifited by a Court Martial.

Article 15th.

If any Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, committed to Prison, shall break thence, and endeavour to escape Punishment, and leave the Service, he shall be punished as a Deserter, and die for it; or suffer such other Punishment as shall, by a Court Martial, be inflifited:

And if any Officer under an Arrest shall leave his Confinement, before lie is let at Liberty by the Officer who confined him, or by a superior Power, he shall be cashiered for it.

Article 16th.

Whatever Officer, or Soldier, shall misbehave himself before the Enemy, and run away, or shamefully abandon any Fort, Post, or Guard, which they are commanded to defend; or speak Words inducing others to do the like; or who, after Visitory, shall, instead of pursuing the Enemy, leave his Commanding Officer, to plunder and pillage, before the Enemy be intirely beaten and defeated; or whilst any Body of them remains unbroken; every such Offender, being duly convifited thereof, shall be reputed a Disobeyer of military Orders; and shall suffer Death, or such other Punishment as by a Court Martial shall be inflifited on him.

Article 17th.

Whatever publick Stores shall be taken in the Enemy’s Camp, Towns, Forts, or Magazines, whether of Artillery, Ammunition, Cloathing, Forage, or Provision, shall be
