Article 18th.

If any Officer, Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, shall be accused of any Crime, which is punishable by the known Laws of the Land, and not express, mentioned in these our Rules and Articles, the Commanding Officer of every Regiment, Troop, Company, or Party, are hereby required to deliver over such accused Persons to the Civil Magistrate, so soon as applied to; and are also to be aiding and affiiling to the Officers of Justice in the seizing and apprehending such Offender, in order to bring him to Tryal, under Pain of our highest Displeasure.

Article igth.

If any Officer think himself wronged by his Colonel, or the Commanding Officer of the Regiment, and shall, upon Application to him, be refused to be redressed, he is to complain to our General or Commander in Chief of our Forces, in order to have Justice done him; who is hereby required to examine into the fame, and to lay it before us himselfj or by our Secretary at War, in order to receive our further Direction; and, if the Accusation prove false and vexatious, the Complainant shall be punished at the Discretion of a General Court Martial: And if any inferior Officer, or Soldier, shall think himself wronged by his Captain, or Officer commanding the Troop or Company, he is to complain thereof to the Officer commanding the Regiment; who is hereby required to fee Justice done to the Complainant at a Regimental Court Martial; from which, if either Party think himself not fully righted, he may appeal to a General Court Martial; where if upon a Second Hearing, the Appeal shall appear vexatious or groundless, the Appeal-ant shall be punished accordingly:

And if any Colonel or Captain shall be found to have taken away any thing from an Officer or Soldier, or to have wronged him of his Dues, he shall not only make Restitution, but be further punished, according to the Nature of his Offence,

Article 20th.

No Officer or Soldier shall use any reproachful or provoking Speeches or Gestures to another, upon Pain of Imprisonment, and asking Pardon of the Party offended, in Presence of his Commanding Officer:

Nor shall any Officer, or Soldier, presume to fend a Challenge to any other Officer, or Soldier, to fight a Duel, upon Pain of being cashiered, if he be an Officer; or suffering the fevered corporal Punishment, if a Non-commission Officer, or private Soldier: And if any Officer, or Non-commission Officer, commanding a Guard, shall willingly and knowingly fufier any Person whatever to go forth to fight a Duel, they shall be punished as above; and all Seconds also, and Carriers of Challenges, shall be taken as Principals, and punished accordingly.

All Officers, of what Condition soever, have Power to part and quell all Quarrels, Frays, and other Disorders, though of another Company, Troop, or Regiment; and to command Officers to Arrest, and Soldiers to Prison, until their proper Officers be acquainted therewith: And whoever shall refute such Officer, though of inferior Rank, or draw his Sword upon him, shall be punished as a General Court Martial shall appoint: Nor shall any Officer or Soldier upbraid another for refilling a Challenge; fmee, according to these our Orders, they but do the Duty of Soldiers, who ought to subject themselves to Discipline: And we do acquit and discharge all Men, who have Quarrels offered, or Challenges font to them, of all Disgrace, or Opinion of Disadvantage, in their Obedience hereunto: And whosoever shall upbraid them, and offend in this Cafe, shall be punished as a Challenger.

Article 21ft.

The Controversies that happen in a Regiment between the Soldiers and their Officers, relating to their military Capacities, as also between Soldier and Soldier, shall be determined atthe next Regimental Court Martial; which

Regimental Court Martial shall not consist of less than Five Commissioned Officers, and the President, not to be under the Degree of a Captain; who are to judge all such . Matters as are proper for their Determination; which shall be decided according to the Plurality of Voices.

They are also impowered to try Non-commission Officers, and Soldiers, for Neglect of Duty, or other Misbehaviour; and to inflict corporal Punishments, if the Sentence be approved by the Commanding Officer; and, if any Person think himself aggrieved, he may appeal to the next General Court Martial for Redress: But, where any Officer or Soldier is accused of any Crime, which, by these Articles, is punishable with Death, they are to be tried by a General Court Martial.

Article 2 2d.

A General Court Martial shall not consist of less than Thirteen Commission Officers, with their President, who is not to be under the Degree of a Field Officer, or the then Commander in Chief of our Forces in Gurifon, where such Court is held: The Members both of General and Regimental Courts Martial shall, for Orders-fake, take the same Rank in their Sittings, as they do in the Army; and the Judge Advocate General, or feme Person having a Deputation to act for him, shall inform the Court, and prosecute in his Majesty’s Name; and in capital Cafes, administer to the several Members the Oath following:

" You shall well and truly try and determine, accordto your Evidence, in the Matter now before you,

" between our Sovereign Lord the King’s Majesty " and the Prisoner to be tried.

So help you GOD/’

The following Oath shall also be taken by such as are Members, or Judges, in any General Court Martial:

" I A. B. do swear, That I will duly administer Justice,

" according to the Rules and Articles made by his Majesty for the better Government of his Forces;

" and according to an Act of Parliament, now in " Force, for the Punishment of Mutiny, Dci'ertion,

" and other Crimes therein mentioned; without " Partiality, Favour, or Affection; and, if any Doubt " shall arise, which is not explained by the said " Articles, or Act of Parliament, according to my " Conscience, the bell of my understanding, and " the Custom of War in like Cafes: And I do further swear, That I will not divulge the Sentence:

" of the Court, until it shall be approved by his Majesty, the General, or Commander in Chief; ncither will I, upon any account, at any time whatsoever, disclose or discover the Vote or Opinion " of any particular Member of the Court Martial.

'So help me GOD."

All Witnesses shall be examined upon Oath; and no Field Officer shall be tried by any under the Degree of a Captain; nor shall any Sentence of Death be given against any Offender, unless Nine of the Thirteen Officers present shall concur therein: And no Sentence of Death shall be had or given against any Offender, nor any Proceedings on his Tryal, but between the Hours of F.ight in the Morning and One in the Afternoon; ‘nor shall the Sentence of any Court Martial be put in Execution until Report be. made of the whole Proceedings to his Majesty, and his Directions figuified thereupon. All Members of Courts Martial shall behave themselves decently; and, in giving their Votes, begin with the youngest.

Article 23d.

Every Non-commission Officer and Soldier, who shall inlist himself in our Service, shall, at the time of his so in-liffing, or within a Month afterwards at the furthest, be taken before a Justice of the Peace by the inlisting Officer, or the Officer commanding the Troop or Company, in which he is lifted; and shall take the Oath following:

" I swear to be true to our Sovereign Lord King George,

" and to serve him honestly and faithfully, in Defence of his Person, Crown, and Dignity, against " all his Enemies and Opposers whatsoever; and to u observe and obey his Majesty’s Orders, and the

Article 24th*

Every Officer commanding aTroop> or Company, shall, upon due Notice given him by the Commissary of the Musters, or some one of his deputies, assemble the Troop, or Company, under his Command, in the next convenient Place, for their being mustered; and if any Officer or ' Soldier shall happen to be absent from such Muller, by real'on of Sickness, being employed in Recruiting, on Party, or on Furloff, or by a signed Leave from his Colonel or Field Officer commanding the Regiment, the Officer there commanding such Troop, or -Company, shall produce signed Certificates of such lawful Cause of Absence, or they shall not be allowed of at the Mutters: And every Officer that shall be convicted of giving, making, or procuring, any false Certificate, in Order to a false Mutter; or shall, at any time, be found guilty of making a false Mutter, either by Muttering of Servants in the Ranks, or of any Man or Horse not truly belonging to the Troop, or Company; shall be cashiered from our Service.

Article 25th.

No Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, shall, by Leave of his Captain, or inferior Officer, commanding a Troop, or Company, be absent from his Quarters above Twenty Days in Six Months, unless by a signed Leave from the Colonel, or other Field Officer commanding the Regiment; who is also to take care, that no more than Two private Men, at a time, of th same Troop, or Company, may have his Licence of Absence; and, for the Absence of Commission Officers from Garilbns, or Quarters, all Colonels, and Commanding Officers, are to govern themselves according to our Orders for Attendance of Officers in Quarters.

Article 26th.

AH Commissions granted by us, or by any of our Generals, having Authority from us, shall be entered in the Books of our Secretary at War and Commissary General of the Mutters; or not otherwise to be allowed of at the Mutters.

Article 27th.

No Commissioned Officer may be cashiered, or dismissed our Service, but by an Order from us, or by the Sentence of a General Court Martial, approved of by such Generals, or Commanders of our Forces, as, by our Power and Authority, shall appoint the same to be held: But Non-commission Officers may be discharged in like manner as private Soldiers; and, by the Sentence of a Regimental Court Martial, may be reduced to serve as private Soldiers in the Ranks, if their Misbehaviour shall deserve such Punishment

Article 28th.

No Non-commission Officer or Soldier, belonging to any Regiment, Troop, or Company, in our Service, mall be permitted to futtle, or to keep any kind of Publick-house or Shop for the Selling of Liquors, Victuals, or other Merchandize, under Pain of being punished for it by a Regimental Court Martial:

And every Commission Officer, who shall presume to mutter any Person known to be so settling, or offending as above, shall be brought to a General Court Martial, and punished as for making of a false Mutter.

Article 29th.

In all our Barracks, Forts, and Garilbns, or on Guards, where any such Suttlers, not being Soldiers, are permitted to attend our Troops, they shall not fell any kind of Liquors,! Victuals, or keep open House for the Entertainment of Soldiers, after Nine of the Clock at Night, nor before the Beating of the Reveilles in the Morning, under Pain of being difiniffed from all future Suttling, as the Commanding Officer shall be answerable.

Article 30th.

All Officers and Soldiers are to behave themselves orderly in Quarters, and on the March; and whoever shall commit any Watte, or Spoil, either in Walks of Trees,

Patks, Warrens, Fish-porids, Houses, of Gardens, Corn- Articles or fields, Inclosures, or Meadows, or shall inalicioully de-» Wan stroy any Property whatever belonging to any of our Sub* je£ts, or belonging to any Person whatever, unless, by Order of the then Commander in Chief of our Forces, to annoy Rebels, or other Enemies, in Arms against us; he or they that shall be found guilty of offending herein, shall, besides such Penalties as they are liable to by Law, be punished, according to the Nature and Degree of the Offence by the Judgment of a Regimental, or General,

Court Martial.

Article 3ilL

No Officer shall demand Billets for Quartering of more than his effective Men; nor quarter any Women of Children in the House assigned him for the Quartering of Officers and Soldiers, without the Consent of the Owner j nor shall take Money for freeing the Landlords from Quartering of Officers, or Soldiers, under Pain of being cashiered for it.

Article 32d.

Every Officer commanding a Regiment, Tfoop, Chm4 pany, or Party, whether in settled Quarters, or on the March, shall fee his own Quarters, and the Quarters of every Officer and Soldier under his Command, paid according to the Rates specified in the Act of Parliament now in Force; and, upon every Payment to be made in Quarters, the said Officer shall give publick Notice thereof to the Landlords, in order to fee them satisfied, as aforesaid: And in case any such Regiment, Troop, Company, or Party, shall be ordered to march before Money may be come to the Hands of the Commanding Officer, he is hereby required, before his Departure out of any Town or Village, to make up the Accounts with all Persons concerned in Money due to them for quartering Officers and Soldiers, for what time soever he shall have happened to remain there; and grant to every such Party a signed Certificate for the same; therein specifying the Name of the Regiment, Troop, or Company, such Officers or Soldiers do belong to, under Pain of being cashiered for it, upon Proof of having wilfully offended herein.

Article 33d.

On Marches, the Commanding Officers are to apply to the proper Magistrates for the Carriages necessary for the Service; and to pay for them, according to the Act of Parliament in that behalf; taking care not to abuse, or to suffer any under their Command to *beat or abuse, the Waggoners, or other Persons, attending such Carriages; nor to put more than Twenty hundred Weight on any Wain or Waggon so furnished to them by the Country:

And whatever Officer shall be convicted of offending herein, or in refilling to grant Certificates, in case of Failure of Money, as in the preceding Article, shall, by the Judgment of a Court Martial, be cashiered, or otherwise punished, according to the Degree of hia Offence.

Article 34th.

All Officers commanding in Garisons, in Quarters, or on Marches, shall keep good Order, and redress all such Abuses or Disorders as may happen to be committed by any Officer or Soldier under their Command: And if, oil Complaint made to any Commanding Officer of Beating of Landlords, or Extorting of more from them than they are obliged by Law to iurnish; of Soldiers Disturbing of Fairs or Markets, or committing any other kind of Riots, to the disturbing or dilquieting our People; he the said Commander, who shall refofe to fee Justice done on the Offender, and Reparation made to the Party injured, lb far as Part of the Offender’s Pay can’enable him, he shall, upon Proof thereof, be punished by a General Court Martial, as if he himself had personally committed the Crimes or Disorders complained of.

Article 35th.

No Officer or Soldier shall lie out of his Camp, or Quarters, without Leave of his superior Officer; and every Soldier shall repair to his Quarters at the beating or founding the Retreat; and whatever Officer, or Soldier,

Article 36th.

If any Officer shall be found drunk on his Guard, Party, or other Duty, under Arms, he shall be cashiered ifor it; and if any Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, shall be found guilty of the fame, he shall be punished by riding the wooden Horse, Picketing, or some other such corporal Punishment as is prafilifed in the Army for such like Offences.

Article 37th.

If any Centinel quit his Poll before he be relieved from it or shall be found ilceping on his Poit, he shall be confined till the next Regimental Court Martial; and, upon Proof thereof, be condemned to run the Gauntlet; which is a Punishment we think not fitting to be otherwise in-flifited than by the Judgment of a General, or Regimental Court Martial.

Article 38th.

No Trooper, Dragoon, or Foot Soldier, shall hire another to do his Duty for him; nor shall any such be excused from Duty, but in Cafes of Sickness, Disability, or Leave of Absence; and every Soldier, found guilty of hiring his Duty, as also the Party io hired to do another’s Duty, shall be ppniffied at the next Regimental Court Martial; and every Non-commission Officer, conniving at such Hiring of Duty as abovesaid, shall be reduced for it; and every Commission Officer, knowing and allowing of such ill Practices in our Service, shall be punished by the Judgment of a General Court Martial: And if he shall protect any Person from his Creditors, under his Pretence of his being a Soldier, except such as do actually serve in the Ranks, and constantly do all the Duties of a Soldier, according to the true Intent and Meaning of the Act of Parliament- in that behalf, he shall be cashiered For it

Article 39th.

No Officer, or Soldier, shall, by Firing of Arms, Drawing of Swords, or otherwise, make Alarms in Camp or Quarters, under Pain of such Punishment as the next Regimental Court Martial shall judge proper.

Article 40th.

And to the end that Officers and Soldiers may not, by lying under Confinement be hindered from doing their Duty, and others be obliged to do it in their room; we hereby direfit, That, upon every Offence committed, and not immediately punishuble by such corporal Punishments, as the there Commanding Officer shall think htmielf impowered to inflifit, he shall forthwith acquaint his Colonel, pr the Officer commanding the Regiment, therewith; who is all, with all convenient Speed, to summon Officers for composing a Regimental Court Martial, for the Tryal and Punishment of such Crimes; or, within the Space of Five Days at fartheit, after Confinement of any such Offender; and, for all Crimes, Offences, and Differences, which, at a Regimental Court Martial, they shall not judge themselves impowered to decide, and punish, foe Officer then commanding the Regiment shall send to our Secretary at War foe Proceedings, Proois, and Examina* lions, made thereon, in order to obtain our Order, or foe Order of our General, or Commander of our Forces, for a General Court Martial thereupon.

Article 41ft

Whosoever shall make known the Parole, or Watchword, without Orders of his foperior Officer, to any other than the Commissioned and Non-commission Officers, who ought to know the same; and whoever, upon his Guard, or Patrol, foaU give any other Word than that given by foe proper Oncer; shall be brought to next Regimental Court Martial, and be punished as their Judgment, and the Circumstances of his Offence, may require.

Article 42d.

Whatever Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, shall at a Regimental Court Martial, be convifiled of having fold, or willingly spoiled, any of the Ammunition delivered to him out of our Stores, shall run the Gauntlet; and if any Commissioned Officer, Store-keeper, or Commissary of Provisions, Forage, Ammunition, Arms, or other Stores, for the Use of our Forces, shall, at a General Court Martial, be convifiled of embezzling, felling, or wilfully spoiling, any such Stores committed to his Charge, he shall be camiered for it.

Article 43d.

Every Non-commission Officer, or Soldier, of Horse, Foot, or Dragoons, who shall, at a Regimental Court Martial, be found guilty of having fold, or wilfully loft, or spoiled, his Horse, Arms, Cloaths, or Accoutrements, or of pilfering and (leafing his Comrades, or other Soldiers, Cloaths, Arms, or Accoutrements, shall be subjefifc to such weekly Stoppage, not exceeding One Half-part of his Pay, as the Court Martial shall judge sufficient for repairing the fame; and suffer Confinement, or such other corporal Punishment, as in their Judgment, the Nature of his Offence may deserve; but no Deduction out of any particular Man’s Pay, otherwise than is, or shall be, direfited by a Regulation under our Sign Manual, may be made, unless for Crimes of the above Nature, and authorized by foe Sentence of a Regimental Court Martial; nor any general Stoppage or Deductions in Regiments, Troops, or Companies, but by our particular Warrant, or foe Warrant of foe General commanding our Forces.

Article 44th.

No Officer commanding a Guard, or Provost Marshal belonging to our Forces, shall refuse to receive, and keep, any Prisoner committed to their Charge by any Officer of our Forces; nor shall release any such Prisoner, without Orders from the then Commander in Chief; nor suffer any Prisoner to escape, under Pain of being punished for it by the Judgment of a General Court Martial, according to the Degree of his Offence; and every such Officer, to whose Charge Prisoners are committed, i3 hereby required, within Twenty-four Hours after such Commitment, or so soon as he is relieved from his Guard, to

five, in Writing, to foe said Commander in Chief, the James of the Prisoners, and of the Committers, and, as far as he knows, of the Crimes alleged against them, under Pain of his being punished for his Disobedience at a Regimental or General Court Martial.

Article 45th.

When any Commission Officer shall happen to die, or be killed in our Service, the Major of the Regiment, or Officer doing Major’s Duty in his Absence, shall immediately secure all his Effefits and Equipage, then in Camp or Quarters, and, before foe next Regimental Court Martial, make a just Inventory thereof; to the end that his lawfol Executor may, after the Payment of his Debts in Quarters, and Interment, receive the Overplus, if any be, to his or their proper Use:

And when any Non-commission Officer, or Soldier,

' shall happen to die, or be killed, as above, the Captain, or then Commanding Officer, of foe Troop, or Company, stall, in Presence of Two other Commission Officers, or other credible Witnesses, take Account of all he dies possessed of, over and above his Regimental Cloathing, Arms, and Accoutrements, to be accounted for as is above direfited.

Article 46th.

The aforegoing Rules and Articles shall be read and published at the Head of every Regiment, Troop, and Company, mustered, or to be mustered, in our Service, once every Two Months at fartheit; and are to be duly observed by all Officers and Soldiers in our Service; and also by our Companies of Gunners, and other Military Officers of our Trains of Artillery, with such Alerations only that relate to the Payment of Soldiers Quarters, and Carriages; which, in the Kingdom of Ireland, are to be regulated by the Lord Lieutenant thereof; and, in our Islands, Provinces, and Garison, beyond the Seas, by the respective

A Petition of Joseph Mart, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in January 1706, the Earl of Peterborough contracted and agreed with, and gave Orders to the Petitioner, at Cajlillo Plano, in the Kingdom of Vatentia, for the Raising of a Regiment of Foot, and Fifty Horse, for the Service of her late Majesty Queen Anne, to be put upon the English Establishment and Pay; the said Earl then declaring, That he was impowered by her late Majesty so to do: 'fiat the Petitioner raised Eight Companies of Foot, and Fifty Horse; of which toe laid Earl having Notice, gave Orders to Mr. Furley, his Secretary at War, to make and issue out Commissions to the Petitioner, as Colonel of the said Regiment, and Captain of One of the Companies; declaring, That the said Regiment was raised by his Order, for the Service of the Queen, and was to be put upon the English Establishment: That the Commissions were accordingly issued; the said Earl therein reciting, That, by virtue of the Power and Authority granted to him by the Queen, to raise and form Troops of die Natives of , he did constitute the Petitioner Colonel of the said Regiment: And the said Commissions expressly mention, 16

That the Petitioner, and the rest of the Officers of that Regiment, should enjoy, have, and receive, the same Honours, Privileges, and Pay, as the other Officers who served her Majesty in the like Stations and Polls: That the Petitioner, with his said Regiment, and Fifty Horse, immediately after issuing of the said Commissions, which were dated the 4th of February 1706, N. S. served under the Command of lieutenant General , at the Siege of Aticant; and, after the Taking of that Town, in de-

fending several important PalTes, the Town and Castle of Denia, the Town of Satavia, and the Town of Alcoy, where the Petitioner, and his Regiment, were made Prisoners of War: That the Petitioner, and Regiment, being, without the lead Doubt, taken and accepted by all Persons to be one of her Majesty’s Regiments, the Petitioner was induced, at his own Charge and Credit, to maintain and pay the said Regiment, upon the Intreaties, and frequent Delarations, of the said Ear!, my Lord Gall-way, General Richards, and other English Generals, that he would run no Risque in so doing, in regard his said Regiment was upon the English Establishment: That, the Petitioner having hereby entirely exhausted his own Fortunes, and engaged his Credit, his Family is reduced to the utmost Extremity: That, upon a Petition to his Maj. jesty, to be paid what was due to him, his Majesty was pleased to refer the Petitioner’s same to the Consideration of the Commissioners appointed to Hate and determine the Debts due to the Army; recommending a speedy Dispatch therein: That the said Commissioners, not finding the Petitioners said Regiment mentioned in the Lift of those who are upon the English Establishment, that served in Spain, are of Opinion, that they are not authorized, by the Powers now granted to them, to proceed to state the Petitioner’s Demand: That he humbly hopes the Honour of the British Nation will provide, that he be no Sufferer for what he has done for the Service of Great Britain: And praying, That in the Bill now brought in, and depending, for appointing Commissioners to take, state, and determine, the Debts of the Array, a Clause may be inserted to im* power the said Commissioners named to state and adjuli the Petitioner’s Demand; and that he may be paid what shall thereupon appear to be jufllydue to him.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same as it appears to them, to the House:

Mr. Lomther prefen ted to the House, according to Order, a Bill for discharging such insolvent Debtors as are now in Gaol, and who were actually Prisoners the Twenty -fifth of December 1716: And the same was received.

Mr. Gyles Erie, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for regulating the Forces to be continued in his Majesty’s Service; and for Payment of the said Forces, and of their Quarters; and for pnnishing Mutiny and Desertion; was committed; the Amendments they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, with an Amendment to One of them, agreed unto by the House.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, to prevent Constables, or such other Persons as shall be employed in Quartering or Billetting of Officers or Soldiers, receiving or demanding of Money, or any Reward, for or on Account of excusing any Perifoh from quartering, or receiving into his House, any Officer or Soldier:

And the said Clause was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the Clause was amended; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, to impower the Justices of the Peace to require the Constables, and other Persons quartering or billetting Soldiers, to give them an Account, in Writing, of the Number of Officers and Soldiers quartered or billetted; and also of the Names of the Housekeepers, Streets, and Signs; to the end there may be no Abuses in Quartering or Billetting of the Soldiers:

And the said Clause was twice read, with a Blank; which was filled up:

And the Clause was amended; and then the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

And other Amendments were made to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morn-, ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Methods for preventing the Walie of the Gold and Silver Coins of this Kingdom.

v Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill for taking off the Obligation and Encouragement for coining Guineas, for a certain time therein mentioned.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for opening the Port of Exeter, for the Importation of Wool from Ireland.

Ordered, That all Committees be adjourned.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of the Tanners, Curriers, and Shoemakers, in and about the Town of Newbury, in the County of Berks, on behalf of themselves, and all others employed in the Leather-trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Leather-trade is very much ' decayed of late Years, by reason of the Exportation of Bark to Ireland, where no Duty is paid for Leather; which hath occasioned several Persons to leave their Trades in this Kingdom, and retire to Ireland', to the great Diiadvantage of the Leather-trade: And pray, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the Exportation of Bark.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Tanners in Malmsbury, and Places adjacent, on behalf of themselves, and others, fife. was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Exportation of English Bark is so prejudicial to the English Trade in Leather, that, unless a speedy Course be taken to prevent it, the English Trade tnuft be utterly loft, and our Hides and Skins not worth the Tanning in England: That, by a Statute of King James the First, it was Enacted, That no Person should engross any oaken Bark to fell agaiu, or fell any oaken Trees, but between the First o I April and the last of June; which’ said Statute

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Traders, and others, id Running the City of Worcester, on behalf of themselves, and other French Owners of Land in and about the said City, was pre- Brandy-fented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in the County of Worcester, and other Counties, there groweth considerable Quantities of wild Pears, and Crab-apples, that is much used by Distillers in making Brandy: That the Brandy drawn from this Fruit is found to be fit for Exportation to foreign Parts, especially when mixed with Brandy drawn from Sugar or Moloffes: That the inland Trade for British Brandy is much obstructed by the Running of great Quantities of French Brandy; to the Prejudice of the fair Trader: That a great deal of our Brandy would be exported into foreign Parts; but the Brandy manufactured in this Kingdom is kept from being shipped out by reason of the Duties laid on low Wines, and Spirits, without Provision for a Drawback on Exportation as is allowed on most Manufactures that pay a Duty; which makes them too dear for Merchants to buy, because they are under-fold in foreign Markets: And praying, That the Running of French Brandy may be prevented, and the Exportation of Brandy made in this Kingdom be encouraged.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the more effectual preventing the clandestine Running of Goods, be read.

A Petition of the Commissioners for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of London ana Westminster, and Suburbs thereof was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the Petitioners taking Notice, That there is a Bill depending to impower the Commissioners appointed to put in Execution the Acts of the Ninth and Tenth Years of her late Majesty’s Reign, for building fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof, to direct the Parish Church of St. Gyles's in the Fields, in the County of Middlesex, to be rebuilt, instead of One of the Fifty new Churches; That, by several Acts of Parliament, Duties are granted for the Increase of the Number of Churches in and near those populous Cities, by building Fifty new Churches; That it is the exprefe Intent and Purpose of those Acts, that, by such Increaling of the Number of Churches, Provision should be made for the better Instruction of the Inhabitants in the true Christian Religion, as professed in the Church of England, and established by the Laws of this Realm; That an Act passed in this ^relent Parliament, for enabling his Majesty to pursue ms pious and gracious Intentions to provide for the Maintenance of the Ministers, who were to attend the Service of God in the new Churches to be erected; the Petitioners therefore think, that a Work, declared by Parliament pobe lb much for the Honour of God, the spiritual Welfare of the Subjects of this Realm, and the Interest of the Established Church, cannot be duly and effectually carried on, if any Part of the Duties appropriated, by the said fevered Acts, to the Building of Fifty new Churches, be applied to the Rebuilding of any of the old ones: And praying, That the Premises may be taken into Consideration.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee;

It passed in the Negative.

That the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petitions of Sir Bazill Dirwell, Baronet, Lieutenant of Dover Castle, and Sir Thomas , Sir Thomas Hales,

VOL. 18.

That the Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and find the same as followeth; viz.

Samuel Walton of Dover, Carpenter, laid, That since the Act of Parliament, of the Eleventh and Twelfth of King William, for the Repair of Dover Harbour, a new Cross-wall has been built, and other Works done, for penning in the Water, and deepening the Harbour, which, at Niep-tides, is 14 or 15 Foot deep, and, at Spring-tides, 20 Foot from the Pier-head to the said Cross-wall; so that a Ship of Three hundred Tons, loaden, may come into the Harbour; and there is scarce a Storm but some Ship or other comes into the Harbour for Shelter:

And further laid. That in stormy Weather, the Harbour hath been stopped up, but very rarely, with Beach; so that a Ship could not then enter; but that the same has been cleared by the Back-water the next Tide, or in 48 Hours after.

Captain Saunders said, That many Ships have been feved in Dover Harbour since the said A of Parliament; and knows, that Ships of 300 or 400 Tons have entered in Stress of Weather j but cannot fey the Harbour is now better than it was 40 Years since; because then Men of War used frequently to ride there: and the Harbour is now sometimes choked with Beach, which the Backwater clears very often the next Tide; yet if the Piers be not kept up, and the new Works carried on, the Harbour, and Two-thirds of the Town of Dover, will be utterly loft, in a short time, by Stress of Weather.

Thomas Pafcall of Dover, and Warden of Pilots, said. That he has been a Pilot 37 Years, and carried many Ships into Dover Harbour, without Anchors or Cables, in

great Storms, the Wind at N. N. E. where they have been saved; and that he carries in a9 large Ships now as formerly, the Water being deepened by the new Works; so that a Ship of 300 Tons may enter the said Harbour, and ride in the Bason; and Hundreds of Ships have been 9 B saved

738 17* Fe«

Dover Pier, saved Cnee the fialon was made; and fa id. That the Sole-bay, Deal Castle, and Men of War, have

careened in the Bason; and may do it in Winter or Summer; and the Harbour will be loft, if the new Works be not continued.

John Huggett, Pilot of ,said, That on Monday last, he came from Dover, when there was in the Harbour so Ships from Ireland, from 100 Tons to a lesser Burthen; and also Two Ships from Hamburgh, of above 200 Tons each; and believes, that if more Money were laid out, and the Pier-heads further carried out into the Sea, it would be more useful for Navigation, though the Harbour is much better now than before the new Works made by the Acts of Parliament; there being 12 or 14 Foot Water in the Baton, at Low-water: 50 Years Ago, Men of War frequently used the said Harbour.

Cuthbert Hodgson, of Dover, Captain, said, That about Ten Years since, in the time of the hard Frost, above 40 Sail of Ships, from 20 to 160 or 200 Tons Burthen, were laved in Dover Harbour; and several other Ships in Distress have been there saved, without Rudders; and said, That the Harbour is much better now than Eleven Years ago, when he first came to Dover; and, if the new Works be not continued, the Harbour will be choaked up, and intirely loft.

Sir Peter Eyton, of London, Merchant, said, That he

has known Dover Harbour 50 Years; and formerly there was no Beach there: That, in the Dutch Wars, 2 or 300 Ships were there saved; and many Ships have been saved by the said Harbour, in great Storms, the being no Place of Safety; and if a Mould, or Head, were carried out to the Westward of the South Head, it w'ould very much prevent the Beach from (lopping the Moudi of the Harbour; and that the Harbour will, be utterly loft, if nothing more be done.

Thomas Thompson of Yarmouth: That he was twice in Dover Harbour; once in the Solebay Man of War, where (he careened in King William's Reign; and the other time, being about two Years since, in the Betty Gaily, of 250 Tons, whereof he was Chief Mate: She put into Dower Harbour without Anchors or Cables, laden with Lead and Red-herrings, and drew between 14 and 15 Foot Water; and believes it is a very good Harbour for the Safety of Shipping.

Mr. Ogburne: That being recommended by Sir Henry Sheers to the Commissioners of Dower, to have the Direction of the Works, pursuant to Sir Henry Sheers' Project, lie directed the Performance of the Traverse-wall, projected by Sir Henry Sheers, in order to pen up the Water, that Ships might be afloat in the Bason; and also by the Discharge of Four Sluices, to carry off the Beach, brought thither by South-weft Winds: That the making a Jetty-head, or Turn-water, Westward of the South Pier-head, to Low-water-mark, was necessary to prevent the Beach from choaking the Mouth of the Harbour: That he thinks it necessary to keep the Works in Repair: That he was there about Two Years since, when the South Pier-head was repairing; believes the Methods then used to be very necessary; and that the Works already begun will want a considerable Sum of Money to complete them.

Alexander Kenton, of London, Captain, faith. That about Eight-and-Twenty Years since, being Master of the Ship Ruby, Burthen 200 Tons and upwards, and being in the Downes, there happening a violent Storm, which drove several Ships from their Anchors; (bme being loft on the Goodztiyn Sands, and others drove on the Coast of France, where they were loft; he feved his Ship in Dover Pier; where he refitted her, and proceeded on his Voyage to Italy-:

And feith, That about a Year ago, being at Dower, he viewed the Works there; and was of Opinion, if the same were carried on, and completed, it would make a good Harbour for One hundred and Fifty Ships; and believes it would cost Ten or Twelve thou fend Pounds to &niih it: That, in the late War, he saw 10 or 12 Ships, from 200 to 300 Tons, drawing from 13 to 14 Foot

Water loaden in the Harbour; and if the Jetty-head, or Break-water, which is begun, was carried out to Low-water-mark, it would greatly prevent the Beach from choaking the Harbour.

Peter Omer, of London, Captain, fays, That the Harbour of Dover is for a publick Benefit, if the Works begun were completed; and knows, that, last Winter, io or 12 Sail of Ships, of 140 Tons, and under, came in at one Tide.

Thomas Rooth, Haven-master of Dover, produced to the Committee an Account of Merchant Ships and Vessels, exclusive of the Packets and Ships belonging to the Town of Dower, which daily came in, and Jailed out of that Harbour, in the Month of January last; viz. Came in 81; failed out 77: And also, another Lift of Merchant Ships, not belonging to Dover, but in the Harbour, the 31st of January last, in N° 17, from 20 to 150 Tons Burthen.

Cornelius Smith, of Dover, Pilot: That Dover Harbour is a good Tide-harbour, and very useful for the Safely of Shipping; there being no other Harbour between Sheerness and the Isle of Wight; and the Packet-boats can go out of the Pier and Harbour in the same Tide, as at Calais; which cannot be done from any other Harbour in Great Britain: The Victualling Hoys also, which carry Provision to his Majesty’s Navy, when in the Downes, at any time, if the Weather permit to lay the Ships on board, can go out of Dover, and deliver, come back the next Tide, take in more, and go out again the same Tide:

That he saved a Ship, of above 500 Tons, loaden with Masts and Deal, when the Water was up to her lower Deck, and nobody on board, and conduced her into the Pier of Dover; lne drawing 17 Foot Water:

That be also carried a Ship, of 150 Tons, bound to the East Indies, Captain Peirfon Commander, to the upper Part of the Harbour:

In the Year 17084 several Transport Ships, from 160 to 300 Tons, came into Dover Pier, to take in Horses and Soldiers, to make a Descent in France:

That his Majesty’s Ship the Solebay was carried in there, and careened ;.and his Majesty’s Ship, the Swift came very often in there to careen:

That, about Two Years since, an East India, Ship, of Two hundred Tons, John Scarlet, of Deal, being Pilot, parted from his Anchoirs and Cables, and feved the Ship, by coming into Dover Pier:

That a Ship, of about Two hundred Tops, Captain Ingle Commander, bound for the Straits, loft his Mafia, and saved his Ship and Cargo, by coming into Dower Pier: That the Harbour of Dover has saved many Ships of great Value, in the late War, from the Enemy; there being, on the Spring Tide, 20 Foot Water; on the Niep, as the Wind is, 13, 14, and 15.

Mr. Samuel Walton, Overseer of the Work, delivered to the Committee an Estimate, by which it appears, that there is dill wanting, to complete Sir Henry Sheers' Projection, 14,700l.; and that be conceives there are several other Works very necessary to be added to the said Scheme, for the Security of the said Harbour; the Doing whereof will ainount.to .5,610/. more.

Then the Merchants of London brought several Persons, in Opposition to the aforesaid Evidence.

Mr, Tobias Bozoles, of London, Merchant, said, That he has known Dover Harbour above 30 Years; and thinks it no better now than 20 or 30 Years since; for that when a stormy Wind at South-weft happens, it raises such a Bar of Beach, that Ships of finall Burthen cannot get in or out of the Harbour; but fhere is a Back-water, which, in feme time, clears the Beach again: That, about Ten Years ago, the Ship Jenny, of about i 60 Tons, came, with the Wind at South-weft, and beat en the Bar, could not get over: The Ship Recovery also, of 160 Tons Burthen, (truck on the Bar, and was like to be loft, because there was not sufficient Water to carry her over; and this was since the Bason, and other new Works, have been made in the said Harbour.

Captain That he has used the Seas 25 Years; but never made for Dover Harbour, because it is so dangerous for Vessels to enter it: That he had rather keep at Sea than run the Hazard of his Ship; and that, about 18 Years ago, he knows many Ships received Damage by going into that Harbour.

Mr. Micajah Perry, Merchant, said, That he has been a considerable Trader for 50 Years last past; and yet none of the Ships he was concerned in ever used Dover Harbour, because ’tis dangerous; and, if he was exempt from the Duty, he would not make use of it

Mr. Moor, Matter of a Ship, said, That about Eight Years since, he got into Dover Harbour by the Help of a Pilot; but, at the same time, another Ship, having also a Pilot on board, run against the Pier-head, and funk her; and thinks no Ship can safely enter the Harbour in foul Weather.

Captain Jennings laid, That he has used the Seas for 50 Years; and that he had rather lie in the Downes than ' venture into Dover Harbour; but believes the Harbour may be of Service to small Ships in time of War.

Matthew Butterwick, of London, Ship-matter, laid, That, about 20 Years since,' he put into Dover Harbour, and could not get out, though his Vessel drew but Nine Foot Water, the Wind blowing into the Harbour; and other Ships then patted by into the Doxvnes:

And said, He thinks Dover the most unnecettary Harbour in England.

Peirfey, of Brighthcmfon, Ship-matter, said, That,

in January last, he entered Dover Harbour at High-water; but another Ship, drawing Seven Foot, run against the Pier-head at falling-water, and was loft: And Peircy said, That, about Four or Five Years ago, he walked cross the Beach.

Captain Tyfack said, That, Four Years ago, he went into Dover Harbour with a Ship of 150 Ton Burthen,

which was hauled into the Bason, where flie lay aground; which is very unfit for that Pm pole, being a hard Chalk, and uneven; and his Ship received Damage.

Robert Parker, of Ramsgate, said, That lie had used the Norway Trade for Four Years past; and, when his Ship was aground in Dover Harbour, flie was twice gulled over, when the Sluices were let out: That, last Year, Twelve Sail of Ships under Dungeness patted by Dover Harbour at near High-water, Two whereof endeavoured to get in, but could not: And said, The Harbour is not better now than Ten Years ago.

Chefman PeirJe: That, about Seven Years since, he was in a Pink which drew but Ten Foot Water; and never a Pilot would undertake to carry her into Dover Harbour.

Captain Frost said, That, about Nine Years since, 20 light Transport Ships, from 150 to 300 Tons Burthen, were ordered for Dover, to take in Horses and Soldiers for Service of the Government; and they all arrived in the Harbour; but his Ship of 300 Tons lay so uneasy on the Shingles, That the Horses could not be taken on board.

A Petition of several Merchants, and Owners of Ships, within the City of London, on behalf of themselves, and others concerned in Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That by an Act, made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of King William the Third, a Duty of Three Pence per Ton is laid on all Ships or Vessels, from Twenty to Three hundred Tons, within this Realm, that shall pass or repafe by Dover; excepting Ships loaden with Coals, Grindstones, Purbeck or Portland Stones, which are to pay only Three Halfpence per Ton; no Coaster or Fisherman is, by the Act, obliged to pay the said Duty above Once in one Year; all Ships and Vessels belonging to Weymouth, Port of Ramsgate, Melcomb Regis, Lyme'Regis, and Great Yarmouth, are excepted from paying any Duty: That above Twenty Thousand-Pounds hath been collected towards repairing Dower Pier, by Ships passing and repairing, that have not received any Benefit thereby; the Entrance into the Pier being narrow, and so choaked up with loose Gravel-stones when the Wind blows hard, that no Vessel of Fifty Tons can go in or out: And praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, or otherwise, against the Bill now dependingJ or exempted from paying this Duty any longer, except upon such Ships as enter the Pier.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for inlarge-ing the Term of Years granted by the Acts, of the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of King the Third, and the Second and Third Years of Queen Ann, for Repair of Dover Harbour, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard before the Committee, by their Counsel, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the Counsel be heard for the said Bill, if the Petitioners for the said Bill think fit.

The Translation of the said Memorial is as follows: viz.

Translation, from the Swedish, of the Memorial presented by Resident Jackson to the Swedish Chancery,

July the 16th, 1714.

Whereas the many serious Representations, which the underwritten Resident of her Majesty the Queen of 'Great Britain hath already, from time to time, made both to her Royal Highness berself, as well as to your Excellencies, and the Royal Chancery, in order to obtain the Releasement of the several British Ships this Year brought up by the Sivedish Ships of War, and Capers, have not hitherto had the expected Effect; but, on the contrary, more and more of her Majesty’s Subjects Ships are daily seized, and sent up to sundry Ports, and con-filcated, without the lead: Regard had to the Passports, which, conform to the Treaties between the Two Crowns, they are all provided with: the Underwritten does therefore find himself obliged, in Obedience to the exprefe Commands he has lately received from the Queen his most gracious Mistress, hereby to addrels himself again to your Excellencies, and the Royal Chancery; and ear-neftly press, that you will be pleased so to remonstrate this Affair again to her Royal Highness, and the Senate, that all the said detained Ships, together with their Lade-ings, according to the annexed Lift, may not only, without Delay, be given free, and set at Liberty to proceed . on their intended Voyages; especially seeing most of them are freighted to fetch naval Stores for her Majesty’s immediate'Service; but that likewise the necessary Orders may be given to the proper Officers to forbear, hereafter,

' the like violent Proceedings; they being direCHy contrary to the plain Tenor of the subsisting Treaties, which is the established Law between the Two Kingdoms; that all such Ground of Complaint, as can wound the Friend-ship between the Two Nations, may thereby be removed; as also the ill <Consequences prevented, which otherwise may probably result from the Continuance of such unjust Treatment; where to the Underwritten does further desire anfl expect of your Excellencies, and the Royal Chancery, such an Answer as may serve for his most gracious Queen’s further Regulation herein.

Stockholm, the 16th July, 1714. R. Jackson.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, Merchants, Owners and Masters of Ships, and other Traders and Inhabitants, of the Town and Port of Poole, was presented to the" House, and read; setting forth, That the Channels, Creeks, Quays, and Wharfs, of, and belonging to, their Harbour of Poolebeing very much choaked up, and obstructed, by means of the very great Bar of moveable Sand lying at the Entring into their said Channel and Harbour; which will require very great Sums of Money to cleanse and make commodious for the Shipping using their Port; having been at great Expences for several Years past on that Account: And praying, That they may be exempted from the Duties chargeable on Shipping towards the Repair of Dover Pier.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for inlarging the Term of Years granted by the Acts, of the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of King William the Third, and the Second and Third Years of Queen Anne, for the Repair of Dover Harbour, is committed.

HIS Majesty, being at present engaged in several Negotiations of the uttermost Concern to the Welfare of these Kingdoms, and the Tranquillity of Europe; and having lately received Information from abroad, which makes him judge, that it will give Weight to his Endeavours, if a Nava! Preventing Mr. Solicitor General reported from the Committee, Robbery, tec. who were appointed to draw up Realons, to be offered to the Lords at a Conference, for disagreeing to feme of the Amendments, made by their Lordships, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the further preventing Robbery, Burglary, and other Felonies; and for the more effectual Transportation of Felons, and unlawful Exporters of Wool; That they had drawn up Realons accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read, Paragraph by Paragraph; and, with an Amendment, agreed unto by the House; and are as follow; viz.

That the Commons agree to all the Amendments, made by your Lordships, to the said Bill, except the Clause B, and the Word " Deer-Stealers," in the Title of the Bill: To which the Commons disagree;

ill, Because they conceive, That unlawful Hunting or Courting of Deer in Forests, Chaces, Purlieus, #c. or being aiding or assisting the rein, is very uncertain, as well with regard to the Nature of the Offence, as to the Place where it may be supposed to be committed; whereby innocent Persons may be liable to prosecutions upon frivolous Pretences:

2d, The Power of Conviction and Transportation being given to a Quarter Sessions of the Peace, there is too much Reason to apprehend, that an ill Use may be made of such a Power upon some Emergencies, where there are Animosities and Divisions in the Country:

3d, They disagree to the Word " Deer-Stealers," in the Title of the Bill; it being only the Consequence of that Amendment, to which the Commons disagree.

Sir tlichard Steele reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Colonel Joseph Marti, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is aa follows; viz.

That the Committee, upon the Examination of the Allegations in the said Petition, do find, That Colonel Marti, in the Beginning of the Year 1706, N.S. did raise, and form, a Regiment of Foot, upon the Promise and Encouragement of the Earl of Peterborough, to be upon the English Establishment and Pay; and that, upon the like Declarations and Promiles from my Lord and General Richards, he paid, and maintained, the said Regiment of Foot from the Fourth Day of February 1706.

N. S. to the Eleventh Day of January 1708:

That the Committee cannot but observe, as it appeared to them, That the said Colonel Marti used so much Industry, that he raised, and completely formed, this Regiment of Foot in the Space of Ten Days; and immediately marched against the Enemy:

That the Committee find, by Testimonials, Certificates, and Letters fro*11 the English Generals, and the Magistrates and Inhabitants of Catalonia and That the said Marti tehaved himselfj on all Occasions, with great Zeal, Fidelity and Bravery, in the Service:

That Colonel, Marti laid before the Committee an Account, and Demand, for his Regiment of Foot confiding of Two hundred Men; whereof he was constituted Colonel, as his Petition sets forth; and which, upon his own Credit, he has paid and satisfied for Two Years, amounting to the Sum of 15,096/. 18 10 in Part whereof

he has received 1,257/.; so that, upon the Balance, there remains due to him, according to this Account, l3,839?. i8j. 10 d.:

Mr. Solicitor General reported, That they had met the Lords at a Conference; and that it was managed on the Part of the Lords by the Earl of Stamford -, who acquainted the Managers, That the lairds do insist upon the Amendments to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the further preventing Robbery, Burglary, and other Felonies;

15 and

4 Geo. I. 198 — 20" Martii. 7^9

and for the more effectual Transportation of Felons, and' unlawful Exporters of Wool; which this House had disagreed unto; for which the Lords gave their Realbns; which Mr. Solicitor General read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, with the Bill, and Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the said Reasons were read; and are as follow; viz.

The Lords having taken into Consideration the Rea-fons given by the Commons, at the last Conference, for their disagreeing with the Amendments, made- by their Lordships to the Bill for the further preventing Robbery, Burglary, and other Felonies; and the more effectual Transportation of Felons, and unlawful Exporters of Wool; which relate to Deer-Stealers; their Lordships do infill on those Amendments:

Because the Crime of Deer-stealing is, of late, very greatly increased, and carried on by Force and Numbers, in divers Parts of the Kingdom; to the great Terror of private Families, and of those entrusted in the Keeping of Deer; and to the apparent Hazard of the Lives of many of his Majesty’s Subjects; for the Prevention of which, the Laws already in being are found to be ineffectual: The Lords cannot but observe, That, though the Commons disagree to the whole Clause; yet their Objection seems only to relate to Part thereofto the Uncertainty of the Words Forests, Chaces, and Purlieus; which Words their Lordships find used in the Act, of the Third and Fourth of King William and Queen Mary, intituled, An Act for the more effectual Discovery and Punishment of Deer-Stealers; although the Conviction, by that Act, is much easier, being to be before One or more Justices of Peace; whereas, by the Clause now in question, such Conviction must be by-Indictment, which necessarily requires Two Juries: And therefore, as well for that the Boundaries are, as their Lordships conceive, sufficiently certain, as for that theft: Words have flood lb long in the afore-mentioned Act, their Lordships conceive it proper to Use the same Words, they relating to the same Offence; though the Clause in question is to enact a further Punishment.

Resolved, That this House doth infill upon their Disagreement with the Lords to the said Amendments.

Resolved, That a free Conference be desired with the Lords, upon the Subject-matter of the last Conference.

Ordered, That Mr. Yonge do go to the Lords, and desire the said’free Conference.

8$ Maritf, Sir Joseph Tredenham reported a Conference had with the Lords upon the Subject-matter of the Lords Amendments to the Bill, sent up by the Commons, intituled, An additional Act for appointing and enabling Commissioners to examine, take, and state, the publick Accounts of the Kingdom: And that the Lords were not satisfied with the Reasons given by the Commons touching the said Amendments: And, amongst the Rea-fons offered by the Lords, it is reported in the Words following; viz.

" The Lords do agree, That, in the Act, passed in the Nineteenth of King Charles the Second, for taking Accounts, the Commissioners thereby constituted were " named by the Commons; and the Lords did agree to " it, both because they approved of the Number and " Quality of the Persons; and because, they being not " Members of the House- of Commons, they might al-

ways be sent for at the Pleasure of the Lords, to explain any Matters relating to those Accounts: But, the " Lords having now had Experience, by the lait Act,

" which constituted no Commissioners but only such as were of the House of Commons, That their Lordships cannot have those Commissioners at any time before them, to answer such Questions or explain such Doubts, as their Lord ships may have occasion to inquire into; or even to intimate such Points as seem to have been omitted either in the Accounts, or the Observations made thereupon; is One very great Reason why the Lords have found it necessary to name such in this Bill as their Lordships may, from time to time, receive Informations from; without which, their Lordlliips examining into the Accounts will prove defective " and dilatory."

And, after Consideration of the said Report, it was

Resolved, That this House doth insist upon their Disagreement with the Lords in the Amendments to the said Bill: And,

Resolved, That a free Conference should be desired with the Lords, upon the Subject-matter of the lift Conference.

Ordered, That the Members who managed the said Conference, do meet this Afternoon at Four a Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber, and prepare for the said Conference.
